editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: I This is he whom you read, the man you ask for, Martial, known the whole world over For his witty little books of epigram: To whom, devoted reader, the honour you have given While he yet lives and feels it Few poets have after their ashes.

I You could indeed have carried three hundred epigrams, But who would carry you, and read you through, my book? Now learn what merits a tight little volume has. This is the first: that less paper is wasted on me; Next, that the copyist will finish it in a single hour, And will not be a slave only to my trifles; The third point is this: that if by chance someone reads you, Bad though you may be throughout, you will not be tiresome. A guest will read you over his mixed five-measures, but Before the cup, once set down, has had time to grow cool. Do you think yourself made safe by such brevity? Alas for me—to how many even so you will seem long!

I This, whatever it is, is sent to you from a far-off shore By the Gaul called by the name of the Roman toga. You read this book, and perhaps you praise the earlier one: Both that and this are mine—choose which you think the better. Of course the one born in our mistress city should please more: A home-bred book must surely surpass a Gallic one.

I Caesar's life-giving day, more sacred than that light which Ida shared, when she bore Cretan Jove, come long, I pray, and richer in years than Pylian Nestor, and shine forever with this face, or one still finer. Let him long honour Pallas in Alban gold, and let the great oak-crown pass through such mighty hands; let him keep the ages that return in the vast cycle and the rites that Romulean Tarentos holds. Great things, you gods, we ask—but owed to the earth: for so great a god, what prayers could be too bold?

I This I send you, Caesar—whether you enjoy the hills of Palladian Alba and look from there toward Trivia, from there toward Thetis, or whether the truth-telling sisters learn your responses where the smooth wave of the suburban strait lies still, or whether Aeneas's nurse pleases you, or the Sun's daughter, or white Anxur with its health-giving waters— this I send, O happy guardian and safety of the world, while you are safe we believe Jove is kind. Only accept it: I'll think that you have read it and indulge, swollen with Gallic credulity.
I This sixth little book is sent you here, Martialis, dear to me above all others: if you polish it with attentive ear, it will dare, less anxious and trembling, to come into Caesar's great hands.

I Receive the rough breastplate of warlike Minerva, the very thing the wrath of Medusa's snaky hair dreads. While unused, Caesar, it may be called a cuirass: once it rests on your sacred breast, it will be the aegis.

I Book, about to enter the laurelled household of our lord, learn to speak more holily, with modest lips. Withdraw, naked Venus; this little book is not yours: come to me, you, Caesar's own Pallas, come.

I While Janus lends the years their winters, Domitian his autumns, and Augustus his summers, while the great light of the German Kalends claims the mighty title of the subdued Rhine, while the Tarpeian rocks of the highest Father stand, while the suppliant matron with voice and incense appeases the sweet godhead of divine Julia: the lofty glory of the Flavian line shall remain with the sun and the stars and with the Roman light. Whatever the unconquered hand has founded belongs to heaven.

I If I seem too much a book, too long, my final flourish late, read just a little: I'll be a slim small thing for you. Three and four times over my page is finished off with a tiny poem: make me as short as you yourself desire.

I Where are you headed, where, my idle book, dressed in no everyday Sidonian dye? Surely not to see Parthenius? No doubt: you'll go and return unrolled, unread: he reads no books, only petitions; nor has he time for the Muses—else he'd have time for his own. Do you reckon yourself blessed enough, if lesser hands take hold of you? Make for the portico of neighbouring Quirinus: no idler crowd is to be had at Pompey's, or by Agenor's daughter's, or at the fickle owner of the first ship's. There are two or three there who'd unroll the bookworms of my trifles, but only when the wagers and stale gossip about Scorpus and Incitatus are done.

I While the nets are idle and the baying Molossian hounds, and the wood is quiet, no boar found, you can give your leisure, Priscus, to a brief little book. The hour is not a summer one, nor is the whole of it lost on you.

I So that mackerel-fry want no wrapper and olives no overcoat, And the grubby bookworm fear no pinching famine, Squander, my Muses, the Nile's papyrus — my loss is your ruin: Look, drunken midwinter calls for fresh jokes. My dice-throw fights no duel with the high-and-mighty piece, My ivory shakes no double-six against the dog: This page is my walnuts, this page is my dice-box; Such gaming brings me neither loss nor gain.

I While the knight and his lord the senator delight in their dinner-suits, And the freedman's cap suits our Jove well; While the slave fears no aedile as he rattles the dice-box, Seeing the icy ponds so near at hand: Take the alternating lots of rich and poor: Let each guest give his own gifts to his own. "These are trifles and trumpery, and things cheaper still." Who doesn't know it? Or who denies what's so plain? But what better to do, Saturn, on your soggy days, Which your own son gave you in place of heaven? Would you have me write of Thebes, or Troy, or wicked Mycenae? "Play," you say, "with nuts." I've no wish to lose my nuts.

II You who long to have my little books with you wherever you go, And want them as companions of a long road, Buy these, that parchment compresses into small leaves: Give book-cases to the great; one hand can hold me. Yet, that you may not be ignorant where I am for sale, and wander Astray through the whole city, with me for guide you shall be sure: Look for Secundus, the freedman of learned Lucensis, Behind the threshold of Peace and the forum of Pallas.

II Crete gave a great name, Africa a greater, Which Scipio as victor holds, and Metellus too; A nobler one Germany bestowed for the Rhine subdued, And even as a boy, Caesar, you were worthy of this name. Your brother earned the Idumaean triumphs with your father, But the laurel that comes from the Chatti is all your own.

II Whose gift do you wish to become, little book? Make haste to provide yourself a protector, Lest, snatched off quickly to a sooty kitchen, You wrap young tunny-fish in your soggy paper, Or be a wrapper for incense or pepper. You flee into the bosom of Faustinus? You are wise. Now you may walk anointed with cedar oil, And, handsome with the twofold honour of your front, Revel in your painted bosses, And let delicate purple clothe you, And your proud title blush with scarlet. With him for protector, fear not even Probus.

II Lately Horatius alone, among them all, watched the show in a black cloak, while the commons, the lesser ranks and the greatest, sat in white beside their sacred prince. Suddenly snow fell from the whole sky: now Horatius watches in a white cloak.

II Matrons and boys and maidens, to you our page is dedicated. You, whom too-saucy naughtiness and naked wit delight too much, read the four wanton little books: the fifth book jokes with our lord; which Germanicus may read, his cheek unblushing, before the Cecropian maiden.

II It was sport to betray the bonds of sacred wedlock, sport too to cut the undeserving males. Both you forbid, Caesar, and to the peoples to come you bring relief, bidding them be born without violation. Now no man will be eunuch or adulterer with you as guardian: but before—O the morals!—even a eunuch was an adulterer.

II A breastplate for our lord, proof against Sarmatian arrows and surer than the Getic hide of Mars, woven from the smooth hooves of countless boars, safe even against the thrust of an Aetolian spear: happy in your lot, for it will be granted you to touch that sacred breast and grow warm with our god's spirit. Go, his companion, and earn great triumphs unscathed, and lead the way to the palm-embroidered robe — but quickly, give him back.

II Janus, begetter and father of the calendar, when he lately saw the conqueror of the Hister, thought all his faces not enough for himself, and wished he had more eyes: and, speaking at once with every tongue, he promised to the lord of the earth and god of all things the Pylian old age of Nestor, four times over. Add, father Janus, your own, we pray.

II Though you are poor toward friendship, Lupus, you are not so toward your mistress, and your cock alone has no complaint of you. That adulteress grows fat on wheaten cunts, while black flour feeds your dinner-guest; Setine wine, that would inflame the snows, is strained for your mistress, while we drink the dark poisons of a Corsican jar; a night is bought from you with no small part of your father's lands, while your deserted comrade ploughs fields not his own; your mistress shines, translucent with Erythraean pearls, while your client is led off, made over to debt, as you fuck; a litter borne up by eight Syrians is given to the girl, while your friend will be the naked weight of a pauper's bier. Go now, Cybele, and cut off the wretched catamites: this, this was the cock worthy of your knives.

II Rushed out before its time, the work of my tenth little book, that slipped from my hands, I've now called back again. Some pieces you'll know, but planed smooth by a recent file; the larger part is new: reader, be kind to both, reader, my wealth: when Rome had given you to me, "I've nothing greater to give you," she said. "Through this you'll flee the sluggish streams of thankless Lethe, and survive in the better part of yourself. The wild fig splits Messalla's marble, and the bold muleteer laughs at Crispus' half-broken horses: but theft does pages no harm, and the ages serve them, and these monuments alone know nothing of dying."

II The grim eyebrow, the stern brow of hard Cato, the daughter of Fabricius the ploughman, the masked airs and the rule of morals, and whatever we aren't, in the dark—out you go. Look, my verses cry "Hurrah, Saturnalia!": under your reign, Nerva, it's both allowed and a pleasure. Sour readers, go memorize knotty Santra: I've nothing to do with you: this book is mine.

II You who lately used to be sent from the City to the nations, now, hurrah, you'll go a foreigner to Rome, my book, from the race of gold-bearing Tagus and grim Salo, the native rivers which my mighty land gives me. Yet you'll be no stranger, nor can you now be called a newcomer, you, whose brothers the high house of Remus holds in such number. By your own right, seek the venerable threshold of the new temple, where the halls are given back to the Pierian choir. Or, if you prefer, you'll walk to the head of the Subura; there are the high halls of my consul: eloquent Stella dwells in his laurel-crowned home, bright Stella, thirster after the Hyantean water; there a Castalian spring is proud with its glassy torrent, whence the nine mistresses are said often to have drunk: he will give you to people and senators and knights to read, and will read you through himself with not too dry cheeks. Why ask for a title? Let two or three verses be read, and all, my book, will cry that you are mine.

II Turn up your nose as long as you like, be one big nose, The kind Atlas himself, asked to bear it, would refuse, And go ahead, outsneer the great sneerer Latinus: Still you can't say more against my trifles Than I have said myself. Why grind tooth on tooth By gnawing? You need meat, if you want to be full. Don't waste your effort: keep your venom for the men Who admire themselves — I know these things are nothing. Yet even this "nothing" is not too little, if you come With a fair ear and no scowl on your morning face.

II At whatever point you like you can end this little book: Every piece is wrapped up in two lines. You ask why headings are written in? I'll explain: So that, if you prefer, you may read the headings alone.

III You would rather live in the bookshops of the Argiletum, Little book, though our book-cases stand empty for you. You do not know, alas, you do not know the disdain of Rome our mistress: Believe me, the crowd of Mars is far too shrewd. Nowhere are there greater sneers: young men and old And boys too have the nose of a rhinoceros. When you have heard a great "Bravo!" and are blowing kisses, You will be tossed in a shaken blanket up to the stars. But you, that you may not so often suffer your master's erasures Nor have the grim pen mark down your jokes, Long, you wanton thing, to flit through the airs of heaven: Go, fly; but you could have been safer at home.
III Sextus, you owe nothing, you owe nothing, Sextus—we admit it. For a man owes, Sextus, only if he can pay.

III [You hide your lovely face with a black cosmetic, But you spoil the water with your unlovely body. Believe the goddess herself tells you in our words: "Either uncover your face, or bathe in your tunic."]

III Look how thick a fleece of silent waters streams down on Caesar's face and into his lap. Yet he indulges Jove, and with head unmoved laughs at the waters thickened by sluggish frost, he who is used to tiring the star of northern Bootes and ignoring Helice with his dripping hair. Who plays with dry waters and sports from the sky? I suspect these snows belong to Caesar's boy.

III Degis, now a dweller on our bank, Germanicus, who came to you from the servant waters of the Hister, glad and amazed at having just seen the world's protector, is said to have spoken thus to his companions: "How much better is my lot than my brother's, who is allowed so near to behold the god whom from afar he worships."

III Be born, name promised to Dardanian Iulus, true offspring of the gods; be born, great boy: to whom your father may hand the eternal reins after the ages, and may you rule the world, old, with one older still. Julia herself with snowy thumb will spin you golden threads and weave the whole fleece of Phrixus.
III Why do I not send you my little books, Pontilianus? So that you, Pontilianus, may not send me yours.

III 'Five would have been enough: for six or seven little books is too much: what pleasure is it still to play, Muse? Let there be shame and an end: now Fame can add nothing more to me — my book is thumbed everywhere; and when Messala's stones lie shattered by decay and Licinus' tall marbles are dust, still mouths will read me, and many a stranger will carry my songs home to his native land.' I had finished, when the ninth of the sisters answered thus, her hair and dress dirty with perfume: 'Can you, ingrate, abandon your sweet trifles? Tell me, what better will you do in your idleness? Or does it please you to change the slipper for the tragic buskin, or to thunder harsh wars in even measures, so that a swollen schoolmaster may declaim you in a raucous voice and the grown girl and the good boy may hate you? Let the over-grave and over-severe write such things, the wretches whom the lamp sees at midnight. But you, dip your charming little books in Roman salt: let life recognize and read its own ways. Though you may seem to sing on a narrow reed, let your reed outdo the trumpets of many.'

III How much you have already given to the gods above, Caesar, and to heaven, if you should call it back and choose to be the creditor, though a great auction be held on aethereal Olympus and the gods be forced to sell whatever they have, Atlas will go bankrupt, and there will not be a whole ounce on which the very father of the gods could settle with you: for what can he pay you for the Capitoline temples, what for the honour of the Tarpeian foliage? What can the Thunderer's matron pay for her twin roofs? Pallas I pass over: she manages your affairs. Why speak of Alcides, and Phoebus, and the pious Laconians? What of the Flavian temple added to the Latian sky? You must wait and endure, Augustus, of necessity: for Jupiter's coffer has nothing to pay you with.

III The quips of home-bred slaves, the foul tooth, and the vile abuse of a hawker's gutter tongue, stuff a peddler of cracked Vatinian cups wouldn't take if bought with a brimstone match, some sneaking poet scatters about and wants them taken for mine. Do you believe it, Priscus? That a parrot should speak in a quail's voice, and Canus long to be a bagpiper? Far from my little books be black repute; a gem-bright rumour bears them on a snow-white wing: why should I labour to be known so vilely, when silence can be had for free?

III Not only urban leisure delights in my Pimpleian Muse, nor do I give these things to empty ears, but my book is thumbed by a stiff centurion amid Getic frosts, at the Martian standards, and Britain is said to chant my verses. What good is it? My purse knows nothing of this. Yet what enduring pages we could compose, what battles blast on the Pierian trumpet, when the kindly gods have given an Augustus back to earth, and a Maecenas too, if they gave you one, Rome!

III What Maecenas, a knight sprung from royal forefathers, was to Flaccus and Varius and supreme Maro, that, Priscus Terentius, garrulous fame and the aged page will say you were to me among the nations and the peoples. You make my genius, you, if I seem to have any power; you give me the right to a freeborn idleness. Bravo for your spirit, which few have, and for your character, such as Numa, such as a cheerful Cato might have. To be generous, to bestow, to enlarge a slender estate, and to give what the easy gods scarcely granted, is now allowed and lawful. But you under a harsh prince and in evil times dared to be good.

III The whole crowd of Xenia in this slender little book Will cost you four coins, bought and paid. Four is too much? It could go for two, And the bookseller Tryphon would still turn a profit. These couplets you may send to your guests as gifts, If coins are as scarce for you as they are for me. You will find each thing's own name written above it as a heading: Skip whatever is not to your taste.
III. Citron-Wood Writing-Tablets Had we not been cut into thin leaves of wood, We'd be the noble burden of a Libyan tusk.

IV If by chance, Caesar, you should touch our little books, Lay aside the frown of the lord of the earth. Your triumphs too are used to bearing jests, And a general is not ashamed to be matter for a quip. With the same look with which you watch Thymele and the mimic Latinus, With that, I pray, may you read our songs. Your censorship can permit harmless games: Wanton is my page, but my life is honest.

IV O how coaxing you are, Ammianus, to your mother! How coaxing your mother is to you, Ammianus! She calls you brother and is called sister. Why do such naughty names attract you both? Why does it not please you to be what you are? Do you think this a game and a joke? It is not: A mother who longs to be called a sister Is happy to be neither mother nor sister.

IV Go to Rome, my book: if anyone asks where you have come from, Say from the region of the Aemilian Way. If he asks in what land, in what city we are, You may answer that I am at Cornelius's Forum. He will ask why I am away: confess much briefly: "He could not bear the tedium of the empty toga." "When is he coming?" he will say: you answer: "A poet He went out; he will come when he is a lyre-player."

IV What a dried marsh of a stagnant pool stinks of, what the raw fumes of the Albulan springs, what the stale reek of a saltwater fish-tank, what a lazy he-goat pressing on a she-goat, what an old soldier's worn-out marching boot, what a fleece twice steeped in purple dye, what the fasts of women keeping the Sabbath, what the panting breath of sad defendants, what filthy Leda's dying lamp, what wrestlers' grease made from Sabine lees, what a fox in flight, a viper's den— all that, Bassa, I would rather smell than smell of you.

IV Myrtale tends to reek of much wine, but to fool us she gobbles laurel leaves and, careful, mixes her neat wine with foliage, not water. Whenever you see her coming toward you, Paulus, flushed, with bulging veins, you may well say, "Myrtale has been drinking laurel."

IV Greatest censor and prince of princes, though Rome already owes you so many triumphs, so many temples newly born, so many reborn, so many spectacles, so many gods, so many cities: Rome owes you more—that she is chaste.
IV Since Oppianus, Castricus, was sickly in complexion, he took to writing verses.

IV What a great gathering of the world, hurrah, at the Latin altars takes up and pays vows for its leader! These are not the joys of men alone, Germanicus, but the very gods, I think, are now performing rites.

IV Though Galla can be fucked for two gold pieces, and for more than fucked, if you add as many again: why does Galla get ten gold pieces from you, Aeschylus? Galla does not suck for so much. What, then? She keeps quiet.

IV You who read of Oedipus and murky Thyestes, of Colchian witches and Scyllas—what but monsters do you read? What good to you is the rape of Hylas, what Parthenopaeus and Attis, what good the sleeper Endymion? Or the boy stripped of his slipping wings? Or he who hates the waters that love him, Hermaphroditus? What pleasure in the empty mockeries of a wretched page? Read this, of which life can say, "It's mine." Here you'll find no Centaurs, no Gorgons or Harpies: my page tastes of a human being. But you don't wish, Mamurra, to know your own habits, nor to know yourself: read the Origins of Callimachus.

IV The rites and household gods of the Phrygians, which Troy's heir chose to snatch rather than Laomedon's wealth about to burn, and Jupiter, now inscribed for the first time in eternal gold, and his sister and the perfect daughter of the supreme father, and you, Janus, who now enter a third name in the purple calendar for Nerva; I beg you with reverent voice: preserve, all of you, this leader, preserve the senate; let the one live by the prince's morals, the other by his own.

IV The longer labour of my eleventh and tenth little book has been compressed and pared into a short work. Let the idle read more, those to whom you gave safe leisure: read these, Caesar; perhaps you'll read those too.
IV. Incense That Germanicus may rule heaven's court late, and long Reign on earth — offer pious incense to Jove.
IV. Five-Leaved Tablets The lord's happy threshold steams with slaughtered bullocks When high honor is granted on the fivefold wax.
V I give you a sea-fight, you give me epigrams: You wish, I think, Marcus, to swim along with your book.

V May I lose my health, Decianus, if I would not be glad To be with you all day and all night long. But there are two miles that keep us apart: These become four, when I go to come back again. Often you are not at home, even when you are; often you are denied: Often you have time only for your cases, or for yourself. Still, to see you, I do not mind going the two miles: Not to see you, I do mind going the four.

V Do you wish to be recommended, little book, since you will run Into the city without me, to many, or will one suffice? One will suffice, believe me, to whom you will be no stranger, Julius, a name forever on my lips. You will seek him at once at the threshold of the first Covered Way: The home that Daphnis held, he now holds. He has a wife, who will receive you in her hands and lap, Though you come all dusty. Whether you see them together, or her, or him first, You will say this: "Marcus bids you good day," And that is enough: let a letter recommend others: he errs Who thinks he must be recommended to his own friends.

V An honest man and poor, true in tongue and heart, what do you want, Fabianus, making for Rome? You cannot pass for a pimp or a party-reveller, nor summon trembling defendants with a grim voice, nor seduce the wife of a dear friend, nor get it up for frigid old women, nor peddle empty smoke around the Palatine, nor clap for Canus, nor clap for Glaphyrus: how, poor wretch, will you live? "A reliable man, a loyal friend—" That's nothing: you'll never make a Philomelus that way.

V Sextus, eloquent attendant of Palatine Minerva, who enjoy the nearer genius of the god— for you are allowed to know our lord's nascent cares and the leader's secret heart—: let there be a place, even in some corner, for my little books too, where Pedo, where Marsus, where Catullus will be. Beside the heavenly songs of the Capitoline war set the great work of buskined Maro.
V I've bought a country estate for much money: lend me a hundred thousand, Caecilianus, I ask. You give me no answer? I believe you say in silence "You won't repay": that, Caecilianus, is why I ask.

V If you regard the longing of the people and the senators, Caesar, and the true joys of the Latin toga, give back our god to the prayers that beg for him. Rome envies her own foe, though many a laurel come his way: that foe sees the lord of the earth at closer range, and the barbarian is terrified by your face — and enjoys it.
V While you give rings to girls, Macer, you have ceased, Macer, to have any rings.

V To you, supreme tamer of the Rhine and parent of the world, chaste prince, the cities give thanks: they will have peoples; now it is no crime to bear children. No longer does the boy, cut by the greedy dealer's art, mourn the losses of his stolen manhood, nor does the wretched mother give to her prostituted infant the petty fee that the haughty pander would count. What modesty did not exist even in the bedchamber before your day has begun, thanks to you, even in the brothel.

V Whoever, scorning the matron's robe and the purple, has wronged with impious verse those he ought to honour, let him wander the city, an exile from bridge and slope, and last among the hoarse-voiced beggars beg for the dog's mouthfuls of vile bread; let a long December and a dripping winter and the closed archway prolong his bitter cold: let him call blessed and shout out the good fortune of those borne by on the bier of death. And when the threads of his last hour have come, and the slow day, let him feel the snarling of dogs, and beat off the harmful birds with a flapping rag. Nor let his punishment end with death, but now flayed by the lash of stern Aeacus, now crushed beneath restless Sisyphus' mountain, now parched amid the waters of the babbling old man, let him wear out all the fables of the poets: and when the Fury bids him confess the truth, let his conscience, betraying him, cry out, "I wrote it."

V So great is your reverence for the right and the just, Caesar, as was Numa's: but Numa was poor. A hard thing it is, not to surrender morals to wealth, and, when you've outdone so many Croesuses, to be a Numa. If the old fathers, those mighty names, should return, if one might empty the Elysian grove: unconquered Camillus will court you, for freedom's sake, Fabricius, while you give it, will want gold; Brutus will rejoice with you as leader, to you bloody Sulla will hand over command, when he's about to lay it down; Magnus will love you, with Caesar a private man, and Crassus will give you all his wealth. Even Cato himself, recalled from the infernal shades of Dis, if he were restored, would be a Caesarian.

V You poems, who lately were going to shore-set Pyrgi, go now by the sacred way—no longer dusty. The mildest of the nobles of the Ausonian court has come, Nerva: now one may enjoy all of Helicon: upright honour, cheerful clemency, cautious power return now; the long fears have turned their backs. This, pious Rome, your peoples and nations pray: may such a leader always be yours, and this one for long.
V. Pepper The waxy fig-pecker glowing with its plump rump, When luck deals it your way — if you're wise, add pepper.
V. Ivory Writing-Tablets Lest the dull wax darken your tired eyes, Let black lettering paint the snow-white ivory.

VI While the eagle bore the boy through the airs of heaven, The freight clung unharmed to the fearful talons: Now its own prey prevails upon the lions of Caesar, And the hare plays safe within the enormous mouth. Which do you think the greater marvel? For each there stands The highest author: these are Caesar's deeds, those Jove's.

VI Go now, bid me publish my little books. With scarcely two pages read, you, Severus, look to the colophon at the end, And draw out long yawns. These are the very things which, when I read them over, You used to snatch and copy down—but on Vitellian tablets; These are the things you carried, one by one, in your bosom Through all the dinners, through the theatres; These are they, or anything better you may not know of. What good is so lean a little book to me, That it is no thicker than its boss, If it takes you three days to read it whole? Never was idleness more supine. So soon, weary traveller, do you give out, And when you ought to run to Bovillae, Do you seek to change horses at the Camenae? Go now, bid me publish my little books.

VI The third day after the Ides of May is counted to you, Marcellinus, to be twice celebrated by your rites. This day reckons up the heavenly birth of your father, This day first sips your own blooming cheeks. Though it gave great gifts of a pleasant life, That day never granted more to a father.
VI You want to be thought chaster than a modest virgin and seem of tender innocence, Malisianus, when you are filthier than the man who recites poems made in Tibullus's metre in Stella's house.

VI If it is not too burdensome or too troublesome, Muses, ask your Parthenius: so may a later and once-blessed old age end your days with Caesar safe, and may you be happy with envy in your favour, so may Burrus soon feel himself a parent: admit my timid and brief page within the threshold of the holier court. You know the times of Jove serene, when he shines with his own calm face, with which he is wont to deny suppliants nothing. There's no cause to fear unjust prayers: my page never asks for great or troublesome things, which, adorned with cedar oil and purple, has grown up with black end-knobs. Don't hold it out, but keep it as if you offered and did nothing. If I know the lord of the nine sisters, he'll ask of his own accord for the purple little book.
VI There are three actors, but your Paula, Lupercus, loves four: and Paula loves even the mute role.

VI Has Caesar, turned toward us at last from the Hyperborean shores, already made ready to take the Ausonian roads? The sure informant is missing, yet every voice proclaims it: I believe you, Rumour — you are wont to speak the truth. The public dispatches of victory attest the general joy; the spears of Mars grow green with laurelled point. Once more, hurrah, Rome cries great triumphs for you, and unconquered, Caesar, you resound within your city. But now, that our gladness may rest on firmer ground, come yourself, the messenger of the Sarmatian laurel.

VI Nothing is more tiresome than old Euctus' antiques — I'd sooner have crockery shaped from Saguntine clay — when he tells the mad pedigree of his silver and, garrulous, turns wine musty with his words. 'These cups belonged to Laomedon's table: to win them, Apollo built the walls with his lyre. With this mixing-bowl fierce Rhoetus joined battle with the Lapiths: you see a piece weakened by the fight. These two bowls are reckoned of long-lived Nestor: a dove, polished by a Pylian thumb, gleams there. Here is the cup in which Aeacus' grandson bade neat wine be mixed more freely and stronger for his friends. In this dish most lovely Dido toasted Bitias when the banquet was given to the Phrygian man.' When you have marvelled much at the ancient embossings, you'll drink Astyanax from Priam's cups.

VI I wished to say 'Good morning' to you, Afer, on your return from the Libyan tribes, for five days running: 'He's not free' or 'He's asleep' was said, twice and three times, as I came back. That's enough now: you don't want to be greeted, Afer; farewell.

VI Happy are they whose lot it was to see the leader flashing among Arctic suns and stars. When will that day come, when field and tree and every trim window will be bright with a Latian bride? When the sweet delays, the long dust raised by Caesar, and all Rome to be seen along the Flaminian Way? When will you ride forth, knights and Moors in painted Nilotic tunics, and the people's voice be one: "He comes"?

VI In the festive days of the scythe-bearing old man, over which the ruling dice-box holds sway, you permit me, I think, felt-capped Rome, to play in unlaborious verse. You've smiled; so it's allowed, we're not forbidden. Pale cares, depart far from here; whatever comes to hand, let me speak it without peevish forethought. Mix the half-measures, boy, such as Pythagoras gave to Nero, mix them, Dindymus, but more frequent ones: I can do nothing sober; drinking, fifteen poets will come to my aid. Now give kisses, but Catullan ones: which if they prove as many as he named, I'll give you the Sparrow of Catullus.
VI. Spelt-Gruel I send spelt-gruel; let a rich man send you mead. If the rich man won't send it, you'll have to buy.
VI. Three-Leaved Tablets Then you'll think our triple tablets no cheap gift, When your girl writes on them that she will come.

VII The Dove, the darling of my friend Stella— Though Verona hear me say it— Has beaten, Maximus, the Sparrow of Catullus. My Stella surpasses your Catullus By as much as a dove is greater than a sparrow.

VII You declaim prettily, Atticus, plead cases prettily, Write pretty histories, pretty poems, Compose mimes prettily, epigrams prettily, A pretty grammarian, a pretty astrologer you are, And you sing prettily and dance, Atticus, prettily, You are pretty at the art of the lyre, pretty at the art of ball. Since you do nothing well, yet do everything prettily, Do you want me to say what you are? You are a great busybody.

VII Farewell now, you wretched hundred farthings, The dole of a weary client who walks before the patron, Which the boiled bath-attendant used to share out. What are you thinking, O hunger of friends? The doles of the proud patron have been withdrawn. "There are no more tricks: now a salary must be paid."

VII Why, boy Hyllus, do you refuse today what you gave yesterday, turned harsh so suddenly, who were just now so soft? But already you plead your beard, your years, your hairs. O night, how long you are, that make a man old in one go! Why mock us? Yesterday, Hyllus, you were a boy— tell us, by what reasoning are you a man today?

VII As fires renew the Assyrian nests each time the one bird has lived ten generations, so new Rome has shed her old age and herself taken on the face of her protector. Now, I pray, forgetting the well-known complaint, Vulcan, spare us: we are the throng of Mars, but of Venus too: spare us, father: so may your wanton wife forgive the Lemnian chains and patiently love.

VII Since the Julian law was reborn for the peoples, Faustinus, and Chastity was ordered to enter our homes, it's less than, or surely not more than, thirty days, and already Telesilla is marrying her tenth husband. She who marries so often does not marry: by the law she's an adulteress. I'm less offended by a more straightforward harlot.

VII Though the wintry Bear and rude Peuce and the Hister, hot with the beat of hooves, and the Rhine, now three times broken in his unruly horn, hold you taming the realms of a treacherous race, O supreme ruler of the world and parent of the globe: still you cannot be absent from our prayers. There we are with you, in eyes and hearts, Caesar, and you alone so possess the minds of all, that the very crowd of the great Circus does not know whether Passerinus or Tigris is running.

VII Is this pleading causes, is this speaking eloquently, Cinna — in ten hours, Cinna, to say nine words? But just now, in a mighty voice, you demanded four water-clocks. Oh, Cinna, how long you can keep silent!

VII As though it were a small injury to our sex to have prostituted males for the people's filthy use, the cradle had already become the pander's, so that, snatched from the breast, the boy demanded sordid coins with his wailing: immature bodies paid unspeakable penalties. The Ausonian father did not bear such monstrosities, the same who lately came to the aid of tender youths, that savage lust might not make men barren. Before, boys and young men and old men loved you, but now infants too love you, Caesar.

VII Father of nymphs and streams, Rhine, and all who drink the Odrysian frosts, so may you ever enjoy your flowing waters, nor may the barbarian wheel of an insolent oxherd grind you trodden underfoot; so may you go with your golden horns restored and Roman now on either bank: the Tiber, your master, begs you give back Trajan to his own peoples and to the City.

VII Now at last, Paula, you won't say to your stupid husband, whenever you want to go far off to your lover, "Caesar bade me come to the Alban estate at dawn, Caesar to Circeii." That trick is gone now. You may be a Penelope under prince Nerva: but the itch and your old nature forbid it. Unhappy one, what will you do? Pretend a sick friend? Your husband himself will cling, the companion of his lady, and go with you to brother and mother and father. What frauds, then, do you plot, so ingenious? Another adulteress might perhaps say she was hysterical and wanted to take the waters at the lake of Sinuessa. How much better you manage it, whenever it pleases you to go and screw, you who'd rather tell your husband the truth, Paula!
VII As many hairs as she bears on the whole of her head, if Ligeia has so many years, she's three years old.
VII. Beans If the pale beans foam for you in their red crock, You can often turn down the dinners of the fancy.
VII. Parchment Tablets Take these for wax, though it be called parchment: You'll erase them whenever you want to write afresh.

VIII That you follow the doctrines of great Thrasea and perfect Cato In such a way that you would have yourself survive, And do not rush bare-breasted upon drawn swords— You do, Decianus, what I would wish you to do. I have no use for the man who buys his fame with blood cheaply given; The man I want is one who can be praised without dying.

VIII If anything seems to you, reader, in these pages Either too obscure or too poor in Latin, The fault is not mine: the copyist spoiled them, While he hurried to reckon up the verses for you. But if you think it was not he but I who erred, Then I shall believe you have no understanding at all. "Yet these things are bad." As if we denied the obvious: These things are bad, but you make nothing better.
VIII "Quintus loves Thais." What Thais? "One-eyed Thais." Thais lacks one eye, he both.

VIII The first and second hours wear out the morning callers, the third sets the hoarse pleaders to work, into the fifth Rome stretches her varied labours, the sixth is rest for the weary, the seventh will be the end, the eighth till the ninth suffices for the gleaming wrestling-grounds, the ninth bids us crush the piled-up couches: the tenth is the hour for my little books, Euphemus, when your care prepares the ambrosial feast and good Caesar relaxes with heavenly nectar and holds in his great hand a modest cup. Then let my jokes in: with timid step my Thalia fears to go in loose stride to Jove at morning.

VIII The edict of our lord and god, by which the seating is made more certain and the knight has recovered his unmixed rows, while Phasis just now was praising it in the theatre, Phasis, red in his purple cloak, and boasting, proud, with swollen mouth: "At last one may sit more comfortably, now the equestrian dignity is restored, we're not crowded by the mob nor soiled": while he reclined and reported such things, Leitus ordered those purple and arrogant cloaks to get up.

VIII Two praetors, four tribunes, seven pleaders, ten poets were lately seeking a certain girl's hand from a certain old man. He, without delay, gave the girl to Eulogus the auctioneer. Tell me, Severus—did he act foolishly?

VIII Now be merry, Muses — if ever for me, be merry now and play: the god comes back victor from the Odrysian world. You first, December, make the people's prayers sure: now we may cry aloud, 'He comes!' Happy in your lot! You could refuse to yield to Janus, if you gave us the joys that he will give. The garlanded soldier shall play at festal taunts, when he walks as comrade among the laurelled horses. It is right to hear jests and lighter songs, Caesar, for you too — if the very triumph loves a game.

VIII Though you give the swift years their beginning, Janus, and renew long ages with your face, though pious incense beg of you first, vows greet you, the lucky purple honour you, every dignity court you: yet you prefer this — that it fell to the Latin city in your month, Janus, to see its god come home.
VIII Fabius left you nothing, Bithynicus, you to whom you used to give, if I remember, six thousand a year. He gave more to no one: don't complain, Bithynicus: he has left you six thousand a year.
VIII Paula wants to marry me; I'm unwilling to marry Paula: she's an old woman. I'd be willing, were she older still.

VIII The scent of yesterday's balsam-resin that lingers faintly, the last whiff that falls from curling saffron; fruit ripening in a winter chest, a field luxuriant with springtime trees; silk from the empress's Palatine presses, amber rewarmed by a maiden's hand; a jar of dark Falernian, broken far off, a garden that keeps Sicilian bees; the perfume-jars of Cosmus and the altars of the gods, a garland just now slipped from rich locks: why name them one by one? They're not enough; mix them all: this is how my boy's kisses smell in the morning. You want to know his name? If for the sake of the kisses, I'll tell. You've sworn: you want to know too much, Sabinus.

VIII Rome, goddess of lands and nations, to whom nothing is equal and nothing second, when, lately glad, she was counting up the years to come of Trajan over so many ages, and saw in so great a leader a soldier brave and young and warlike, she said, glorious in such a guardian: "Nobles of the Parthians and leaders of the Seres, Thracians, Sauromatae, Getae, Britons, I can show you a Caesar; come."
VIII. Coarse Meal Steep your plebeian pots with Clusine porridge, So that, full, you may drink sweet new wine on an empty stomach.
VIII. Vitellian Tablets Though a girl has not yet read these, She knows what the Vitellian tablets want.
IX You wish to be thought a fine fellow and a great man at once, Cotta: But the man who is a fine fellow, Cotta, is a trifling man.
IX I wrote; Naevia wrote nothing back. She will not give, then. But I suppose she had read what I wrote: she will give, then.
IX Cinna is said to write little verses against me. He does not write, whose poems no one reads.
IX Daughter of Sotas the doctor, Labulla, you leave your husband and chase after Clytus, you give and you love: you are going to ruin.
IX I was ill: but you came at once to me, Symmachus, attended by a hundred students. A hundred hands chilled by the north wind touched me: I had no fever, Symmachus—now I have.
IX You sleep in Pompey's theatre, Laevinus: and you complain if Oceanus wakes you?
IX Though Cascellius counts sixty years, he is a clever man: when will he be eloquent?

IX Bleary-eyed Hylas lately wished to pay you, Quintus, three-quarters of the debt; now, one-eyed, he wants to give half. Take it as soon as you can; the chance of gain is brief: if Hylas goes blind, he'll pay you nothing at all.
IX Though you dine abroad gladly, Cantharus, you shout and slander and threaten. Lay aside your fierce spirit, we warn you: you cannot be both a free-spoken man and a glutton.

IX By elevens of feet and syllables and with much salt yet nothing crude, that Martial known to the nations and known to the peoples—why do you envy?— I'm no better known than Andraemon the racehorse.
IX Bright with Jove's foliage, fame of the Roman buskin, Memor breathes again, restored by Apelles' art.
IX Palma governs our Iberians, mildest Caesar, and a foreign peace enjoys the gentle yoke. So we render glad thanks for so great a gift: you have sent your own ways into our regions.
IX. Lentils Take this lentil, the Nile's gift, sent from Pelusium: It is cheaper than gruel, dearer than the bean.
IX. The Same Because you see them so small, you think they're sent to a girl. You're wrong: this tablet asks for money too.

X Gemellus seeks the hand of Maronilla in marriage, And longs and presses and entreats and gives. Is she so lovely? No—nothing is more hideous. What then is sought and pleases in her? She has a cough.

X Because you give me kisses, Postumus, with half a lip, I praise you: you may take away half of this too. Do you wish to give a still greater and unspeakable gift? Keep this half whole for yourself, Postumus.

X Your father, Philomusus, settled two thousand a month on you, And paid it out to you every day, Since each tomorrow's want forever cramped your luxury, And your daily allowance had to feed your vices. The same man, dying, left you his sole heir. He disinherited you, Philomusus, your father did.

X While my little book is new, its brow not yet shaved smooth, while the page, not quite dry, fears to be touched, go, boy, and carry the light gift to a dear friend who has earned to be the first to hold my trifles. Run, but well equipped: let a Punic sponge go with the book—it suits my kind of gifts. Many erasures, Faustinus, cannot mend my jokes: one erasure can.

X "What shall I call this—that fame is denied the living, and that rare is the reader who loves his own age?" These, no doubt, Regulus, are the ways of envy, that it should always prefer the old to the new. So, ungrateful, we seek out old Pompey's shade, so old men praise Catulus's paltry temples; Ennius was read while you, Rome, still had Maro, and his own age laughed at the Maeonian, the seldom-crowded theatre applauded crowned Menander, only Corinna knew her Naso. Yet you, O my little books, do not be in haste: if glory comes after death, I'm in no hurry.

X When I lately happened to ask Jove for a few thousand, "He will give it," he said, "who gave me my temples." Temples indeed he gave to Jove, but to me no thousands did he give: I'm ashamed, ah, to have asked Jove for so little. But how unfrowning, how clouded by no anger, with how calm a face he had read my prayers! Such is he when he grants diadems to suppliant Dacians and goes and comes along the Capitoline ways. Tell me, I pray, O maiden who shares our Thunderer's secrets, if he refuses with that face, with what face does he grant? So I; and so to me, briefly, with her Gorgon laid aside, Pallas: "What has not yet been given, fool, do you count as refused?"

X Eros is sodomized, Linus sucks: Olus, what is it to you what either of them does with his own skin? Matho fucks for a hundred thousand: Olus, what is it to you? You will not be the poorer for it — only Matho. Sertorius dines till dawn: Olus, what is it to you, when you are free to snore the whole night through? Lupus owes Titus seven hundred thousand: Olus, what is it to you? Don't you give Lupus a penny, or trust him with one. The thing you ignore is the one that concerns you, Olus, the one that ought to be more your care. You owe for your shabby toga: this concerns you, Olus. No one now will trust you for a farthing: this too. Your wife is an adulteress: this concerns you, Olus. Your grown-up daughter now demands a dowry: this too. I could name fifteen things that concern you: but what you do, Olus, is nothing whatever to me.
X Bassus bought Tyrian cloaks of the finest dye for ten thousand. He made a profit. 'Did he buy so cheaply?' you say. No — he won't pay.
X You want to marry Priscus: I'm not surprised, Paula; you're wise. Priscus doesn't want to marry you: and he too is wise.

X While you, who enter the year with laurel-wreathed rods, wear down a thousand thresholds at the morning round, what am I to do here? What do you leave for us, Paulus, who are of Numa's common crowd and the packed throng? Shall I, who sees me, call him lord and king? This you yourself do—but how much more smoothly! Shall I follow litter or chair? You don't refuse to carry it, you fight to go ahead through the middle of the mud. Shall I rise more often to one reciting verse? You stand and stretch both hands together toward his face. What shall the poor man do, who isn't allowed to be a client? Your purple has dismissed our togas.
X Turnus turned his mighty genius to satire. Why not to the songs of Memor? He was his brother.
X Africanus has a hundred million, yet he hunts legacies. Fortune gives too much to many, enough to none.
X. Fine Flour You could count neither the merits nor the uses of fine flour, Since it serves the baker as often as the cook.
X. Larger Sheets There's no reason to think the gift a paltry one, When a poet gives you blank sheets of paper.

XI Since the knight has been given his twice five coins, why Do you alone, Sextilianus, drink twice ten times that? By now the hot water would have failed the slaves who fetch it, If you, Sextilianus, did not drink your wine neat.

XI That you see Selius with clouded brow, Rufus, That, walking, he wears down the portico till late, That his dull face keeps something mournfully silent, That his ugly nose nearly touches the ground, That he beats his breast with his right hand and tears his hair: He is not mourning the death of friend or brother; Both his sons are alive—and may they live, I pray— His wife is safe, and his goods and his slaves, His tenant and his bailiff have squandered nothing. What, then, is the cause of his grief? He dines at home.

XI If your girl, Quintus, is neither Thais nor one-eyed, Why do you think the couplet was aimed at you? But is there some likeness? Did I say Thais for Lais? Tell me, what is alike in Thais and Hermione? Yet you are Quintus: let us change the lover's name: If Quintus does not want her, let Sextus love Thais.

XI While you swell, puffed up with an empty name, and are ashamed, poor wretch, to be a Saturninus, you stirred up unholy wars beneath the Arcadian Bear, like the man who bore the arms of his Egyptian wife. Had the fate of this name so slipped your mind, that the heavy wrath of the Actian sea once buried? Or did the Rhine promise you what the Nile did not give him, and grant you more than the northern waters? That Antonius too fell by our arms, who set beside you, traitor, had been a Caesar.
XI Sardonyxes, emeralds, diamonds, jaspers—my Stella turns them all, Severus, on one knuckle. Many gems on his fingers, more in his verse you'll find: hence, I think, this cultured hand.

XI That there's no Pylades in this age, no Orestes, you wonder? Pylades, Marcus, drank the same wine, nor was better bread or thrush given to Orestes, but the dinner was equal and the same for both. You devour Lucrine oysters, watery clams feed me: my palate is no less wellborn than yours, Marcus. Cadmean Tyre clothes you, rich Gaul clothes me: do you want me, dressed in coarse wool, to love you in purple? For me to be your Pylades, let someone be my Orestes. This is not done by words, Marcus: to be loved, love.
XI You force me, Pudens, with my own pen and hand, to correct my little books. Oh, how excessively you approve of me and love me, you who want to own my trifles in the original!

XI The Rhine already knows you have reached your city; for it too hears the voices of your people: the Sarmatian tribes also, and the Hister and the Getae, the very shout of strange rejoicing has terrified. While long-drawn joys revere you in the sacred Circus, no one noticed the horses run, though sent forth four times. Rome has loved no leader, nor you, Caesar, so much: even she could not love you more, much as she'd wish.

XI A name born with violets and roses, by which the best part of the year is named, which tastes of Hybla and Attic flowers, which smells of the proud bird's nest; a name sweeter than blessed nectar, by which Cybele's boy would rather be called, and he who mixes the Thunderer's cups; which, if you sound it in the Parrhasian hall, the Venuses and Cupids answer; a noble name, soft, delicate, I wished to speak in no rough verse: but you, stubborn syllable, rebel. Yet poets say 'Eiarinos' — but Greek ones, to whom nothing is denied and whom it befits to sound 'Ares, Ares': we are not allowed to be so eloquent, we who cultivate the sterner Muses.

XI You talk of nothing but Theseus and Pirithous, and you think yourself, Calliodorus, a match for Pylades. May I die, if you deserve to hand Pylades his chamber-pot or to feed the swine of Pirithous. "And yet," you say, "I gave my friend five thousand and a toga washed, at most, three or four times." What of it, since Orestes never gave Pylades anything? He who gives, however much, refuses more.

XI Take away, boy, the cups and the embossed work of the tepid Nile, and hand me goblets with a careless hand, worn by the lips of our fathers, clean from an unshorn servant; let the ancient honour be restored to our tables. A gem-cup befits you to drink from, who break Mentor's work into a chamber-pot for your whore, Sardanapalus.

XI Give greetings, Muse, to your Parthenius and mine: for who drinks more freely from the Aonian stream? Whose lyre comes brighter from the Pimpleian cave? Whom does Phoebus love more of the Pierian flock? And if perhaps—but this is scarcely to be hoped—he has leisure, ask him to hand our poems to the leader himself, and only to commend the timid and brief little book with four words: "Your Rome reads this man."
XI. Barley Take what the muleteer would give to his uncomplaining mules. This gift I gave the innkeeper, not to you.
XI. Letter-Paper Whether sent to a slight acquaintance or a dear comrade, This paper is wont to call them all its own.

XII Where you go up to the Herculean heights of cool Tibur, And the white Albula steams with its sulphurous waters, The fourth milestone from the city marks the farms, The sacred grove, and the acres dear to the Muses. Here a rough portico used to offer shade in summer— Ah, what an unheard-of crime that portico nearly dared! For suddenly it collapsed in ruin, just when, beneath that pile, Regulus had been carried by his pair of horses. Surely Fortune feared our complaints, Which were no match for so great a hatred. Now even the losses please us; the very danger is worth so much: Had the roof stood, it could not have proved the gods exist.

XII What am I to call this, that your kisses smell of myrrh, And that you never have a scent that is your own? This makes me suspicious, Postumus, that you always smell good: Postumus, he does not smell good who always smells good.

XII You gave your guests good perfume yesterday, I admit—but you carved nothing. It is a fine joke, to smell sweet and go hungry. The man who does not dine, Fabullus, but is anointed, That man seems to me truly dead.
XII You refuse no one, Thais; but if that does not shame you, let this at least shame you, Thais—to refuse nothing.

XII That proud Masclion bears nodding weights on his brow with the pole that props them, or that great Ninus lifts with all his muscles seven boys or eight, seems no hard feat to me, when my Stella with one finger, this one or that, carries ten girls.
XII Fabulla swears the hair she bought is her own: does she, Paulus, perjure herself?

XII So may my lord read me, Faustinus, with serene brow, and take in my jests with the ear he is used to, as truly my page has never injured even those it justly hates, and no fame that comes by a blush can please me. What good is it, when certain men want my work to seem theirs, if any darts of mine drip with the blood of Lycambes, and someone spews viper's venom under my name — one who cannot bear the rays of Phoebus and the day? I play harmlessly: you know this well. I swear by the genius of mighty Fame, and by the Castalian band, and by your ears, which are like a great divinity to me, reader free of every inhuman spite.
XII Why I would not wish to marry a rich wife, you ask? I do not want to be the bride to my wife. Let the matron be beneath her husband, Priscus: not otherwise do woman and man become equals.

XII You who make for the Aemilian peoples and Apollo's Vercellae and the fields of the Phaethontean Po, may I not live, Domitius, if I don't let you go gladly, though without you no day is pleasing to me: but the longing is worth this, that even by one summer's reaping you ease your neck, scorched by the City's yoke. Go, I pray, and drink in whole suns with greedy skin— oh, how handsome you'll be, while you're abroad! And you'll come back unrecognized by your pale-faced friends, and the wan crowd will be jealous of your cheeks. But the colour the road gives you, Rome will swiftly snatch away, though you come back black as a Nile-bred face.
XII Let the right of seven children be granted you, Zoilus, so long as no one gives you a mother, no one a father.
XII. Grain Take three hundred bushels from the Libyan tenant's harvest, So that the field by the city does not starve.
XII. Ivory Money-Boxes These boxes it is wrong to fill with anything But yellow coin: let cheap wood carry silver.

XIII When chaste Arria handed the sword to her own Paetus, The blade she had herself drawn from her own vitals, "If there be any faith," she said, "the wound I made does not pain me: But the wound you will make, Paetus—that one pains me."
XIII Both the judge demands his fee, and the advocate demands his. I advise you, Sextus, to pay the creditor.

XIII While you will not have the fish, will not carve the fowl, And spare the boar, Naevia, that is more than rotten, You accuse and storm at the cook, as if he had brought Everything raw. I shall never be so raw as that.

XIII Claudia Peregrina weds my Pudens, Rufus: joy to your torches, O Hymenaeus, joy. So well does rare cinnamon blend with its nard, so well Massic wine with Attic honeycombs; no better are elms joined to tender vines, no more does the lotus love the water, the myrtle the shore. Fair Concord, dwell forever on that bed, and let Venus be always kind to so matched a yoke: let her love him grown old one day, and let her, even when old, not seem old to her husband.

XIII I am, I confess, and always was, Callistratus, poor, but no obscure or ill-known knight; I'm read throughout the world and people say "That's the man", and what death gives to few, life has given me. But your roofs rest on a hundred columns, your strongbox lashes freedman's wealth, the great soil of Nile's Syene serves you, and Gallic Parma shears your countless flocks. This is what I and you are: but what I am, you cannot be; what you are, anyone from the crowd can be.

XIII Who would not think you, Julia, shaped by Phidias's chisel, or the work of Pallas's art? The white marble answers with no silent image, and living grace gleams in your calm face. Your hand—not rough—plays with the Acidalian knot that it snatched, little Cupid, from your neck. To call back the love of Mars and the supreme Thunderer, let Juno ask the girdle of you, and Venus herself.

XIII When dusky Lycoris heard that the ivory of an old tusk turns white under the suns of Tibur, she went up to the Herculean hills. What power the air of lofty Tibur has! In a short while she came back black.
XIII He was called a fool: I bought him for twenty thousand. Give me back my money, Gargilianus: he has his wits.

XIII That the Celtiberian Salo leads me to gold-bearing shores, that I long to visit my homeland's hanging roofs, you bring this about, Manius, dear to me from my simple years and cherished in friendship since boyhood's days; in the Iberian lands there is no other man sweeter, more worthy of true love than you. With you I could have loved, as a guest, the Gaetulian huts of the parched African and the Scythian cabins. If your mind is the same, if our care is mutual, in whatever place, Rome will belong to us two.

XIII Whoever you are who tread the Flaminian Way, traveller, do not pass by this noble marble. The delight of the city, the wit of the Nile, art and grace, sport and pleasure, the glory and grief of the Roman theatre, and all the Venuses and Cupids are buried in this tomb, with Paris.
XIII The rich have a kind of profit, Auctus, in their anger: to hate costs less than to give.
XIII. Beets To give the bland beets flavor — the dinners of workmen — How often, alas, the cook will cry for wine and pepper!
XIII. Wooden Money-Box If anything is still left in the dregs of our little box, It will be a gift. There's nothing? Then the box itself will be.

XIV The dalliance, Caesar, the games and the sport of lions We have seen—the arena gives you this too— When the hare, caught again and again by the gentle tooth, Came back, and ran at large through the open jaws. How can the greedy lion spare the prey it has caught? And yet it is said to be yours: therefore it can.

XIV Selius leaves nothing untried, nothing unattempted, Whenever he sees he must dine at home. He runs to the Europa colonnade, and praises you, Paulinus, and your Achillean feet—without end. If Europa has done nothing, then the Saepta are sought, To see if the son of Phillyra or of Aeson can do anything. Cheated here too, he haunts the Memphitic temples, And sits by your seats, you sorrowful heifer. Thence he makes for the roofs hung on a hundred columns, And thence the gifts of Pompey and the double grove. He scorns neither the baths of Fortunatus nor of Faustus, Nor the dark of Gryllus and the Aeolia of Lupus: For he bathes in the hot baths again and again and again. When he has done everything, but the god refusing, Washed, he hurries back to the box-thickets of warm Europa, In case some friend there is taking a late walk. By you, you wanton bull, and by your girl, Invite Selius to dinner, I beg you.
XIV Starving Tuccius was making for Rome, Having set out from Spain. The tale of the doles met him on the way: He turned back from the Mulvian Bridge.

XIV Silius, glory of the Castalian sisters, who with mighty voice crush the perjuries of barbarian rage and the treacherous wiles of Hannibal, and force the fickle Carthaginians to yield to the great Africani: set your sternness a little aside, while wandering December, with coaxing dice, rattles its uncertain dice-boxes here and there and plays at heads-or-tails with the wickeder die, and grant some leisure to my Muses; read with no grim brow, but relaxed, my little books, soaked in playful jests. So perhaps tender Catullus dared to send his Sparrow to great Maro.

XIV Nanneius, used always to sit in the front row, back when one could grab a seat, twice and three times moved on, shifted his camp, and almost as a third party, among the very chairs, sat down behind a Gaius and a Lucius. From there, his head covered with a hood, he peers out and watches the games, unseemly, with one eye. And from there, poor wretch, thrown out, he passes into the gangway, and half-propped on the edge of a back bench, and ill-received, on one knee, he pretends to a knight that he's sitting, to Leitus that he's standing.
XIV You declare you can write eloquent verses, Laberius: why then won't you? Whoever can write eloquent verses, let him not write, Laberius: I'll think him a man.

XIV An unspeakable disaster has befallen my girl, Aulus; she has lost her plaything and her darling: not such as Catullus' tender mistress Lesbia mourned, robbed of the naughtiness of her sparrow, nor such as the Ianthis my Stella sang of wept for, whose black dove flies in Elysium: my light is not caught by such trifles or such fancies, nor do such losses move my mistress's heart: she has lost a boy who was counting twice ten years, whose cock was not yet a foot and a half long.

XIV That his pale Cilician orchards may not fear the winter, and a too-strong breeze nip the tender grove, window-panes set against the wintry south-winds admit the clear suns and the cloudless day. But to me is given a cell, not wholly closed by a window, in which not even Boreas himself would care to stay. So you bid an old friend lodge, cruel man — better, then, that I be the guest of your tree.

XIV This friend whom your table, whom your dinner has won you — do you think his is a heart of faithful friendship? He loves the boar and the mullets and the udder and the oysters, not you. If I dined as well, he would be my friend.

XIV Though the cushioned carriage carry your smooth-skinned servants for you, and the Libyan rider sweat in the long dust, though spread couches ring more than one Baiae for you and Thetis grow pale, smeared with your perfume, though Setine wine break the bright crystal cups, nor Venus sleep on softer down than yours: you lie at the night-time threshold of a haughty whore, and the deaf door, alas, is wet with your tears, nor do sighs cease to scorch your wretched breast. Shall I tell you why things go badly with you, Cotta? They go well.
XIV Heirs, do not bury the short farmer: for to him earth, however little, is heavy.

XIV Use the runaway horse more sparingly, I warn you, Priscus, and don't go so violently after hares. Often the hunter has paid the price to his quarry, and fallen shaken from his fierce horse, never to return. The plain too has its traps: though there be neither ditch nor mound nor rocks, level ground is wont to deceive. There'll be no lack of one to give you such spectacles, but let him fall by a less envied fate. If spirited dangers delight you, let's lie in wait for Tuscan boars—that valour is safer. What good to you are reckless reins? More often, Priscus, it's been given to them to break a rider than a hare.
XIV. Lettuce The lettuce that used to close our grandfathers' dinners, Tell me — why does it now begin our feasts?
XIV. Ivory Dice When no die has shown you the same face twice, You'll say I have given you a great gift.

XV O Julius, to be named before none of my companions, If long fidelity and grey old loyalty count for anything, Your sixtieth consul is now almost upon you, And your life counts scarcely a few more days. You will not do well to put off what you may see can be denied you, And to reckon that alone yours which has already been. Cares await you, and labours linked in chains; Joys do not stay, but fly away in flight. Grasp these with both hands and with your whole embrace: Even so they often slip and flow from the depths of your lap. It is not, believe me, the part of a wise man to say "I shall live": Tomorrow's life is too late; live today.
XV That you toast your cup to no one, You do a kind thing, Hormus, not a proud one.
XV No one in the whole city gives more credit than Cordus. "Though he is so poor, how?" Blind, he loves.

XV When yesterday you asked me for a thousand sesterces for six or seven days, Caecilianus, I said "I haven't got it"; but you, pleading a friend's arrival, ask me for a dish and a few vessels. Are you a fool? Or do you think me one, my friend? I refused you a thousand sesterces—shall I give you five thousand?

XV This is the fifth book of my jokes, Augustus, and no one complains of being hurt by my verse, but many a reader rejoices at an honoured name, to whom by my gift lasting fame is given. "Yet what do these things profit, though they honour many?" Granted they profit not—still they delight me.
XV While an ant was wandering in Phaethon's shade, an amber drop entangled the slender creature. So she, who lately had been despised while life remained, has now been made precious by her own death.

XV What boy is this who keeps off from the bright waters of Ianthis? Is it Hylas, fleeing his mistress the Naiad? How well it is that the Tirynthian is worshipped in this grove and guards these amorous waters so close at hand! You may tend these springs in safety, Argynnus: the Nymphs will do nothing — but beware lest he himself should wish it.

XV While the new glory of the Pannonian war is recounted, and every altar makes offering to Jupiter the home-bringer, the people give, the grateful knights give, the senate gives incense, and a third gift enriches the Latin tribes: these secret triumphs too Rome has recorded, nor was that laurel of your peace any less, in that you trust to the holy devotion of your own. A prince's greatest virtue is to know his own.
XV The wicked Chloe inscribed on the tombs of her seven husbands that she had made them. What could be plainer?

XV You say you yield to none of our friends. But, granting this is true, what, I ask, Crispus, do you do? When I begged five thousand sesterces as a loan, you refused, though your heavy strongbox couldn't hold your cash. When did you give me a peck of beans or grain, though a Nile-bred tenant farms your acres? When was a short toga sent in the cold of winter's time? When did half a pound of silver come to me? I see nothing else by which we might believe you a friend, than that you tend to fart in my presence, Crispus.

XV I have pages that Cato's wife and the dreadful Sabine women might read: this whole little book I want to laugh and be more wanton than all little books. Let it be drenched with wine and not blush to be dirty with rich Cosmian pomade, let it play with boys, love girls, and not speak in roundabout phrases of that from which we're born, the parent of us all, which holy Numa called a cock. Yet remember that these verses are of the Saturnalia, Apollinaris: this little book does not have my morals.

XV Whatever was gleaming in the Parrhasian hall has been given to our eyes and our gods. Jupiter marvels at the Scythian flames of green gold, and is amazed at the proud king's luxuries and weighty playthings: these are the cups that befit the Thunderer, these are they that befit the Phrygian servant. We are all now blessed, together with Jove; but lately—it shames me, ah, it shames me to confess— we were all poor, together with Jove.
XV. Smokeless Firewood If the country near Nomentum is your estate, Bring your own firewood to the villa, rustic — my advice.
XV. Gaming-Dice Let me, the die, not equal the dice in number, so long As my throw is often bigger than theirs.
XVI Some things are good, some middling, more are bad, Of those you read here: no otherwise, Avitus, is a book made.

XVI Zoilus is ill: it is his bedclothes that bring on this fever. If he were well, what would his scarlet covers do? What the couch from the Nile, what the cloth dyed with stinking Sidon? What does sickness display but foolish wealth? What have you to do with doctors? Dismiss all your Machaons. Do you want to get well? Take my bedclothes.

XVI You give a show of gladiators, Cerdo, you princeling of cobblers, And what the awl bestows on you, the sword snatches away. You are drunk: for never would you do this sober— To wish to play, Cerdo, with your own hide. You have played with hide: but, believe me, remember Now to keep, Cerdo, within your own skin.

XVI That you were no stepson to your stepmother, Gallus, was the rumour, while she was your father's wife. Yet while your father lived, it could not be proved. Now your father is nowhere, Gallus; the stepmother is at home. Let great Tullius be called back from the shades below and Regulus himself defend you—still you cannot be acquitted: for she who does not cease to be a stepmother after the father, Gallus, never was one.

XVI That I prefer to write what pleases, though I could write serious things—you are the cause, friendly reader, you who read and sing all my songs throughout Rome: but you don't know how much such love costs me. For if I chose to defend the temple of the scythe-bearing Thunderer and sell words to anxious defendants, many a sailor would send me Spanish casks and my pocket would grow grimy with varied coin. But now my little book is a guest and a reveller, and my page pleases only for free. Yet the ancients were not content with praise alone, when the least gift to a poet was an Alexis. "Nicely said," you say; "it delights me and we'll praise it always." You play dumb? You'll make me a pleader, I think.
XVI You who terrify men with your member and perverts with your sickle, guard these few acres of secluded soil. So may no aged thieves enter your orchards, but a boy and a fair girl with long hair.
XVI There is no cash at home, Regulus; the only thing left is to sell the gifts you gave me: will you buy them?

XVI You who were long a baker, Cyperus, now plead causes and seek two hundred thousand: but you spend, and you keep on borrowing. You do not retreat from the baker's trade, Cyperus: you make bread, and you make flour-dust of your fortune.

XVI The counsellor of his beauty, the mirror, and his sweet hair that boy, most pleasing of all the court to his master, who marks the spring season with his name, set up as hallowed gifts to the Pergamene god. Happy the land esteemed with such a gift! Nor would it wish to have Ganymede's locks.
XVI He pierced his dowried wife's heart with a sharp reed, but while Aper was at play: Aper knows how to play.

XVI You who are too solemn, reader, can leave now wherever you like: I wrote these for the city's toga; now my page grows wanton with Lampsacene verse and clashes the cymbals with a Tartessian hand. O how often you'll strike your cloak with stiffened member, though you be graver than Curius and Fabricius! You too, girl, will read the naughtiness and the games of my little book, moist with desire, though you be from Patavium. Lucretia blushed and put down my book, but in Brutus' presence; Brutus, withdraw: she'll read.
XVI You sold, Labienus, three little fields; you bought, Labienus, three catamites: you bugger, Labienus, three little fields.
XVI. Turnips These turnips I give you, that rejoice in winter's frost, Romulus is wont to eat — up there in heaven.
XVI. The Dice-Tower The cheating hand that knows how to throw loaded dice, If it throws through me, will gain nothing but wishes.
XVII Titus urges me to keep pleading cases, And often tells me, "It is a great thing." A great thing, Titus, is what the farmer does.

XVII A barber-woman sits at the first entrance of the Subura, Where the bloody scourges of the torturers hang And many a cobbler besets the Argiletum. But that barber-woman, Ammianus, does not shave, Does not shave, I say. What does she do, then? She fleeces.

XVII A tart, long carried round at the second course, Burned the hands cruelly with too much heat; But Sabidius's gullet burned more: so at once He puffed at it three and four times with his cheeks. It did indeed grow cool, and seemed to let the fingers in, But no one could touch it: it had become a turd.
XVII You bid me write verses against Lycisca, Paulus, such that, reading them, she may blush and be enraged. O Paulus, you are wicked: you want to have her all to yourself.

XVII While you recount grandfathers and ancestors and great names, while a knight like me is to you a sordid match, while you say you cannot marry, Gellia, anyone but a man of the broad stripe—you've married, Gellia, a chest-bearer.
XVII You bid yourself be called Cinna, Cinnamus. Isn't this, I ask, Cinna, a barbarism? If you'd been called Furius before, by that reasoning you'd be called Fur—Thief.

XVII Library of a charming country house, from which the reader sees the neighbouring city, if among holier songs there be any place for wanton Thalia, you may set on even the lowest shelf these seven little books I have sent you, marked by their author's own pen: this erasure makes their value. But you, dedicated by my small gift, who will be sung, famed through the whole world, guard this pledge of my heart, library of Julius Martialis.

XVII I pleaded your case, Sextus, agreed on two thousand: that you sent me a thousand coins — what is this? 'You told nothing,' you say, 'and the case was lost by you.' You owe so much the more, Sextus, because I blushed.

XVII Venerable grandson of Latona, who with gentle herbs prevail upon the Parcae's threads and their short distaffs, this hair, praised by his master, a granted vow, that boy of yours sent from the Latian city; he added too a shining disc to the hallowed locks, by whose verdict his happy face was kept safe. Preserve his youthful charm, that he be no fairer in long hair than in shorter.

XVII If you call promising and not giving a gift, Gaius, I'll outdo you in my gifts and presents. Take whatever the Asturian digs in Galician fields, whatever the golden flood of rich Tagus holds, whatever the black Indian finds in Red Sea weed, whatever the lone bird guards in its nest, whatever shameless Tyre boils up in Agenor's cauldron: take whatever everyone has—the way you give.
XVII Not every page of my book is for the night: you'll find, Sabinus, something to read in the morning too.

XVII Why your fever won't leave you, Laetinus, for so many days, you ask, and keep groaning. It's carried about with you and bathes with you alike; it dines on mushrooms, oysters, sow's udder, boar; it often gets drunk on Setine and often on Falernian, and drinks no Caecuban except through snow-cooled water; it reclines wreathed in roses and dark with balsam, it sleeps on down and a purple couch. Since it reclines so handsomely, since it lives so well at your house, do you want your fever to go to Dama instead?
XVII. A Bundle of Cabbage-Shoots Lest the pallid stalks turn your stomach, Let the green cabbage be greened in soda-water.

XVIII Why does it please you, Tucca, to mix with old Falernian The new must stored in Vatican jars? What great good have the worst of wines done you? Or what harm have the best of wines done you? About us it is easy; but it is a crime to slaughter Falernian And to give cruel poison to Campanian wine. Your guests, perhaps, have deserved to perish: But so precious a jar did not deserve to die.

XVIII I angle for your dinner—shame on me, but I angle for it, Maximus— You angle for another's: so now we are equals. I come in the morning to pay my respects; you are said to have gone To pay yours before me: so now we are equals. I am your own attendant and walk before the swollen king; You attend another: so now we are equals. It is enough to be a slave; I will not be an underling's underling. He who is a king, Maximus, should have no king.
XVIII Your preface complained that your throat had caught a chill. Since you have made your excuse, Maximus, why recite?

XVIII Where the gate near the Vipsanian columns drips and the slick stone is soaked with constant rain, into a boy's throat, as he passed beneath the dripping roof, a mass of water fell, heavy with winter ice: and when it had finished the poor boy's cruel fate, the tender blade melted in the warm wound. What has savage Fortune not claimed as her right? Or where is death not, if water cuts our throats?

XVIII That in December, the month when napkins fly and slender ladles and wax tapers and papers and the sharp jar of Damascus plums goes to old men, I sent you nothing but home-born little books, perhaps I may seem stingy or unkind— I hate the crafty and wicked arts of gifts: gifts mimic hooks: for who does not know that the greedy scarus is caught by the swallowed fly? Whenever a poor man gives nothing to a rich friend, O Quintianus, he is generous.
XVIII Saloninus rests in the Spanish lands, where no better shade sees the Stygian halls. But to mourn is wrong: for he who left you, Priscus, lives on in the better part by which he wished to live.

XVIII Though your face is such that no woman could fault it, though no blemish marks your body, why so rarely does a lover want you and come back for more? Do you wonder?
