The fault is no light one, Galla: every time I set to work and we are moved with mingled loins, your cunt is not silent — while you yourself are. Would to the gods you spoke and it kept quiet: I am offended by your cunt's chatter. I would rather you broke wind: for that, says Symmachus, is not without use, and the thing raises a laugh as well. But who can laugh at the silly noises of a cunt? When it sounds off, whose cock and whose mind does not collapse? Say something at least, drown out that clamorous cunt, and if you are so dumb, learn to talk at least from that quarter.

XVIII If you brought out your epigrams, Cerrinius, before the public, you could be read either alongside me or even ahead of me: but so great is your regard for an old friend, that my fame is dearer to you than your own. So Maro did not attempt the songs of Calabrian Flaccus, though he knew how to surpass the Pindaric measures, and yielded to Varius the glory of the Roman buskin, though he could speak more powerfully in the tragic voice. Gold and wealth and lands a friend will often give: he who is willing to yield in talent will be rare.

XVIII I have — and may I have it long with you as guardian, Caesar — a tiny country place, and small are my household gods in the city too. But from a low valley, to give what it can to the thirsty gardens, the curved pump raises laboured-up waters: my dry house complains that no dew refreshes it, though the Marcian water sounds in a fountain near me. The water you give to my household, Augustus, will be for me Castalia's spring or Jove's own rain.

XVIII To cheat Macer of his Saturnalian tribute you long in vain, my Muse: it's not allowed: he asks for it himself, and demands the customary jokes, not gloomy verse, and complains that my trifles have gone silent. But now he has time only for the surveyors' long account-books. Appian Way, what will you do, if Macer reads these?

XVIII You gave me, Lupus, a farm near the city; but I've a bigger farm in my window. Can you call this a farm, name this a farm? In which a rue-sprig makes Diana's grove, which the wing of a chirping cicada covers, which an ant eats up in a single day, for which a closed rose-petal is a garland; in which no more grass is found than a leaf of Cosmus or raw pepper; in which neither a cucumber can lie straight nor a whole snake make its home. The garden scarcely feeds a single caterpillar, the gnat dies once the willow-bed's consumed, and a mole is my digger and ploughman. The mushroom can't gape open, the fig can't smile, the violets can't spread out. A mouse ravages the borders, and by the farmer is feared like a Calydonian boar, and the crop, snatched by flying Procne's claw, lies in a swallow's nest; and though he stand there without sickle or member, there's no room for half a Priapus. The finished harvest scarcely fills a snail-shell, and we store the new wine in a pitch-sealed nut. You made a mistake, Lupus, but by a single letter: for at the time you gave me a praedium, a farm, I'd have preferred you'd given me a prandium, a lunch.

XVIII While you, Juvenal, perhaps wander restless in the clamorous Subura, or tread the hill of mistress Diana; while across the thresholds of the more powerful your sweat-soaked toga fans you, and the greater and lesser Caelian wear you out as you roam: me, after many Decembers come round again, my Bilbilis, proud of its gold and iron, has received and made a countryman. Here lazily I cultivate, by sweet labour, Boterdum and Platea—these are the rougher names of Celtiberian lands—: I enjoy a vast and shameless sleep, which often not even the third hour breaks, and now I pay myself back in full for whatever I had stayed awake through three times ten years. The toga is unknown, but at my request the nearest garment from a broken chair is given. When I rise, the hearth receives me, proud with a heap from the neighbouring oak-wood, which the bailiff's wife crowns with many a pot. The hunter follows, but the kind you'd wish to have with you in a secret wood; the smooth bailiff doles out tasks to the boys and asks to lay aside his long hair. So I love to live, so I love to die.
XVIII. Cut Leeks As often as you've eaten the strong-smelling threads Of Tarentine leek, give your kisses with lips sealed.
XVIII. Counters If you play the wars of the cunning brigands, This piece of glass will be your soldier and your foe.
XIX If I remember rightly, Aelia, you had four teeth: One cough spat out two, and another two. Now you can cough in safety the whole day long: A third cough has nothing left to do there.
XIX Do you believe you make me happy, Zoilus, by a dinner? Happy by a dinner, Zoilus—and then by yours? The guest must recline on the Arician slope to beg, Whom your dinner, Zoilus, makes happy.

XIX Near the Hundred Columns a she-bear is shown, Where sculpted beasts adorn the plane-tree grove. While, playing, the handsome Hylas tried its gaping jaws And thrust his tender hand into its mouth, But a wicked viper lurked in the dark bronze And lived with a worse life than the beast. The boy did not feel the trap, until the fang sank in, While he died. O the crime, that the bear was false!

XIX This thick weave, nursling of a Sequanian weaver, which, though foreign, bears a Spartan name— coarse, but in icy December not to be scorned— I send you as a gift, an outlandish endromis: whether you rub the sluggish wrestling-grease or the warm trigon, or snatch the dusty handballs in your grip, or share out the feathery weight of the loose ball, or seek to outrun swift Athas in the race— so that the piercing cold not enter your dripping limbs, nor a sudden rainbow weigh you down with rain. Wrapped in this gift, you will laugh at winds and showers: not even in Tyrian linen would you be so safe.

XIX If there's any faith in truth, O greatest Caesar, no ages can be preferred to your times. When was it allowed to see worthier triumphs? When did the Palatine gods deserve more? Under what leader was warlike Rome fairer and greater? Under what prince was liberty so great? Yet there is this fault—and no slight one, though it's the only one— that the poor man cultivates ungrateful friendships. Who lavishes wealth on an old and faithful comrade, or whom does a knight, not unrelated, attend? To have sent a ladle of a half-pound at the Saturnalia, or ten full scruples of a flame-coloured toga, is luxury, and the swollen patrons call these gifts: one who might jingle gold pieces will perhaps be the only one. Since these patrons don't exist, be you, Caesar, our friend: no virtue of a leader can be sweeter. Long since you've been laughing, Germanicus, with silent nose, that I give you advice useful to me.

XIX Not of violence nor murder nor poison, but my lawsuit is about three she-goats: I complain that my neighbour stole them. This the judge demands be proved to him: you thunder of Cannae and the Mithridatic war and the perjuries of Punic frenzy and the Sullas and Mariuses and Muciuses with great voice and your whole hand. Now speak, Postumus, about the three she-goats.

XIX This fragment, which you think cheap and useless wood, was the first keel of an unknown sea. The crashing Cyaneae of old could not break her, nor the grimmer wrath of the Scythian strait: the ages have conquered her — but though she has yielded to the years, the little plank, saved, is holier than the whole ship was.
XIX Cinna wishes to seem poor; and he is poor.
XIX You praise the baths of Ponticus, who dines well, in three hundred verses, Sabellus. You want to dine, Sabellus, not to bathe.

XIX Marius neither invites to dinner nor sends gifts, nor stands surety, nor will lend, nor even has anything to lend. Yet a crowd's not lacking that courts the barren friend. Alas! how foolish are your togas, Rome!
XIX You ask why I won't marry you, Galla? You're eloquent. My cock often commits a solecism.
XIX In the baths Aemilius takes lettuce, eggs, mackerel, and denies that he dines at home.
XIX. Headed Leeks Wooded Aricia sends the finest leeks: See the green hair upon the snow-white stalk.

XX Tell me, what madness is this? Before the summoned crowd that watches, You alone, Caecilianus, devour the mushrooms. What shall I pray for, worthy of so great a belly and gullet? May you eat such a mushroom as Claudius ate.
XX Paulus buys his poems; Paulus recites his own poems. For what you buy you may rightly call your own.

XX Tell me, Muse, what my friend Canius Rufus is doing: Is he committing to immortal pages The deeds of Claudian times, to be read hereafter? Or what a lying historian fastens on Nero? Or does he rival the tales of wicked Phaedrus? Is he wanton in elegy, or severe in epic? Or grim in the buskins of Sophocles? Or, at leisure in the school of poets, Does he tell jokes dipped in Attic charm? If he has left there, is he treading the portico of the temple, Or strolling slowly through the spaces of the Argonauts? Or in the sun of delicate Europa again, Among the warm box-trees, after midday, Does he sit or walk, free of biting cares? Does he bathe in the baths of Titus or Agrippa, Or in the bath of shameless Tigellinus? Does he enjoy the country place of Tullus and Lucanus? Does he run to Pollio's sweet fourth milestone? Or, set out now for seething Baiae, Does he sail, lazy, on the Lucrine pool? "Do you want to know what your Canius is doing? He is laughing."
XX Caerellia calls herself an old woman, though she's a doll; Gellia calls herself a doll, though she's a hag. You could bear neither one, Collinus, nor the other: one is absurd, the other sickening.

XX If with you, dear Martialis, I were allowed to enjoy carefree days, to dispose of leisured time and alike be free for true life: we'd know neither the halls nor the houses of the powerful, nor grim lawsuits and the gloomy forum, nor proud ancestral busts; but riding, talk, little books, the Field, the colonnade, shade, the Virgin's water, the baths— these would always be our haunts, these our labours. Now neither of us lives for himself, and feels the good suns flee and pass away, which perish for us and are charged to our account. Does any man, who knows how to live, delay?

XX I asked you, Phoebus, to lend me a hundred thousand sesterces, when you'd said to me, "You ask nothing, then?" You inquire, you hesitate, you delay, and for ten days you torment me and yourself: now, Phoebus, I ask—refuse.

XX Nothing is more wretched or more gluttonous than Santra. Invited at last to a proper dinner, which for so many days and nights he had angled for, three times he asks for boar's sweetbreads, four for loin, and for both haunches of a hare and its two shoulders, nor does he blush to perjure himself over a thrush and to snatch the dingy fibres of oysters. He smears his filthy napkin with gobs of cake; in it too are stowed away preserved grapes and a few seeds of pomegranates and the unsightly skin of a hollowed-out sow's womb, and a runny fig and a flabby mushroom. But when the napkin already bursts with a thousand thefts, he hides in his warm bosom gnawed vertebrae and a headless turtledove with its head devoured. Nor does he think it shameful to gather with a long arm whatever the crumb-collectors and the dogs have left. And the edible loot is not enough for his gullet: he fills his flask at his feet with mixed wine. When he has carried all this home up two hundred stairs and shut himself, anxious, in his bolted room, that glutton — the next day he sells it.
XX Though you make two hundred verses every single day, Varus, you recite nothing. You have no sense — and you have sense.

XX This ground, which lies all open and is covered with marble and gold, was conscious of our infant lord, happy, oh, with what wailings it rang, and what crawling hands it saw and held up: here had stood the venerable house that gave the world what Rhodes gave the starry sky, what pious Crete. The Curetes shielded Jove with clashing arms, such as the half-male Phrygians could bear: but you the father of the gods protected, and for you, Caesar, the thunderbolt and aegis served as javelin and shield.

XX Take a little book not learned enough and too little grave, yet not quite rustic either, to eloquent Pliny for me, my Thalia— go, carry it: the labour's brief, once done, to climb the steep path of the Subura. There you'll see at once the Orpheus slick on the summit of his dripping theatre, and the wondering beasts, and the king's own bird that bore off the ravished Phrygian to the Thunderer; there is the small house of your Pedo, engraved with an eagle's lesser wing. But take care not to knock, drunk and at the wrong hour, on his eloquent door: he gives whole days to austere Minerva, while he toils for the ears of the hundred men at what the ages and posterity might be able to set even beside the pages of Arpinum. You'll go more safely to the late lamps: this is your hour, when Lyaeus rages, when the rose reigns, when the hair is drenched: then let even rigid Catos read me.

XX You who, being sour, read sour Latin words, read six wanton verses of Caesar Augustus, you envious one: "Because Antony fucks Glaphyra, Fulvia has decreed this penalty for me, that I fuck her too. That I should fuck Fulvia? What if Manius begged me to bugger him, would I do it? I think not, if I were sane. 'Either fuck or let's fight,' she says. But what, since my prick is dearer to me than life itself? Let the trumpets sound!" You absolve, no doubt, my witty little books, Augustus, you who know how to speak with Roman frankness.
XX Why Themison hasn't a wife, Fabullus, you ask? He has a sister.
XX. Wild Turnips The Amiternine field rears these in its happy gardens: You may eat the Nursine kind more sparingly.
XX. A Pen-Case Drawing the case, remember to arm it with pens: We've given the rest; you supply the lighter things.

XXI When his right hand, aiming at the king, was deceived by the attendant, He thrust it, doomed to perish, into the sacred fire. But the kindly foe could not endure so cruel a marvel, And bade the man, snatched from the flames, depart: The hand that Mucius could burn with fire he scorned, Porsena could not bear to look upon. Greater is the fame and glory of the cheated right hand: Had it not erred, it would have done less.
XXI You give kisses to some, to others, Postumus, you give your right hand. You say, "Which do you prefer? Choose." I prefer the hand.
XXI A slave, his brow branded, saved his proscribed master. This was not the master's life, but his disgrace.
XXI That there are no gods, that heaven is empty, Segius declares: and his proof is that he sees himself made rich while he denies all this.

XXI Quintus instead of Decimus, Macer instead of Crassus, Regulus, the rhetor Apollodotus used to greet. Now he returns each man's greeting by his own name. How much care and toil can do! He wrote it down and learned it by heart.

XXI While glad Venus joined the everlasting Ianthis to Stella the poet, she said, "I could give no more." This before the lady; but more wickedly that into his ear: "See you commit no fault, you ruinous man. Often, in fury, I have beaten wanton Mars, when he was straying before lawful beds. But since he's mine, no rival has wronged me: Juno would wish to have so well-behaved a husband." She spoke, and struck his breast with her secret thong. The blow pleases: but you now, goddess, beat the gods.

XXI This is that day, conscious of a mighty birth, which gave Lucan to the nations and to you, Polla. Alas, cruel Nero, no shade more hateful than yours, this at least ought not to have been permitted you.

XXI Phosphor, give back the day: why do you delay our joys? With Caesar coming, Phosphor, give back the day. Rome asks it. Do the sluggish wains of placid Boötes carry you, that you come on too slow an axle? You could have led off Cyllarus from the Ledaean star: Castor himself will now yield you his own horse. Why do you hold back the eager Titan? Already Xanthus and Aethon want the reins; Memnon's kindly mother is awake. Yet the slow stars do not yield to the shining light, and the moon longs to see the Ausonian leader. Now, Caesar, come even by night: though the stars stand still, the day will not fail the people when you come.
XXI Artemidorus has a boy, but he sold his farm; Calliodorus has a farm in exchange for a boy. Tell me, Auctus, which of these has done the better business: Artemidorus loves, Calliodorus ploughs.

XXI To write what Modestus himself can scarcely understand and Claranus scarcely—what good is it, I ask, Sextus? Your books need no reader, but Apollo: in your judgment, Cinna was greater than Maro. So let yours be praised, by all means: but my poems, Sextus, may they please the grammarians, so long as they please without them.

XXI Lydia is as loose as the arse of a bronze horseman, as the swift hoop that rings with shrill bronze, as the wheel struck so often by the leaping vaulter, as an old shoe soaked in muddy water, as the wide-meshed nets that wait for wandering thrushes, as the awnings denied to Pompey's south wind, as the bracelet slipped from a consumptive catamite, as a mattress widowed of its Leuconian stuffing, as the old breeches of a poor Briton, and as the foul gullet of a Ravenna pelican. They say I fucked her in a sea-water pool. I don't know; I think I fucked the pool.

XXI Who would think you, Marcella, a townswoman of grim Salo and born in our regions? So rare, so sweet is your wit. The Palatine will say, if it has heard you even once, that you're its own; no girl born in the heart of the Subura will rival you, nor a nursling of the Capitoline hill; nor will the glory of a foreign-born child soon arise more fit to be a Roman bride. You bid my longing for the mistress city be gentler: you alone make Rome for me.
XXI. Asparagus The tender shoot that grew in seaside Ravenna Will be no more pleasing than wild asparagus.
XXI. A Stylus-Case Here you'll have a stylus-case armed with its own iron: Give it to a boy, and it will be no slight gift.

XXII Why now, hare, do you flee the gentle mouth of a peaceful lion? It has not learned to crush such tiny beasts. Those claws are kept for mighty necks, Nor does so great a thirst rejoice in thin blood. The hare is prey for hounds; it does not fill those vast jaws. The Dacian boy need not fear the arms of Caesar.
XXII What have I to do with you, O Phoebus and you nine sisters? See, the merry Muse harms her own poet. Postumus used to give me half his kisses before; Now he has begun to give them with both lips.

XXII You had given, Apicius, sixty million to your belly, And still there remained ten million loose to you. Burdened by this, as if you could not bear hunger and thirst, You drained off poison in a final draught. Nothing you ever did, Apicius, was more gluttonous.

XXII Having endured her first bridal night, still to be soothed toward her husband, Cleopatra had plunged herself into the gleaming pool, fleeing his embrace. But the water betrayed her hiding: she shone, though covered wholly by the water. So lilies hidden are counted through clear glass, so thin crystal forbids roses to lie concealed. I leaped in, and diving through the shallows snatched struggling kisses: the clear water, you forbade more.

XXII If I did not wish and deserve to see you at home in the morning, let your Esquiline, Paulus, be farther off for me. But I'm a near neighbour to the Tiburtine pillar, where rustic Flora looks on ancient Jove: the steep path of the Suburan slope must be climbed, and the filthy stones, with a step never dry, and one can scarcely break through the long mule-trains and the marble you see dragged with much rope. Worse still is this: that after a thousand labours the doorkeeper tells me, Paulus, you're not at home, exhausted. This is the end of my vain effort and my soaked little toga: it was scarcely worth so much to see Paulus in the morning. The dutiful man always has unkind friends: unless you sleep in, you cannot be my patron.
XXII That you marry your bedfellow, Proculina, and make him now a husband whom you lately made a lover, so that the Julian law cannot brand you: you don't marry, Proculina—you confess.

XXII The day of the Apollonian bard, memorable for his great birth, returns: throng of the Muses, favour the rites. This day deserved, when it gave you, Lucan, to the earth, that Baetis should be mingled with Castalia's water.
XXII You invite me to boar, Gallicus, you set pork before me. I'm a half-breed, Gallicus, if you fool me.

XXII You believe, perhaps, Pastor, that I beg for wealth on the same grounds as the common, thick-witted crowd begs, that Setine soil may wear out my hoes and a Tuscan field clank with countless fetters of slaves; that a hundred Moorish round tables stand on Libyan tusks and golden plate rattle on my couches, that no crystal but the great be worn by my lips and my Falernian make black snows; that a Canusian-cloaked Syrian sweat under my chair-pole and my chair be thronged with well-dressed clients; that a guest grow hot, drenched, at the hands of my servant, whom you'd not exchange even for Ganymede; that a muddy mule daub my Tyrian cloaks and a Massylian wand steer my horse. None of these is the reason: I call the gods and stars to witness. What then? That I may give, Pastor, and build.
XXII Why do I often come out with a plastered chin, or my sound lips painted with white lead, Philaenis, you ask? I don't want to kiss you.

XXII That you wear away the soft kisses of snowy Galaesus with your hard mouth, that you lie with naked Ganymede, (who denies it?) that's too much. But let it be enough; at least spare their groins, don't trouble them with a fucking hand. In smooth boys this sins more than the cock does, and the fingers hasten and make a man of him: hence the goatish smell and the quick hairs and a beard to amaze his mother, and the baths displease in broad daylight. Nature divided the male: one part is born for girls, one for men. Use your own part.
XXII How unbecomingly one-eyed Philaenis is, do you want me to tell you briefly, Fabullus? Philaenis would be more becoming blind.
XXII. Hard-Skinned Grapes A grape unfit for cups and useless to Lyaeus, Yet to you, if you're not drinking, I'll be nectar.
XXII. A Toothpick Mastic is better: but if you lack a leafy point, A quill can clear your teeth.

XXIII You invite no one, Cotta, except a man you have bathed with, And the baths alone furnish you a dinner-guest. I used to wonder why you never asked me, Cotta: Now I know—it was naked that I displeased you.
XXIII I will not tell, though you keep asking me, Who the Postumus in my little book is, I will not tell: for what need is there To offend these kissings, Which can avenge themselves so well?
XXIII Since you hand all the courses back to your slaves, Why is the table not set for you at your feet?

XXIII While you dawdle too long and slowly debate who should be first for you and who second among those the Greek epigram has matched: Callimachus himself, Thalia, has yielded the palm of his own will to eloquent Bruttianus. And if he, sated with Attic wit, should sport with the salt of Roman Minerva, make me, I pray, second after him.

XXIII You had clothed yourself in grass-green colours, Bassus, while the laws of the theatre seats were silent. But after the gentle censor's care bade them be reborn, and the knight, made surer, obeys Oceanus, you shine in no clothing but what is soaked with scarlet or dyed with purple, and think thus to fool him. There are no four-hundred-thousand cloaks, Bassus, or my Cordus would have a horse before all others.
XXIII You bid my member always stand for you, Lesbia: believe me, what's a finger isn't a prick. Though you press me with coaxing hands and words, your face is commanding against you.

XXIII Come, Phoebus, but as great as you were when you yourself gave the second plectrum to the Latin lyre as it thundered war. What shall I pray for, on so great a day? You, Polla, cherish your husband often, and let him feel himself cherished.

XXIII I seem to you savage and too much a glutton, Rusticus, because over a dinner I flog the cook. If that seems to you a trivial cause for the lash, then for what cause would you have the cook beaten?

XXIII O you to whom it has fallen to grow golden with the virgin's gold, tell me, Carus, where is your Palladian honour? 'You see, look, my master's face gleaming in marble? My crown came of itself to those locks.' The pious oak of the Alban olive may well be livid, that the oak first crowned the unconquered head.

XXIII Happy Antonius Primus now counts off in tranquil age his fifteen Olympiads gone by, and looks back on days that are past and on years made safe, nor does he now fear the waters of Lethe drawing near. No day, as he recalls them, is unwelcome or hard; there was none he wouldn't wish to remember. A good man enlarges for himself the span of his life: this is to live twice—to be able to enjoy a former life.

XXIII Sila is ready to marry me on any terms whatever; but on no terms do I want to marry Sila. When she pressed me, though, I said: "You'll give me ten million in gold as dowry, my bride; what could be less than that? Nor will I fuck you, though your husband, even on the first night, nor will I share a bed with you; I'll embrace my own mistress, and you won't forbid it, and at my bidding you'll send me your maid. While you watch, the servant will give me wanton kisses, whether he's mine or yours. You'll come to dinner, but you'll recline so set apart that our cloaks aren't touched by yours. You'll give me kisses rarely and not of your own accord, nor give them like a wife, but like an old mother. If you can endure all this, if you refuse to bear nothing, you'll find someone, Sila, who'll want to marry you."
XXIII Teeth and hair—and you're not ashamed—you use, all bought. What will you do for an eye, Laelia? That's not for sale.
XXIII. Chian Figs The Chian, like aged wine that Setia sent, Carries with it both its own liquor and its own salt.
XXIII. An Ear-Pick If your ear is troubled by a fretful itch, We give you arms suited to such cravings.

XXIV You see that man there, Decianus, with unkempt hair, Whose grim brow even you yourself dread, Who talks of the Curii and the liberating Camilli? Do not trust the face: he was married yesterday—as a bride.

XXIV If unjust fortune should bring you a sad charge in court, Pale, squalid, I will cling beside you, paler than the accused: If she should bid you, condemned, leave your native land, Over seas, over crags I will go, the exile's comrade. She gives you riches: are these things shared between two? Do you give me a part? Is it much? Candidus, do you give anything? With me, then, you will be wretched: but if the god with serene face Should nod assent, happy, Candidus, you will be alone.

XXIV Harmful to the vine and the rose, a he-goat stood at the altar, Ready to die, a welcome victim, Bacchus, for your hearth. When a Tuscan soothsayer wished to slay him to the god, He had told by chance a rough and uncouth man To cut quickly the testicles with a sharp sickle, That the foul stench of the unclean flesh might depart. While, bending over the green altar, he cut with his knife The struggling neck and pressed it down with his hand, A huge rupture appeared at the angry rites. The countryman seized it with the iron and cut it off, Thinking that the ancient rites of sacrifice required this And that the old gods were worshipped with such entrails. So you, who lately were a Tuscan, now a Gallic soothsayer, While you cut the goat's throat, became a gelding yourself.
XXIV Every woman she had as a friend, Fabianus, Lycoris has carried out to burial: let her be my wife's friend.

XXIV Hermes, the warlike delight of the age, Hermes, skilled in all weapons, Hermes both gladiator and trainer, Hermes, the throng and terror of his own school, Hermes, whom Helius fears, but him alone, Hermes, to whom Advolans falls, but to him alone, Hermes, taught to conquer and not to wound, Hermes, his own understudy, Hermes, the riches of the seat-sellers, Hermes, the care and toil of the gladiators' women, Hermes, proud with the warlike spear, Hermes, menacing with the sea-god's trident, Hermes, fearsome with the drooping helmet, Hermes, the glory of universal Mars, Hermes, all things in one and three times one.
XXIV Nothing is more wanton than Charisianus: at the Saturnalia he walks about in a toga.

XXIV You who try to set me at odds with my Juvenal, what will you not dare to say, treacherous tongue? With you inventing crimes, Orestes would have hated Pylades, the love of Pirithous would have abandoned Theseus, you could have parted the Sicilian brothers, and the Atridae — a greater name — and the offspring of Leda. This I call down on you for such deserts and such ventures: that you do, my tongue, the thing I think you do.

XXIV If by chance I ask anything in a timid, slender little book, grant it, if my page has not been shameless. And if you will not grant it, Caesar, allow it to be asked: incense and prayers never offend Jupiter. He who shapes sacred faces in gold or marble does not make gods: the man who prays does.

XXIV Who, having imitated the Palatine features in his likeness, outdid Phidian ivory with Latian marble? This is the face of the world, these the lips of serene Jove: so that god thunders, when he thunders without a cloud. Not the crown alone did Pallas grant you, Carus; she gave the master's image, which you worship.

XXIV The Kalends of March, my birthday, a day lovelier than all the Kalends, on which the girls send me a gift, to your hearths I add this fiftieth and seventh cake and this casket of incense. If it suits you to grant a petitioner, on these years add, I pray, twice nine more, so that, not yet sluggish with excessive age, but with the three stages of life completed, I may seek the groves of the Elysian girl. After such a Nestor's span I'll ask for not one more day.

XXIV While I escort you and walk you home, while I lend you my ear as you chatter, and praise whatever you say and do, how many verses, Labullus, could have been born! Does it not seem a loss to you, if what Rome reads, the visitor seeks out, the knight doesn't mock, the senator keeps, the lawyer praises, the poet carps at, perishes because of you? Labullus, is this right? Could anyone bear it? That your tally of little toga'd clients should be larger, mine of my own books smaller? For nearly thirty days now one single page has scarcely been finished by me. So it goes, when a poet doesn't want to dine at home.

XXIV O pleasant solitude of my carriage, a gift more welcome to me than coach or chariot, gift of eloquent Aelianus! Here you may, here, Iuvatus, speak whatever comes to your mouth: no black driver of a Libyan horse, no girt-up runner goes ahead; nowhere is there a muleteer: the ponies will keep silent. O if Avitus were here to share it, I'd not fear a third ear. How well the whole day would pass like this!
XXIV. Quinces If quinces soaked in Attic honey Are set before you, say: "These honey-apples please me."
XXIV. A Golden Hairpin Lest your damp hair stain the bright silk, Let a pin fix and hold up your twisted locks.

XXV Publish your little books at last, Faustinus, to the people, And bring out the polished work of your learned heart, Such as the Cecropian citadels of Pandion would not condemn Nor our old men pass over in silence. Do you hesitate to admit Fame as she stands before your doors, And does it irk you to bear off the rewards of your own labour? Let the pages, fated to outlive you, begin through you also To live: glory comes too late to the ashes.
XXV You never give, Galla, you always promise to the man who asks. If you always deceive, then now, Galla, I ask you—say no.
XXV If you wish, Faustinus, to cool a boiling bath That Julianus himself would scarcely enter, Ask the rhetorician Sabineius to bathe. He chills the Neronian hot baths.

XXV Shores of Altinum that rival the villas of Baiae, and you, wood that witnessed Phaethon's pyre, and you, fairest of the Dryads, who wed Antenor's Faunus, Sola, the maiden, by the Euganean lakes, and you, Aquileia, blessed by the Ledaean Timavus, where Cyllarus drank the seven streams: you shall be the rest and harbour of my old age, if my leisure should ever be my own.

XXV "You don't have four hundred thousand, Chaerestratus: get up, look, Leitus is coming: stand, flee, run, hide." Is there anyone, ah, who calls him back and leads the departing in? Is there any friend, ah, who opens his ample wealth? Whom shall we give to our pages and to fame and to the talk of nations? Who would not wish to go down whole to the Stygian lakes? Is not this, I ask, better than to spatter the stage with a red shower and be drenched with lavished saffron? Than to give four hundred thousand to a horse that won't feel it, so that Scorpus's golden nose may gleam everywhere? O rich man in vain, O dissembler of your friend, do you read this and praise it? What fame you're losing!

XXV Marcellinus, true offspring of a good father, whom the bristling Bear covers under the Arcadian ridge, hear what your old, ancestral friend would wish for you, and keep these prayers in a mindful heart: let your valour be cautious, nor let rash ardour bear you into the midst of swords and savage weapons. Let the irrational want wars and fierce Mars; you can be both your father's soldier and your leader's.

XXV Though you only ever write sweet epigrams, whiter than white-leaded skin, and there is in them no grain of salt nor any drop of bitter gall — yet, you fool, you want them read! Even food does not please when robbed of the bite of vinegar, nor is a face charming that lacks a dimple. Give honey-apples and insipid figs to a baby: for me, the Chian fig that knows how to sting has flavour.
XXV You saw me ill just once, Oppianus, hardly at all; I'll see you often.

XXV Whenever we have looked at your Hyllus giving the wine, you mark us, Afer, with a more troubled eye. What, I ask, what crime is it to watch a soft servant? We look at the sun, the stars, the temples, the gods. Shall I turn away my face, as if a Gorgon held out the cups to me and sought my eyes and face? Alcides was grim, and one could look at Hylas; one may play with Mercury and Ganymede. If you don't want a guest to watch your tender servants, invite, Afer, men like Phineus and the Oedipuses.

XXV That Mucius lately seen in the morning arena, who laid his own limb upon the fire— if he seems to you patient and hard and brave, you've the wits of the people of Abdera. For when, with the torturing shirt set before him, he's told "Burn your hand," it's more to say "I won't do it."
XXV That over-lustful member, known to not a few girls, has stopped standing for Linus. Tongue, beware.

XXV When I ask you for money without a pledge, "I have none," you say; yet, if my little field stands surety for me, you have it: what you won't trust me with, Telesinus, your old comrade, you trust to my cabbages and trees. Look, Carus has charged you as defendant: let my little field attend. You seek a companion for exile: let my little field go.
XXV. Pine-Nuts We are Cybele's fruit: keep your distance, traveler, Lest our downfall crash upon your luckless head.
XXV. Combs What will this boxwood do, which will find no hair, Given to you with its many-cleft teeth?

XXVI Sextilianus, you drink as much, all by yourself, As five tiers of benches: you could be drunk so often on water; Nor do you beg only the coins of neighbours sitting near you, But the cash from benches further off. This vintage is not pressed by Paelignian wine-presses, Nor was that grape born on Tuscan slopes, But the lucky jar of old Opimius is drained dry, And the Massic cellar empties out its black casks. Go beg the dregs of Laletania from a tavern-keeper, If, Sextilianus, you drink more than ten times.

XXVI That Naevia breathes a querulous, bitter cough, And keeps spitting into your lap, Do you now think, Bithynicus, that you have the matter settled? You are wrong: Naevia is flattering you, not dying.

XXVI You alone have estates, and you alone, Candidus, have cash, You alone have gold plate, you alone the murrine ware, You alone the Massic, you alone the Caecuban of Opimius, And you alone have wit, you alone genius. You alone have everything—imagine my wanting to deny it!— But your wife, Candidus, you have in common with the public.

XXVI That all year I have not seen you at home in the morning, shall I tell you, Postumus, how much I have lost? Sixty sesterces, I think, twice; thrice twenty, I think. Forgive me: I buy my little toga for more, Postumus.
XXVI That I called you the alpha of the cloaked men, Cordus, lately, when I was joking on some page, if perchance this verse stirred your bile, you may call me the beta of the toga-wearers.
XXVI Our Sotades stands in peril of his head. You think Sotades is a defendant? He isn't. Sotades has lost the power to get it up: he licks.

XXVI Go find my friend Apollinaris, Scazon; and if he has leisure — don't come at him as a bother — give him this, such as it is, of which he himself is some part: let his ears take in this witty song. If you see yourself received with a fully open brow, ask him to support it with his well-known favour. You know with what love of my trifles he burns: not even I can love you more. If you want to be safe against the spiteful, go find my friend Apollinaris, Scazon.

XXVI The Gangetic ravisher feared not so many tigers in the Eastern fields, fleeing white on his Hyrcanian horse, as your Rome has seen, Germanicus, new tigers: it could not even count its own delights. Your arena, Caesar, surpasses the Erythraean triumphs and the wealth and riches of the conquering god: for when he drove captive Indians beneath his chariot, Bacchus was content with a pair of tigers.

XXVI He who dares to send poems to eloquent Nerva will give pale woad-perfume to you, Cosmus, violets and white privet to the Paestan gardener, Corsican honey to the bees of Hybla: but yet even a small Muse has some grace; the cheap olive is sought after when the boar is set aside. Nor let it be a wonder to you that my Thalia, aware of her modest bard, fears your judgement: even Nero himself is said to have feared your ears, when as a young man he played a wanton work for you.

XXVI Varus, lately noble through the Latian vine in the Paraetonian towns, leader to be remembered by a hundred men, but now, promised in vain to Ausonian Quirinus, you lie, a stranger's shade, on the shore of the Nile. It wasn't granted to sprinkle your cold face with tears, nor add rich incense to the mournful pyres. But it's given you—a name to live by eternal song: can you deny even this, deceitful Nile?

XXVI O my dear repose, O my coaxing care, Telesphorus, such as was never before in my embrace: give me kisses, boy, moist with old Falernian, give me cups made smaller by your lips. If you'd add to these the true joys of Venus, I'd say Jove's no better off with Ganymede.
XXVI You say you've been fucked by robbers, Saenia: but the robbers deny it.
XXVI. Service-Berries We are service-berries, binding too-loose bowels: You'll give this fruit to a boy more fittingly than to yourself.
XXVI. Hair-Dye Chattian foam fires the Teutonic hair: You can be smarter with captive locks.

XXVII Last night I had told you— After ten half-pints downed, I think— That you should dine with me today, Procillus. At once you thought the thing as good as done, And made a note of my unsober words By a precedent far too dangerous: "I hate a drinking-mate with a good memory," Procillus.

XXVII When Selius, praising you, spreads his nets for a dinner, Take him along, whether you read aloud or plead as advocate: "Perfect! weighty! quick! cleverly! bravo! divine!" "That is what I wanted! Now your dinner is earned—be quiet."

XXVII You never invite me back, though you often come when invited: I forgive you, Gallus, if only you invite no one. But you invite others: the fault is on both sides. "What?" you ask. I have no sense, and you, Gallus, have no shame.

XXVII You often praise my little books, Augustus. Look, the envious man denies it: do you praise them the less? What of this—that you gave me not only honouring words, but gifts no other man could give? Look, again the spiteful one gnaws his blackened nails. Give all the more, Caesar, that he may suffer.

XXVII Talent and study and manners and birth you have of a knight, I admit: the rest you have of the plebs. Don't let your fourteen rows of benches be worth so much that you sit pale at the sight of Oceanus.

XXVII Twice my neighbour, Nepos—for you too dwell near Flora and you too dwell in old Ficeliae— you have a girl whose face is sealed with her father's likeness, a witness born to her mother's chastity. Yet don't be too sparing of your aged Falernian, and rather leave the jars full of money. Let her be dutiful, let her be rich, but let your daughter drink new wine: the amphora, now new, will grow old along with its mistress. Let the Caecuban vintage nourish not only the childless: fathers too can live, believe me.

XXVII A boar, ravager of Tuscan acorns and now sluggish from much oak, second in fame to the Aetolian beast, which my Dexter pierced with shining point, lies as prey, the envy of my hearth: let my house-gods grow fat, glad in the dripping savour, and let the festive kitchen blaze with a felled ridge of wood. But the cook will use up a huge heap of pepper and add Falernian mixed with secret fish-sauce: go back to your owner, my fire cannot hold you, ruinous boar: I go hungry more cheaply.
XXVII The man who gives gifts to you, Gaurus, rich and old, if you have wit and sense, says this to you: 'Die.'

XXVII Though you carry depilated balls, Chrestus, and a cock like a vulture's neck, and a head smoother than prostitutes' arses, and not a hair lives on your leg, and savage tweezers cleanse your white lips: yet you talk and thunder, menacing, with grand words of Curii, Camilli, Quintii, Numas, Ancuses, and whatever hairy worthies we ever read of, and you brawl with the theatre and the age. If meanwhile some strongman crosses your path, just freed from his tutor and whose swollen penis the smith has unbuckled: you call him with a nod and lead him off, and I am ashamed to say, Chrestus, what you do with your Cato-like tongue.
XXVII On your birthday, Diodorus, the senate as your guests reclines, and a rare knight is not left out, and your dole hands out thirty coins apiece. Yet no one, Diodorus, thinks you were ever born.

XXVII You're made of iron, Flaccus, if your cock can stand, when your girlfriend begs you for six measures of fish-sauce, or asks for two slices of tunny or a thin mackerel, and doesn't think herself worthy of a whole bunch of grapes; to whom a maid joyfully brings on a red dish some fish-pickle, but only what she'll gulp down at once; or when she's rubbed her brow and laid aside shame and asks five greasy fleeces for a cloak. But let my girlfriend demand a pound of nard from me, or green gems or matched sardonyx, and want only the finest silk from the Tuscan quarter, or ask for a hundred gold pieces as if for small change. Now you think I want to give these things to a girl? No, I don't, but I want a girl worthy of them.
XXVII I drink two ounces, you drink eleven, Cinna: and you complain that we don't drink the same, Cinna?
XXVII. Soap If, gray-haired, you mean to change your long-lived locks, Take Mattiac balls — but why, when you're bald?
XXVIII Whoever believes that Acerra reeks of yesterday's wine Is mistaken: Acerra always drinks till dawn.

XXVIII Laugh heartily at whoever calls you, Sextillus, a catamite, And give him the middle finger. But you are no sodomite, Sextillus, nor a fornicator, Nor does the hot mouth of Vetustina please you. You are none of these, I admit, Sextillus: what are you then? I do not know, but you know there are two things left.
XXVIII You marvel that Marius's little ear smells foul. You do this, Nestor: you chatter into his little ear.

XXVIII You gave tender Lupercus, Chloe, cloaks Spanish, Tyrian, and scarlet, a toga washed in warm Galaesus, Indian sardonyx, Scythian emeralds, and a hundred lords of fresh-struck coin: and whatever he keeps asking you keep giving. Alas, poor sleek plucked thing, alas for you: your Lupercus will leave you stripped bare.

XXVIII That Mamercus should speak and think well, you could bring about by no manners, Aulus: though you outdo the Curvian brothers in piety, the Nervas in calm, the Rusos in courtesy, the Macers in honesty, the Mauricuses in fairness, the Reguli in oratory, the Pauli in jests: he gnaws everything with rusty teeth. You might believe him perhaps a spiteful man: I believe him a wretched one, whom no one pleases.

XXVIII That famous freedman of Melior, who fell with all Rome grieving, the brief darling of his dear patron, Glaucias, buried beneath this marble, lies in a tomb joined to the Flaminian way: pure in morals, untouched in modesty, quick of wit, blessed with beauty. The boy had just completed twice six harvests and was barely adding one more year. You who weep at such things, traveller, weep at nothing.

XXVIII So may the wood of Tiburtine Diana grow for you and the often-felled grove make haste to come back, nor may your olives, Fuscus, yield to Tartessian presses, and may the vats give the good must of an ample crop; so may the forums admire you, the palaces praise you, and many a palm adorn your twin doors: while mid-December gives you a little leisure, weigh — but with a sure ear — the jests you read. 'You wish to know the truth? That is a hard task.' But you, Fuscus, can say what you want said to you.

XXVIII Tell me, toga, welcome gift of an eloquent friend, of what flock do you wish to be the fame and pride? Did the Apulian grass of Ledaean Phalanthus bloom for you, where Galaesus waters the tilled fields with Calabrian streams? Or did Baetis, the Tartessian nurse of the Spanish fold, also wash you in a Hesperian sheep? Or did your wool number among many-branched Timavus, which pious Cyllarus drank with his star-bearing mouth? It became you not to be stained with Amyclaean dye, nor was Miletus worthy of your fleece. You outdo the lilies and the privet not yet fallen, and the ivory that chills on the Tiburtine hill; the Spartan swan will yield to you, and the Paphian doves, the gem dug from the Erythraean shallows will yield: but though these gifts rival the first snows, they are not whiter than their Parthenius. I would not prefer the embroidered weavings of proud Babylon, which the Semiramian needle makes various; nor would I admire myself more in Athamantian gold, should you give me, Phrixus, the Aeolian sheep. Oh, what laughter will my cloak stir up, when seen together with my Palatine toga!

XXVIII Sweet glory of the stage, fame of the games, I am that Latinus, your applause and your delight, who could have made a spectator of Cato, who could relax the grave Curii and Fabricii. But my life took nothing from our theatre, and I am called an actor by my art alone; nor could I be pleasing to our lord without good character; that god looks more deeply into men's minds. Call me the parasite of laurelled Phoebus, so long as Rome knows me the servant of her own Jove.

XXVIII Loveliest sire of the years and of the shining world, whom the public vows and prayers first invoke, once you dwelt in cramped quarters as a thoroughfare, where teeming Rome wore down the middle of the road: now your thresholds are ringed with Caesar's gifts, and you count as many forums, Janus, as you bear faces. But you, holy father, grateful for so great a gift, keep watch over the iron bars with their bolt forever fastened.
XXVIII Frenzied Nasica burst in on the doctor Euctus and buggered Hylas. This one, I think, was sane.

XXVIII Hermogenes is as great a thief of napkins as Massa, I think, scarcely was of money; though you watch his right hand and hold his left, he'll find a way to make off with your napkin: so the stag's breath sucks up the cold snake, so Iris draws up the waters that will fall from on high. Lately when discharge was sought for wounded Myrinus, Hermogenes filched four napkins; when the praetor wished to drop the chalk-white napkin, Hermogenes stole the praetor's napkin. No one had brought a napkin, while thefts were feared: Hermogenes stole the cloth from the table. And if even this is lacking, Hermogenes is not afraid to strip the middle of the couches and the feet of the tables. Though the spectacles glow with no small sun, the awnings are drawn back when Hermogenes comes. The anxious sailors hasten to furl their canvas, whenever Hermogenes appears at the harbour. The bald linen-clad priests flee, and the rattle-bearing throng, when Hermogenes has stood among the worshippers. Hermogenes never brought a napkin to dinner, from dinner Hermogenes always carried one home.
XXVIII. A Jar of Syrian Figs These that came to you packed in a twisted cone — Had the cottana been bigger, they'd have been figs.
XXVIII. A Sunshade Take this parasol to beat the fierce sun: Even if there's wind, your own canopy will shield you.

XXIX Rumour reports, Fidentinus, that you recite my little books To the public no otherwise than as your own. If you want them called mine, I will send you the poems for nothing: If you want them called yours, buy this—that they may not be mine.

XXIX Rufus, you see that man wearing down the front benches, Whose hand even from here gleams with its sardonyx, And whose cloaks have drained off Tyrian dye so many times, And whose toga is bidden to outdo untouched snows, Whose oiled hair reeks of all the Marcellan colonnade, And whose smooth arms gleam with the hair plucked out, On whose foot sits no day-old crescent-marked strap, And scarlet leather paints his unblemished foot, And many plasters cover his star-spangled brow. You do not know what it is? Take off the plasters: you will read it.
XXIX These chains, with their twin fetter, Zoilus dedicates To you, Saturn—the rings he wore before.

XXIX Their own great number stands against my little books, dear Pudens, and the crowded work wearies and gluts the reader. Rare things please: so the first fruits hold more favour, so winter roses earn their price; so a grasping mistress's scorn commends her, nor does an ever-open door keep the young man. Persius is counted more often in his one book than trifling Marsus in his whole Amazonis. You too, whatever of my little books you reread, think it the only one: so it will be worth more to you.
XXIX Whenever you send me a hare, Gellia, you say: "You'll be handsome, Marcus, for seven days." If you don't mock, if you tell the truth, my light, you've never eaten a hare, Gellia.

XXIX Not of the household's commons, nor a slave of the greedy auction-block, but a boy worthy of his master's holy love, when he could not yet feel his patron's gifts, Glaucias was already Melior's freedman. This was granted to his character and his beauty: who was more charming than he? Or who was fairer with Apollo's face? For the extraordinary, life is brief and old age rare. Whatever you love, pray it not please too much.

XXIX Thestylus, sweet torment of Voconius Victor, than whom no boy is better known in all the world, so may you be lovely even when your curls are laid aside, and may no girl please your poet: set aside your master's learned little books awhile, while I read small verses to your Victor. And Maecenas, when Maro sang of Alexis, still knew the dusky Melaenis of Marsus.
XXIX He who writes couplets, I think, wants to please by brevity. But what good is brevity, tell me, if it makes a book?

XXIX Philaenis, who had measured out the ages of Nestor's old age, have you been snatched so soon to the infernal waters of Dis? You did not yet count the long years of the Euboean Sibyl: she was greater by three months. Ah, what a tongue is silent! A thousand auction-blocks could not outdo it, nor the throng that loves Sarapis, nor the curled-haired band of the morning schoolmaster, nor the bank that sounds with the Strymonian flock. Who now will know how to draw down the moon with the Thessalian wheel, who, as a bawd, to sell this man's bed or that? May the earth lie light on you and soft sand cover you, that the dogs may not be unable to dig up your bones.

XXIX The dish you used to send me at Saturn's season, you've sent, Sextilianus, to your mistress; and the gown you'd give on the Kalends named for Mars, out of my green toga is the dinner-suit bought. Now the girls have begun to cost you nothing: you screw, Sextilianus, with my gifts.

XXIX When you begin to handle my limp manhood with your old hand, Phyllis, I'm done in by your thumb: for when you call me your mouse, your eyes, I scarcely think I can recover in ten hours. You don't know flattery: say "I'll give you a hundred thousand and I'll give you the well-tilled acres of Setine soil; take wine, a house, slave-boys, gold plate, tables." There's no need of fingers: rub me like this, Phyllis.

XXIX Since you, a senator, tread sixty thresholds in the morning, I seem to you an idle knight, because I don't run about the city from first light and carry home, weary, a thousand kisses. But you do it to give new names to the purple calendar or to seek the lands of the Nomads or the Cappadocians: but for me, whom you force to break off my sleep in the middle and to bear and endure the morning mud, what's to be gained? When my straying foot comes out of broken leather and a sudden shower of thick water falls, and the home-born slave, called for, doesn't come with my stolen cloak, a servant comes up to my chilled ear and says, "Laetorius asks you to dine with him." For twenty coins? Not I: I'd rather go hungry, than that dinner be my wages while a province is yours, and we do the same and not earn the same.
XXIX. A Jar of Damson Plums Take plums wrinkled with the rot of foreign age: They tend to ease the burden of a costive belly.
XXIX. A Broad-Brimmed Hat I'll watch with you in the Pompeian theater: For often the man in charge denies the people the awnings.
XXX Diaulus had been a surgeon, now he is an undertaker. He began to be a doctor in the only way he could.

XXX By chance I was asking for a loan of twenty thousand sesterces, Which would have been no heavy gift even to a giver. For the man I asked was a prosperous old comrade, And one whose money-chest scourges its loose-flowing wealth. He said to me, "You will be rich, if you plead cases." Give me what I ask, Gaius: I do not ask for advice.

XXX No dole is given; you recline as a guest for free: Tell me, Gargilianus, what do you do at Rome? Whence comes your shabby toga and the rent of your dark cell? Whence the farthing? Whence the means to keep Chione? Though you may say you live by the highest reason, That you live at all you do with no reason at all.

XXX Far from the Baian lake, we warn you, fisherman, flee, lest you go off guilty. These waters are swum by sacred fish that know their master and lick that hand than which nothing in the world is greater. What's more, they have names, and at their master's voice each comes when called. Once an impious Libyan, in this deep, while drawing his prey with trembling rod, suddenly, his eyes snatched away, went blind, and could not see the fish he'd caught, and now, hating the sacrilegious hooks, he sits by the Baian lake, a beggar. But you, while you may, withdraw guiltless, casting only honest food into the waves, and revere the delicate fish.

XXX Varro, not to be disowned by the Sophoclean buskin, nor less to be admired in the Calabrian lyre, put off your work, let neither eloquent Catullus's stage detain you, nor elegy with her dressed hair; but in smoky December read these poems, not to be scorned, sent you in their own month: unless perhaps it seems to you handier and better to lose, Varro, the Saturnalian nuts.

XXX Had you given me six thousand sesterces at once, when you said to me, "Take it, take it up, it's a gift," I'd owe you, Paetus, as if for two hundred thousand. But now, since you gave it after long delay, after seven, I think, or nine Kalends, do you want me to tell you something truer than truth? You've wasted six thousand sesterces, Paetus.

XXX You give yourself to Parthians, to Germans, to Dacians, Caelia, nor do you spurn the beds of Cilicians and Cappadocians; to you sails a Memphitic fornicator from the Pharian city, and a black Indian from the Red Sea waters; nor do you flee the circumcised loins of Jews, nor does the Alan pass you by on his Sarmatian horse. What is your reason, since you are a Roman girl, that no Roman cock pleases you?

XXX The show now watched in Caesar's arena was the highest glory in the days of Brutus. You see how the brave hand holds the flames and delights in its punishment and reigns over the astonished fire! He stands as his own spectator, and loves the noble death of his right hand: it feeds on the whole sacrifice; and had the punishment not been snatched from the unwilling man, the fiercer left hand was getting ready to go into the failing flames. After such a glorious deed, it irks me to know what it did before: it is enough for me to know the hand I saw.

XXX Antistius Rusticus died on the savage shores of the Cappadocians. O land guilty of a grievous crime! Nigrina brought back in her bosom the bones of her dear husband and complained the long roads were not enough; and when she gave the holy urn to the tomb she envies, she felt herself twice widowed of her snatched husband.

XXX O sweet shore of temperate Formiae, you, when he flees the town of stern Mars and wearied sheds his restless cares, Apollinaris prefers above all places. Not the sweet Tibur of his pious wife, nor his Tusculan or Algidan retreats, does he so admire, nor Praeneste and Antium; no charming Circe nor Dardanian Caieta is missed, nor Marica nor the Liris, nor Salmacis bathed in the Lucrine spring. Here the surface of Thetis is brushed by a gentle wind; the sea doesn't languish, but a living stillness of the deep bears the painted skiff with a helping breeze, just as, from a girl who has no love of summer's heat, a healthful coolness comes from the waved purple fan. Nor does the line seek its prey in the long sea, but the fish, hooked from couch and little bed, is watched as it draws the line from high above. If ever Nereus feels the reign of Aeolus, the table laughs at the storms, safe in its own supply: the fishpond feeds the turbot and home-bred bass, the dainty lamprey swims to its keeper, the namer of names calls the well-known mullet, and the old red mullets, bidden, come forth at the summons. But when does Rome allow the enjoyment of these things? How many days at Formiae does the year reckon to one held fast by the City's pressing affairs? O happy doorkeepers and bailiffs! These things are prepared for the masters; they serve you.
XXX You say lawyers and poets have foul-smelling mouths. But a cocksucker's, Zoilus, smells worse.
XXX Aper is dry, sober; what's that to me? That's how I praise a slave, not a friend.
XXX. Luna Cheese Cheese stamped with the image of Etruscan Luna Will furnish a thousand lunches for your boys.
XXX. Hunting-Spears They'll meet the boars and wait for the lions, They'll go in against bears, if only the hand be steady.

XXXI To you, Phoebus, Encolpos vows all the hair from the crown of his head, The darling of his master the centurion, When Pudens shall have won the deserved reward of the first rank. Cut the long locks soon, Phoebus, While no down soils the tender face And while the milk-white neck becomes the flowing mane; And, that master and boy may long enjoy Your gifts, make him shorn quickly, a man late.
XXXI Often I have had Chrestina. You ask how good she is? There is nothing, Marianus, that can surpass it.

XXXI You have, I confess, acres of wide-spreading field, And your town house holds many estates, And many a debtor serves your money-chest's mistress, And a mass of gold sustains your feasts. Yet do not look down, Rufinus, on lesser men: Didymus had more, Philomelus has more.

XXXI That you wish to be named and read in my little books, and think that some honour comes to you in this, may I die if it is not most welcome to me, and I want to have set you among my pages. But you bear a name imposed against the sisters' spring, which your hard mother gave you; one that neither Melpomene nor Polyhymnia could utter, nor pious Calliope with Phoebus. So adopt some name the Muses can welcome: "Hippodame" is not always nicely said.

XXXI See how the troop leaps over the gentle bullocks and how the easy-natured bull loves its own burden. This one hangs from the very tips of the horns, that one, ranging, runs along the shoulders and brandishes his weapons all over the ox. But the savage beast stays rigid, unmoved: the sand would be no safer, and the level ground could deceive them more. Their gestures don't tremble; but for the prize at stake the boy is unconcerned, the herd anxious.
XXXI You yourself know and allow, Charidemus, that your wife is laid by the doctor: you want to die without a fever.

XXXI The birds of the noisy farmyard and the mothers' eggs, and the yellow Chian figs ripened by gentle heat, and the rough young of the bleating she-goat, and olives no longer able to bear the cold, and greens beneath the chilly frosts — do you believe these were sent you from my farm? Oh, how diligently you err, Regulus! My little fields bear nothing but me. Whatever your Umbrian bailiff or your tenant or the country marked at the third milestone or the Tuscans send you, or the men of Tusculum, all that is born for me in the whole Subura.

XXXI You confess something not very pretty about yourself, Dento, you who, having taken a wife, seek the rights of a father. But now stop wearying our lord with begging little books, and return at last from the city to your homeland: for while you are far off, your wife long deserted, and you seek three sons, you'll find four.

XXXI When Velius clung as comrade to Caesar's Northern arms, he vowed this bird to Mars on behalf of his leader; the moon had not yet finished twice four circuits, and already the god demanded the vows owed him: of itself the goose hastened gladly to its altar and fell, a small victim, on the holy hearth. You see eight coins hanging from the bird's open beak? These were lately hidden in the entrails: the victim that makes offering for you, Caesar, with silver, not blood, teaches that there is now no need of the knife.

XXXI You sold a slave yesterday for twelve hundred coins, Calliodorus, so you might dine well—once. And you didn't dine well: a mullet bought at four pounds was the show and headpiece of the meal. One wants to cry out: "This is no fish, you scoundrel, no fish: it's a man; a man, Calliodorus, you're eating."

XXXI Caecilius is the Atreus of gourds: just as if they were the sons of Thyestes, he mangles them and cuts them into a thousand parts. You'll eat these right away in the relish course, he'll serve these in the first or second course, the third course will set these before you, from these he'll prepare late after-dinner dishes. From these the baker makes silly little cakes, from these he builds up multiple wafers and dates known to theatre audiences. From these comes a varied hash for the cook, so you'd think it was lentils and beans set out; it imitates mushrooms and little sausages, and the tail of a tunny and small sprats. From these the steward tries out his arts, so that, sly fellow, he may store in a rue-leaf Capellian conserves of varied flavour. So he fills the bowls and the dishes and the smooth platters and hollowed trays. This he calls elegant, this he thinks charming, to set out for so many courses a single penny.

XXXI This grove, these springs, this woven shade of trailing vine-shoots, this channelled stream of running water, and the meadows and the rose-beds not to yield to twice-bearing Paestum, and the herb that's green in January's month and doesn't freeze, and the tame eel that swims in enclosed waters, and the white tower that holds birds of the same hue, are the gifts of my mistress: when I returned after seven lustres, Marcella gave me this home and these little realms. If Nausicaa would grant me her father's gardens, I could say to Alcinous, "I prefer my own."
XXXI. Vestine Cheese If you'd take a frugal breakfast without meat, This lump comes to you from the Vestine flock.
XXXI. A Hunting-Knife If you groan that your spear, with its long shaft, is knocked aside, This short blade will go at the huge boar hand to hand.
XXXII I do not love you, Sabidius, nor can I say why: This only can I say—I do not love you.

XXXII I have a quarrel with Balbus; you do not want to offend Balbus, Ponticus: I have one with Licinus—here too is a great man. Patrobas, my neighbour, often harasses my little field; You are afraid to go against a freedman of Caesar. Laronia refuses and keeps back my slave; You answer, "She is childless, rich, old, a widow." A friend who is a slave, believe me, is poorly served: Let him be free who wants to be my master.

XXXII I cannot do an old woman. You complain, Matrinia? I can Do even an old woman, but you are dead, not old. I can do Hecuba, I can do Niobe, Matrinia, but only If the one is not yet a dog, the other not yet a stone.
XXXII It both hides and shines, sealed in a Phaethontian drop, so the bee seems shut in its own nectar. A worthy reward she won for all her toils: one may believe she herself chose to die so.
XXXII Crispus, Faustinus, in his last will did not leave his wife a farthing. "To whom did he leave it, then?" To himself.

XXXII While the war-goddess of civil strife still wavered and soft Otho could perhaps have won, he condemned a Mars that would cost much blood and pierced his whole breast with a sure hand. Let Cato, while he lives, be even greater than Caesar: but in dying—was he greater than Otho?

XXXII Atticus, you who revive the name of an eloquent line and do not let a mighty house fall silent, the pious throng of Cecropian Minerva attends you, quiet seclusion loves you, every sage loves you. But other youths a trainer with a battered ear cultivates, and the grimy masseur snatches their undeserving wealth. No ball, no bladder, no rustic football at the baths prepares you, nor the dull blow of a bare stump, nor do you stretch crooked arms in the sticky wrestler's grease, nor, roaming, do you snatch the dusty handballs, but you only run near the snowy waters of the Virgin, or where the bull glows with Sidonian love. To play, through the various arts that every field serves, when one is free to run, is sloth.

XXXII Gliding down through the silent air, a coaxing dove flowed into the very lap of seated Aretulla. Chance would have made sport of this, but the bird stayed unwatched and, though free to fly, would not go off. If a pious sister may hope for better things, and if prayers avail to bend the lord of the world, this bird perhaps comes to you from the Sardinian shores of the exile as a messenger that your brother will return.

XXXII I want her who is easy, who roams in a little cloak, I want her who has already given herself to my boy, I want her whom a single denarius buys outright, I want her who, one alone, suffices three at once. Let the cock of thick-witted Bordeaux possess the woman who demands money and sounds off grand words.

XXXII This picture, tended with violets and roses, whose features it recalls, Caedicianus, you ask? Such was Marcus Antonius Primus in his middle years: in this face the old man sees his younger self. Would that art could shape the character and the soul! No tablet on earth would be more beautiful.

XXXII You've neither toga nor hearth nor a bedbug-worn bed, nor a mat patched from absorbent marsh-reeds, nor slave-boy nor older man, no maidservant nor infant, nor bolt nor key nor dog and cup. Yet you affect, Nestor, to be called and to seem poor, and seek to have a place among the people. You lie and flatter yourself with empty honour. It's no poverty, Nestor, to have nothing.

XXXII O disgrace of the Julian Kalends, I saw, Vacerra, your baggage, I saw it; which, not held back for two years' rent, your red-haired wife carried, with her seven locks, and your white-haired mother with your huge sister. I thought they were Furies risen from the night of Dis. You followed these ahead, dry with cold and hunger, and paler than aged boxwood, the Irus of your times. You'd think the Arician slope was on the move. A three-legged cot went along and a two-legged table, and with a lantern and an earthenware bowl a chamber-pot was pissing through its broken side; the neck of an amphora lay under a greening brazier; that there'd been sprats or worthless mackerel the shameless smell of the jar confessed, such as scarce comes from a sea-water tank. Nor was a square of Toulouse cheese lacking, nor a four-year-old wreath of black pennyroyal and bald ropes with garlic and onions, nor your mother's pot full of vile resin, with which the Summemmian wives are stripped of hair. Why do you seek a house and mock the bailiffs, when you could, Vacerra, live free of charge? This parade of baggage belongs on the bridge.
XXXII. Smoked Cheese Not every hearth, not every kind of smoke, But the cheese that has drunk Velabran smoke has flavor.
XXXII. A Belt-Dagger This will be the soldier's glory and an omen of welcome honor, A weapon fit to gird a tribune's side.

XXXIII Gellia does not weep for her lost father when she is alone, But if anyone is present, the bidden tears leap forth. He does not mourn who seeks to be praised for it, Gellia; He grieves truly who grieves with no witness by.

XXXIII Why do I not kiss you, Philaenis? You are bald. Why do I not kiss you, Philaenis? You are red-haired. Why do I not kiss you, Philaenis? You are one-eyed. The man who kisses these, O Philaenis, sucks cocks.
XXXIII I prefer a freeborn girl, but if she is denied me, A freedwoman is my next condition: A slave-girl comes last: but she will beat them both, If, in face, she seems to me freeborn.
XXXIII Though you have chests full of laboured books, why, Sosibianus, do you publish nothing? "My heirs," you say, "will bring out my poems." When? It was high time, Sosibianus, that you were read.
XXXIII A pleader is said to carp at my poems: who he is, I don't know: if I find out, woe to you, pleader.

XXXIII Nothing more pitiable, Matho, than Sabellus the sodomite have you seen, than whom nothing was happier before. Thefts, runaways, deaths of slaves, fires, mourning afflict the man, and now, wretched, he even goes with women.

XXXIII Though your toga is filthier than mud, Cinna, while your shoe is whiter than the first snow, why, fool, do you drench your feet with your dragging cloak? Gather up your toga, Cinna — look, your shoe is ruined.

XXXIII From your praetorian crown you send me a leaf, Paulus, and bid it bear the name of a saucer. With this gauze your stage-platform was lately smeared, which the wave of red saffron washed pale. Or is it gold-leaf scraped off by the nail of a crafty servant, which I think comes from the foot of your couch? That leaf can feel a gnat flying far off and be stirred by the wing of the tiniest butterfly; it flutters, suspended on the heat of a small lamp, and breaks at the light touch of poured wine. With this spit are smeared the date-palms of January's Kalends, which the shabby client brings with his stingy penny. Less limp grow the colocasia on their slender stalk, more fully the lilies fall in too much sun; nor does the wandering spider run on so thin a web, nor does the hanging silkworm press out so light a work. Thicker stands the chalk on old Fabulla's face, thicker the bubble swells on struck water; stronger is the bladder that keeps curled hair, and the Batavian foam that changes Latin locks. With such a skin the chick is clothed in the Ledaean egg, such patches sit on the crescent-marked brow. What have you to do with a saucer, when you could send a spoon, when you could send me even a little ladle — I speak too grandly — when you could send a snail-shell, in short, when you could send, Paulus, nothing?
XXXIII If you hear applause in any bath, Flaccus, know that Maro's cock is there.

XXXIII Simpler than the old Sabines, Munatius Gallus, who surpass the Cecropian sage in goodness, so may chaste Venus grant you to keep your daughter's husband's bright house with her wedding-torch unbroken: that you, if perchance ill-will calls verses dipped in green verdigris to be mine, do as you do—drive them from me, and don't insist that anyone who is read writes such poems. My little books have learned to keep this rule: to spare persons, to speak of vices.

XXXIII Time and again the Green has reached the palm since Nero's death, and as victor carries off more prizes. Go now, gnawing envy, say you yielded to Nero: it was no doubt not Nero who won, but the Green.
XXXIII To buy boys Labienus sold his gardens. Now Labienus has nothing but a fig-grove.
XXXIII. Trebulan Cheeses Trebula bore us; a double grace commends us, Whether we are tamed by gentle flame or by water.
XXXIII. A Dagger A dagger, which a short groove marks with a curving vein. Salo dipped it, hissing, in his icy waters.

XXXIV With your doors unguarded and forever open, Lesbia, You sin, and do not hide your stolen pleasures, And the onlooker delights you more than the lover himself, Nor are your joys agreeable to you if they lie hidden. But the courtesan drives off the witness with a curtain and a bolt, And rarely does a chink gape in the brothel of Summemmius. From Chione at least, or from Ias, learn some modesty: Even the tombs hide their filthy harlots. Does my censure seem to you too harsh? I forbid you, Lesbia, to be caught—not to be had.

XXXIV Though Phileros pleases you, ransomed at the cost of your whole dowry, You suffer your three sons, Galla, to die of hunger. Such indulgence is shown to a grey cunt, Which not even chaste Venus could now become. May the gods make you the everlasting mistress of Phileros, O mother, no worse than Pontia herself.
XXXIV Why you both deserve and do not deserve your name, I will tell. You are cold and you are black: you are not, and you are, Chione—Snow.
XXXIV Though your toga is dirty, still he speaks the truth, Attalus, whoever says you have a snow-white toga.

XXXIV To you, father Fronto, mother Flaccilla, I commend this girl, my kisses and my darling, that little Erotion may not shudder at the dark shades and the monstrous jaws of the hound of Tartarus. She would have completed the cold of her sixth winter, had she not lived just so many days too few. Among such aged patrons let her play, wanton, and chatter my name with lisping mouth. Let no hard turf cover her soft bones, and you, earth, do not be heavy on her: she was not heavy on you.

XXXIV Give me kisses, Diadumenus, pressed close. "How many?" you ask. You bid me number the waves of Ocean and the shells scattered along the Aegean shores and the bees that wander on the Cecropian mount, and the voices and hands that sound in the full theatre when the people suddenly see Caesar's face. I don't want as many as Lesbia, won over, gave to clever Catullus: he wants few who can count them.

XXXIV By what means, Severus, you ask, could the worst man of all, Charinus, have done one thing well? I'll tell you, but quickly. What is worse than Nero? What is better than the Neronian baths? At once, behold, one of the spiteful is not lacking, who speaks thus with rancid mouth: 'What? Do you prefer this to all the gifts of our lord and god?' I prefer the Neronian baths — to the bathing-place of a catamite.
XXXIV You say you own the original silver of Mys. A thing made without you — is that the more original?

XXXIV Jupiter laughed at the lies of his Idaean tomb, while he saw the Flavian temple of Augustus' sky, and amid the tables, now flowing with abundant nectar, as he himself handed the cups to his own Mars, looking on Phoebus and Phoebus' sister alike, with whom were Alcides and the pious Arcadian: 'You gave me,' he said, 'monuments in Cnossos: see how much better it is to be Caesar's father.'

XXXIV May the gods grant you, Caesar Trajan, whatever you deserve, and ratify forever what they've been willing to bestow: you who restore his rights to the patron stripped of them —he'll be no exile to his own freedmen—, you deserve the power to keep the whole client safe: which—if only one may prove the truth—you can.
XXXIV Aper bought a house, but one that not even an owl would want as its own: so black and old a hovel it is. Sleek Maro owns the gardens next to him. Aper will dine well, but won't live well.

XXXIV Thirty-four harvests I have spent with you, Julius, if I remember rightly. Of these the sweets are mixed with the bitter, but still the pleasant were the more; and if every pebble, this way and that, distinct and two-coloured, were sorted out, the white throng would beat the blacker. If you'd avoid certain bitter things and guard against sad bites of the heart, make yourself too close a comrade to no one: you'll rejoice less and you'll grieve less.
XXXIV. Onion-Bulbs Since your wife is an old woman and your parts are dead, Bulbs can do nothing for you but fill your belly.
XXXIV. A Sickle A leader's settled peace bent me to gentle uses. Now I belong to the farmer; before, I was the soldier's.

XXXV You complain, Cornelius, that the verses I write are too little severe, And not such as a schoolmaster might read aloud in class: But these little books, like husbands with their wives, Cannot please without a cock. What if you bade me write a wedding-hymn In language not of a wedding-hymn? Who clothes the Floralia, and grants To courtesans the modesty of the matron's robe? This is the law laid down for jesting songs: They cannot give pleasure unless they tickle. So lay aside your severity, I beg, And spare my sports and jokes, And do not seek to castrate my little books. Nothing is uglier than a Priapus gelded.
XXXV Since your legs are like the horns of the moon, You could, Phoebus, wash your feet in a drinking-horn.
XXXV You behold the fish, a famous masterpiece of Phidian art: Add water, and they will swim.

XXXV With facing brows we saw soft does charge together and fall by an equal lot of fate. The dogs watched the prey, and the proud hunter stood amazed that nothing was left for his knife. Whence did such light spirits burn with such fury? So bulls fight, so heroes fall.

XXXV While scarlet-clad Euclides was shouting that he gets two hundred thousand back from his Patran estates and more from his suburban land near Corinth, and traced his long pedigree from fair Leda, and resisted Leitus, who was making him get up: from the proud, noble, wealthy knight's bosom a great key suddenly fell. Never, Fabullus, was there a more good-for-nothing key.

XXXV Seven water-clocks, demanded by you in a loud voice, the unwilling judge, Caecilianus, granted. But you speak much and long, and half-reclining drink lukewarm water from glass flasks. That you may at last sate both voice and thirst, we ask that you now drink, Caecilianus, from the water-clock.

XXXV A slave with his black loins girt in leather stands by, whenever you bathe in warm water all over. But my slave, Laecania — to say nothing of myself — has a Jewish weight under his bare skin, and young men and old bathe naked with you. Or is your slave's cock the only real one? Do you, married woman, seek out the women's recesses, and bathe apart, you cunt, in your own water?
XXXV Since you are alike and matched in life, a wretched wife, a wretched husband, I wonder you don't get on well together.

XXXV By these arts, Philomusus, you always earn your dinner, inventing much, but reporting it as if true.
