You know what Pacorus deliberates in the Arsacid court, you count the Rhenish and Sarmatian forces, you unseal the words of the Dacian leader committed to paper, you see the victor's laurel before it comes, you know how often dark Syene is drenched by the Pharian Jove, you know how many ships go from the Libyan shore, on whose head the Julian olives are born, to whom the aethereal father destines his own garlands. Away with your arts; today you'll dine at my house on this condition, Philomusus: that you tell nothing new.

XXXV Let all girls read Sulpicia, who wish to please one man alone; let all husbands read Sulpicia, who wish to please one bride alone. She doesn't recount the frenzy of the Colchian nor tell of dire Thyestes' banquet; nor does she believe there was a Scylla or a Byblis: but she teaches chaste and honest loves, games, delights, and pleasantries. Whoever judges her poems rightly would say none is more mischievous, would say none is more pure. Such, I'd believe, were Egeria's jests in dewy Numa's grotto. With her as fellow-pupil or as teacher, you'd have been more learned and chaste, Sappho: but had hard Phaon seen Sulpicia beside you and at once, he'd have loved her. In vain: for neither as the Thunderer's wife nor as the girl of Bacchus or Apollo would she live, with her Calenus torn away.
XXXV Since you invite three hundred strangers to me, you wonder and complain and quarrel that I don't come, though invited, to your house. I dine alone, Fabullus, but not gladly.

XXXV As though you lived openly with me, Callistratus, you're often used to tell me you've been buggered. You're not so candid, Callistratus, as you want to be believed. For whoever tells such things keeps more untold.
XXXV. Lucanian Sausage I, the Lucanian, come as daughter of the Picene sow: From me a welcome garland rings the snow-white gruel.
XXXV. A Little Axe When the sad auction was held to pay off debts, This was bought for four hundred thousand.

XXXVI If to you, Lucanus, or to you, Tullus, there were given Such a destiny as the Spartan sons of Leda have, There would be a noble contest of devotion between the two, Since each would wish to die before the other for his brother, And the first to go down to the shades below would say: "Live out your time, brother; live out mine."

XXXVI I would not have you curl, but neither tousle, your hair; I would not have your skin gleaming, nor would I have it dirty; Let there be no beard of the mitred, nor the beard of the accused: I want a man, Pannychus, neither too much so nor too little. Now your legs are bristly with hairs, and your chest With shaggy bristles, but your mind, Pannychus, is plucked smooth.

XXXVI What a new and lately made friend does for you, This you bid me do for you, Fabianus: That, unkempt, I should always greet you at first light, And your sedan drag me through the middle of the mud, That, weary, at the tenth hour or later, I should follow you to Agrippa's baths, when I bathe at Titus's. Have I earned this, Fabianus, through thirty Decembers, That I be always a raw recruit to your friendship? Have I earned this, Fabianus, with a toga worn and my own, That you do not yet believe I have earned my discharge?
XXXVI Your beard is grey, your hair is black: you cannot dye your beard—that's the reason—but you can, Olus, dye your hair.
XXXVI A certain man, praised in my little book, Faustinus, pretends, as if he owed nothing: he's cheated me.
XXXVI Your member is as big, Papylus, as your nose, so that you can smell it whenever you get it up.

XXXVI When my unfinished farmhouse refused to bear the rains and dripping Jupiter, and swam in winter waters, many a tile to pour off the sudden showers came, sent by your gifts. Behold, rough December roars with Boreas' shriek: Stella, you roof the house — you do not roof the farmer.

XXXVI Laugh, Caesar, at the royal wonder of the pyramids; now barbaric Memphis is silent about her Eastern work: how small a part is the Mareotic labour beside the Parrhasian hall? The day sees nothing brighter in the whole world. You'd think the seven hills rise together; Thessalian Pelion bore a lower Ossa; it so enters the air that, hidden among the bright stars, its serene peak thunders below the cloud and is filled with the secret godhead of Phoebus before Circe sees the face of her rising father. Yet this house, Augustus, which strikes the stars with its summit, is the equal of heaven — but less than its lord.

XXXVI The Phrygian boy, the known joy of the other Jove, had seen the Ausonian servant just now with his hair laid aside: 'What your Caesar, look, has allowed his own youth, allow yours, greatest ruler,' he said; 'Already my first down hides in long hair, already your Juno laughs at me and calls me a man.' To him the aethereal father said, 'O sweetest boy, it is not I, but the thing itself, that denies you what you ask: our Caesar has a thousand servants like you, and that great hall scarcely holds his star-like males; but if shorn hair gives you a manly look, who else will there be to mix me nectar?'

XXXVI Whatever the wicked smokehouses of Massilia ripen, each cask that takes its age from the fire, comes from you, Munna: to your wretched friends you send across the straits, down the long roads, your savage poisons; and at no easy price, but one that would content a jar of Falernian or Setine dear to its own cellars. Why you don't come to Rome in so long a time, this, I think, is the reason: that you'd not drink your own wines.

XXXVI Gaius Julius marks this day for me with a white gem— hurrah, behold, he's been given back to my prayers: it's a joy to have despaired, as if the sisters' threads were already cut; those who feared nothing rejoice less. Hypnus, why do you dally, lazy one? Pour out immortal Falernian, such vows demand an old cask: let's drink five measures, and six, and eight, so that he may be Gaius and Julius and Proculus.

XXXVI Four pounds of silver, or two, to a friend, and a toga for the cold and a short cloak, and now and then gold pieces clinking in the hand, enough to last two Kalends— because no one but you, Labullus, gives these, you're not, believe me, a good man. What then? To speak the truth, you're the best of the bad. Give me back the Pisos and Senecas and Memmiuses and Crispuses, but the earlier ones: you'll become at once the last of the good. Do you want to glory in running, in your feet? Beat Tigris and swift Passerinus: there's no glory in outrunning little donkeys.
XXXVI. A Small Box of Olives This olive, brought up smuggled from the Picene presses, Both opens the feast and the same olive ends it.
XXXVII You receive the burden of your belly in wretched gold—and feel no shame— You drink from glass, Bassus: so it costs you more to shit.

XXXVII Whatever is set down, you sweep up from here and there, The teats of a sow's udder and a rib of pork And a moor-hen meant to be shared by two, Half a mullet and a whole bass And the side of a lamprey and the thigh of a fowl And a wood-pigeon dripping with its own gravy. When these are stowed in your dripping napkin, They are handed to a slave to be carried home: We recline, an idle company. If you have any shame, put back the dinner: I did not invite you, Caecilianus, for tomorrow.
XXXVII You prosperous friends know only how to take offence. You do not act prettily, but it pleases you: go on, do it.

XXXVII "Coranus owes a hundred, Mancinus two hundred, Titius three hundred, Albinus twice that, Sabinus a million and another, Serranus the same; from his apartment-blocks and estates, three million clear, from his Parman flocks come twice three hundred a year": all day long, Afer, you tell me this, and I know it better than my own name. You must pay out something, that I may bear it: ease my daily nausea with cash— I cannot listen to all that for free, Afer.

XXXVII A girl sweeter to me than the aged swans, softer than the lamb of Phalantine Galaesus, daintier than the shell of the Lucrine pool, to whom you'd prefer neither Erythraean pearls, nor the just-polished tooth of the Indian beast, nor virgin snows nor the untouched lily; who outdid in hair the fleece of the Baetic flock and the knots of the Rhine and the golden dormouse; whose breath was fragrant as the rose-gardens of Paestum, as the first honey of Attic combs, as a lump of amber snatched from the hand; compared to whom the peacock was unlovely, the squirrel unpleasing, and the phoenix common: Erotion is still warm on her fresh pyre, whom the bitter law of cruellest fates finished in her sixth winter, and not even all of it, my love and joy and play— and yet my Paetus forbids me to be sad, beating his breast and tearing his hair the same: "Aren't you ashamed to weep at a little slave-girl's death? I," he says, "have buried a wife, and yet I live, a famous, proud, noble, wealthy wife." What can be braver than our Paetus? He inherited twenty million, and yet he lives.

XXXVII Charinus has, of his split backside, right up to the navel, no remnant left, and yet he itches right up to the navel. O with what an itch the wretch suffers! He has no arse, yet he's a pervert.

XXXVII You know the quaestor's deadly sign, Castricus? It is worth your while to learn a new mark of death: whenever he wiped his nose, running with cold, he had ordered that to be the fatal sign for the throat. A foul icicle was hanging from his loathsome nose, when fierce December blew from his dripping jaw: his colleagues held his hands — what more do you ask? The poor wretch, Castricus, was not allowed to blow his nose.

XXXVII That you give back the bills to Caietanus, Polycharmus, do you suppose you have made him a gift of a hundred thousand? 'He owed it,' you say. Keep the bills to yourself, Polycharmus, and lend Caietanus another two thousand.

XXXVII Though you are yourself at home and dress in the middle of the Subura, your hair, Galla, is made for you in your absence, and you lay aside your teeth at night as you do your silks, and you lie stowed in a hundred boxes, nor does your face sleep with you, and you wink with that eyebrow that was brought out for you in the morning, and no reverence for your grey cunt moves you, which you can now number among your forebears. Yet you promise six hundred delights; but the cock is deaf, and though it be one-eyed, it nonetheless sees you.

XXXVII Most holy worshipper of justice and even-handed laws, who rule the Latian forum with truth-telling lips, to your townsman, Maternus, your old comrade, if you're sending anything to the Galician Ocean—. Or do you think it better to drag ugly frogs and slender needle-fish on the Laurentian shore than to send the captive mullet back to its own rocks, since it would seem to weigh less than three pounds? And to dine on an insipid clam at the head of the table, and on what a small thin-shelled mussel covers, rather than oysters not envious of Baian shells, which the slave-boys gulp, their master not forbidding? Here you'll noisily drive the reeking fox into the nets, and the filthy prey will bite your dogs: there the wet lines, lately scarce drawn up from the fishy deep, will entangle my hares. While I speak, look—the fisherman returns with empty basket, the hunter stands by, proud of a captured badger: every dinner comes from the city market to the sea. If you're sending anything to the Galician Ocean—.
XXXVII Zoilus, what pleasure is it to gird your gem with a whole pound of gold and ruin the poor sardonyx? That ring was lately fit for your legs: the same weight does not suit fingers.
XXXVII You long too much to seem a man of sharp nose. I want a man of nose, not one all polyps.
XXXVII. Citrons Either these came from the leaves of the Corcyrean garden, Or these were the fruit of the Massylian dragon.
XXXVII. A Book-Box Unless you give me choice little books, I'll let in the moths and the savage worms.
XXXVIII The book you recite, Fidentinus, is mine: But when you recite it badly, it begins to be yours.
XXXVIII You ask, Linus, what my Nomentan farm yields me? This my farm yields me: that I do not see you, Linus.

XXXVIII What cause draws you, or what confidence, to Rome, Sextus? What do you hope or seek from it? Tell me. "I will plead cases," you say, "more eloquent than Cicero himself, And in the three forums none will be my equal." Atestinus pleaded cases, and Civis—you knew them both— But neither earned even his rent in full. "If nothing comes of this, I will compose poems: When you hear them, you will say they are the work of Maro." You are mad: all who are there in chilly cloaks You see are Nasos and Virgils. "I will haunt the great halls." That trade has barely fed Three or four; the rest of the crowd is pale with hunger. "What shall I do? Advise me: for I am resolved to live at Rome." If you are an honest man, Sextus, you can live—by chance.
XXXVIII Galla, say no: love sates itself, unless its joys are torment. But don't, Galla, say no too long.

XXXVIII Calliodorus has an equestrian fortune—who doesn't know it?— Sextus, but Calliodorus also has a brother. He who says "Split the four hundred thousand" is dividing a fig: do you think two can sit on one horse? What have you to do with your brother, with troublesome Pollux? If you had no Pollux, you'd be Castor. Since you are one, will you, Calliodorus, sit as two? Get up: you're committing a solecism, Calliodorus. Or imitate Leda's brood—if you can't sit with your brother—: take turns, Calliodorus, in sitting.

XXXVIII You see how little Regulus, not yet three full years old, listens and praises his father himself? And how, at the sight of his sire, he leaves his mother's lap and feels his father's praises to be his own? Already the shouting and the Hundred Men and the dense crowd of the ring and the Julian hall please the infant. So the spirited horse's offspring delights in the great dust, so the calf longs for battles with its soft brow. Gods, preserve, I pray, the mother's vows for her, the father's for him, that Regulus may hear his son, and she hear two.

XXXVIII So vast you are, and such, our Severus' Polyphemus, that even the Cyclops himself could marvel at you. But Scylla is no smaller. If you should join the two wild monsters, each would become the other's terror.

XXXVIII He who excels in stubborn devotion toward one who will feel the good of his generosity may perhaps be angling, or claiming a return: but he who keeps on giving to a name left behind, after the shade and the tomb, what does he seek, except to grieve more sparingly? It matters whether you are good or wish to seem so. This you do, Melior, with Fame for witness, you who, careful of the rites of the buried, do not let the name of Blaesus perish, and, lavish from your bountiful coffer, to honour his birthday, what you give to the mindful and pious band of scribes you make a thing of Blaesus. This will be your tribute long, while life remains, this too after your ashes.

XXXVIII Though you play, Agathinus, at the highest perils with speed, yet you cannot make your shield fall. It follows you against your will, and, turned back through the thin air, sits on your foot or your back, your hair or your nail; though the boards be slippery with Corycian saffron-spray and swift south-winds snatch the denied sails, the neglected shield walks over the boy's untroubled limbs, and wind and water harm the artist not at all. Though you wish to err, when you have done everything, you cannot be foiled: it takes art to make your shield fall.

XXXVIII O the soft fifteen years, Calenus, which the god granted and brought to completion in wedlock with your Sulpicia! O every night and hour that was marked with the precious pebbles of the Indian shore! O what battles, what struggles on both sides the happy little bed and the lamp beheld, drunk with Nicerotian perfumes! You've lived three lustres, Calenus: this whole age is reckoned to you, and you count only the days of a husband. If, long besought, Atropos would give you back from those one single day—but one— you'd rather have it than four times Nestor's age.
XXXVIII A mule-driver, Aulus, just sold for twenty thousand. You wonder at so steep a price? He was deaf.

XXXVIII This man, who paces day and night among the women's chairs, too well known in the whole city, gleaming of hair, dark with ointment, glistening with purple, soft of face, broad of chest, smooth of leg, who, a shameless companion, often clings to your wife— there's no reason to fear him, Candidus: he doesn't fuck.
XXXVIII. Beestings What the shepherd stole, while the kids could not yet stand, From the mothers' first milk — beestings — we give.
XXXIX You give scarlet and violet robes to a notorious whore: Do you wish to give the gift she has earned? Send her a toga.
XXXIX A boy like the Trojan cup-bearer, Faustinus, One-eyed Lycoris loves. How well the one-eyed girl sees!

XXXIX You have collected silver of every kind, and you alone have Myron's old craft, you alone the hand of Praxiteles and Scopas, you alone the chasing of Phidias's tool, you alone the labours of Mentor. Nor do you lack genuine Gratian pieces, nor what is overlaid with Galician gold, nor embossed plate from ancestral tables. Yet among all your silver I wonder why you have none, Charinus, that is pure.

XXXIX Thirty times in a year, Charinus, when you sealed your last will, I sent you cakes soaked in Hyblaean thyme. I'm worn out: have pity now, Charinus: seal less often, or do once for all what your cough keeps falsely promising. I've emptied my money-boxes and my purse: though I'd been richer than Croesus, I'd be poorer than Irus, Charinus, if you so often ate up my bean-soup.

XXXIX You've been made the father of seven, Cinna, by Marulla— not of children: for none is yours, nor a friend's son nor a neighbour's, but, conceived on cots and mats, they betray their mother's thefts by their own heads. This one, who walks as a Moor with curled hair, admits he's the offspring of Santra the cook. But that one, with snub nose and swollen lips, is the very image of Pannychus the wrestler. Who doesn't know the third is the baker's, whoever knows and sees blear-eyed Dama? The fourth, with a pervert's brow and fair face, was born to you from your bedfellow Lygdus: bugger your son, if you like: it's no crime. But this one, with pointed head and long ears, which twitch the way donkeys' usually do, who can deny is the son of Cyrta the fool? The two sisters, that one dark and this one red, are the children of Crotus the flute-player and Carpus the bailiff. Already you'd have a full flock of Niobids, if Coresus and Dindymus weren't eunuchs.

XXXIX When Caelius could no longer endure or suffer the various rushing about, the wandering mornings, the haughtiness and the 'good morning' of the powerful, he began to feign the gout. And while he wants too much to prove it real, and smears and binds his healthy soles and walks with a laboured step — such is the power of care and the art of pain! — Caelius stopped feigning the gout.

XXXIX There was no place before to hold the banquets of the Palatine table and its ambrosial feasts: here it is fitting to drink the sacred nectar, Germanicus, and the cups mixed by a Ganymede-hand. Be willing, I beg, to be a late guest of the Thunderer: but if you are in a hurry, Jupiter, come yourself.

XXXIX This first light dawned for the Palatine Thunderer, on which Cybele would have wished to have borne Jove; on this too holy Caesonia, my Rufus' wife, was born: no girl owes more to her mother. The husband rejoices in the double lot of his prayers, that it has fallen to him to love this day for both.

XXXIX That you swear you were born when Brutus was consul, Lesbia, you lie. Were you born when Numa was king, Lesbia? There too you lie. For, as your centuries report, you're said to be moulded from Prometheus' clay.

XXXIX You'd been the rocker of my cradle, Charidemus, and the guardian and constant companion of my boyhood. Now my towels darken with my shaven beard, and the girl complains, pricked by my lips; but to you I've never grown up: you our bailiff dreads, you the steward, you the very household fears. You allow us neither to play nor to love; you want nothing for me and want everything allowed for you. You scold, watch, complain, draw sighs, and your anger scarcely keeps off the rods. If I've put on Tyrian clothes or oiled my hair, you exclaim, "Your father never did such things"; and you count my measures with knitted brow, as if that cask came from your own cellar. Stop it; I can't bear a freedman Cato. My girl will tell you I'm a man now.
XXXIX I hate you, Sabellus, because you're pretty. A pretty fellow is a rancid thing—and a Sabellus. In short, I'd rather have a war than a Sabellus. May you waste away, pretty Sabellus!
XXXIX. A Kid The wanton beast, no friend to the green vine, Pays the price; tender as he was, he has already harmed the god.
XXXIX. A Bedroom Lamp The sweet lamp, confidante of your couch: Do whatever you please, I'll keep silent.
XL You who draw down your face and do not read these lines with pleasure, May you envy everyone, you spiteful man, and no one envy you.

XL Tongilius is said to be badly burned with semi-tertian fever. I know the man's tricks: he is hungry and thirsty. Now sly nets are spread for the fat thrushes, And the hook is cast for mullet and bass. Let the Caecuban be strained, and what the year of Opimius ripened, Let dark Falernian be stored in a thrifty glass. All the doctors have ordered Tongilius to bathe: O fools, you believe it is a fever? It is gluttony.
XL A lizard, drawn by the hand of Mentor, set into the bowl, Lives, and the silver is feared.

XL While the halls of the Pisos stood with all their lineage and learned Seneca's house, three times to be reckoned; above such great realms I preferred you alone, Postumus: you were poor and a knight, but to me you were a consul. With you, Postumus, I counted thirty winters: we had a couch in common, one and shared. Now you can give, now lose, full of honours, lavish with wealth: I wait, Postumus, to see what you do. You do nothing, and it's too late to seek another patron.— Does this please you, Fortune? "Postumus has cheated."
XL You painted Venus, Artemidorus, and you worship Minerva: and you wonder your work has displeased?
XL No woman could be preferred to you, Lycoris: no woman can be preferred to Glycera. She will become what you are: you can't be what she is. What time does! Her I want, you I wanted.

XL Here lies that old man, known in the imperial court, who bore both gods with no humble breast; whom his children's piety mingled with the holy shade of his wife: both possess the Elysian grove. She fell first, cheated of her green youth: he lived nearly thrice six Olympiads. But whoever saw your tears, Etruscus, believed him snatched from you in years cut short.

XL Not of a garden nor of a happy vine, but of a thin grove, Priapus, are you guardian, from which you were born and can be born again; I warn you, keep off thieving hands and save the wood for your master's hearths: if this fails, you too are firewood.

XL When Diodorus sought Rome from the Pharos he had left, for the Tarpeian crowns, Philaenis vowed, for her husband's return, that, as a simple girl, she would lick the part that even chaste Sabine women cherish. His ship scattered by grim storms, sunk in the waves and overwhelmed by the sea, Diodorus swam to fulfil the vow. O too slow and sluggish husband! Had my girl made this vow on the shore, I would have come back at once.
XL Since I was always being told that my Polla was secretly with a lover, I burst in, Lupus. It was no lover.

XL Lupercus loves beautiful Glycera, and holds her alone and rules her alone. When, sadly complaining that he'd not fucked her in a whole month, he wanted to give Aelianus the reason he asked for, he answered that Glycera's teeth ached.

XL You lie, I believe it: you recite bad poems, I praise them: you sing, I sing: you drink, Pontilianus, I drink: you fart, I pretend not to notice: you want to play at dice, I'm beaten: there's one thing you do without me, and I keep silent. Yet you provide me nothing at all. "When I'm dead," you say, "I'll treat you well." I want nothing: but die.
XL. Eggs If the white flows round the saffron yolks, Let Spanish mackerel-sauce season the eggs.
XL. A Tallow Candle Fortune gave you the lamp's handmaid, Who, wakeful, sees the whole darkness through.

XLI You think yourself a wit, Caecilius. You are not, believe me. What then? A vulgar slave— The kind that hawker across the Tiber is, Who barters pale sulphur-matches For broken glass; the kind who sells Soaked chickpeas to the lounging crowd; The kind who keeps and owns the vipers; The kind the cheap boys of the salt-sellers are; The kind that hoarse cook is who carries round Steaming sausages through the lukewarm cook-shops; The kind some second-rate street-poet is; The kind that shameless dancing-master from Gades is; The kind the chattering mouth of an aged catamite is. So cease at last to seem to yourself What only to yourself, Caecilius, you seem— You who could outdo Gabba in your salt, And Tettius Caballus himself. It is not granted to everyone to have a nose: He who jests with stupid impudence Is no Tettius—but a horse.

XLI "Laugh if you are wise, O girl, laugh," The Paelignian poet, I think, had said. But he had not said it to all girls. Yet, granted that he said it to all girls, He did not say it to you: you are no girl, And you have three teeth, Maximina, And those plainly pitch-black and box-yellow. So, if you trust your mirror and me, You ought to dread laughter no otherwise Than Spanius the wind, or Priscus a hand, Than chalked Fabulla dreads the rain-cloud, Than white-leaded Sabella dreads the sun. Put on a look more severe Than the wife of Priam or his elder daughter-in-law. Avoid the mimes of comic Philistion And livelier dinner-parties And whatever, with witty impudence, Loosens the lips in clear laughter. It becomes you to sit beside a grieving mother Or one mourning her husband or her loyal brother, And to have time only for the tragic Muses. But you, following our advice, Weep, if you are wise, O girl, weep.

XLI Because you lent me thrice fifty thousand Out of such great wealth as your heavy chest weighs down, You think yourself, Telesinus, a great friend to me. You great, because you give? No—I, because you get it back.
XLI Why, about to recite, do you wrap wool round your neck? That would suit our ears better.

XLI Though you are more unmanned than a flabby eunuch, and softer than the catamite of Celaenae, whom the gelded Gallus of the frenzied mother bewails, you talk of theatres and rows and edicts, and of robes and the Ides and brooches and fortunes, and point out the poor with your pumiced hand. Whether you may sit on the knights' benches, I'll see, Didymus: you may not sit on the husbands'.
XLI He who recites with throat and neck wrapped in wool, denies that he can speak or can keep silent.
XLI You seem to yourself, Sempronius Tucca, to be a man of the world: the world's ways, Sempronius, are as bad as they are good.
XLI 'Gloomy Athenagoras has not sent us the gifts he is wont to send in mid-winter's month.' Whether Athenagoras is gloomy, Faustinus, I shall see: certainly Athenagoras has made me gloomy.

XLI Ponticus, that you never fuck, but use your left hand as a concubine, and your hand serves Venus as a mistress — do you think this is nothing? It is a crime, believe me, and a great one, greater than you yourself can conceive in your mind. Horace, surely, fucked but once to beget three; Mars once, that chaste Ilia might give twins: all would have been lost, had each of them, masturbating, entrusted his foul pleasures to his own hands. Believe that Nature herself says this to you: 'That which you waste with your fingers, Ponticus, is a man.'

XLI In the new month of Janus, Proculeia, you abandon your old husband and bid him keep his goods to himself. What, I ask, what's happened? What's the cause of this sudden grief? You give me no answer? I'll tell you: he was made praetor. The purple for the Megalensian games would have cost a hundred thousand, even if you gave the shows too sparingly, and the people's festival would have carried off twice ten thousand. This is no divorce, Proculeia: it's profit.

XLI While the shepherd Amyntas pampered his flock too much and delighted in the fame and luxury of his herd, he overweighed the branches yielding to their load and the bending wood, and fell himself, chasing the shaken wealth. The father forbade the grim grove to outlive the dire ruin and condemned the guilty timber to the pyres. Let your neighbour Iollas, Lygdus, have the fat swine: it's enough for us that you count me the flock.
XLI It's not enough, Tucca, that you're a glutton: you want both to be called one and to seem one.
XLI. A Suckling Pig Let him set before me a nursling fed on pure milk By its sluggish mother; let the rich man feed on Aetolian boar.
XLI. A Many-Nozzled Lamp Since I light the whole banquet with my flames And carry so many nozzles, I am called a single lamp.

XLII When Porcia had heard the fate of her husband Brutus, And her grief sought the weapons taken from her, "Do you not yet know," she said, "that death cannot be denied? I had believed my father taught this by his fate." She spoke, and drank with eager mouth the burning coals. Go now, you tiresome crowd, and deny her steel.
XLII Zoilus, why do you spoil the bath-water with your washed backside? To make it filthier, Zoilus, plunge in your head.

XLII Because you try to bury the wrinkles of your belly with bean-meal, Polla, you smear your stomach, not my lips. Let the flaw, perhaps a trifling one, lie simply open: What is concealed is believed to be a great evil.

XLII If anyone could grant me what I ask, hear, Flaccus, what sort of boy I'd want to ask for. First, let the boy be born on Nile's shores: no land knows better how to give naughtiness. Let him be whiter than snow: for in dusky Mareotis that colour is the fairer, the rarer it is. Let his eyes vie with the stars, and soft locks lash his neck: I don't like curled hair, Flaccus. A small brow, a nose slightly and lightly hooked, lips that redden, rivals of Paestan roses. Let him often force me unwilling, and be unwilling when I'm willing, let him often be freer than his master; let him fear the boys, and often shut out the girls: a man to the rest, let him be a boy to me alone. "Now I know, and you don't fool me: for in my judgement too it's true. Such," you'll say, "was my Amazonicus."

XLII A cunning thief will carry off your coins with the chest broken open, impious flame will lay your ancestral home in ruins: a debtor will deny alike the interest and the principal, the barren field won't return the seed cast in: a deceitful mistress will rob your steward, the wave will overwhelm your ships piled with merchandise. Beyond fortune's reach is whatever is given to friends: the wealth you give away is the only wealth you'll always have.

XLII Unless you bathe at Etruscus's little baths, you'll die unwashed, Oppianus. No waters will so caress you, not the springs of Aponus, untried by girls, not soft Sinuessa and the scalding floods of Passer or proud Anxur, not Phoebus's shallows and royal Baiae. Nowhere is so bright a clear sky at leisure: the very light is longer there, and the day withdraws from no place more slowly. There the quarries of Taygetus gleam green and stones vie in varied beauty, which the Phrygian and the Libyan cut deep. Rich onyx breathes out dry heat and the serpentine stones glow with a thin flame: if Spartan customs please you, content with the dry vapour, you may plunge in raw Virgin or Marcian water; which shines so bright, so clear, that you'd suspect no water there and believe empty marble gleams. You're not attending, and with idle ear you've long heard me as if carelessly. You'll die unwashed, Oppianus.

XLII If anyone should wish to vie with you in gifts, let him also dare, Castricus, in verses. We are slight in both, and ready to be beaten: hence sleep is ours, and deep quiet pleases us. You ask, then, why I gave you such bad verses? Do you think no one gave apples to Alcinous?
XLII If a bigger dole among the rich has not corrupted you, as it does, then, Matho, you may bathe a hundred times at my expense.

XLII So, Apollo, may you enjoy the rich Myrine plains, so may you ever delight in your aged swans, so may the learned sisters serve you, nor let your Delphi lie to anyone, so may the Palatine court you and love you: quickly, at your asking, may good Caesar grant Stella twice six fasces and nod assent. Then happy I, and bound by a vow, will lead to your rustic altars a bullock with gilded horns, to fall for you. The victim is born, Phoebus; why do you delay?

XLII Your down is so faint, so soft, that breath and the suns and a light breeze wear it away. A coming quince hides itself in similar fuzz, which gleams when stripped by a maiden's thumb. Whenever I've pressed five firmer kisses on you, I become bearded, Dindymus, from your lips.

XLII Though you ask for lively epigrams, you set out dead subjects. What can be done, Caecilianus? You bid Hyblaean honey, or Hymettian, be born for you, yet you set Corsican thyme before the Cecropian bee!

XLII Bearded Callistratus was married to rugged Afer, on the same terms a virgin is wont to wed a man. Torches blazed before them, bridal veils covered their faces, nor were your words, Talassus, lacking to you. A dowry too was named. Does this not yet seem to you, Rome, enough? Are you waiting for him to give birth as well?
XLII. Cling-Stone and Stoneless Fruit We do not give you stoneless fruit and clingstones from Libyan boughs, But from Nomentan trees.
XLII. A Wax Candle This candle will give you fire by night: For your boy has filched away the lamp.

XLIII We were twice thirty, Mancinus, summoned by you, And nothing was set before us yesterday but a boar, No grapes kept from the late-bearing vines, Nor honey-apples to rival the sweet combs, No pears that hang tied to the long broom-shoots, Nor pomegranates that mimic short-lived roses; Rustic Sassina sent no milk-white cones of cheese, Nor came the olive from Picene jars: The boar alone—and that the smallest, such as could be killed By an unarmed pygmy. And nothing was given from it; we all only looked on: That is how the arena too serves us up a boar. After such deeds, may no boar be set before you, But may you be set before the boar that took Charidemus.

XLIII "Friends share all in common"—these things are yours, Candidus, "in common," Which you, grandiloquent, harp on night and day: A toga washed in Spartan Galaesus clothes you, Or one Parma gave from a choice flock: But me a hide clothes that bore the rages and horns of the bull, One the first ball would not have called its own. The land of Cadmus sent you Agenorean cloaks: You would not sell my scarlet for three coins. You hang up Libyan disks on Indian tusks: A table of beech is propped up with a potsherd for me. Huge mullets adorn your gold-inlaid dishes: Of one colour in my plate, you blush, my little crab. Your troop could vie with the Trojan catamite: But for a Ganymede my own hand comes to my aid. Out of such wealth, to an old and faithful comrade You give nothing, and you say, Candidus, "Friends share all in common"?
XLIII You counterfeit youth, Laetinus, with dyed hair, So suddenly a raven, you who were lately a swan. You do not fool everyone: Proserpina knows you are grey: She will tear the mask from your head.

XLIII I did not call you a pervert, Coracinus: I am not so rash or bold, nor one to tell lies gladly. If I called you a pervert, Coracinus, may Pontia's flask be angry with me, may Metilus's cup be angry with me: I swear by the Syrian tumours, I swear by the Berecyntian frenzies. What did I say, then? This light, trifling thing, which is well known, which you yourself won't deny— I said, Coracinus, you go down on women.
XLIII Thais has black teeth, Laecania snow-white. What's the reason? This one has bought hers, that one has her own.

XLIII While happy Baiae indulges you, Castricus, and the white nymph swims in the sulphurous waters, the leisure of my Nomentan farm restores me and a cottage not burdened by its own acres. This is my Baian sunshine and soft Lucrine, this, Castricus, is your wealth to me. Once I would run to the praised waters wherever I pleased and not dread long journeys, now I delight in the neighbourhood of the city and easy retreats, and it's enough, if I'm allowed to be lazy.

XLIII The first thing, Cinna, is to grant whatever I ask of you; the next thing after, Cinna, is to refuse quickly. I love the man who grants; I do not hate, Cinna, the one who refuses: but you neither grant, Cinna, nor quickly refuse.

XLIII Fabius buries his wives, Chrestilla her husbands, and each shakes a funeral torch over the marriage-bed. Match the victors, Venus: the end that waits these two is that one Libitina carry the pair away together.

XLIII This god who, seated, softens the hard rocks with his outstretched lion-skin, great in a little bronze, and gazes with upturned face at the stars he bore, whose left hand is warm with his club, his right with wine: this is no recent fame, no glory of our chisel; you see the noble gift and work of Lysippus. This godhead the table of the Pellaean tyrant possessed, who, conqueror, lies in a world soon subdued; to this Hannibal as a boy swore at the Libyan altars; this bade grim Sulla lay down his power. Offended by the swollen terrors of varied courts, he now rejoices to dwell in private households, and as he was once the guest of gentle Molorchus, so the god wished to be learned Vindex's.
XLIII Now, Phileros, your seventh wife is buried in your field. No man's field, Phileros, yields more than yours.

XLIII Caught with a boy, wife, you scold me with grim words and reply that you too have an arse. How often Juno said the same to the wanton Thunderer! Yet he lies with sturdy Ganymede. The Tirynthian bent over Hylas, laying down his bow: do you think Megara had no buttocks? Fleeing Daphne tormented Phoebus: yet the Oebalian boy bade those flames depart. Though Briseis lay much turned away, the smooth friend was nearer the son of Aeacus. So stop giving masculine names to your possessions, and think, wife, that you have two cunts.

XLIII You read me eloquent verses on lewd matters, Sabellus, all too many, such as neither the girls of Didymus know nor the wanton little books of Elephantis. There are in them new figures of love, such as a desperate fornicator might dare, what the catamites perform and keep silent, in what entanglement five are coupled, by what chain more are held together, what is allowed when the lamp is put out. It wasn't worth so much, your being eloquent.
XLIII. The Same Stoneless fruit, gathered from suburban boughs, is sent, And home-grown clingstones too. What have you to do with Libya's?
XLIII. A Corinthian Candelabrum Candles gave us our ancient name: The oily lamp knew nothing of our thrifty fathers.

XLIV That the wanton runs of hares and the games of lions Are carried by my larger sheet and my smaller, And that I do the same thing twice—if that, Stella, seems Too much to you, then you too serve me a hare twice over.

XLIV If I have bought a boy, or a well-combed toga, Or three, say, or four pounds of silver, That Sextus, the moneylender at once, Whom you know as my old comrade, Fears and takes care that I may not chance to ask for something, And whispers to himself, but so that I may hear: "I owe seven thousand to Secundus, Four to Phoebus, eleven to Phyletus, And there is not a farthing in my chest." O the great wit of my comrade! It is hard, Sextus, to refuse when you are asked, How much harder before you are asked!

XLIV That no one meets you gladly, That, wherever you come, there is flight and a vast Solitude around you, Ligurinus, Do you wish to know what it is? You are too much a poet. This is a fault exceedingly dangerous. No tigress roused, her cubs torn from her, No viper scorched by the noonday sun, Nor the wicked scorpion is so feared. For who, I ask, could bear such ordeals? You read to me standing, you read to me sitting, You read to me running, you read to me on the privy. I flee to the hot baths: you buzz in my ear. I seek the swimming-pool: I am not allowed to swim. I hurry to dinner: you hold me as I go. I come to dinner: you put me to flight as I sit. Weary, I sleep: you rouse me as I lie. Do you want to see how much harm you do? A man just, upright, innocent—you are feared.

XLIV Here is Vesuvius, lately green with shady vines, here the noble grape had pressed its dripping vats: these ridges Bacchus loved more than the hills of Nysa, on this mount the Satyrs lately led their dances. This was Venus's seat, dearer to her than Sparta, this place was famous for the name of Hercules. All lies sunk in flames and dismal ash: the gods themselves would not have wished this allowed them.

XLIV What has happened, I ask, what suddenly has happened, that when I invited you to dinner, Dento— who would believe it?—you dared four times to refuse? And you don't look back and you flee me when I follow, whom you used just now to seek at the baths and theatres and in every gathering-room. So it is—you've been caught by a richer table, and a bigger kitchen has snatched the dog. Soon, but quickly, recognized and dropped, when the rich cookshop has grown tired of you, you'll come back to the bones of your old dinner.

XLIV You believe, Calliodorus, that you joke wittily and that you alone are steeped in much salt. You grin at everyone, you sling gibes at everyone; so you think you can please as a dinner-guest. But if I should say something not nicely, but truly, no one will toast you, Calliodorus.

XLIV That great Caesonius of yours, Ovidius, is the man here, whose face the living wax still keeps. Nero condemned him; but you dared to condemn Nero, and to follow the fate of the exile, not your own: a noble comrade you went across Scylla's seas with the banished man, you who had lately refused to go as comrade of a consul. If names entrusted to my pages are to live, and it is granted me to survive my own ashes: the crowd now present and to come shall hear that you were to him what he was to his own Seneca.

XLIV Titullus, I warn you, live: it is always too late; even were you to begin under your tutor, it is too late. But you, poor Titullus, do not live even as an old man, but wear down every threshold as a caller, and in the morning sweat, wet with the kisses of the city, and, splashed before all the horses in the triple forum and the temple of Mars and the colossus of Augustus, you run through them all, at the third hour and the fifth. Snatch, heap up, carry off, possess: it must be left behind. Though your proud strongbox grow pale with packed coins, though a hundred pages of account-books be unrolled, your heir will swear you left nothing, and over your bier, while you lie there — a board or a stone — while your couch, stuffed with paper, swells for you, he will proudly kiss your weeping eunuchs; and your sorrowing son, whether you will or no, the first night will sleep with your catamite.

XLIV Just now I was asking Vindex's Alcides whose work and happy labour he was. He laughed — for so he is wont — and with a slight nod said, 'Poet, do you not know Greek? The base is inscribed and gives the name.' I read 'Lysippus' work'; I had thought it Phidias'.

XLIV Quintus Ovidius, soon to see the Caledonian Britons and green Tethys and Father Ocean, so you leave Numa's hills and the Nomentan leisure, and neither country nor hearth holds the old man back? You put off your joys, but Atropos doesn't put off her threads, and every hour is charged to you. You'll have proved to a dear friend—who wouldn't praise it?— that sacred loyalty is worth more to you than life; but be at last returned, to remain among your Sabines, and count yourself among your own friendships.

XLIV You're childless and rich and born when Brutus was consul: do you believe your friendships are true? There are true ones, but those you had when young, when poor. The friend who's new—he loves your death.

XLIV Unicus, you who bear a name joined to me by kindred blood, and whose heart is near to mine in pursuits; since you make poems yielding only to your brother, you're no less in talent, but first in family love. Lesbia could love you, with witty Catullus, coaxing Corinna could follow you, after Naso. Nor would the west winds fail, if it pleased you to set sail; but you love the shore. This too you have of your brother's.
XLIV. A Sow's Udder You'd think it not yet an udder: so from its generous teat It flows, and the nipple swells with living milk.
XLIV. A Wooden Candelabrum You see it's wood; unless you watch the lights, you'll have A great blaze made out of your candelabrum.
XLV That the labour I publish may not perish in little books, Let it rather be said, "Him then in answer he addressed."
XLV The cock that would not stand for you has been cut off, Glyptus. Madman, what had you to do with the knife? You were already a eunuch.

XLV Whether Phoebus fled the table and dinner of Thyestes, I do not know: we, Ligurinus, flee yours. That is indeed splendid and furnished with proud dishes, But nothing at all pleases while you recite. I do not want you to set before me turbot or a two-pound mullet, Nor do I want mushrooms, nor oysters: be silent.

XLV These offerings, Phoebus, for his son the Palatine Parthenius joyfully gives from a full incense-box, that Burrus, who marks his first five years with a new cycle, may fill out countless Olympiads. Make the father's vows come true: so may your own tree love you, and your sister rejoice in her sure virginity, so may you shine in perpetual bloom, so may Bacchus's locks at last be not so long, Phoebus, as yours.
XLV You call yourself beautiful, Bassa, you call yourself a girl. That's what she who is neither tends to say, Bassa.

XLV You've had your sport, it's enough: marry, you wanton cunts: no Venus is allowed you but the chaste. Is this chaste Venus? Laetoria marries Lygdus: she'll be a fouler wife than she was lately a harlot.

XLV Mighty friend of eloquent Seneca, next to dear Serenus, or before him, this is that Maximus, whom on many a page the lucky letter greets in close array. Him you followed through the Sicilian waves, O Ovidius, not to be passed over by any tongue, and you scorned the rage of a raving lord. Let antiquity admire its Pylades, who clung as comrade to the exile of his parent: who would compare the dangers of the two? You clung, a comrade, to the exile of Nero.

XLV Priscus Terentius is given back to me, Flaccus, from the shores of Etna: let a milk-white gem mark this day; let the cloudy amphora drip and grow bright through the slow strainer, the jar made smaller under its hundredth consul. When will so fair a night fall to my table? When shall I be allowed to grow warm with so deserved a wine? When Cytherean Cyprus gives you back to me, Flaccus, there will be so good a cause for my excess.

XLV A soldier, Marcellinus, you lately bore the Hyperborean Bears and the sluggish stars of the Getic sky: behold, the rocks of Prometheus and the fabled mountain, how near to your eyes they now are to be approached! When you see the rocks that rang with the old man's boundless laments, you'll say, 'He himself was harder.' And you may add this: 'He who could bear such things had deserved to fashion the human race.'

XLV If my little books say anything gentle and sweet, if a flattering page sounds anything that honours you, you think this fat and would rather gnaw the rib, when I serve you the flank of a Laurentian boar. Drink Vatican wine, if you delight in vinegar: my flagon doesn't suit your stomach.

XLV Whenever you've entered the threshold of a placarded cell, whether a boy or a girl has smiled on you, you're not content with door and curtain and bolt, and demand a greater secrecy for yourself: any chink, if there's the least suspicion of one, is smeared over, and the holes that are bored by a wanton needle. No one is of so tender and anxious modesty, Cantharus, who either buggers or fucks.
XLV You who cover with a goatskin the temples and crown of your bare, bald head, he spoke wittily to you, Phoebus, who said your skull was shod.
XLV. Pullets If we had Libyan birds and Phasian pheasants, You'd be getting those — but now take the fowls of the yard.
XLV. A Peasant's Ball This peasant-ball that swells with stiff feathers Is less loose than the bladder-ball, less tight than the hard.

XLVI When you say, "Quick, do it if you're doing it," Hedylus, at once My passion droops and falters, weakened. Bid me wait: held back, I will go the faster. Hedylus, if you're in a hurry, tell me—not to hurry.

XLVI As flowery Hybla is painted in various colours When the bees plunder the brief Sicilian spring, So your presses glow with the cloaks laid up beneath them, So your chest sparkles with countless festal robes, And your whites could clothe a whole tribe, Which the Apulian land bore with more than one flock. You watch, unmoved, the winter of your scantily clad friend —what a crime!—and fear the worn cold of his side. What would it have cost you, hard-hearted man, to defraud two rags —what do you fear?—not yourself, Naevolus, but the moths?

XLVI You demand of me endless service in the toga: I do not go, but I send you my freedman. "It is not the same," you say. I will prove it is much more: I should scarcely keep up with your litter; he will carry it. If you fall into a crowd, he will thrust them all back with his shoulder: My side is weak and freeborn. Whatever you say in your case, I myself shall be silent: But he will bellow you a triple "Bravo!" There is a lawsuit: he will hurl abuse in a mighty voice: Shame forbids me to use strong words. "So you will do nothing for me as a friend?" you say. Whatever, Candidus, my freedman cannot do.

XLVI The Saturnalia made Sabellus rich: deservedly Sabellus swells with pride, and thinks and proclaims that no one among the pleaders is more blessed. These airs and high spirits are given Sabellus by half a peck of grain and crushed beans, and three half-pounds of incense and pepper, and a Lucanian sausage with a Faliscan paunch, and a Syrian flask of black boiled wine, and figs frozen in a Libyan jar with onions and snails and cheese. From a Picene client too there came a little box that holds but scant olives, and, polished with the potter's coarse tool, a seven-piece dinner-set of Saguntum, the yellow earthenware of a Spanish wheel, and a napkin striped with a broad purple band. More fruitful Saturnalia than these Sabellus has not had in ten years.

XLVI Since I want no kisses but those I've snatched in struggle, and your anger pleases me more than your face, to ask you often, Diadumenus, I often beat you: and I achieve this—that you neither fear nor love me.
XLVI The Blue team's four-horse chariot is whipped constantly, yet doesn't run: it's doing a great thing, Catianus.

XLVI While you want to commend your gift to me in song and long to speak more learnedly than Maeonian lips, you torment both me and yourself alike for many days, and your Thalia, Priscus, says nothing of mine. You can send the rich your Muses and your sounding elegies: but to the poor give gifts in prose.

XLVI As great as your honesty, so great is the innocence of your beauty, boy Cestus, chaster than chaste Hippolytus! Diana would wish you with her and teach you to swim, Cybele would rather have you whole, a Phrygian; you could succeed to Ganymede's couch, but, hard, you'd give your lord kisses only. Happy the bride who will vex her tender husband, and the girl who will first make a man of you!

XLVI Gellius is always building: now he sets thresholds, now he fits keys to doors and buys locks, now these, now those windows he remakes and changes; so long as he builds at all, he does anything — that he may say to a friend begging for money that one word, Gellius: 'I'm building.'
XLVI You want, Matho, to say everything finely. Sometimes say it well too; say it neither way; sometimes say it badly.

XLVI Now you get it up only in sleep, Mevius, and your prick begins to piss between your feet, and the worn-out member is rubbed by weary fingers but doesn't lift its dead head, however coaxed. Why do you vainly harass poor cunts and arses? Aim higher: there an old woman's member lives.
XLVI Difficult and easy, pleasant and bitter, you're the same: I can't live with you, nor without you.
XLVI. Early Peaches We were once cheap peaches on our mother boughs: Now, grafted, we are precious peaches.
XLVI. A Triangle-Ball If you know how to drive me back with skilled left hands, I'm yours. You don't? Then, bumpkin, give back the ball.
XLVII Lately he was a doctor, now Diaulus is an undertaker: What the undertaker does, the doctor too had done.

XLVII I warn you, flee the sly nets of a notorious adulteress, You who are smoother, Gallus, than the shells of Cythera. Do you trust to your backside? The husband is no sodomite: There are two things he does: he forces the mouth, or he forces the front.

XLVII Where the Capene Gate drips with its great drops And the Almo washes the Phrygian iron of the Mother, Where the sacred field of the Horatii is green And the little shrine of Hercules seethes with crowds, Faustinus, Bassus was riding in a loaded wagon, Hauling all the riches of a blessed countryside. There you would see cabbages of noble stalk And both kinds of leek and low-growing lettuce And beets not useless to a sluggish belly, There a wreath heavy with fat thrushes And a hare mauled by a Gallic hound's tooth And a milk-fed pig fed on beans not yet shelled. Nor did the runner go idle before the carriage, But the courier carried eggs safe in hay. Was Bassus making for the city? No—he was going to the country.
XLVII Phaethon is painted for you on this panel in encaustic. What do you mean, making Phaethon twice-burned?
XLVII Philo swears he's never dined at home, and it's true: he doesn't dine, whenever no one has invited him.

XLVII Nymph, who, household to my Stella, glide from the pure spring and pass beneath your master's jewelled roof, whether Numa's wife sent you from Trivia's caves, or you come ninth from the troop of the Camenae: Marcus pays his vows to you with this sow, because, sick, he drank your water on the sly. You, content now with my offence, grant me safely the joys of your spring: let my thirst be healthy.

XLVII Licinius Sura, most renowned of learned men, whose grave and ancient tongue brought back our forefathers, you are given back to us — heavens, by what gift of the fates! — all but released, having tasted of Lethe's water. Our prayers had already lost their fear, and untroubled sorrow wept, and you were as good as done with our tears: but the ruler of silent Avernus would not bear the spite, and himself gave back the snatched distaff to the Fates. You know, then, what great laments a false report of death has stirred among men, and you enjoy your own posterity. Live as one whose life is snatched, and pluck fugitive joys: let your returned life lose not a single day.
XLVII Part of your jaws is clipped, part of you is shaved, part is plucked. Who would think it is one head?

XLVII Democrituses, Zenos, and tangled Platos, and whatever moulders in shaggy busts, you talk of, as though the successor and heir of Pythagoras. Your beard, indeed, hangs no shorter than theirs: but what is shameful in goatish, foul in hairy men, you gladly take a stiff one in your soft buttocks. You, who know the principles and weight of the sects, tell me, Pannychus, what doctrine is it to be buggered?

XLVII Why does Lattara avoid all the baths beloved by crowds of women? So as not to fuck. Why does he not stroll idly in Pompey's shade, nor seek the threshold of Inachus' daughter? So as not to fuck. Why does he drench his body, muddy with Spartan ointment, in the cold water of the Virgin? So as not to fuck. Since he thus shuns all contact with the female sex, why does Lattara lick a cunt? So as not to fuck.
XLVII Gallus and Lupercus sell their poems. Now deny, Classicus, that poets are sane.
XLVII. Picentine Loaves Picentine grain so swells with snowy juice That a light sponge bloats when it takes up water.
XLVII. A Bladder-Ball Off with you, young men: a gentle age suits me: The bladder-ball befits boys at play, and old men.

XLVIII From these jaws the keepers have not rescued bulls, Through which the fleeing prey, the hare, goes and returns; And, what is more wondrous, it comes out swifter than its foe, And carries off something from so great a nobility. It is not safer when it runs on the empty sand, Nor is it shut up in its cage with such good faith. If you seek to escape the bites of hounds, you reckless hare, You have the mouth of a lion to flee to for refuge.

XLVIII A tavern-keeper and a butcher and a bath, A barber and a board and gaming-pieces And a few books—but for me to choose them: One comrade not too unpolished, And a tall slave-boy long kept smooth, And a girl dear to my boy: Grant me these, Rufus, even at Butunti, And keep the Baths of Nero for yourself.
XLVIII Olus built a poor man's cell, but sold his Estates: now Olus has a poor man's cell.

XLVIII You love to be buggered; once buggered, Papylus, you weep. Why, Papylus, grieve at the deed you wish done? Do you repent the obscene itch? Or do you weep more at this, Papylus—that you have stopped being buggered?

XLVIII What does love not compel? Encolpos cut his hair against his master's wish—though not forbidden— Pudens allowed it and wept: so the father gave up the reins, complaining of bold Phaethon: so Hylas was carried off, so Achilles, discovered, laid down his hair gladly, his mother grieving. But you, don't hurry—don't trust to short hair— and come slowly, beard, in return for so great a gift.
XLVIII That the toga-clad crowd shouts so loud a "Bravo!" for you, it's not you, Pomponius—your dinner is eloquent.

XLVIII Though he has nearly three hundred tables, Annius has servants instead of tables: the dishes run past, the platters fly. Keep these feasts to yourselves, you elegant folk: I am put off by a dinner that walks about.

XLVIII Crispinus does not know to whom he gave his Tyrian mantle, while he changes his dress and puts on the toga. Whoever has it, give the cloak back to its shoulders, we beg: it is not Crispinus who asks you this, but the mantle. Not just anyone is fit for garments steeped in purple, nor does that colour suit any but the elegant. If loot delights you and the madness of foul gain, take the toga — with it you can cheat better.

XLVIII When you swore I was heir to a fourth part of your estate, Garricus, by your sacred rites and your own head, I believed it — for who readily condemns his own hopes? — and kept fostering the hope with gifts I gave. Among them I sent a Laurentine boar of rare weight: you'd think it from Aetolian Calydon. But you at once invited the people and the senate, and pale Rome still belches up my boar: I myself — who would believe it? — was a guest, and not the lowest, yet no rib was given me, no tail sent my way. What can I hope for from your quarter-share, Garricus? Not one ounce of my own boar came to me.

XLVIII The crowd of the Pharian heifer announces the eighth hour, and the spear-armed cohort returns and now takes its turn. This hour tempers the baths, the earlier breathes out excessive vapours, and the sixth glows with immoderate Nero's heat. Stella, Nepos, Canius, Cerialis, Flaccus—are you coming? The couch holds seven; we are six; add Lupus. The bailiff's wife has brought me mallows to relieve the belly, and the varied riches the garden holds, among which is squat lettuce and trimmed leek, nor is belching mint lacking, nor the lustful herb; sliced eggs will crown rue-flavoured mackerel, and there'll be a sow's udder dripping from the tunny-brine. These for the relish; one little dinner will be set on a single table: a kid snatched from the jaws of a savage wolf, and tidbits that need no carver's knife, and workmen's beans and tender young greens; a chicken too, and a ham already surviving three dinners, will be added. To the well-fed I'll give ripe apples, wine without dregs from a Nomentan flagon, which was three years old in Frontinus' second consulship. Add jokes without gall, and a freedom not to be feared the next morning, and nothing you'd wish you'd left unsaid: let my guest talk of the Green and the Blue, nor will our cups make anyone a defendant.
XLVIII Silius haunts these monuments of great Maro, he who owns the acres of eloquent Cicero. As heir and master of his tomb and home neither Maro nor Cicero would prefer another.

XLVIII If you set out mushrooms and boar as though they were cheap things and you think these aren't what I pray for, I'm willing: but if you believe I'm made fortunate by them and want me written down as heir for five Lucrine oysters, farewell. The dinner's elegant, I admit, most elegant, but tomorrow it'll be nothing—nay, today, nay, at once—nothing, which the wretched sponge of a condemned mop may know, or any dog and the broken pot beside the road: this is the end of mullets and hares and sow's udder, the sulphurous colour and the executioner feet. Not the Alban revel would be worth so much to me, nor the Capitoline banquets and those of the pontiffs; let a god himself charge me with nectar, it'll turn to vinegar and the treacherous flat wine of a Vatican cask. Seek other guests, master of banquets, whom the proud realms of your table may take: let my own friend invite me to hasty cutlets: this dinner, which I can return, pleases me.
XLVIII. Mushrooms It's easy to send silver and gold, a cloak and a toga: Mushrooms — those are hard to send.
XLVIII. Hand-Balls The swift athlete snatches these up in Antaeus' dust, Who makes his great neck big with futile toil.

XLIX Man not to be left unspoken among the Celtiberian peoples, And glory of our Spain, You shall see lofty Bilbilis, Licinianus, Renowned for horses and for arms, And old Caius white with snows, and Vadavero Holy with its broken crags, And the sweet grove of delicate Boterdus, Which fruitful Pomona loves. You shall swim the gentle ford of warm Congedus And the soft lakes of the Nymphs, And brace your slackened body in the brief Salo, that hardens iron. There Voberca itself shall offer to the man at lunch Wild beasts to be shot close by. You shall break the clear heat in the golden Tagus, Shaded by the shadows of trees; The chilly Derceita shall quench your greedy thirst, And Nutha, that surpasses snows. But when grey December and winter's unbridled storm Bellow with the hoarse north wind, You shall seek again the sunny shores of Tarraco And your own Laletania. There you shall slaughter does entangled in soft nets, And boars bred at home, And burst the cunning hare with a strong horse, And leave the stags to your bailiff. The neighbouring wood shall come right down to your hearth, Ringed with grimy children. The huntsman shall be called, and the guest shall come to you At a shout from close at hand. Nowhere a crescent-marked boot, nowhere the toga, Nor garments rank with purple dye; Far off the bristling Liburnian and the querulous client, Far off the imperious commands of widows; No pale defendant shall break your deep sleep, But you shall sleep the whole morning through. Let another earn a great and frantic "Bravo!": Pity you the fortunate, And enjoy true joy without pride, While your Sura is being praised. Not shamelessly does my life ask what is left to it, When my fame has what is enough.
XLIX I do not want to marry Telesina: why? She is an adulteress. But Telesina gives to boys. I do.
XLIX You mix Veientan for me, while you drink Massic: I would rather smell these cups than drink them.

XLIX He does not know, believe me, what epigrams are, Flaccus, who calls them only sport and jokes. He plays more who writes the breakfast of savage Tereus, or your dinner, indigestible Thyestes, or Daedalus fitting liquid wings to his boy, or Polyphemus pasturing Sicilian sheep. All windy bombast is far from my little books, nor does my Muse swell in a madman's tragic robe. "Yet everyone praises, admires, adores those works." I admit it: they praise those—but they read these.

XLIX When just now I happened to see you sitting alone, Labienus, I thought you three. The number of your bald head deceived me: you have hairs on this side, you have them on that, such as might even suit a boy; the head's bare in the middle, and not one hair is marked on the long expanse. This mistake profited you in December, then, when the Emperor sent out the dinners: you came back with three little bread-baskets. Such, I believe, was Geryon. You should avoid, I advise, Philip's colonnade: if Hercules sees you, you're done for.

XLIX I'm not carved from brittle elm, nor is this column, that stands stiff and erect, made of any chance wood, but begotten from living cypress: which fears neither the ages run a hundred times nor the rot of long old age. You, whoever you are, O wicked man, fear this. For if with greedy hand you harm even the smallest grapes of this vine, there will grow—though you may wish to deny it— a fig grafted on you from the cypress.
XLIX I send you small gifts from my suburban garden: eggs for your throat, Severus, apples for your appetite.

XLIX As great as the table of the Giants' triumph is recounted, and as great a night as that was for all the gods above, when the good father reclined with the common folk of the gods and the Fauns were allowed to ask Jupiter for wine: so great are the banquets that celebrate your laurels, Caesar; our joys gladden the very gods. Every knight feasts with you, and the people and the fathers, and Rome takes ambrosial fare with her leader. Having promised great things, how much greater you have given! A dole was promised us; a full dinner was served.

XLIX This is that toga, much sung in my little books, which my reader has learned by heart and loves. It was once Parthenius', a memorable gift to the bard: in it I went, a knight to be admired, while it shone, splendid, with new and glossy wool, and while it was worthy of the name of its giver: now an old thing, scarcely fit for a shivering pauper, which you could rightly call snow-white. What does long time, what do the years not consume? This toga is no longer Parthenius'; it is mine.

XLIX Though you drink your amethyst-coloured measures and are soaked in dark Opimian, you toast me with a Sabine just now broached and say to me, Cotta, "Will you have it in gold?" Does anyone want leaden wine in a golden cup?

XLIX There's no hour, Phyllis, in which you don't despoil me, mad with love: with such cunning you plunder me. Now the sly maid weeps for a mirror left behind, or a gem falls from your finger or a stone from your ear; now smuggled silks can be made profit of, now a dry onyx-jar of Cosmus is produced for me; now a worm-eaten jar of dark Falernian is sought, to expiate your dreams with a babbling crone; now, that I may buy a great pike or a two-pound mullet, a rich girlfriend has announced a dinner to you. Have some shame and at last some regard for truth and fairness: I deny you nothing, Phyllis; deny me nothing, Phyllis.

XLIX Linus, tutor of the long-haired throng, whom rich Postumilla calls the master of her affairs and to whom she entrusts her gems, her gold, her wines, her concubines: so may your patroness, proved by your unending loyalty, prefer you to all others: come, I pray, to the aid of my wretched madness and guard now and then carelessly those who badly scorch my heart, whom both by night and by day I long, in my desire, to see in my embrace, the lovely, snow-white, matched, twin, big ones—not boys, but pearls.
XLIX. Fig-Peckers Since the fig feeds me, since I graze on sweet grapes, Why didn't the grape, rather, give me my name?
XLIX. Dumb-Bells Why do strong arms waste themselves on the foolish dumb-bell? Digging a vineyard exercises men better.
L If your cook, Aemilianus, is called Mistyllus, Why should not mine be called Taratalla?
L That you suck cocks and drink water, Lesbia—you do no wrong. You take water, Lesbia, where you have need of it.

L This, and no other, is your reason for inviting me to dinner, That you may recite, Ligurinus, your little verses. I have taken off my sandals; at once a huge book is brought Among the lettuces and the fish-sauce: A second is read through, while the first courses are delayed: There is a third, and the second course has not yet come: And you recite a fourth and a fifth book at last. It is rank, if you serve me a boar so many times over. But if you do not give your wicked poems to the mackerel, You will dine alone now, Ligurinus, at home.
L Why, Thais, do you keep calling me old? No one, Thais, is too old to be sucked off.

L Whenever I dine at home, unless I've invited you, Charopinus, at once there are huge hostilities, and you could run me through the middle with drawn sword, if you learn my hearth grew warm without you. So I'm not allowed even once to steal a meal? Nothing is more shameless than this gullet of yours, Charopinus. Stop now, I beg, watching my kitchen, and let my cook for once put one over on you.

L When poor Telesinus cultivated honest friends, he wandered shabby in his chilly little toga: since he began to court obscene perverts, he alone buys silver, tables, estates. Do you want to grow rich, Bithynicus? Be an accomplice: pure kisses will give you nothing, not even the least.

L Fountain of the mistress, queen of the place that Ianthis delights in, glory and darling of a famous house, since your bank is adorned with so many snow-white attendants and your water gleams with a Ganymede-like band: what is the Alcides doing, hallowed in that grove? Why does the god keep a cave so near to you? Does he, perhaps, watch over the known loves of the Nymphs, lest so many Hylases be carried off at once?

L What labour is in this dish? Learned Mys' work, or Myron's? Is this the hand of Mentor, or, Polyclitus, yours? It is not dulled by any dark tarnish, nor does the cloudy mass hate the fires that test it; true amber gleams less than this yellow metal, and the lucky boss outshines snowy ivory. The work does not yield to its material: so it rings the disc round, as the full moon shines with all its lamp. A goat stands, decked with the Aeolian fleece of Theban Phrixus: his sister might have wished to be carried by this one; not even the Cinyphian shearer would harm him, and you, Lyaeus, would yourself wish him fed on your vine. On the beast's back rides a golden Cupid with twin wings, and the Pallas-lotus sounds from his tender mouth: so the dolphin, delighting in Methymnaean Arion, bore the languid burden, not silent, through the seas. Let your hand, Cestus, steep this fine gift for me with worthy nectar — not one of the master's herd, but your own; Cestus, glory of the table, mix Setine wine: the boy himself, the goat himself, seem to us to thirst. Let the letter of Instantius Rufus give the number of cyathi: for he is the author to me of so great a gift: if Telethusa comes and brings the promised joys, I'll be kept for my mistress, Rufus, by your four measures; if she's doubtful, I'll be dragged on through seven; if she fails her lover, to cut my cares' throat I'll drink both names.

L You prove to me, Gaurus, that my talent is so small, because I make poems that please by their brevity. I confess it. But you, who write in twice six books the grand battles of Priam — are you a great man? We make a living Brutus' boy, we make a living Langon: you, Gaurus, make a great Giant of clay.

L Let mournful Victory break her Idumaean palms, beat, Favour, your bare breast with a savage hand; let Honour change his garb, and you, sad Glory, fling your garlanded hair to the cruel flames as an offering. Alas, the crime! cheated of your first youth, Scorpus, you fall and so soon yoke the black horses. That goal, always too swiftly hastened and brief for your chariots—why was it so near to your life too?

L There was but one poor man left to tend the now nearly deserted ashes and holy name of Maro. Silius resolved to come to the aid of the longed-for shade, and Silius, himself no lesser bard, honours the bard.

L You have laurel-groves and plane-groves and airy pine-groves and baths for more than one, all to yourself, and a high portico stands for you on a hundred columns, and the onyx gleams, trodden under your foot, and the fleeing hoof claps the dusty hippodrome, and the splash of falling water sounds everywhere; long halls stand open. But there's nowhere a place for diners or for sleep. How well you don't live!
L. Truffles We truffles, who burst the nursing earth with our tender crown, Are the fruit second only to mushrooms.
L. An Oil-Cap Lest the foul wrestler's grease soil your shining hair, With this cap you can tuck away your oiled locks.

LI No neck but the first will do for the fierce lions. Why do you flee these teeth, you ambitious hare? No doubt you wish them to descend from mighty bulls To you, and to break necks they cannot see. You must despair of the glory of a mighty fate: You cannot die thus, a slender prey, beneath such a foe.

LI Though there is often but a single denarius in your whole chest, And that, Hyllus, more worn than your own arse, Still the baker will not take it from you, nor the tavern-keeper, But anyone proud of an excessive prick. Your unhappy belly watches the feastings of your backside, And the one is forever starving, wretch, while the other gorges.

LI When I praise your face, when I admire your legs and hands, You are wont to say, Galla, "Naked, I shall please more," And you always avoid the baths we share. Surely, Galla, you are not afraid I shall not please you?

LI When you didn't have six thousand, Caecilianus, you rode about widely in a huge six-bearer litter: after blind fortune gave you two million and the coins burst your purse, look—you've become a footman. What should I wish you for your merits and such great praises? May the gods give you back your sedan, Caecilianus.

LI This man, who carries a left hand weighed down with books, whom a light chorus of clerks crowds round, who, with notebooks brought out from this side and that and with letters, lends a grave countenance, like Cato and Tullius and Brutus, though the racks should force him, Rufus, cannot manage a Latin "Greetings," nor a Greek "Chaire." If you think I'm making this up, let's greet him.
LI That you dine without me so often, Lupercus, I've found out how to do you harm. I'm angry: you may keep calling and sending and asking— "What will you do?" you say. What will I do? I'll come.

LI If it irks you, Urbicus, to buy my trifles, yet you would like to know my wanton songs, seek out Pompeius Auctus — perhaps you know him; he sits at the front of the temple of Mars the Avenger: steeped in law and polished by the varied wear of the toga, he is not my reader, Urbicus, but my book. So he holds my absent verses by heart and recites them, that not a letter perishes from my pages: in short, if he wished, he could seem to have written them; but he prefers to favour my fame. You may pester him from the tenth hour — for he will not be free enough before — a little supper will hold the two of you; he will read, you drink; though you don't wish it, he will sound off; and when you have said 'That's enough now,' he will read.
LI A truly beautiful woman — but Asper loves her blind. So Asper, as the case stands, loves more than he sees.

LI What you always begged of the gods against your brother's wish, this, Lucanus, has fallen to you — to die first. He envies you; for Tullus wished, though he is younger, to go first to the Stygian shades. You dwell in Elysium, and now, an inhabitant of the lovely grove, you long to be without your brother for the first time; and if he comes by turns from the bright stars, in Pollux's place you warn Castor not to return.

LI Now Tyrian Taurus looks back on the stars of Phrixus' ram, and winter flees the alternating Castor; the field laughs, the ground is clothed, the tree is clothed, the Attic mistress weeps for Ismarian Itys. What days, Faustinus, what a Ravenna has Rome stolen from you! O suns, O tunic-clad repose! O grove, O springs, and the firm shore of the moist sand, and Anxur splendid with its sea-waters, and the couch that watches more than one stretch of water, which sees from here the river's boats, from there the sea's! But there is no Theatre of Marcellus or Pompey, nor there the triple baths, nor the fora joined four times, nor the topmost shrine of Capitoline Thunderer, nor the temples that shine next to their own heaven. How often, weary, I think you say to Quirinus: "What's yours, keep for yourself: what's mine, give back to me."

LI So great is the column that hangs on Titius, as the girls of Lampsacus worship. He, with none to attend and none to trouble him, bathes in great baths—his own. Yet Titius bathes in cramped quarters.
LI That our Fabullinus is so often deceived, do you wonder, Aulus? A good man is always a novice.
LI. A Dozen Thrushes A garland woven of roses, perhaps, for you, or rich nard, But for me a garland made of thrushes is what pleases.
LI. Strigils Pergamon sent these. Scrape yourself with the curved iron: The fuller won't wear out your towels so often.

LII I commend to you, Quintianus, my own books— If I may still call them my own, The books your poet recites: If they complain of harsh slavery, Come as their liberator and give security enough, And, when that man calls himself their owner, Say they are mine, manumitted by my hand. If you cry this out three and four times, You will put shame upon the plagiarist.
LII Dasius knows how to count those about to bathe: he charged Big-breasted Spatale for three: she paid.

LII You had bought a house, Tongilianus, for two hundred thousand: A mishap too frequent in the city carried it off. Ten times that was collected. I ask: can you not seem yourself To have set fire, Tongilianus, to your own house?
LII If you don't stop riding behind your team of goats, Hedylus, you who were just now a fig will soon be a wild fig.

LII What you've done for me I remember and will always keep in mind. Why then am I silent, Postumus? Because you talk. Whenever I begin to recount your gifts to someone, at once he cries, "He told me himself." Some things two don't do nicely: one is enough for this task: if you want me to speak, be silent yourself. Believe me, Postumus, gifts, however huge, are spoiled by the chattering of their giver.

LII In this tomb lies, carried off in his boyhood years, Pantagathus, his master's care and grief, skilled with barely-touching blade to trim the straying hair and dress the shaggy cheeks. Though you be, as you should, kind and light, earth, you cannot be lighter than the craftsman's hand.

LII It is gratifying, Auctus, that you read my little books to Celer, if, that is, what you read, Auctus, pleases Celer too. He governed my own people and the Celtic Iberians, and there was no surer good faith in all our world. A greater reverence the more disturbs me, and I think my ears are those not of a hearer, but of a judge.

LII A boy barber, but of such skill as not even Nero's Thalamus had, to whom the beards of the Drusi fell, I lent to Rufus, Caedicianus, when asked for once, to even out his cheeks. While, as bidden, he goes over the same hairs, his judgement guided by the mirror in his hand, and paints the skin and makes a long second going-over of the close-cut hairs, my barber came back to me with a beard.
