LII If you believe me, Quintus, what you deserve, I love your birthday, Ovidius, the Kalends of April, as I love my own Kalends of March. Happy each light and day for us, to be marked with the better pebbles! This gave me life, but that gave me a friend. Your Kalends, Quintus, give me more.
LII Numa had seen the eunuch Thelys in a toga, and said he was a convicted adulteress.

LII You'll dine well, Julius Cerialis, at my house; if you've no better engagement, come. You can keep the eighth hour; we'll bathe together: you know how close Stephanus' baths are to me. First you'll be given lettuce, useful for moving the belly, and shoots cut from their leeks, then a salted tunny, larger than a slender mackerel, but one that eggs and rue-leaves will cover; nor will more be lacking, turned over warm ash, and a cheese curdled at the Velabran hearth, and olives that have felt the Picene frost. This is enough for the relish. You want to know the rest? I'll lie, so you'll come: fish, shellfish, sow's udder, and the fat birds of the poultry-yard and the marsh, which even Stella's not used to serve except at a rare dinner. And I promise more: I'll recite nothing to you, though you may read me your Giants over and over, or your rural verse next to immortal Virgil's.

LII Wont to wreathe his brows with the Pierian garland, no less a voice celebrated by trembling defendants, here he lies, here that Rufus of yours, Sempronia, whose very ash burns with love of you. You're told as a sweet tale in the Elysian field, and Tyndareus' daughter herself is amazed at your abduction: you're the better, who came back when your ravisher was deserted, while she refused to follow her husband even when sought back. Menelaus laughs and hears of the Trojan loves: your abduction absolves Phrygian Paris. When one day the glad places of the pious receive you, no shade in the Stygian home will be better known: Proserpina does not see the abducted as strangers, but loves them: that love will win you the favour of the mistress.
LII. Ducks Let the whole duck be served; but only in the breast And neck has it flavor: give the rest back to the cook.
LII. A Horn Oil-Flask A bullock lately wore me on his brow: Yet you took me for true rhinoceros-horn.

LIII There is one page in our little books that is yours, Fidentinus— But marked with the sure stamp of its true owner, Which exposes your poems for the manifest theft they are. So, set among them, a Lingonian hooded cloak, with its greasy nap, Pollutes the city's violet-purple stuffs; So Arretine pots violate vessels of crystal; So, when by chance the black raven strays on the banks of Cayster, It is laughed at among the swans of Leda; So, where the sacred grove resounds with the many-voiced nightingale, The wicked magpie offends the Cecropian laments. Our books need no informer, no judge: Your page stands against you and says to you, "You are a thief."

LIII Do you wish to become free? You lie, Maximus, you do not wish it: But if you do wish to become so, this is the way you can. You will be free, Maximus, if you refuse to dine out, If the Veientan grape masters your thirst, If you can laugh at the gold dishes of wretched Cinna, If you can be content with a toga like mine, If plebeian Venus is bought for you with a couple of asses, If you cannot enter your own house without stooping. If you have this strength, if such power of mind is yours, You can live more free than the Parthian king.
LIII I could do without your face, And your neck and hands and legs, And your breasts and buttocks and hips, And, not to labour through them one by one, I could do without you whole, Chloe.

LIII This man whom you often see within the inner shrine of our Pallas and the threshold of the new temple, Cosmus, an old man with staff and wallet, whose hair stands grey and rotting, and a filthy beard falls on his chest, whom a coarse cloak covers, wife of his bare pallet, to whom the crowd he meets gives food he's barked for— you think him a Cynic, deceived by the false image: he's no Cynic, Cosmus. What then? A Dog.

LIII Why write of Medea, why, friend, write of Thyestes? What use to you, Bassus, are Niobe or Andromache? The fittest subject for your pages, believe me, is Deucalion, or, if he doesn't please, Phaethon.
LIII He bathed with us, dined merrily, and the same man was found dead in the morning—Andragoras. You ask the cause of so sudden a death, Faustinus? In his sleep he'd seen the doctor Hermocrates.

LIII You sent me everything at the Saturnalia, Umber — all the gifts the five days had brought you: twelve three-leaved tablets and seven toothpicks; with these came a sponge, a napkin, a cup, a half-peck of beans with a basket of Picentine olives, and a black flask of Laletanian must; small Syrian figs came with wrinkled prunes and a jar heavy with the weight of Libyan figs. I reckon the whole gift was scarcely worth thirty sesterces — and eight strapping Syrians brought it. How much more conveniently, with no labour at all, a single boy could have carried me five pounds of silver!

LIII As loud a roar as is heard through the Massylian wilds, whenever the wood rages with countless lions, when the pale shepherd calls back to the Punic huts his frightened bulls and his witless flock: so great a terror lately growled in the Ausonian sand. Who would not have thought it a herd? It was one, but one whose laws even the lions themselves would tremble at, to whom the marble-painted Nomad would give a diadem. Oh, what glory round his neck, what honour the golden shadow of his crescent mane scattered, when he stood! How the great hunting-spears became his broad breast, and what joys he took from a noble death! Whence, Libya, came so happy a glory to your forests? Had he come, perhaps, from the yoke of Cybele? Or rather, Germanicus, did your brother or father himself send this beast to you from the Herculean star?

LIII On your birthday, Quintus, I wished to give you small gifts; you forbid it: you're an imperious man. I must obey your warnings; let it be done as we both wish and as pleases us both: you, Quintus, give to me.

LIII I am that Scorpus, glory of the clamorous Circus, your applause, Rome, and your brief delight, whom envious Lachesis snatched in his ninth third-year, and, counting my palms, believed to be an old man.

LIII Though Claudia Rufina was born of the blue-painted Britons, what hearts of the Latin race she has! What beauty of form! The Italian mothers might believe her Roman, the Athenian their own. The gods do well that fruitful she bore to a holy husband, that, still a girl, she hopes for sons-in-law and daughters-in-law. So may it please the gods above that she delight in one spouse and always delight in her three children.

LIII Though you have so much money and wealth, Paternus, as a rare citizen has, you give away nothing and brood over your hoard, like the great serpent the poets sing was the guardian of the Scythian grove. But the cause, as you yourself recall and boast, is that you're the son of dire rapacity. Do you really seek out fools and simpletons, to mock and to rob of their wits? To this vice you have always been a father.
LIII. Turtle-Doves When I have a fat turtle-dove, goodbye, lettuce: And keep your snails to yourself. I've no wish to spoil my appetite.
LIII. A Rhinoceros Lately admired in our lord's Ausonian arena, Here for you is the one for whom the bull was a ball.

LIV If, Fuscus, you have still any room to be loved— For you have friends on this side, friends on that— We ask one place, if one is left, And do not refuse me because I am new to you: All those old friends of yours were once new. Only look at the one newly offered for the part, And see whether the new friend can grow old in it.

LIV What your wife suspects about you, Linus, And in what part she wants you more chaste, She has proved well enough by sure tokens, She who has given you a eunuch for a guard. There is nothing keener than she, nor more malicious.
LIV Since I cannot give what you demand, Galla, when you ask, You could much more simply, Galla, say no.

LIV O you who have been allowed to touch the Tarpeian oaks and crown your deserving locks with the first wreath, if you are wise, Collinus, make use of all your days and always think the last is at hand for you. No one has won by prayer from the three wool-spinning girls a respite: they keep the day they have fixed. Be richer than Crispus, steadier than Thrasea himself, more elegant than splendid Melior though you may— Lachesis adds nothing to the wool, unwinds the sisters' spindles, and one of the three always says no.
LIV My rhetor has become an improviser: he didn't write down "Calpurnius," and he greeted him.

LIV If you forbade Sextilianus, Aulus, to say "so many men" and "so many women," he'd scarcely string three words together, poor man. "What does he mean by it?" you ask. I'll tell you what I suspect: Sextilianus loves so many men and so many women.
LIV Of women most beautiful, who have been or are, but most worthless, who have been or are, oh, how I would wish you to become, Catulla, either less beautiful or more chaste!

LIV If a thrush were ripening for me on a Picene olive, or a Sabine wood were stretching my nets, or light prey were drawn in by the growing reed and the limed twig held the entangled birds: my dear kinship would give you its customary gift, nor would a brother or grandfather come before you. Now the field hears poor starlings and the chaffinches' complaints and grows green in spring with the chattering sparrow; hence the ploughman, greeted, answers the magpie, hence the rapacious kite flies near the topmost stars. So I send you the little gifts of a small farmyard: if you accept such things, you'll often be a kinsman.
LIV You set out good dishes, Olus, but you set them covered. It's ridiculous: I can have good ones that way too.

LIV The ointments and the cassia and the myrrh that smells of funerals and the incense half-burned from the midst of a pyre and the cinnamon you snatched from the Stygian bier, shameless Zoilus, give back from your vile pocket. Your wanton hands learned from your feet to sin. I don't wonder you're a thief, who were a runaway.
LIV Red of hair, black of face, short of foot, weak of eye, you do a great thing, Zoilus, if you're good.
LIV. A Ham Let mine be Cerretane, or it may be one sent From the Menapii: let the elegant gorge on gammon.
LIV. A Baby's Rattle If some wailing little home-born slave hangs at your neck, Let this chattering rattle shake in his tender hand.

LV If you wish to know briefly the prayer of your Marcus, Fronto, bright ornament of camp and toga, This is what he seeks: to be the ploughman of his own, not a great, estate, And he loves homely leisure among small things. Does any man, fool that he is, court the painted cold of Spartan marble, And carry the morning greeting "Good day," When he could—blessed with the spoils of wood and field— Spread out his full nets before the hearth, And draw up the leaping fish on the quivering line, And bring out yellow honey from the red jar? When his plump farm-wife loads his uneven table, And ash, bought from no one, makes ready his own eggs? Let no one love this life who does not love me—that is my wish— And let him live, pale, among the duties of the town.
LV You want to be courted, Sextus: I wanted to love. I must obey you: as you command, you shall be courted: But if I court you, Sextus, I shall not love.

LV Because wherever you come, we think Cosmus is moving house And cinnamon pours, spilled from a shaken bottle, I would not have you please yourself, Gellia, with foreign trifles. You know, I suppose, my dog could smell as sweet that way.

LV Lucius, glory of your times, who do not let old Caius and our Tagus yield to eloquent Arpi: let the man born among Argive cities sing in song of Thebes or Mycenae, or famous Rhodes, or the Ledaean wrestling-grounds of lustful Sparta: let us, sprung from Celts and Iberians, not be ashamed in grateful verse to name the harsher names of our land: Bilbilis, supreme in its fierce metal, which beats the Chalybes and Norici, and Platea ringing with its own iron, which, with a slender but restless current, Salo, temperer of arms, surrounds, and the guardianship and dances of Rixamae, and the festive banquets of Carduae, and Peteris red with woven roses, and the ancient theatres of our fathers, Rigae, and the Silai, sure with the light javelin, and the lakes of Turgontum and Turasia, and the pure shallows of little Tvetonissa, and the holy oak-grove of Burado, through which even the lazy traveller strolls, and the fields of curving Vativesca that Manlius works with sturdy young oxen. At these so rustic names, dainty reader, do you laugh? Laugh you may— these so rustic I prefer to Butunti.

LV Tell me, whom do you carry, queen of the birds? "The Thunderer." Why does he hold no thunderbolts in his hand? "He's in love." With what fire does the god burn? "A boy's." Why do you look back gently at Jove, with open beak? "I'm speaking of Ganymede."

LV That you always reek black with cassia and cinnamon and the nest of the proud bird, fragrant with Niceros's leaden boxes, you laugh at us, Coracinus, who smell of nothing: I'd rather smell of nothing than smell good.

LV If you send back gifts to no one, Chrestus, then don't give to us or send any back: I will believe you generous enough. But if you make returns to Apicius and Lupus, to Gallus and Titius and Caesius, you shall lick — not mine, for it is honest and small — but the one that comes from burnt Jerusalem, the cock lately condemned to tribute.

LV Since the age of our grandfathers yields to our times, and Rome has grown greater with her leader, you wonder that the genius of sacred Maro is wanting, and that no one sounds wars with so great a trumpet. Let there be Maecenases, Flaccus, and Marones will not be lacking; even your own farm will give you a Virgil. Tityrus had lost the acres next to wretched Cremona, and grieved, sick at heart, for his sheep driven away: the Tuscan knight laughed, and pushed back grudging poverty and bade it depart in swift flight. 'Take riches,' he said, 'and be the greatest of bards; you may even love our Alexis.' That loveliest boy stood by his master's table, pouring dark Falernian with a marble hand, and gave the sipped cups from rosy lips, cups that could have tempted Jupiter himself. The astonished poet forgot plump Galatea and Thestylis, her red cheeks burnt at harvest; at once he conceived Italy and 'arms and the man,' he who lately had barely wept the Gnat with rude lips. Why speak of the Varii and Marsi and the enriched names of bards whom it would be great labour to count? So I'll be a Virgil, if you give me Maecenas' gifts? A Virgil I'll not be: I'll be a Marsus.

LV On the day of kinsmen, when birds are sent in plenty, while I prepare thrushes for Stella, and for you, Flaccus, a huge and burdensome crowd comes to mind, in which each man counts himself first and mine. To oblige two is my wish; to offend more is hardly safe; to send gifts to many is grievous. By the only means I can, I'll win pardon: I'll give thrushes neither to Stella nor to you, Flaccus.

LV Whenever Marulla has weighed in her fingers an erect member and long taken its measure, she names the pounds, the scruples, the half-ounces; the same one, after the work and its exercises, when it lies slack like a loosened thong, Marulla says by how much it's lighter. So that's no hand of hers, but a balance-scale.

LV That Lupus urges you, Urbicus, to become a father, don't believe it; there's nothing he'd want less. It's the art of legacy-hunting to seem to want what you don't; he prays you won't do what he asks you to do. Let your Cosconia only say she's pregnant: Lupus will turn paler than a woman in labour. But, so you may seem to have used a friend's advice, die in such a way that he thinks you've become a father.

LV Whoever bids you give yourselves for free, girls, is the most tasteless and most shameless of men. Don't give for free, but kiss for free. This Aegle refuses, this, greedy, she sells. But let her sell: to kiss well, how great a thing it is! Yet she sells this too, and at no light plunder: either she demands a pound of Cosmian perfume, or eight new pieces from the fresh mint, so the kisses won't be mute, won't be stingy, won't deny entry with closed lips. Yet she does one thing kindly, just one: she who refuses to give a kiss for free doesn't refuse to lick for free, Aegle.
LV. A Gammon It's fresh: hurry, don't keep your dear friends waiting, For with an old gammon I want nothing to do.
LV. A Whip You'll get nowhere with this whip, lash as you will, If a horse of the purple team runs for you.
LVI The vintage, harassed by unceasing rains, is sodden: You cannot, much as you wish, sell unwatered wine, tavern-keeper.

LVI Among the peoples of Libya, your wife, Gallus, is ill spoken of On the foul charge of immoderate greed. But these are sheer lies: she is not at all in the habit Of taking. What is she in the habit of, then? Of giving.
LVI I would rather have a cistern than a vineyard at Ravenna, Where I could sell water for so much more.

LVI Because you send huge gifts to old men and widows, do you want me to call you generous, Gargilianus? Nothing is fouler, nothing more vile than you alone, who can call your snares gifts: so the deceitful hook indulges greedy fish, so the cunning bait deceives the foolish beasts. What it is to be lavish, what it is to give, I'll teach you, if you don't know: give, Gargilianus, to me.

LVI To what schoolmaster you should hand your son, Lupus, you ask, anxious, and inquire a long time. Avoid, I advise, all the grammarians and rhetors: let him have nothing to do with the books of Cicero or Maro, let him leave Tutilius to his own fame; if he makes verses, disown the poet. Does he want to learn the money-making arts? See that he learns lyre-playing or flute-playing; if the boy seems of dull wit, make him an auctioneer or an architect.

LVI That your legs are stiff with bristles and your chest with shaggy hair, do you think, Charidemus, you fool report? Pluck out, believe me, the hairs from your whole body and testify that you depilate your buttocks. "What's the reason?" you say. You know many say many things: make them think, Charidemus, that you get buggered.

LVI You have grasped the stars and the sky with pious mind, Rabirius, who with wondrous art build the Parrhasian palace. If Pisa prepares to give temples worthy of Phidian Jove, she will seek these hands of yours from our Thunderer.

LVI Though you bestow great gifts so often, about to give greater, conqueror of leaders, conqueror even of yourself, you are loved by the people not for your rewards, Caesar; for you the people love your rewards, Caesar.

LVI Spendophorus, the master's armour-bearer, seeks the Libyan cities: prepare, Cupid, the darts you would give the boy, those with which you pierce young men and soft girls: but let the spear too be smooth in his tender hand. Breastplate, shield, and helmet I give back to you; that he may safely enter battles, let him go naked: neither javelin, sword, nor arrow harmed Parthenopaeus while he was free of the helmet. Whoever is pierced by this boy will die of love. O happy, if such a good fate awaits anyone! While you are a boy, come back; while your face is smooth, and let not Libya make you a man, but your own Rome.

LVI You bid me, Gallus, serve you all day long and run three, four times through your Aventine. Cascellius pulls out or repairs the aching tooth, you, Hyginus, burn off the lashes hostile to the eyes; Fannius cuts not, but removes the dripping uvula, Eros erases the grim brands of stone; Hermes is called the Podalirius of ruptures: who heals the broken, tell me, Gallus, who is it?

LVI That you praise death too much, Chaeremon the Stoic, do you want me to admire and look up to your spirit? This virtue a jug with a broken handle makes for you, and the gloomy hearth that warms with no fire, and the mat and the bedbug and the frame of a bare cot, and a short toga, the same by night and by day. O how great a man you are, who can do without the dregs of red vinegar and straw and black bread! Come now, let your mattress swell with Leuconian wool and combed purple gird your couches, and let the boy sleep with you who, mixing the Caecuban just now, tormented your guests with his rosy mouth: O how you'll long to live three times Nestor's years and want to lose nothing of any day! In tight straits it's easy to despise life: he acts bravely who can be wretched.

LVI You fall ill ten times a year or oftener, and this harms not you but us, Polycharmus: for every time you get up, you ask your friends for recovery-gifts. Have some shame: now, Polycharmus, fall ill just once.
LVI. A Sow's Womb You, perhaps, are more taken with a maiden hog's: The mother-sow's womb, from a pregnant pig, takes me.
LVI. Tooth-Powder What have I to do with you? Let a girl take me: I'm not used to polishing bought-in teeth.

LVII You ask, Flaccus, what sort of girl I would have, or not? I want one neither too easy nor too hard. What lies between, and between the two, is what I approve: I want neither what torments nor what cloys.

LVII This man you see strolling with idle steps, Who in amethyst-purple cuts through the middle of the Saepta, Whom my Publius does not surpass in cloaks, Nor Cordus himself, the alpha of cloak-wearers, Whom a toga-clad and long-haired troop follows, And a fresh sedan with its linen and its straps: Just now, just now he pawned at Cladus's counter For scarcely eight coins a ring, to get himself a dinner.
LVII A cunning tavern-keeper cheated me lately at Ravenna: When I asked for it mixed, he sold me wine neat.

LVII While the alluring pools of wanton Lucrinus hold me and the caves that steam with their pumice springs, you dwell in the realm of the Argive settler, Faustinus, where the twentieth milestone leads you from the city. But the bristling breast of the Nemean monster burns, and it is not enough that Baiae glow with their own fire. So, sacred springs and pleasant shores, farewell, home alike of Nymphs and of Nereids. In icy winter outdo the Herculean hills, but now yield to the cool of Tibur.
LVII When I call you "lord," Cinna, don't be pleased with yourself: I often return your slave's greeting that way too.
LVII You feign fake hair with ointment, Phoebus, and your dirty bald head is covered with painted locks. There's no need to bring a barber to your head: a sponge, Phoebus, can shave you better.
LVII Gabinia made an Achilles out of Castor — out of a Pollux: he had been a good boxer; now he will be a horse-tamer.

LVII He had three teeth, all of which he spat out together while Picens himself sat at his own tomb; and he gathered in his lap the last fragments of his loose mouth, and buried them in heaped-up earth. Though some day his heir need not gather the dead man's bones, Picens has already done himself this office.

LVII Nothing is more worn than Hedylus' cloaks: not the handles of old Corinthian bronzes, nor the leg made slippery by a ten-year fetter, nor the chafed neck of a broken-down mule, nor the ruts that cut the Flaminian Way, nor the pebbles that shine on the shore, nor the hoe polished by a Tuscan vineyard, nor the pale toga of a dead clansman, nor the cracked wheel of a lazy muleteer, nor the side of a bison shaved by its cage, nor the now-aged tusk of a fierce boar. There is one thing, though — he himself won't deny it: Hedylus' arsehole is more worn than his cloaks.
LVII You used to send a pound of silver; it's become a half-pound, but of pepper. I don't buy pepper that dear, Sextus.

LVII You wonder that I send poems to learned Severus, when I'm inviting you, learned Severus, to dinner? Jupiter is full of ambrosia and lives on nectar; yet we give Jove raw entrails and unmixed wine. Since everything is granted you by the gift of the gods, if you don't want what you have, then what will you accept?

LVII Why I often make for the little fields of dry Nomentum and the squalid home of my villa, you ask? There's no place, Sparsus, for a poor man to think or to rest in the city. The schoolmasters deny him life in the morning, the bakers at night, the coppersmiths' hammers all day long; here the idle money-changer rattles his dirty table with a heap of Nero's coin, there the beater of Spanish gold-dust beats the worn stone with his gleaming club; nor does the god-frenzied throng of Bellona cease, nor the babbling shipwrecked man with his bandaged stump, nor the Jew taught by his mother to beg, nor the bleary-eyed hawker of sulphur-wares. Who can count up the losses of lazy sleep? He'll tell how many bronze pans the hands of the city beat, when the cut Moon is flogged by the Colchian wheel. You, Sparsus, know nothing of this, nor can you know, luxurious in your Petilian realms, where your level house looks down on the mountain-tops, and there's countryside in the city, and a Roman vine-dresser, and no greater vintage on the Falernian hill, and within your boundary a wide drive for the chariot, and sleep in the depths, and quiet broken by no tongues, and no daylight unless let in. Us the laughter of the passing crowd wakes, and Rome is at our bedside. When, worn out with weariness, it pleases us to sleep, we go to the villa.
LVII. Egyptian Beans You'll laugh at the Nile's vegetable and its clinging strings, When you drag the troublesome threads with bite and hand.
LVII. Behen-Nut Oil What neither Virgil nor Homer names in song, This is made of perfume and of the behen-nut.

LVIII A slave-dealer asked me a hundred thousand for a boy: I laughed, but Phoebus paid it on the spot. This grieves my cock, and it complains of me in private, And Phoebus is praised to my disgrace. But my cock has just made Phoebus a present of Two million: give me that, and I will buy at a higher price.
LVIII Sleekly combed, you laugh at my threadbare clothes, Zoilus. They are threadbare indeed, Zoilus, but they are mine.

LVIII Our Faustinus's villa at Baiae, Bassus, Is not laid out in idle myrtle-groves And barren plane and clipped box, holding the wide field's ungrateful spaces, But rejoices in a real and rough countryside. Here Ceres is crammed and pressed into every corner, And many a jar is fragrant with the wine of old autumns; Here, after November, with winter already at hand, The rough pruner brings back the late grapes. Fierce bulls bellow in the deep valley, And the calf, with hornless brow, itches for a fight. The whole flock of the dirty farmyard roams about, The shrill goose and the jewelled peacocks And the bird that owes its name to its reddening feathers, The painted partridge and the spotted Numidian hens And the pheasant of the impious Colchians; Proud cocks tread the Rhodian hens; The cotes resound with the clapping of doves, Here moans the wood-pigeon, there the waxen turtle-dove. The greedy pigs follow the bailiff's wife's lap, And the soft lamb awaits its full-uddered mother. The milk-white home-born slaves ring the bright hearth, And the festive household gods are lit by a great heap of wood. No idle tavern-keeper grows pale with white leisure, Nor does the slippery wrestling-master waste his oil, But he sets a sly net for the greedy thrushes Or draws up the caught fish on a quivering line Or brings back a doe entangled in the toils; The kindly garden gives the cheerful townsmen exercise, And, with no schoolmaster bidding them, the long-haired Wanton boys gladly obey the bailiff, And the dainty eunuch enjoys the work. Nor does the rustic caller come empty-handed: One brings pale honey with its own combs And a cone of cheese from the Sassinate wood; One offers up drowsy dormice, This one a bleating kid from its bristly mother, Another capons forced to be chaste. And the strapping daughters of honest tenants Offer their mothers' gifts in woven wicker. When the work is done, the glad neighbour is invited; Nor does a greedy table keep back tomorrow's feast, All eat, and the well-fed servant does not know How to envy the drunken guest. But you, near the city, possess an elegant famine, And from a high tower you survey nothing but laurels, Secure, with Priapus fearing no thief; And you feed your vine-dresser on town-bought grain And, at your leisure, carry to your painted villa Greens, eggs, fowl, fruit, cheese, new wine. Ought this to be called a country place, or a town house far off?
LVIII In the dark you mourn your lost husband, Galla. By now, I think, you're ashamed to weep for a husband, Galla.

LVIII Tomorrow you'll live, tomorrow, you keep saying, Postumus. Tell me, that "tomorrow," Postumus—when does it come? How far off is that "tomorrow," where is it? Or where is it to be sought? Surely it doesn't hide among the Parthians and Armenians? That "tomorrow" already has the years of Priam or Nestor. That "tomorrow"—tell me—for how much could it be bought? You'll live tomorrow? Today it's already too late to live, Postumus: he is wise, whoever, Postumus, lived yesterday.

LVIII While it delights you, Aulus, to behold the Arcadian Bear close at hand and bear the stars of the Getic sky, O how nearly was I, snatched to the Stygian waters, made to see the dark clouds of the Elysian realm! Though weary, my eyes were seeking your face, and "Pudens" was forever on my cold lips. If the wool-spinning sisters draw me threads not black and that voice has no deaf gods, safe yourself, with me safe, you'll be carried back to the Latin cities and return, a famous knight, with the rewards of your service.

LVIII You have married six or seven catamites by now, Galla, while their combed hair and dressed beards please you too much. Then, having tried their flanks and loins like a soaked thong, and parts that no tired hand could force to stand, you desert the unwarlike marriage-beds and the soft husband; and again and again you fall back into beds of the same kind. Look for some man forever talking of Curii and Fabii, shaggy and grim with harsh rusticity: you'll find one — but that grim crowd has its catamites too. It is hard, Galla, to marry a real man.
LVIII Since your cloaks are so thick, Artemidorus, I could rightly call you Sagaris.

LVIII Nymph, queen of the sacred lake, to whom welcome Sabinus gave temples that will endure, a pious gift, so may mountain Umbria forever tend your springs, nor may your Sassina prefer the waters of Baiae: receive kindly my anxious gifts, these little books; be the Pegasean spring to my Muses. — 'Whoever gives his own songs to the temples of the Nymphs, shows himself what ought to be done with such books.'

LVIII While I tended the calm retreats of sea-girt Anxur, Frontinus, and Baiae nearer still and the shore-house, and the grove that the inhuman cicadas, when the Crab seethes, never knew, and the river-fed lakes, I had leisure to honour with you the learned Pierians: now the greatest Rome wears me down. When is a day my own here? I'm tossed on the deep of the City, and life perishes in barren toil, while I feed the harsh acres of a suburban farm and the household gods near you, holy Quirinus. But not only he loves who, night and day, frequents your thresholds, nor do such losses befit a poet. By the venerable rites of the Muses, by all the gods I swear: even unattentive, I love you.

LVIII When you see I want it and feel me hard, Telesphorus, you ask for great things—suppose I want to refuse: am I allowed?— and unless I've said "I'll give" on oath, you withdraw those buttocks, which grant me so much in return. What if my barber, when the drawn razor is over me, should then beg liberty and riches? I'd promise; for at that moment it's not a barber asking, it's a robber: fear is a commanding thing: but once the razor is safe in its curved case, I'll break the barber's legs and his hands together. But to you I'll do nothing, except that my cock, washed with wool, will tell your greedy avarice to go suck itself.
LVIII Your wife calls you a chaser of maids, and she herself is a chaser of litter-bearers: you're a matched pair, Alauda.
LVIII. Goose-Liver Look how the liver swells, bigger than the big goose itself! Amazed, you'll say: "Where, I ask, did this grow?"
LVIII. Saltpetre-Foam Are you a rustic? You don't know my Greek name: I'm called "foam of nitre." Are you Greek? Then aphronitrum.

LIX The dole at Baiae gives me a hundred farthings. What does such starvation do amid such luxuries? Give me back the dark baths of Lupus and Gryllus: When I dine so badly, why, Flaccus, should I bathe so well?

LIX I am called Mica: you see what I am, a little dining-room: From me, look, you behold the Caesarean dome. Break the couches, call for wine, take roses, anoint yourself with nard: The god himself bids you remember death.
LIX The cobbler Cerdo gave you a show, well-dressed Bologna, The fuller gave one at Modena: now where will the tavern-keeper give one?

LIX While a viper crept among the weeping Heliads' boughs, an amber drop flowed onto the beast in its path: and while it marvels to be held in the rich dew, it stiffened, suddenly bound by the congealed ice. Don't be proud of your royal tomb, Cleopatra, if a viper lies in a nobler sepulchre.

LIX That I send you no silver, that I send you no gold, this I do, eloquent Stella, for your own sake. Whoever has given great things wished great things sent back to him; by my earthenware you'll be relieved of that.

LIX Baccara both grieves and complains that the cold doesn't reach him, because of his six hundred shaggy cloaks, he longs for dark days and winds and snows, and hates the winter days, if they've turned warm. What harm have my cloaks done you, cruel man, which a light breeze can lift from one's shoulders? How much simpler, how much more humane it would be to put on your shaggy cloaks even in the month of August!
LIX Our friend Caecilianus, Titus, never dines without a boar. A fine dinner-guest Caecilianus keeps!

LIX Do you see this man content with one eye, beneath whose worn brow a bleary socket gapes? Don't despise the fellow: nothing is more thievish than he; not even Autolycus' hand was so peppered. Take care to keep a wary eye on this dinner-guest: then he rages, and one-eyed sees with both eyes; the anxious servants lose their cups and spoons, and many a napkin hides in his warm bosom; nor does he fail to filch a cloak slipped from an elbow, and often goes off covered with two mantles; nor was the cheat ashamed to cheat a drowsing slave of the lamp, though it be burning. If he has seized nothing, then with crafty art he goes round a boy and steals his own slippers.

LIX Mamurra, having wandered long and much in the Saepta, here where golden Rome torments its own wealth, inspected the soft boys and devoured them with his eyes, not those whom the front stalls prostitute, but those whom the boards of the secret platform keep and whom neither the public nor my sort sees. Then, sated, he stripped the covers from tables and round tops and asked for the rich ivory displayed up high, and, measuring four times the tortoiseshell six-couch table, groaned that it was not big enough for his citrus-wood top. He consulted his nose, whether the bronzes smelled of Corinth, he found fault even with your statues, Polyclitus, and, complaining that some crystal was spoiled by bits of glass, he marked ten murrine cups and set them aside. He weighed old goblets, and any cups ennobled by Mentor's hand, and counted green gems in painted gold, and whatever, larger, rings from a snow-white ear. Sardonyxes, indeed, he sought at every table and set a price on great jaspers. When at last, wearied, he was leaving at the eleventh hour, he bought two cups for a penny and carried them himself.

LIX If a page is used up on a single subject, you skip it, and the shorter, not the better, pleases you. A rich dinner is set out, furnished from every market for you, but only the tidbit delights you. I've no need of too dainty a reader; I want one who isn't satisfied without bread.
LIX Charinus wears six rings on each finger, and never takes off his rings at night, nor when he bathes. You ask what the reason is? He has no ring-case.

LIX Rome gives you so many kisses, returned just now after fifteen years, as Lesbia did not give Catullus. The whole neighbourhood presses you, the hairy farmer with his goatish kiss; here the weaver besets you, there the fuller, here the cobbler who's just kissed his leather, here the master of a dangerous chin, here the lame man on his right side, there the bleary-eyed, and the cocksucker and the fresh cunt-licker. Now it wasn't worth so much for you to return.
LIX. Dormice The whole winter through I sleep, and I am fatter At that season when nothing but sleep feeds me.
LIX. Balsam-Oils Balsams enchant me; these are the perfumes of men: Reek of Cosmus' luxuries, you young wives.

LX Though you enter the wide mouth of the grim lion, hare, The lion still thinks its tooth is idle. On what back will it rush, on what shoulders fall? Where will it fix the deep wounds it deals to bullocks? Why do you weary in vain the lord and king of the woods? He feeds on nothing but the beast he has chosen.

LX You bed the wife, boy Hyllus, of an armed tribune, While you fear only a boy's punishment. Woe to you—while you play, you will be gelded. Now you will tell me, "That is not allowed." What? Is what you do, Hyllus, allowed?

LX Since I am invited to dinner, no longer for sale as before, Why is not the same dinner given me as is given you? You take oysters fattened in the Lucrine pool, I suck a mussel through a slit shell: You have mushrooms, I take pig-fungus: You deal with turbot, but I with a bream: A golden turtle-dove fills you with its huge rump, A magpie dead in its cage is set before me. Why do I dine without you, Ponticus, when I dine with you? Let it profit me that the dole is gone: let us eat the same.

LX Let men make for Ardea and the Castran fields at midsummer and the land that burns under the Cleonaean star, since Curiatius condemned the airs of Tibur, sent to the Styx among its praised waters. You can shut out fate in no place: when death has come, in the midst of Tibur there is Sardinia.

LX Though you bark at us on and on and provoke us with your shameless yelping, I'm resolved to deny you outright this fame, which you've long sought, that in my little books, such as they are, you should be read throughout the world. For why should anyone know you existed? You must perish unknown, poor wretch. Yet perhaps there'll be no lack, in this city, of one or two or three or four willing to gnaw the dog's hide: but I keep my nails from this scab.
LX My Rome praises, loves, recites my little books, and every pocket holds me, every hand holds me. Look—a certain man reddens, pales, gapes, yawns, hates. This I want: now my songs please me.

LX Reverend ruler of the Tarpeian court, whom, while our chief is safe, we believe the Thunderer, since each man wearies you with prayers for himself and begs you to grant what you gods are able: do not be angry, Jupiter, as at a proud man, that I ask nothing for myself. For Caesar I must pray to you; for myself I must pray to Caesar.
LX You could equal the summit of the Palatine colossus, Claudia, if you became a foot and a half shorter.

LX Whether you were born in Paestan or in Tiburtine fields, or whether the soil of Tusculum blushed with your bloom, or whether the bailiff's wife gathered you in a Praenestine garden, or whether you were lately the glory of Campanian country: that you may seem a fairer garland to my Sabinus, let him think you come from my Nomentan farm.
LX Munna asked Caesar for the privilege of three pupils, though he's always been used to teaching two.

LX You ask whether Phlogis or Chione is more fit for Venus? Chione is the prettier; but Phlogis has an itch, an itch that could stiffen Priam's leather and not let old Pelias be old, an itch that everyone wants his own girl to have, which Crito can cure, not Hygia: but Chione feels no work, nor with any cries does she help, you'd think her absent or made of marble. If, gods, one might win so great a boon from you and you'd be willing to give gifts so precious, you'd make Phlogis have the body that Chione has, and Chione the itch that Phlogis has.

LX Day, child of Mars, on which we first saw the rosy lamp and the great face of the starry god, if you'll be ashamed to be honoured in the country and at green altars, you who used to be honoured by me in the Latian city: forgive me that I don't want to be a slave on my own Kalends, and that I want to live on the day I was born. To grow pale on one's own birthday, lest the hot water fail for Sabellus; and that Alauda may drink clear unmixed wine, to strain the muddy Caecuban through an anxious bag; and to go to and fro among one's own tables; to receive these and those, and rise the whole dinner long, treading marble colder than ice: what sense is it to endure and suffer of one's own accord what you'd refuse if a king and master bade you do it?
LX. Rabbits The rabbit delights to dwell in burrowed caves. He it was who showed the foe the hidden paths.
LX. Bean-Meal Wash A welcome gift it will be, and not useless to a chafed belly, If you seek Stephanus' baths by broad daylight.

LXI Verona loves the verses of her learned bard, Mantua is blessed in Maro, The land of Aponus is reckoned rich in its Livy And its Stella, no less than in Flaccus, The rainy Nile applauds Apollodorus, The Paeligni resound with Naso, And eloquent Corduba speaks of its two Senecas And of its one and only Lucan, Merry Gades delights in its Canius, Emerita in my Decianus: In you, Licinianus, our Bilbilis shall glory, And it will not be silent about me.

LXI When your cheeks bloomed with their first doubtful down, Your shameless tongue licked men's middles. Now that your foul head has earned the loathing of undertakers And the disgust of the wretched hangman, You use your mouth otherwise, and, seized by excessive spite, You bark at every name there is. Better that so harmful a tongue should cling to the groin: For when it sucked cocks, it was cleaner.
LXI You say whatever you ask is nothing, you shameless Cinna: If you ask nothing, Cinna, I refuse you nothing, Cinna.

LXI That a friend gave you two hundred thousand, Mancinus, you lately boasted with proud lips, delighted. Four days ago, in the poets' school, while we chatted, you said cloaks bought for ten thousand were a gift from Pompulla, and a true sardonyx ringed three times with veins, and two gems like the waves of the sea, you swore Bassa and Caelia had given. Yesterday at the theatre, while Pollio sang, when you suddenly left, in flight you babbled that three hundred thousand had come to you in legacy, and a hundred in the morning, and a hundred after noon. What such great wrong have we, your friends, done you? Have pity now, cruel man, and be silent at last. Or, if that tongue of yours cannot keep still, tell us, some time, what we'd like to hear.

LXI Who is that curly-haired fellow, Marianus, always clinging to your wife? Who is that curly-haired fellow? Who whispers I-don't-know-what into your lady's tender ear and presses her chair with his right elbow? On all of whose fingers a slim ring runs, whose legs bear not a hair to mar them? You give me no answer? "He manages my wife's affairs," you say. To be sure, he's a steadfast, hard man, who shows the agent in his very face: Aufidius of Chios won't be sharper than this. O how you deserved, Marianus, the slaps of Latinus: you'll be the successor, I believe, to Panniculus. He manages your wife's affairs? That curly fellow, any affairs? Not your wife's affairs—your affairs he manages.

LXI Pompullus has done a great thing, Faustinus: he'll be read and scatter his name throughout the whole world. "So may the light race of the fair-haired Usipi fare well, and whoever does not love the Ausonian empire." Yet Pompullus's writings are said to be ingenious. "But for fame that's not enough, believe me: how many eloquent men feed bookworms and moths, and only cooks buy up learned poems! There's something more, something that grants the ages to pages: a book that will live must have a genius."

LXI The reckless huckster had stolen the whole city, and no man's threshold was his own at his own door. You ordered the narrow alleys to grow, Germanicus, and what had lately been a footpath became a road. No pillar now is girt with chained flasks, nor is the praetor forced to walk through the mud, nor is a razor blindly drawn in the thick crowd, nor does the black cookshop seize whole streets. Barber, taverner, cook, butcher keep to their own thresholds. Now it is Rome; lately it was one big shop.

LXI Charinus is livid, he bursts, he rages, he weeps, and seeks high branches to hang himself from: not now because I am sung and read throughout the world, nor because, smart with bosses and cedar-oil, I am scattered through all the nations Rome holds: but because I have a summer place in the country near the city, and ride on mules not, as before, hired. What shall I call down, O Severus, on the livid man? This I pray: may he have mules and a suburban farm.

LXI In the Tartessian lands there is a most famous house, where rich Corduba loves the placid Baetis, where the tawny fleeces grow pale with native metal and living gold-leaf coats the Hesperian flock. In the midst of the house, embracing the whole household, stands a Caesarian plane-tree with thick foliage, which the happy right hand of the unconquered guest set, and from that hand the shoot began to grow. The grove seems to feel its planter and master: so it is green and seeks the high stars with its branches. Often beneath this tree the drunken Fauns have played, and a late pipe has frightened the silent house; and while nocturnal Pan fled through the lonely fields, often beneath this leafage a rustic Dryad hid. And the household gods smelled of Lyaeus the reveller, and the shade grew gladder for the spilled wine; the grass was reddened, strewn with yesterday's garlands, and no one could call the roses his own. O tree beloved of the gods, O tree of great Caesar, fear not the iron and the sacrilegious hearths. You may hope for the perpetual honours of your leaves: no Pompeian hands planted you.

LXI Here rests Erotion, a too-hasty shade, whom her sixth winter slew by the crime of fate. Whoever you'll be, after me the ruler of my little field, to her slight shade pay each year its due: so may your hearth endure, your household be unharmed, and this stone be the only thing to mourn on your land.

LXI A husband with his tongue, an adulterer with his mouth, Nanneius, filthier than the cheeks of the Summemmian whores; whom, when obscene Leda saw naked from her Suburan window, she shuts up her brothel and prefers to kiss his middle rather than his top; he who lately went through all the tubes of the guts and with a sure and knowing voice would tell whether boy or girl was in the mother's womb: —rejoice, cunts; for your business is done— he can't get his fucking tongue up. For while, sunk in a swelling womb, he clings and hears inside the wailing infants, an unseemly disease unstrings his gluttonous part. He can be neither pure now nor impure.

LXI That I'd make verses and a brief, lively poem against you, you fear, Ligurra, and you long to seem worthy of this fear. But you fear in vain and long in vain. Libyan lions rush upon bulls, they're no trouble to butterflies. I'd advise you to seek, if you toil to be read, some drunken poet of a dark archway, who writes with rough charcoal and crumbling chalk poems that men read while shitting. This brow of yours is not to be branded with my mark.
LXI. Heath-Cocks Among the flavors of birds, the taste of the Ionian Heath-cock is said to be the first.
LXI. A Horn Lantern I, the road's guide, am carried golden, my flame shut in, And the small lamp is safe in my bosom.

LXII Laevina, chaste, and yielding to none of the ancient Sabine women, And, though her husband is gloomy, gloomier still herself, While she gives herself now to the Lucrine, now to Avernus, And while she is often warmed by the waters of Baiae, Fell into the flames: pursuing a young man, she left Her husband and came as Penelope—and departed Helen.

LXII That you pluck your chest, your legs, your arms, That your shaved prick is girt with short hairs: This you do, Labienus—who does not know it?—for your mistress. For whom do you do it, Labienus, that you depilate your arse?

LXII Because you buy boys for a hundred thousand, often two hundred, Because you drink wines laid up under King Numa, Because not very spacious furniture costs you a million, Because a pound of wrought silver carries off five thousand, Because a golden carriage is got for the price of a farm, Because your mule cost more than the house you bought: Do you believe, Quintus, you provide all this with a great soul? You are wrong: a petty soul, Quintus, buys these things.
LXII Black Lycoris has moved to Hercules' Tibur, believing all things turn white there.

LXII By your own right you may stay in my gardens, guest, if you can lay your limbs on the bare ground, or if a great supply of furnishings is carried with you: for mine has already given up the ghost for guests. No mattress—not even an empty one—covers the broken couches, the rotten webbing lies with its cord snapped. Yet let the lodging be shared between us two: I bought the gardens; that's the greater part: you furnish them; that's the less.
LXII Salanus has lost his only son, a father: do you delay to send gifts, Oppianus? Alas, cruel crime and the wicked Fates! Whose vulture will this corpse be?

LXII Behind open doors you bugger grown men, Amillus, and you want to be caught while you do it, so that no freedman or your father's slaves may tattle, nor a dark client with sidelong gossip. The man who calls others to witness he is not sodomized, Amillus, often does the thing he does without a witness.
LXII Picens writes epigrams on the back of the paper, and grieves that he does it with the god turned away.
LXII That Philaenis wears garments dyed with purple both night and day, she is not ostentatious nor haughty: she delights in the smell, not the colour.

LXII Schoolmaster, spare the simple throng: so may the long-haired boys flock to hear you and the chorus love your dainty desk, nor any reckoner or swift clerk be ringed by a larger circle. The white days glow with the flaming Lion and seething July cooks the parched harvest. Let the Scythian hide, fringed with rough thongs, with which Marsyas of Celaenae was flogged, and the grim canes, the sceptres of pedagogues, rest and sleep until the Ides of October: in summer, if boys keep well, they learn enough.
LXII Lesbia swears she's never been fucked for free. It's true. When she wants to be fucked, she pays.

LXII Great king of the ancient pole and of the former world, under whom there was sluggish rest and no toil at all, no lightning too regal nor men worthy of the lightning, no earth split open to the Shades, but rich for itself: glad and gracious, come to these solemn joys of Priscus: it befits you to be present at your own rites. You, best father, give back to his homeland, in the sixth winter, peace-making Numa, returned from the Latian city. Do you see how, like an Ausonian market, the procession hangs for you, and how great an honour runs riot? How no stinting hand and the coins of a lavish table, what wealth, Saturn, is counted out for you? And that there may be a reward for these deserts and greater thanks, both a father and a frugal man thus honours your rites. But you, holy one—so may you ever be loved in your December— bid these days often return for him.
LXII. Fattened Hens The easy hen is fed on sweet meal, And fed in the dark. The gullet is ingenious.
LXII. A Bladder-Lantern If I'm not horn, am I any dingier? Or does the man Who comes against me take me for a bladder?
LXIII You ask me to recite my epigrams to you. I will not. You do not want to listen, Celer, but to recite.

LXIII You had a hundred thousand sesterces, your sole fortune, Milichus, Which you spent to buy Leda on the Sacred Way. Milichus, it is extravagance, if you, a rich man, loved at such a price. "I do not love," you will now say: this too is extravagance.

LXIII Cotilus, you are a fine fellow: many say this, Cotilus. I hear it: but what is a fine fellow? Tell me. "A fine fellow is one who arranges his curled locks in order, Who always smells of balsam, always of cinnamon; Who hums the songs of the Nile, the songs of Gades, Who waves his smooth-plucked arms to various measures; Who lounges all day long among the women's chairs And always whispers something in someone's ear, Who reads notes sent from here and there and writes them; Who shrinks from the cloak of his neighbour's elbow; Who knows who loves whom, who flits through the dinner-parties, Who knows well the old pedigrees of Hirpinus the horse." What are you saying? Is this, is this a fine fellow, Cotilus? A fine fellow, Cotilus, is a very fiddling thing.

LXIII While mother Caerellia made for Baiae from Bauli, she perished, sunk by the crime of the mad strait. What glory you have lost! These monstrous deeds, waters, you never showed Nero once, even when bidden.

LXIII "What do you think," you say, "Marcus, of my little books?" So you often ask me, Ponticus, anxious. I admire, I'm astonished: nothing is more perfect than they, Regulus himself will yield to your genius. "You think so?" you say. "So may Caesar be good to you, so may Capitoline Jupiter." No—to you.

LXIII You know you're being courted, you know this courtier is greedy, and you know, Marianus, what the one who courts you wants. Yet you, fool, write him heir in your last will and want him, madman, to take your place. "Still, he sent great gifts." But he sent them on a hook; and can a fish love the fisherman? Will this man weep for your fate with real grief? If you want him to weep, Marianus, leave him nothing.

LXIII You who read the never-dying volumes of eternal Silius, poems worthy of the Latin toga, do you suppose only the Pierian retreats pleased the bard, and the Bacchic garlands on his Aonian hair? He did not touch the rites of buskined Maro before he had filled the work of great Cicero: him the grave spear of the Hundred Men still admires, him many a client speaks of with grateful mouth. After he had ruled the mighty year with its twelve fasces — the year that was hallowed when the world was set free — he handed over his earned years to the Muses and to Phoebus, and now keeps Helicon as his forum.
LXIII Aulus loves Thestylus, but burns no less for Alexis, and perhaps now loves my Hyacinthus too. Go now and doubt whether he loves the bards themselves, when my Aulus loves the bards' darlings.
LXIII All the catamites invite you to dinner, Phoebus. The man whom a cock feeds is not, I think, a clean man.

LXIII Marble small indeed, but not to yield, traveller, to the stones of Mausolus and the pyramids, you read. Twice was my life seen at the Roman Tarentine games, and it lost nothing before the final pyres: Juno gave me five boys, as many girls, and the hands of all closed my eyes. A rare glory of the marriage-bed fell to me too: one member alone was known to my chastity.
LXIII You watch us, Philomusus, when we bathe, and keep asking why my smooth boys are so well-hung. I'll answer you plainly, since you ask: they bugger the curious, Philomusus.

LXIII Corduba, richer than oil-rich Venafrum, no less perfect than the Istrian jar, you who surpass the sheep of white Galaesus, false by no purple dye nor blood, but with your flocks tinted in living colour: tell your poet, I beg, to have some shame, and not recite my little books for free. I'd bear it, if a good poet did it, to whom I could give pains in return. A celibate corrupts without retaliation, a blind man can't lose what he carries off: nothing is worse than a naked robber: nothing is safer than a bad poet.
LXIII. Capons Lest the cock grow lean from a too-drained loins, He has lost his stones. Now he shall be a cock for me.
LXIII. Pipes The drunken flute-girl splits us with her dripping cheeks: Often she has two at once, often a single pipe.
LXIV You are beautiful—we know it—and a girl, that is true, And rich, for who can deny it? But when you praise yourself too much, Fabulla, You are neither rich nor beautiful nor a girl.

LXIV While you fashion yourself now an advocate, now a rhetorician, And cannot decide, Laurus, what you want to be, The age of Peleus and Priam and Nestor has passed by, And it would now be late for you even to stop. Begin: three rhetoricians died in a single year, If you have any spirit, if you have any worth in the art. If the school is condemned, all the forums seethe with lawsuits, Even Marsyas himself could become an advocate. Come, away with you, break off delay: how long shall we go on hoping for you? While you doubt what you are, you can already be nothing.

LXIV The Sirens, the merry bane of sailors, The coaxing deaths and the cruel joy, Whom once no man left, once he had heard them, Wily Ulysses is said to have left behind. I do not wonder: this, Cassianus, I would wonder at, If he had left Canius in mid-story.

LXIV Julius Martialis's few acres, more blessed than the gardens of the Hesperides, recline on the long ridge of the Janiculum: broad retreats jut out over the hills, and the level top, with its modest swell, enjoys a clearer sky, and when mist covers the curving valleys it alone shines with its own peculiar light; the dainty rooftops of the lofty villa are gently raised toward the clear stars. From here you may see the seven sovereign hills and take the measure of all Rome, the Alban and Tusculan hills too and every cool spot that lies near the city, old Fidenae and little Rubrae, and Anna Perenna's fruitful grove that delights in virgin blood. On that side, on the Flaminian and Salarian roads, the traveller is in view, his carriage silent, lest the wheel be a nuisance to sweet sleep, which neither the sailors' chant nor the shout of bargemen can break, though the Mulvian bridge is so near and keels glide swift down the sacred Tiber. This country place, or rather house to be called, its master commends: you'll think it your own, so unenvious and so generous, so kindly open in its hospitality: you'd believe it the pious home of Alcinous or of Molorchus just made rich. You who now think all things small, tame icy Tibur with a hundred hoes or Praeneste, and hand over hanging Setia to a single tenant— so long as, in my judgement, to all these are preferred Julius Martialis's few acres.

LXIV Pour me two measures of Falernian, Callistus, and you, Alcimus, melt summer snows over them, let my dripping hair grow rich with abundant balsam and my temples be wearied with sewn rose-garlands. The Mausoleum so near bids us live, since it teaches that the gods themselves can perish.

LXIV Though you're not born of the rigid Fabian stock, nor such as a ruddy wife bore to Curius beneath the shaggy oak while she brought lunch to her ploughing husband, but the son of a father shaved at the mirror and a toga-wearing mother, and your bride could call you her bride: yet you presume to correct my little books, which fame knows, and to carp at the trifles of a happy man— these trifles, I say, to which the leaders of city and forum do not scorn to turn their whole ear, which the bookcases of eternal Silius deem worthy and which Regulus so often repeats with eloquent voice, and which Sura, neighbour of Aventine Diana, who watches the great Circus's contests more closely, praises, which Caesar himself, the lord, under so great a weight of affairs, does not disdain to unroll two and three times. But you have more sense, your heart with sharpening Minerva is keener, and refined Athens shaped your breast. May I perish if that isn't far wiser which, with slack paunch and great foot and red lung, old and fearsome with its nostrils, the cruel butcher carries about through all the crossroads. Besides, you dare to write against me little verses that no one would know, and waste your miserable papers. But if the heat of my bile should scorch you with anything, it will live and stick and be read throughout the world, nor will Cinnamus erase the brand-marks with his cunning art. But have pity on yourself, and don't, lost in rabid madness, provoke the smoking nostril of a living bear. Though he be gentle and lick your fingers and hands, if grief and bile, if just anger compel him, he'll be a bear: weary your teeth on an empty hide and seek some silent flesh that you can gnaw.

LXIV You who were the most famous barber in all the city, and afterward, by your mistress's gift, were made a knight, you sought out the Sicilian cities and Aetna's realms, Cinnamus, when you fled the grim laws of the forum. By what art will you now bear, useless, your burdensome years? What does an unhappy, fugitive leisure do? You cannot be a rhetor, a grammarian, or a schoolmaster, nor a Cynic, nor a Stoic, nor sell your voice and applause to Sicilian theatres: what is left, Cinnamus, is to be a barber again.

LXIV That you may beg a gift and exact it, Clytus, you are born eight times in one year, and you have only, I think, three or four Kalends that are not your birthday. Though your face be smoother than the worn pebbles of a dry shore, though your hair be blacker than the falling mulberry, though you outdo trembling feathers in softness, or a lump of curdled milk just now, and such a swelling rouse your nipples as an unripe girl keeps for a man, you seem to us, Clytus, already an old man: for who would believe that even Priam or Nestor had so many birthdays? Let there be at last some shame and limit to your robberies. But if you keep playing, and to be born once in one year is not now enough for you, I'll think, Clytus, you were not born even once.

LXIV Caesar, having deigned to come down into the features of great Hercules, gives new temples to the Latin way, where the traveller, as he seeks Trivia's wooded realms, reads the eighth milestone from the mistress city. Before, he was worshipped with vows and abundant blood; now the lesser Alcides himself worships the greater. This man asks him for great wealth, that one for honours; to him this one, untroubled, makes his lesser vows.

LXIV If you should touch my little books, queen Polla, receive my jests with no stern brow. That bard of yours, the glory of our Helicon, when he sang of fierce wars on the Pierian trumpet, did not yet blush to say in wanton verse: "If I'm not even buggered, Cotta, what am I doing here?"
LXIV I don't know what you write to so many girls, Faustus: this I know, that no girl writes to you.
LXIV A cook who outdid his servants in face and hair, Cinna made him. Cinna, you're a gluttonous man.
LXIV. The Same In vain the hen submits to her barren mate. This bird should have belonged to mother Cybele.
LXIV. A Reed-Pipe Why do you laugh at me, joined of wax and reed? Such was the first pipe ever built.
LXV When I say "ficus," you laugh as at a barbarous word, And bid me say "ficos," Laetilianus. We will say "ficus" for the figs we know grow on the tree, We will say "ficos," Caecilianus, for yours.

LXV Why do we see Saleianus sadder than usual? "Is it a slight cause?" you ask. "I have buried my wife." O grievous crime of fate! O heavy blow! Is she, is that rich Secundilla dead, Who gave you a million for her dowry? I would not have had this happen to you, Saleianus.

LXV The fragrance an apple breathes, bitten by a tender girl, The breeze that comes from Corycian saffron; The scent of the grey vine when it flowers with its first clusters, Of the grass that the sheep has just cropped; Of myrtle, of the Arab harvester, of rubbed amber, The smell of a pale fire of eastern incense; Of the clod when it is lightly sprinkled with a summer shower, Of the garland that has rested on hair dripping with nard: Of all these your kisses smell, cruel boy Diadumenus. What if you gave them whole, without grudging?
LXV Philaenis always weeps from one eye. You ask how that comes about? She's one-eyed.

LXV Stars and heaven were given—though his stepmother opposed— to Alcides by the terror of Nemea and the Arcadian boar and the chastised wrestling-grease of the Libyan ring and Eryx, laid low heavily in Sicilian dust, and the woods' terror, who by silent fraud was wont to lead off cattle, walking backward, into his cave—Cacus. Of your arena, Caesar, what small fraction is this seen? The new day brings greater battles in the morning. How many heavier weights fall than the Nemean monster! How many Maenalian boars your spear lays low! Were the Iberian shepherd's triple fight renewed, you have one who could conquer Geryon. Though the Greek Lerna's beast be counted often, what does the wicked Hydra do beside the Nile's beasts? For such great merits, Augustus, the gods gave heaven to Alcides quickly, but to you they'll give it late.

LXV "You make an epigram in hexameters"—I know Tucca says it. Tucca, it's customary; in short, Tucca, it's allowed. "But still, this is long." That too is customary, Tucca, and allowed: if you approve shorter ones, read only the couplets. Let us agree that it's fair for you to skip long epigrams, Tucca, and for me to write them.

LXV A lawsuit, while you count the frosts of twice ten winters, wears you down, Gargilianus — one suit in three courts. Ah, wretched and mad! Does anyone litigate for twenty years, Gargilianus, when he is free to lose?

LXV Here, where the temples of Fortune the Home-Bringer gleam wide and bright, was lately a happy open space: here stood Caesar, handsome with the dust of Northern war, pouring a purple radiance from his face; here Rome, her hair wreathed with laurel and bright in dress, greeted her leader with voice and hand. Other gifts attest the great merit of the place: a sacred arch stands and exults over conquered nations; here twin chariots count many an elephant, the golden figure himself suffices for the huge teams. This gate is worthy of your triumphs, Germanicus; such entrances befit the city of Mars to have.

LXV Alcides, now to be recognized by the Latian Thunderer, since you bear the fair face of the god Caesar, if you had then had these features and this bearing, when the wild monsters yielded to your hands: the nations would not have seen you serve as slave to the Argive tyrant and suffer his savage rule, but you would have given orders to Eurystheus; nor would treacherous Lichas have brought you the perfidious gifts of Nessus, without the law of the Oetaean pyre, untroubled, you would have approached the stars of your highest father, which your punishment gave you; nor would you have drawn out Lydian wool for a haughty mistress, nor seen the Styx and the Tartarean dog. Now Juno favours you, now your Hebe loves you; now, if a nymph saw you, she would send back Hylas.

LXV Though you boast yourself a citizen of the Corinthians, Charmenion, with no one denying it, why am I called your brother, I, born of Iberians and Celts, a citizen of the Tagus? Or do we seem alike in face? You wander sleek with curled hair, I unruly with Spanish locks; you smooth with daily depilatory, I with shaggy legs and cheeks; your speech lisps and your tongue is feeble, my little daughter would speak more forcefully: the dove is not so unlike the eagle, nor the timid gazelle the stiff-maned lion. So stop calling me brother, lest I, Charmenion, call you sister.

LXV Six hundred dine at your invitation, Justinus, for the duty of the day that was your first. Among them, I recall, I used not to be the last; nor was this place an enviable one for me. But the next day you repeat the rites of the festive table: to six hundred today, tomorrow you'll be born for me.

LXV When beautiful Phyllis had given herself to me all night, lavish in every way, and in the morning I was thinking what gift to give, whether a pound of Cosmus or of Niceros, or a sharp weight of Baetic wool, or ten yellow pieces from Caesar's mint: embracing my neck and coaxing me with a kiss as long as the marriages of doves, Phyllis began to ask for a jar of wine.
LXV. Partridges This bird, set out most rarely on Ausonian tables, You often watch at play in your fish-pond.
LXV. Woolen Slippers If by chance there's no slave-boy and you fancy Putting on slippers, the foot will be its own boy.

LXVI You are mistaken, you greedy thief of my books, Who think a poet can be made for the cost That a copying and a cheap roll come to: A "Bravo!" is not got for six or ten coins. Seek out unpublished poems and rough drafts, Which one man alone knows, and which the father of the virgin page Keeps sealed in his book-case, himself the guardian, Pages that have not yet bristled at a hard chin. A book once known cannot change its master. But if there is one with its brow not yet pumiced, Not yet adorned with bosses and parchment wrapper, Buy it: such I have; and no one will know. Whoever recites another's work and seeks fame Ought to buy not the book, but silence.

LXVI Of the whole world of her hair, one curl alone had gone wrong, Not well fixed with an unsteady pin. This crime Lalage avenged with the mirror in which she had seen it, And Plecusa fell, struck by the cruel curls. Cease now, Lalage, to dress those sorry locks, And let no girl touch that mad head. Let a salamander brand it, or the savage razor lay it bare, That your image may become worthy of the mirror.

LXVI Antony committed an equal crime with the swords of Egypt: Each sword cut off sacred faces. That one, Rome, was your head, when, joyful, You drove your laurelled triumphs; this one, when you spoke. Yet Antony's cause is worse than that of Pothinus: The latter did the deed for his master, the former for himself.

LXVI You have always lived a small-town life, Linus, than which nothing at all can be cheaper. On the Ides and on rare Kalends the little toga was shaken out, and one dinner-suit lasted ten summers. The forest sent you boar, the field hare, unbought, the beaten woods gave heavy thrushes, the caught fish came from the river's depth, the red jar poured wine not foreign. No tender page sent from Argive stock, but a rustic crowd stood by the rough hearth. The bailiff's wife, or the hard tenant's bride, was tumbled whenever the wounded vein grew hot with wine. Fire did no harm to your roofs, nor the Dog-star to your fields, no ship was sunk at sea, for you had none. The gambling-die was never slipped you for the coaxing knuckle-bone, but nuts alone were the play of your thrift. Tell me, where is the million your greedy mother left? Nowhere: you've done, Linus, a difficult thing.
LXVI Often greeted, you never greet first yourself: so you'll have, Pontilianus, your "Eternal farewell."

LXVI A girl of not too good a name, such as sit in the middle of the Subura, the crier Gellianus was lately auctioning. When the price stayed low a long time, wishing to prove her pure to all, he drew her toward him, resisting, with his hand and kissed her twice and thrice and four times. What did he gain by the kiss, you ask? The man who'd just bid six hundred withdrew it.
LXVI Fabius left Labienus heir to the whole estate: yet Labienus says he deserved more.

LXVI Pious incense and victims for Augustus, Camenae, give on behalf of your Silius. Lo, he bids twice six fasces return, his son made consul, and with noble rod he bids the Castalian house of the bard resound — Caesar, the first and only safety of the world. There remains still for the rejoicing man to wish for: the lucky purple and a third consul. Though the senate and Caesar may have given sacred honours to Pompey and his son-in-law, whose names peace-making Janus thrice enlarged: Silius prefers thus to count frequent consulships.

LXVI Since you have a wife, beautiful, chaste, a young girl, what need have you, Fabullus, of the rights of three children? What you beg as a suppliant from our lord and god, you will give to yourself, if you can get it up.

LXVI Who, I ask, was so hard, who so haughty, as to order you, Theopompus, made a cook? Does anyone bear to defile this face with the black kitchen, to pollute these locks with greasy fire? Who'll rather hold the wine-cups or the crystal? By what hand will Falernian be better mixed? If such an end awaits star-bright servants, let Jupiter now use Ganymede as a cook.
LXVI You're an informer and a slanderer, and a swindler and a dealer, and a cocksucker and a gladiator-trainer. I wonder why you don't have money, Vacerra.

LXVI You bought your house for a hundred thousand, which you want to sell for that sum or even less. But with sly art you corrupt the buyer, Amoenus, and the hovel lies hidden, ambitious with riches. Jewelled couches gleam with prime tortoise-shell, and rare slabs of Moorish citron-wood; silver and gold a more-than-simple Delphic table bears; boys stand there, whom I'd pray were my own masters. Then you sound out two hundred thousand, and say it's not for less. You sell a furnished house cheap, Amoenus.
LXVI. Doves Do not wrong the tender doves with perjured tooth, If the rites of the Cnidian goddess have been entrusted to you.
LXVI. A Breast-Band You could have bound your chest with a bull's hide: For that skin cannot hold those breasts of yours.
LXVII "You are too free a man," you always tell me, Cerylus. The man who says that against you, Cerylus—is he a free man?

LXVII Wherever you meet me, Postumus, you shout out At once, and your first word is this: "How are you doing?" This, even if you meet me ten times in one hour, You say: I think, Postumus, you have nothing to do.

LXVII You idle, boys, and you know nothing, Lazier than the Vaternus and the Rasina, Through whose sluggish shallows sailing You dip your slow oars to the time-call. Already, as Phaethon sinks, Aethon sweats And the day blazes, and the noonday hour Unyokes the wearied horses. But you, wandering over such peaceful waves, Idly play at leisure in your safe boat. I think you no sailors—but Argo-nauts.

LXVII Poor Gaurus begged the praetor for a hundred thousand sesterces, known to him by an old friendship, and said this alone was lacking to his three hundred thousand, that he might be able, as a proper knight, to applaud his lord. The praetor said, "You know I'll give to Scorpus and Thallus, and would that I gave a hundred thousand only." Ah, shame on the ungrateful, shame on the ill-gotten chest. What you won't give a knight, praetor, will you give a horse?

LXVII When the Attic birds were seeking their winter retreats in the usual way, one bird stayed behind in the nests. The others caught the crime when they returned in spring-time, and her own kind tore the deserter to pieces. Late she paid the penalty: the guilty mother should have been torn apart, but then, when she mangled Itys.
LXVII Why does your Caelia have only eunuchs, you ask, Pannychus? Caelia wants to be laid and not to bear.

LXVII Philaenis the tribade buggers boys, and, fiercer than a husband in her lust, ploughs eleven girls a day. Tucked up, she plays at handball too, grows yellow with sand, and whirls with easy arm the weights heavy for athletes; and, muddied from the crumbling wrestling-ground, she is whipped by the oiled trainer's lash. Nor does she dine or recline before she has vomited up seven measures of neat wine; to which she thinks it right to return when she has eaten sixteen rissoles. After all this, when she lusts, she does not suck — she thinks that too unmanly — but plainly devours the middles of girls. May the gods give you your own mind, Philaenis, you who think it manly to lick a cunt.

LXVII The boy has not yet announced the fifth hour to you, and already you come as my dinner-guest, Caecilianus, though the courts of the hoarse fourth have just put off their sureties and the arena still tires the Floralian beasts. Run, come, Callistus, call back the unwashed servants; let the couches be spread: Caecilianus, sit down. You ask for hot water: cold has not yet come to me; the kitchen is shut and chills still with bare hearth. Come in the morning rather; for why should the fifth hour keep you? To breakfast, Caecilianus, you come late.

LXVII I possessed all night a wanton girl, whose naughtinesses no one can outdo. Tired of a thousand ways, I asked for that boyish thing: she granted it before all my prayers and first words. Laughing and blushing, I asked something more shameless: the lustful girl promised it with no delay. But for me she was pure; for you she won't be, Aeschylus, if you wish to receive this favour on a bad condition.

LXVII Daughter of Pyrrha, stepmother of Nestor, whom Niobe saw white-haired as a girl, whom old Laertes called grandmother, Priam nurse, Thyestes mother-in-law, now outliving all the crows, at last laid in this tomb still itches, bald Plutia, with Melanthion.
LXVII You give me nothing while you live; you say you'll give after death. If you're not a fool, you know, Maro, what I wish.

LXVII You, the May Ides, gave birth to Mercury, on the August Ides Diana returns, the October Ides Maro consecrated. May you often keep the Ides, both these and those, you who celebrate the Ides of great Maro.
LXVII. Wood-Pigeons Ringed wood-pigeons slacken and dull the loins: Let no man eat this bird who hopes to be lusty.
LXVII. A Peacock Fly-Whisk That which keeps the filthy flies from licking your lunch Was once the proud tail of an exquisite bird.

LXVIII Whatever Rufus does, it is nothing but Naevia to Rufus. If he rejoices, if he weeps, if he is silent, of her he speaks. He dines, he toasts, he asks, refuses, nods: there is one Naevia; if there were no Naevia, he would be dumb. When yesterday at dawn he was writing a greeting to his father, "Naevia my light," he wrote, "Naevia my lamp, good morning." Naevia reads this and laughs with downcast face. There is more than one Naevia: why, you fool of a man, do you rave?

LXVIII That I now greet you by your own name, Whom before I used to call king and lord, Do not say that I am insolent: I bought back my freedman's cap with all my baggage. A man must have kings and lords Who has not himself and covets What kings and lords covet. If you can do without a slave, Olus, You can also do without a king, Olus.

LXVIII Thus far the book is written for you, matron. For whom are the inner pages written, you ask? For me. The gymnasium, the baths, the racetrack are in this part: withdraw. We are stripping: spare to see naked men. From here, with modesty laid aside after the wine and roses, Tipsy Terpsichore knows not what she says: With no doubtful figure, but openly she names that thing Which proud Venus receives in the sixth month, Which the bailiff sets as guard in the middle of the garden, Which the chaste maiden looks at with her hand held against it. If I know you well, you were laying down the long book, Wearied; now, eager, you will read it whole.
LXVIII You invite me on a hundred farthings and dine well. Am I invited to dine, Sextus, or to envy?
LXVIII From a northern race I've sent you hair, Lesbia, that you might know how much more golden yours is.

LXVIII Weep for your sin, but weep with all Lucrinus, Naiads, and let Thetis herself feel the grief. Among the Baian waves, snatched away, a boy has died, that Eutychos, your sweet companion, Castricus. This was your partner in cares and your coaxing solace, this was your love, this was our poet's Alexis. Did some wanton nymph see you naked beneath the glassy waves and send back Hylas to Alcides? Or does the goddess now neglect womanish Hermaphroditus, stirred by the embrace of a tender man? Whatever it is, whatever the cause of the sudden seizure, may both earth and water, I pray, be gentle to you.
