LXVIII Forbear, I beg, to commend my Muses, Instantius Rufus, to your father-in-law: perhaps he likes serious things. But if he too admits wanton little books, these I would read even to a Curius or a Fabricius.

LXVIII He who has seen the orchards of the Corcyraean king will prefer, Entellus, the country of your house. That envious winter may not scorch the purple clusters and cold frost devour the gifts of Bacchus, the vintage lives shut in transparent glass, and the happy grape is covered, yet not hidden: so a woman's body shines through silk, so a pebble is counted in clear water. What did Nature not wish to allow to genius? Barren winter is bidden to bear an autumn.

LXVIII What have you to do with us, accursed schoolmaster, head hateful to boys and girls? The crested cocks have not yet broken the silence: already you thunder with savage muttering and lashings. As loudly does the bronze ring from struck anvils, when the smith fits a lawyer to a horse in the middle; gentler the shouting rages in the great amphitheatre, when its crowd cheers the winning shield. We neighbours ask for sleep — not all night long: for to lie awake is light, to lie awake all night is grievous. Dismiss your pupils. Will you take, chatterbox, as much to keep quiet as you take to shout?

LXVIII Though you have neither Ephesus nor Rhodes nor Mytilene, but a house, Laelia, in a patrician quarter, and a mother never tanned, born of swarthy Etruscans, a stern father from the Arician region; "My lord, my honey, my soul"—you keep heaping it up, —for shame!—you, a citizen of Hersilia and Egeria. Let the little bed hear these words, not every bed, but the one a mistress has spread for her wanton man. Do you want to know how you, a chaste matron, talk? Can you, even when you writhe, be more seductive? Though you learn by heart and recite the whole of Corinth, you still won't, Laelia, be wholly a Lais.
LXVIII You ask small things of great men; but the great don't give even these. So that you may be less ashamed, Matho, ask great things.

LXVIII Morning client, the reason I left the city, if you're wise, you'd court ambitious halls. I'm no advocate, nor fit for bitter lawsuits, but lazy and older and a companion of the Muses; leisure and sleep delight me, which great Rome denied me: I'll go back, if there's no rest here either.
LXVIII. Wood-Larks The yellow-green bird is fooled by limed reeds and by nets, While the green grape, still raw, swells with its young wine.
LXVIII. An Ox-Tail Fly-Whisk If your clothes get dirtied with yellow dust, Let this light tail brush it off with gentle strokes.
LXIX Maximus, the Tarentos that once was wont to show a Pan Now shows a Canius.

LXIX You say, Classicus, that you dine out unwillingly: If you are not lying, Classicus, may I perish. Apicius himself was glad to go to dinner: When he dined at home, he was gloomier. Yet if you go unwillingly, why, Classicus, do you go? "I am compelled," you say: true; Selius too is compelled. See, Melior invites you, Classicus, to a proper dinner. Where are your grand words? If you are a man, look—say no.

LXIX Because you write all your epigrams in chaste words And in your poems there is no prick, I marvel, I praise: there is nothing more saintly than you alone: But no page of mine is free of wantonness. So let naughty youths and easy girls read these, And let the older man read them too, if a mistress torments him. But your venerable and saintly words, Cosconius, Ought to be read by boys and virgins.

LXIX You always set out Setine or Massic, Papylus, but rumour denies wines so good: you're said to have been four times widowed by this flask. I neither think it nor believe it, Papylus, nor am I thirsty.

LXIX Antonius, who'll reproach Pharian Pothinus with nothing, and more lightly guilty by the proscription-list than by Cicero: why, madman, do you draw a sword against Roman lips? Not even Catiline would have allowed this crime. The impious soldier is bribed with unspeakable gold, and for such great wealth one voice falls silent for you. What use is the precious silence of that sacred tongue? All men will begin to speak for Cicero.
LXIX I don't wonder that your Bassa drinks water, Catullus: I wonder that Bassus's daughter drinks water.

LXIX This is that Theophila promised to you, Canius, whose breast is steeped in Cecropian endowment: the garden of the great old man might justly claim her for its own, nor would the Stoic throng less wish her theirs. Whatever work you send out through these ears will live: so unwomanly, so uncommon is her taste. Let not your Pantaenis prefer herself too much to her, though she is well known to the Pierian choir. Sappho the lover praised her as she fashioned songs: Theophila was chaster, and Sappho no more learned.
LXIX You admire only the ancients, Vacerra, and praise no poets but the dead. We beg your pardon, Vacerra: it is not worth dying, just to please you.
LXIX When you fuck, Polycharmus, you usually shit at the end. When you are buggered, Polycharmus, what do you do?
LXIX You give your husband watchmen, Polla, but take none yourself. This, Polla, is to wed a man as a wife yourself.

LXIX Reared among the trainers of the amphitheatre, a huntress, fierce in the woods, gentle at home, I was called Lydia, most faithful to my master Dexter, who'd not have preferred to own Erigone's dog, nor the one that, following Cephalus of the Dictaean line, came likewise to the stars of the dawn-bringing goddess. No long span took me, nor useless age, such as were the fates of the Dulichian dog: I was destroyed by the lightning tusk of a foaming boar, great as yours, Calydon, or yours, Erymanthus. Nor do I complain, though snatched so swiftly to the shades below: I could not have died by a nobler fate.
LXIX Just as with your tablets and goblets, Paulus, you hold all your friends to be original masterpieces.
LXIX. Marten-Skins Umbria never gave us Pannonian martens: Pudens would rather send these gifts to his mistress.
LXIX. A Rhodian Cake Don't strike your erring slave's teeth with your fist: Let him eat the cake bright Rhodes sent you.

LXX Go and pay my respects for me, book: you are bidden to go, Dutifully, to the gleaming home of Proculus. You ask the way? I will tell you. You will pass the Castor Near grey-haired Vesta and the home of the virgins; Thence by the sacred slope you shall seek the venerable Palatine, Where many an image of the supreme leader gleams. Let not the radiant mass of the marvellous colossus delay you, That rejoices to surpass the work of Rhodes. Turn your way here, where stand the roofs of dripping Lyaeus And the dome of Cybele with its painted Corybant. Straightway on the left, with bright front, are the household gods And the halls of the lofty house you must approach. Make for this house: fear no pride, no haughty threshold: No door stands more open with every post thrown wide, Nor any that Phoebus and the learned sisters love more nearly. If he says, "Why has he not come himself, then?" You may excuse me thus: "Because, whatever the quality Of what is read here, a mere caller could not have written it."

LXX You do not want anyone to bathe in the tub before you, Cotilus: what is the reason, unless it is this, That you may not be soaked in befouled waters? You may wash first: yet here, of necessity, The prick is washed before the head.

LXX You are the lover of Aufidia, Scaevinus, whose husband you once were; He who was your rival is now her husband. Why does another's wife please you, when your own did not? Can you not get it up unless you feel insecure?
LXX Nothing but a dry rope did his father leave Ammianus, dying, in his last will. Who could have thought it possible, Marullinus, that Ammianus would not want his father dead?

LXX A hundred thousand just poured into him by his patron, in full, Maximus—Syriscus, wandering through the cookshops with their stools around the four baths, ran through it. O what a gullet, to eat up a hundred thousand! And greater still—and not even reclining!

LXX The sixtieth harvest, Marcianus, is past, and now, I think, the second of Cotta, nor does he recall having felt the weariness of a fevered bed even for a single day. He shows his finger—but the indecent one— to Alcon and Dasius and Symmachus. But if our years be well reckoned, and whatever the grim fevers or heavy languor or evil pains took away be separated from the better life: we are infants, and we seem old men. He who thinks the age of Priam and Nestor long, Marcianus, is much deceived and mistaken. To live is not life, but to be well.
LXX Tribade of the very tribades, Philaenis, you rightly call the woman you fuck your 'girlfriend.'

LXX As great as gentle Nerva's calm, so great his eloquence, but modesty restrains his powers and his genius. Though he could drain the sacred Permessis with a full mouth, he chose rather to keep his thirst modest, content to wreathe his Pierian brow with a slender crown, and not to spread sail to his own fame. Yet whoever knows the famous songs of learned Nero knows that this man is the Tibullus of our age.

LXX 'O the times! O the manners!' Tullius once cried, when Catiline was contriving his sacrilegious crime, when son-in-law and father-in-law clashed in dreadful arms and the mournful earth was soaked with civil slaughter. Why do you now say 'O the manners!', why now 'O the times!'? What is there, Caecilianus, that displeases you? There is no savagery of leaders, no madness of the sword; we may enjoy a sure peace and gladness. It is not our times that make your age sordid to you, but your own manners, Caecilianus.

LXX That scarcely one book a year comes out from me, I stand charged of sloth before you, learned Potitus. But how much more justly might you marvel that one comes out, when whole days often slip away from me. At night I visit friends who don't return the greeting, I congratulate many, no one congratulates me, Potitus. Now my gem seals letters to light-bringing Diana, now the first hour snatches me, now the fifth. Now a consul or praetor holds me, and the returning dances, often a poet is heard the whole day through. But you can't safely refuse the pleading lawyer, nor if a rhetor or a grammarian should ask you. After the tenth hour the baths are sought, weary, and a hundred quadrantes. When, Potitus, will the book be done?

LXX Can you sell, Tucca, boys bought for a hundred thousand each? Can you sell, Tucca, weeping masters? Do neither their coaxings nor their words nor their untrained complaints, nor their necks wounded by your own teeth, move you? Oh, the crime! the groin lies bare, the tunic lifted on both sides, and the member made by your hand is inspected. If counted money delights you, sell your silver, tables, murra-cups, lands, house; sell old slaves, they'll forgive you, sell those your father left: just don't sell boys; sell everything, wretch. It's extravagance to buy them—for who doubts or denies it?— but to sell them is far greater extravagance.

LXX When the bandy-legged home-bred slave was lately carrying towels for Aper, and the one-eyed old woman sat over his little toga, and the ruptured rubber gave him a drop of oil, he was a grim and harsh censor of the soused: he kept shouting that the cups should be smashed and the Falernian poured out, that a knight had just drunk after bathing. But after three hundred thousand came from his old uncle, he doesn't know how to go home sober from the baths. O how much carved cups and five long-haired boys can do! Then, when he was poor, Aper wasn't thirsty.
LXX. Peacocks You marvel each time it unfolds its jeweled wings — And can you, hard-hearted, hand this over to the cruel cook?
LXX. A Priapus of Wheat-Bread If you want to be full, you may eat our Priapus: Though you gnaw his very loins, you'll stay clean.

LXXI Let Laevia be drunk in six measures, Justina in seven, Lycas in five, Lyde in four, Ida in three. Let every mistress be counted out in poured Falernian, And, since none of them comes, you, Sleep, come to me.

LXXI Nothing is more candid than you, Caecilianus. I have noticed: Whenever I read a few couplets of mine, You at once recite the writings of Marsus or of Catullus. Do you do me this favour, as though you read worse stuff, That mine may please more by comparison? I believe it: Yet I would rather, Caecilianus, you recited your own.
LXXI When the boy's prick hurts and yours, Naevolus, your arse, I am no prophet, but I know what you do.

LXXI Long I search the whole city, Safronius Rufus, to find a girl who says no: no girl says no. As though it weren't allowed, as though it were shameful to refuse, as though it weren't permitted: no girl says no. Is none then chaste? A thousand are chaste: what, then, does a chaste one do? She doesn't give, yet she doesn't say no.

LXXI Where moist Trebula sends down her chill valleys and the green field is cold in the months of the Crab, country never violated by the Cleonaean lion and a house always friendly to the Aeolian South wind, they call you, Faustinus: pass your long harvests on these hills; Tibur will be your winter now.

LXXI She who is skilled to perform wanton gestures to Baetic music and to play in the Gaditanian style, who could rouse trembling Pelias and Hecuba's husband to Hector's pyre, Telethusa burns and torments her former master: he sold her as a slave-girl, now he buys her back as mistress.

LXXI The wife is poxed with figs, the husband poxed himself, the daughter poxed, and the son-in-law and grandson; neither steward nor bailiff lacks the foul sore, nor the sturdy digger, nor even the ploughman. Since young and old alike are poxed, it is a marvel: one single field has no figs.

LXXI A lion, the fame of the Massylian ridge, and a husband of the woolly flock joined together in wondrous loyalty. You may see it yourself: they are stabled in one cage and each crops the shared feast alike: they delight neither in the woods' offspring nor in mild herbs, but a tender lamb sates their harmonious hunger. What did the terror of Nemea earn, what the bearer of Helle, that they should gleam as bright signs of the high sky? If beasts of flock and field could earn the stars, this ram was worthy of the stars, this lion.

LXXI Whoever you are who wish glad and late fates for your parents, love the brief inscription of this marble. Here Rabirius has buried dear shades in the earth; no old folk lie under a brighter lot: a gentle and last night closed twice six lustres of their wedlock, two funerals burned on a single pyre. Yet he mourns them as snatched in their earliest years. Nothing can be more outrageous than these tears.

LXXI Leda had told her old husband she was hysterical and complains it's necessary for her to be fucked; but, weeping and groaning, she says health isn't worth so much and declares she'd rather have resolved to die. Her husband begs her to live and not desert her green years, and allows what he himself no longer does to be done. At once the male doctors come up and the female ones withdraw, and her feet are lifted. O weighty medicine!
LXXI You deny me nothing, Lygdus, when I ask: yet once, Lygdus, you denied me nothing.
LXXI. Flamingos My red plumage gives me my name, but my tongue Is the gourmet's delight. What if my tongue could chatter?
LXXI. A Pig This pig will make you a good Saturnalia, Fattened among the foaming boars on acorns.

LXXII Do you think, Fidentinus, that by my verses you are a poet, And do you wish to be believed so? So Aegle thinks she has teeth, With bones and Indian horn she has bought; So Lycoris, who is blacker than a falling mulberry, Pleases herself with white lead. By the same reasoning by which you are a poet, When you are bald, you will have a head of hair.

LXXII At yesterday's dinner, Postumus, a thing is said to have been done That I should not wish—for who would approve such deeds?— Your mouth was so battered that not even Latinus himself Strikes the cheap face of Panniculus with such a sound: And what is more wondrous, rumour through the whole city Names Caecilius as the author of this crime. You deny it was done: do you want me to believe this? I believe it. But what of it, Postumus, that Caecilius has witnesses?

LXXII You want to be had, but you will not bathe with me, Saufeia. I suspect some great defect. Either your flabby breasts hang from your chest, Or, naked, you fear to betray the furrows of your belly, Or your torn groin gapes with an endless cleft, Or something of your cunt juts out at its mouth. But none of these is so, I believe; naked, you are most beautiful. If that is true, you have a worse fault: you are a fool.

LXXII You demand, Quintus, that I give you my little books. I haven't got them, but the bookseller Tryphon has. "Shall I pay money for trifles and buy your poems, sane? No," you say, "I won't do anything so foolish." Nor will I.
LXXII He who could call the Thunderer Bacchus's mother could call Semele, Rufus, his father.

LXXII A thief of all-too-noted rapacity, Cilix, wished to plunder a garden, but in the huge garden, Fabullus, there was nothing but a marble Priapus. Not wanting to return empty-handed, Cilix stole Priapus himself.

LXXII So may December be welcome to you, Paulus, nor may there come empty three-leaved tablets and skimpy napkins nor light half-pounds of incense, but may a great defendant or a powerful friend bring you platters and your grandsires' goblets, or whatever rather pleases and takes you; so may you beat Novius and Publius shut in by their stockades and glass robber-pieces; so may the favour of the umpire of the oiled ring give you the palm at bare ball-play, and praise no more the left-handed strokes of Polybius: if any spiteful man says that the songs which drip with black venom are mine, lend me your voice as advocate and cry, as loud and as long as you can: 'My Martial did not write that.'

LXXII Not yet decked with purple, nor smoothed by the rough bite of dry pumice, you hurry to follow Arcanus, little book, whom most lovely Narbo bids return — Narbo, the home of learned Votienus Paternus — to her laws and her yearly fasces: what with equal vows you must wish for, that place and this friend will be granted you. How I'd wish to become my own little book!

LXXII Liber, your brow bound with the Amyclaean crown, who shake Greek lashes with Ausonian hand, since you send me lunches shut in woven wicker, why does no flask come to accompany the feast? Yet if you brought gifts worthy of your name, you know, I think, what gifts ought to have been given me.

LXXII In vain you come to me, Flatteries, pitiful with your worn-down little lips: I'm not going to call anyone lord and god. There's no longer a place for you in this city; go far off, to the felt-capped Parthians, and, foul and grovelling and suppliant, kiss the soles of painted kings. There's no lord here, but an emperor, but the most just senator of all, through whom from the Stygian home there's brought back rustic Truth, with dry hair. Under this prince, if you're wise, beware, Rome, of speaking in your former words.
LXXII Natta calls his stud's tool a little willy, compared to which Priapus is a Gallus.

LXXII Having bought acres of a little field hidden near the tombs and the propped-up roof of a badly-built hovel, you abandon, Pannychus, your urban lawsuits, your estate, and the small but sure rewards of a worn toga. Grain, millet, barley-gruel and beans you used to sell as a man of business; now you buy them as a farmer.
LXXII. Pheasants I was first carried over in the Argo's hull: Before, I knew nothing but the Phasis.
LXXII. A Sausage The sausage that comes to you in midwinter's season Had come seven days before Saturn's feast.

LXXIII There was no one in the whole city who would touch Your wife for free, Caecilianus, while it was allowed: But now, with guards posted, there is a huge Crowd of seducers: you are a man of resource.
LXXIII Lyris wants to know what she does: what she does sober—she sucks cocks.

LXXIII You sleep with well-endowed boys, And what stands for them, Gallus, does not stand for you. What, I ask you, Phoebus, do you want me to suspect? I wanted to believe you a soft man, But rumour denies that you are a catamite.

LXXIII When grievous Vestinus was drawing his last hours and was now about to pass through the Stygian waters, he begged the sisters spinning his final threads to draw the dark strands a little while longer, already dead to himself, while he lived on for his dear friends. Such pious prayers moved the grim goddesses. Then, having divided his great wealth, he withdrew from the light and after this believed he died an old man.
LXXIII Why I don't give you my little books, when you beg and demand them so often, do you wonder, Theodorus? There's a great reason: that you may not give me your little books.

LXXIII No rude settler made me with unskilled blade: you see the noble work of a steward. For the richest cultivator of the Caeretan land, Hilarus, holds these hills and joyful ridges. See how I seem not wooden, with sure face, nor bear the weapons of my groin devoted to the hearth-fire, but for me, of everlasting, never-dying cypress, stands stiff a member worthy of Phidias's hand. Neighbours, I warn you, honour holy Priapus and spare these twice seven acres.

LXXIII You have a house on the Esquiline, a house on Diana's hill, and the patrician quarter holds your rooftops; from here you look on widowed Cybele's shrines, from there on Vesta's, on the new Jupiter from this side, the old from that. Tell me where I may meet you, tell me where to find you: the man who lives everywhere, Maximus, lives nowhere.

LXXIII Instantius, than whom no other is held more sincere in heart, nor first in snow-white candour, if you wish to give strength and spirit to my Thalia and seek songs that will live, give me something to love. Cynthia made you a bard, wanton Propertius; fair Lycoris was the genius of Gallus; lovely Nemesis is the fame of smart Tibullus; Lesbia dictated to you, learned Catullus: neither the Paeligni nor Mantua will scorn me as a bard, if I have some Corinna, some Alexis.

LXXIII You who used to draw out old hides with your teeth and bite the rotten, ancient sole with mud, now hold the Praenestine realms of your deceived patron, in which I am indignant if you ever had a cell; and, drunk, you break the crystal with burning Falernian, and you lust with your master's Ganymede. But my foolish parents taught me my letters: what have I to do with grammarians and rhetors? Break the light reeds and tear up the books, Thalia, if a shoe can give such things to a cobbler.

LXXIII A letter brought me the welcome pledge of an eloquent friend, the austere gift of an Ausonian toga, which not Fabricius, but Apicius would wish to wear, which Maecenas, Caesar's knight, would wish. This would have been cheaper to me, sent by another; not by whatever hand the victim is slain does it appease: sent by you it comes: could I not love your gift, Marcus, I could love my own name. But more than the gift and more welcome than the name itself is the kind service and judgment of a learned man.

LXXIII You always swear you'll come when I ask, Lygdus, and you fix the hour and you fix the place. When I've lain in vain, tense with long lust, my left hand often comes to my aid in your place. What shall I wish you, deceiver, for such deserts and ways? That you carry the parasol, Lygdus, of a one-eyed mistress.
LXXIII You say I'm your heir, Catullus. I won't believe it, Catullus, until I've read it.
LXXIII. Guinea-Fowl Though Hannibal had eaten his fill of Roman goose, The barbarian himself never ate his own native birds.
LXXIII. A Parrot I, a parrot, will learn from you the names of others: This I've learned to say of myself — "Hail, Caesar."
LXXIV He was an adulterer: yet you could deny it, Paula. Now, look, he is your husband: can you deny it now, Paula?

LXXIV Saufeius girt about, before and behind, with a toga-clad crowd, As great a throng as Regulus has when he returns, When he sent his shaven client, acquitted, to the lofty temples— Maternus, do you see him? Do not envy him. May such an escort, I pray, never be yours. These friends and these troops of toga-wearers Fuficulenus and Faventinus furnish him.

LXXIV You smooth your face with depilatory and your bald head with pitch-paste. Are you afraid, Gargilianus, of the barber? What will you do about your nails? For surely you cannot Pare them with resin or with Venetian clay. Stop, if you have any shame, parading your wretched baldness: This, Gargilianus, is usually done to a cunt.

LXXIV You see how brave the battles unwarlike does attempt? How great the anger in such timid beasts? With small brows they burn to charge to the death. Do you wish, Caesar, to spare the does? Send dogs.

LXXIV The young Pompeys Asia and Europe cover, but the father himself the land of Libya covers, if indeed any land covers him. What wonder if he's scattered over the whole world? In one place so great a ruin could not lie.
LXXIV He who reclines lowest on the middle couch, his three-haired bald head streaked with ointment, and picks his loose mouth with clipped mastic-twigs, is lying, Aefulanus: he has no teeth.

LXXIV Glory of Cyllene and the sky, eloquent minister, whose golden wand grows green with a twisted serpent: so may you never lack a store of wanton intrigue, whether you long for Paphos or grow warm for Ganymede, and may your mother's Ides be decked with sacred leaves, and your aged grandfather be pressed with a light burden: this day may Norbana ever keep with her husband Carpus, glad — the day they came together to their first bed. Here this pious priest of wisdom offers you his gifts, here he calls you with incense, himself faithful to Jove too.
LXXIV A gladiator now, you were an eye-doctor before. You did as a doctor what you do as a gladiator.

LXXIV Only the likeness of the boy Camonius does the painting keep, and the small image of the infant remains. No portrait marked his face in its flowering, since the pious father feared to see the mute features.

LXXIV Now spare your weary congratulator, Rome, your weary client. How long, as a morning caller among forerunners and little toga'd men, shall I earn a hundred leaden coins the whole day, when Scorpus in a single hour carries off, victorious, fifteen heavy sacks of glowing gold? I'd not want, as the prize for my little books —for what do they earn?—the Apulian fields: neither Hybla nor the corn-bearing Nile takes me, nor the dainty grape that from the citadel of the Setine slope looks out on the Pomptine marshes. You ask, then, what I long for? To sleep.
LXXIV Baccara the Raetian entrusted his penis to be cured to a rival doctor. Baccara will become a Gallus.

LXXIV While a Nile-borne convoy brings you crystal, take cups from the Flaminian Circus. Are these more daring, or those who send such gifts? But there's a use in cheap glassware: these embossed pieces, Flaccus, tempt no thief, and aren't spoiled by too hot water. What of it, that the guest drinks while his servant's at ease, and the trembling hands haven't feared a mishap? This too is something, that you'll toast in these, if a cup, Flaccus, must be broken by you.
LXXIV. Geese This was the bird that saved the temple of Tarpeian Jove. You marvel? He had not yet made the bird a god.
LXXIV. A Crow Crow, the greeter — why are you held a fellator? No member has ever entered your head.
LXXV The man who would rather give Linus half than lend him the whole, Would rather lose the half.

LXXV A lion, wont to bear unmoved the blows of its master And to suffer, gently, a hand thrust into its mouth, Suddenly unlearned its peace, its savagery returning, As great as ought not to have been even on the slopes of Libya. For two of the boyish band, of tender body, Who were renewing the bloody sand with rakes, The cruel beast destroyed, ill-starred, with its raging tooth: The arena of Mars saw no greater outrage. One wants to cry out: "Cruel, treacherous robber, Learn from our she-wolf to spare children!"

LXXV Your prick, Lupercus, long ago ceased to stand, Yet, madman, you struggle to get it up. But rocket and lecherous bulbs do nothing, And shameless savory now profits you nothing. You have begun to corrupt pure mouths with bribes: Even so, your Venus, urged on, does not come alive. Could anyone marvel enough at this, or believe it— That what does not stand stands you, Lupercus, at a great price?

LXXV O happy in your heart, Nigrina, happy in your husband, and first glory among Latin brides: it delights you to share your inherited wealth with your spouse, rejoicing in a partner who is your fellow. Let Evadne be burned, flung onto her husband's flames, nor let lesser fame bear Alcestis to the stars: you do better: by a sure pledge of life you've earned that your love need not be proved by death.
LXXV She who married you to obey the law, Laelia, Quintus, you may call your lawful wife.
LXXV When you send me a thrush or a slice of cake, or a hare's thigh, or something like these, you say, Pontia, that you've sent me your tidbits. These, Pontia, I'll neither send on nor eat.
LXXV You want to be fucked for free, though you are ugly and old. A most ridiculous thing: you want to give, yet won't pay.

LXXV While the Lingonian, fresh from the Tecta and the Flaminian Way, sought his hired lodgings late at night, he struck his thumb and dislocated his injured ankle and lay stretched full-length upon the ground. What was the Gaul to do, by what means move himself? The huge master had but one little slave, so thin he could scarcely carry the smallest lamp: chance came to the wretch's aid and brought him help. Four branded slaves were carrying a cheap corpse, such as the poor man's pyre receives by the thousand; the feeble companion begs them in a lowered voice to carry the empty body wherever they wish: the load is exchanged, and the great bundle, crammed, is lifted high on the narrow bier. This man of many, Lucanus, seems to me one to whom 'dead Gaul' can rightly be said.

LXXV Not of hard flint or built-up rubble, nor of baked brick, with which Semiramis girt long Babylon, did Tucca make his bath: but of slaughtered groves and pinewood frame, so that Tucca could sail in his bath. The same man, elegant, builds rich warm-baths of every marble that Carystos found, that Phrygian Synnas, that African Nomas sent, and that Eurotas washed with its green stream. But wood is wanting: put the bath under the warm-baths to burn.

LXXV Once Galla demanded twenty thousand from me, and, I confess, she wasn't too dear at the price. A year went by: "You'll give twice five thousand," she said. She seemed to me to ask more than before. Now, six months later, when she asked two thousand, I offered a thousand coins. She wouldn't take them. Two or perhaps three Kalends had passed: of her own accord she asked four gold pieces. I didn't give them. She bade me send a hundred coins: but even this sum seemed to me too heavy. A meagre dole of a hundred quadrantes joined us; this she wanted: I said it had been given to my boy. Could she go any lower? She did. Galla gives for free, gives of her own accord: I say no.

LXXV A slave covered with a bronze sheath bathes with you, Caelia; why, I ask, is it, since he's no lyre-player or flute-player? You don't want, I suppose, to see his member. Why, then, do you bathe with the public? Are we all eunuchs to you? So, lest you seem to be jealous, release, Caelia, the clasp from your slave.
LXXV. Cranes You'll throw your lines into disorder, the whole letter will not fly, If you lose a single one of Palamedes' birds.
LXXV. A Nightingale Philomela weeps the crime of incestuous Tereus, and she Who was a speechless girl is now a chattering bird.

LXXVI O Flaccus, no cheap reward of my cares, Hope and nursling of the Antenorean home, Put off the Pierian songs and the choirs of the sisters; None of those girls will give you a copper. What do you seek from Phoebus? Minerva's chest has the cash; She is the shrewd one, she alone lends to all the gods. What can the ivy of Bacchus give? The tree of Pallas, Black with weight, bows down its various foliage. Besides waters, Helicon has nothing but garlands And the lyres of the goddesses, and a grand but empty "Bravo!" What have you to do with Cirrha? What with naked Permessis? The Roman forum is nearer and richer. There the coins ring out: but round our stages And barren professors' chairs only kisses click.
LXXVI Marius left you five pounds of silver, You to whom he gave nothing himself: did he keep his word to you?

LXXVI You get it up for old women, Bassus, you spurn girls, And not the beautiful, but the dying, please you. Is this not madness, I ask, is this not a crazed prick? When you could have Hecuba, you cannot do Andromache!
LXXVI You sent me six thousand when I asked twelve: to get twice six, I'll ask twice twelve.
LXXVI Mithridates profited by often drinking poison, so that savage toxins could not harm him. You too have taken precautions, dining always so badly, that you could never, Cinna, die of hunger.

LXXVI That guardian of the sacred side and of Mars in the toga, to whom the camp of the supreme leader was entrusted, here lies Fuscus. This, Fortune, we may confess: this stone now fears no enemy threats; the Dacian has taken the great yoke on his subdued neck, and the victorious shade possesses the grove as its slave.

LXXVI That more powerful men tear you to pieces at banquets, porticoes, theatres, and it delights them, whenever you've fallen in their way, to be carried and to bathe with you: do not be too pleased with yourself. You amuse, Philomusus; you are not loved.

LXXVI 'Tell me the truth, Marcus, tell me, please; there is nothing I would hear more gladly.' So both when you recite your little books, and whenever you plead a client's case, you beg me, Gallicus, and always ask. It is hard for me to deny you what you ask. So hear what is truer than truth: the truth, Gallicus, you do not gladly hear.

LXXVI These are those features of my Camonius you behold, this was the boy's face and first form. This face had grown stronger in twice ten years, and the beard rejoiced to paint his cheeks, and the bloom, sipped but once, had just sprinkled the topmost razors: of three, one sister envied and cut the threads with hastened spinning, and the urn brought back to the father the pyre of his absent son. But lest the painting alone speak of the boy, this greater image will be in my pages.

LXXVI Does this, Fortune, seem fair to you? A citizen not of Syria or Parthia, nor a knight from a Cappadocian platform, but a home-bred slave of the people of Remus and Numa, pleasant, honest, harmless—a friend, learned in both tongues, whose one fault, but a great one, is that he's a poet, Mevius shivers in a drab cowl, while the muleteer Incitatus shines in scarlet.

LXXVI You force me, Paetus, to pay you ten thousand sesterces, because Bucco lost you two hundred thousand. Don't let crimes that aren't mine harm me, I beg: you who can lose two hundred thousand, lose ten.
LXXVI A jar is given for twenty coins, a peck for four pieces of bronze. Drunk and bloated, the farmer has nothing.
LXXVI. Woodcocks Woodcock or partridge — what does it matter, if the flavor's the same? The partridge costs more. So it tastes the better.
LXXVI. A Magpie I, the talking magpie, greet you, my master, with sure voice: If you didn't see me, you'd deny I'm a bird.

LXXVII Charinus is in fine health, and yet he is pale. Charinus drinks sparingly, and yet he is pale. Charinus digests well, and yet he is pale. Charinus takes the sun, and yet he is pale. Charinus dyes his skin, and yet he is pale. Charinus licks a cunt, and yet he is pale.

LXXVII Cosconius, you who think our epigrams too long, You might be useful for greasing axles. By that reasoning you would think the colossus long, And call the boy of Brutus short. Learn what you do not know: of Marsus and learned Pedo Often a double page treats a single subject. Those are not long from which you can take nothing away, But you, Cosconius, make even couplets long.

LXXVII Neither mullet nor thrush delights you, Baeticus, Nor is hare ever, nor boar, agreeable to you, Nor do cakes please you, nor a slice of cut pastry, Nor does Libya send, nor Phasis, birds to you: You devour capers and onions swimming in rotten fish-sauce And the flesh of a doubtful gammon, And gurnards delight you and tunny-chunks with grey skin, You drink resined wines, you flee Falernian. I suspect there is some more secret fault of the stomach: For why else, Baeticus, do you eat putrid things?
LXXVII Never have I asked the gods for riches, content with little and happy with my own: Poverty—forgive me—be gone. What is the cause of this sudden, novel prayer? I want to see Zoilus hanged.
LXXVII A certain man is said, Marullus, to have wittily said that you carry oil in your ear.

LXXVII Though you're as poor as wretched Irus is not, as young as Parthenopaeus was not, as strong as Artemidorus was not, even when he won, why do you delight to be the burden of six Cappadocians? You're laughed at and much more disgraced, Afer, than if you walked naked in the middle of the forum. Just so Atlas is pointed at, with his matched mule, and the black beast that carries a Libyan like itself. You ask how hateful your litter is? You shouldn't be carried dead in a six-bearer.
LXXVII You demand, Tucca, that I make you a gift of my little books. I won't: for you want to sell them, not read them.

LXXVII Liber, sweetest care of your friends, Liber, worthy to live in eternal roses, if you are wise, let your hair forever gleam with Assyrian balm, and flowery garlands ring your head; let bright crystal grow dark with old Falernian, and the soft couch grow warm with charming love. He who has so lived, though cut off even in mid-course, has made his life longer than the life that was given him.

LXXVII What is the best banquet, the eloquent page of Priscus disputes, and reports much sweetly, much sublimely, but all with learned heart. You ask what is the best banquet? One at which there will be no flute-player.

LXXVII Nothing was ever more wickedly done by Carus, Maximus, than that he died of a fever: it too committed a crime. The savage, harmful fever should at least have been a quartan! He ought to have been kept for his own doctor.
LXXVII That Vacerra spends hours in all the privies and sits the whole day long, Vacerra wants to dine, not to shit.

LXXVII While he greeted Jove with many prayers, standing bent back right up onto his tiptoes, Aethon farted in the Capitol. Men laughed, but the father of the gods himself, offended, punished his client with a three-night dine-at-home sentence. After this disgrace, poor little Aethon, when he wants to come to the Capitol, first seeks out the Paterclian privies and farts ten and twenty times. But although he's taken care by his cracking, with clenched buttocks he greets Jove.
LXXVII. Swans With failing tongue the swan tunes its sweet songs, Itself the singer of its own funeral.
LXXVII. An Ivory Cage If you have such a bird as Catullus' beloved Lesbia wept for, here it can live.

LXXVIII When the wasting plague gripped his undeserving throat And the black pest crept over his very face, With dry cheeks himself, exhorting his weeping friends, Festus resolved to go to the Stygian pools. Yet he did not defile his pious lips with hidden poison, Nor torment his sad fate with lingering starvation, But ended a holy life by a Roman death, And sent forth his soul by a nobler pyre. Fame may set this death above the fate of great Cato: For of this man Caesar was the friend.
LXXVIII You ask where, in summertime, you may keep your fish? Keep it, Caecilianus, in your hot baths.
LXXVIII You pissed once with the keel running, Paulinus. Do you want to piss again? Then you will be a Palinurus.

LXXVIII Though your sixtieth harvest is already stored away and your white face shines with much grey hair, you dash about, wandering the whole city, nor is there any chair to which you don't carry an unwearied "Good morning" each dawn; without you no tribune may rightly go forth, nor does either consul lack your attendance; ten times you climb back up the sacred Palatine slope and sound nothing but Sigeri and Partheni. Let young men do this: nothing, Afer, is more unseemly than a busybody grown old.

LXXVIII If you suffer from a dismal dinner alone at home, Toranius, you can go hungry with me. You won't lack, if you're used to an aperitif, cheap Cappadocian lettuce and pungent leeks, a slice of tuna will lie hidden in halved eggs. There'll be set out, to be held in scorched fingers on a black dish, green sprouts, which just now left the chilly garden, and a little sausage pressing snowy porridge, and pale beans with reddish bacon. If you'll have the gifts of the second course, shrivelled grapes will be offered you and pears that bear the name of the Syrians, and chestnuts that learned Naples produced, roasted in slow heat: the wine you'll make good by drinking it. After all this, if by chance Bacchus stirs the hunger he usually does, noble olives will come to your aid, such as the Picene branches lately bore, and hot chickpeas and warm lupins. The little dinner is small—who can deny it?— but you'll feign nothing nor hear feigned talk, and you'll recline at ease with your own face; nor will the host read out a fat scroll, nor will girls from wicked Gades keep quivering, lustful, without end, their wanton loins with practised trembling; but the pipe of little Condylus will sound something neither heavy nor coarse. This is the little dinner. You'll follow Claudia. What girl do you want me to put before you?

LXXVIII The famous drinker, Aulus, Phryx, was blind in one eye and bleary in the other. To him Heras the doctor said, "Beware of drinking: if you drink wine, you'll see nothing." Laughing, Phryx said to his eye, "Farewell." He at once orders measures mixed for himself, but frequent ones. You ask the outcome? Phryx drank wine, his eye drank poison.

LXXVIII Since a tail of Saxetan mackerel is served you, and beans dressed for you, if you dine well: yet you send out sow's udder, boar, hare, mushrooms, oysters, mullet — you have, Papylus, neither heart nor taste.

LXXVIII Such games as Phlegraean victory would wish its own, such, Lyaeus, as the Indian procession would wish yours, Stella, celebrant of the Hyperborean triumph, has staged — O modesty! O devotion! — and thinks it too little. Not enough for him is Hermus, dirty with churned gold, and Tagus, which sounds in the Hesperian world. Every day has its gifts: nor does the rich line of prizes cease, and much plunder falls upon the crowd; now wanton tokens come in sudden showers, now the lavish ticket gives the beasts on show, now the bird rejoices to fill safe bosoms and, absent, chooses its owners by lot, that it not be torn apart. Why count the chariots and the thirty prizes of the palm, which not even both consuls are always wont to give? But all is surpassed, Caesar, by so great an honour, that your laurel has you for its spectator.
LXXVIII After the funerals of seven husbands, Galla married you, Picentinus: Galla wants, I think, to follow her husbands.

LXXVIII You'll go, Macer, to shore-set Salonae, and there will go rare loyalty and love of right and that office which, when it drags modesty along as companion, always returns the poorer: happy farmer of the gold-bearing land, you'll send your governor back with an empty purse and wish for delays, and as he departs the Dalmatian will follow him with wet-eyed joy. We'll make for the Celts, Macer, and the fierce Iberians with longing for you. But whatever page is brought from there, marked by the reed of the fishy Tagus, my page will name Macer: so let me be read among the old poets, and don't prefer to me many earlier ones, but let me be lesser to you than Catullus alone.

LXXVIII Use feminine embraces, use them, Victor, and let your cock learn its unknown task. The bridal veil is being woven, now the maiden is being readied, now the new bride will crop your boys' hair. She'll let you bugger her once, the eager husband, while she fears the first wounds of the new weapon: nurse and mother will forbid this happen more often and will say, "She's your wife, not your boy." Alas, what fevers, what labours you'll suffer, if the cunt is a foreign thing to you! So hand the recruit over to a Suburan instructress. She'll make a man of you; a virgin teaches badly.
LXXVIII I've written nothing against you, Bithynicus. You won't believe it and bid me swear an oath? I'd rather give satisfaction.
LXXVIII. Purple Coots Has so small a bird the name of a great giant? And it has the name of the Green-faction's Porphyrion too.
LXXVIII. A Medicine-Case You see the medicine-case of the healing art: you'll have Gifts that Paccius would wish were his own.

LXXIX You always plead cases and always drive at business, Attalus: Whether there is or is not something to drive at, Attalus, you always drive. If business and cases fail, Attalus, you drive mules. Attalus, that you may not lack something to drive—drive out your life.
LXXIX You invite me, Nasica, just when you know I have invited guests. I beg you, hold me excused: I dine at home.
LXXIX Sertorius finishes nothing, begins everything. This man, when he has a woman, I do not think he completes the act.
LXXIX You were always a guest at my Tibur place, Matho. Now you buy it. I've tricked you: I'm selling you your own land.

LXXIX Eleven times you got up at one dinner, Zoilus, and your dinner-suit was changed eleven times, lest the sweat, retained, should cling to your damp clothes and a thin breeze chafe your loosened skin. Why don't I sweat, who dine with you, Zoilus? Because one dinner-suit makes great cold.
LXXIX You're sad and fortunate. Beware lest Fortune know it: she'll call you ungrateful, Lupus, if she knows.
LXXIX I lately drank a consular wine. You ask how old and how generous? Laid down under Priscus' consulship: but the very man who set it before me, Severus, was the consul.

LXXIX All your women friends are either old hags or ugly and fouler than old hags. These you lead as companions and drag with you through banquets, porticoes, theatres. So you are beautiful, Fabulla, so you are a girl.

LXXIX Rome hated before the leaders' servants and the former throng and the Palatine arrogance: but now so great is the love of all for your people, Augustus, that each cares for his own house second. So peaceful are their minds, so great their reverence for us, so calm their quiet, so much modesty in their faces. No one — this is the nature of a powerful court — but the master's manners does a Caesarian have.

LXXIX Torquatus has a mansion at the fourth milestone; at the fourth milestone Otacilius bought a little farm. Torquatus built baths gleaming with varied marble; Otacilius made a cooking-pot. Torquatus laid out a laurel-grove on his land; Otacilius planted a hundred chestnut-trees. When Torquatus was consul, that one was a ward-master, and thought himself no less in so great an honour. As once a great ox burst a tiny frog, so, I think, will Torquatus burst Otacilius.
LXXIX That we came to the first milestone at the tenth hour, we're charged with the crime of slow laziness. That's no fault of the road, no fault of mine, but yours, Paetus, who sent me your mules.
LXXIX I gave you many things you asked for; I gave you more things than you asked for: yet you don't stop asking me always. Whoever denies nothing, Atticilla, sucks.
LXXIX. Whips Play, wanton slaves, but only play: These are sealed up for me, just for the five days.
LXXX The last night of your life, Canus, you went out to beg the dole: You died, I think, Canus, because there was only one.
LXXX While fleeing the foe, Fannius slew himself. Is this not madness, I ask—to die that you may not die?
LXXX You speak ill of no one, you slander no one, Apicius: Yet rumour says that your tongue is a foul one.

LXXX You declaim in a fever, Maro: that this is madness, if you don't know, you're not sane, friend Maro. You declaim while sick, you declaim in a semi-tertian fever: if you can't sweat otherwise, there's a method in it. "Yet it's a great thing." You're wrong; when fever burns your guts, the great thing, Maro, is to keep quiet.

LXXX You may give me, Severus, not a whole hour, if you have time—and you may charge it to me— while you read and assess my trifles. "It's hard to lose a holiday": I ask that you bear and endure this loss. But if you read these with eloquent —but surely we're not shameless?—Secundus, this little book will owe you much more than it owes its own author. For it will be carefree, nor will it see the restless marbles of weary Sisyphus, once the censorial file of learned Secundus, with my Severus, has nibbled it.

LXXX That she might send you new gifts, Caesar, the land of Nile in her eagerness had sent you winter roses. The Memphian sailor laughed at the Pharian gardens as soon as he entered the first thresholds of your city: so great was the glory of spring and the grace of fragrant Flora, so great the splendour of the Paestan countryside; wherever, wandering, he bore his step and his eyes, every path was red with clipped garlands. But you, now bidden to yield to the Roman winter, send us your harvests, Nile, and accept our roses.

LXXX Since now the Roman peace tempers the Odrysian North and the grim trumpets have fallen silent, you may send this little book to Marcellinus, Faustinus: now he is free for pages, now for jests. But if you wish to commend the small gifts of your friend, let a boy carry my songs — not the kind who, gorged on the milk of a Getic heifer, plays on the stiff Sarmatian stream with a hoop, but the rosy youth of a Mitylenean dealer, or a Laconian not yet flogged at his mother's bidding. But to you a captive servant shall be sent from the Hister, one able to pasture your Tiburtine sheep.

LXXX You give us back the wonders of our holy forefathers, nor do you let the hoary ages die, Caesar, when the old rites of the Latin sand are renewed and valour fights with a simpler hand. So with you as guardian, honour is kept for ancient temples, and the hut has its godhead under so cultured a Jupiter; so, while you found new things, you call back the old, Augustus — both what is owed to you and what once was.
LXXX A poor, hungry man married a rich old woman: Gellius both feeds his wife and fucks her.

LXXX Eros weeps, whenever he eyes the cups of spotted murra or the slave-boys or the nobler citron-wood, and draws his groans from deep in his breast, because he can't, poor wretch, buy up the whole Saepta and carry it home. How many do what Eros does, but with dry eye! The greater part laughs at his tears and holds the same within.

LXXX The golden shore of blessed Venus, Baiae, Baiae, the coaxing gifts of proud Nature, though I praised Baiae in a thousand verses, Flaccus, still I'd not praise Baiae worthily enough. But I prefer Martial, Flaccus, to Baiae. To wish for both alike is a greedy man's prayer. But if this were granted you by the gift of the gods, what joys there'd be—Martial and Baiae!
LXXX So as not to praise the deserving, Callistratus praises everyone. He for whom no one is bad, how can anyone be good?
LXXX. Lampreys The great lamprey that swims in the Sicilian deep Cannot dive when its skin is scorched by the sun.
LXXX. Canes Hated too much by boys, dear to schoolmasters, We are the wood made famous by Prometheus' gift.
LXXXI You know you were born of a slave, and sweetly confess it, When you call your father master, Sosibianus.
LXXXI Though your litter may be roomier than a six-bearer chair: Yet, since it is yours, Zoilus, it is a pauper's bier.

LXXXI What have you to do, Baeticus the Gaul, with a woman's pit? That tongue of yours ought to lick men's middles. Why was your prick cut off with a Samian sherd, If a cunt, Baeticus, was so welcome to you? Your head must be gelded: for though you are a eunuch in the groin, Yet you cheat the rites of Cybele: in the mouth you are a man.

LXXXI When Fabulla had read my epigram in which I complain that no girl says no, asked once and twice and three times, she ignored a lover's prayers. Now, Fabulla, promise: I told you to refuse, I did not tell you to refuse forever.
LXXXI You'll always be poor, if you're poor, Aemilianus. Wealth is now given to none but the rich.

LXXXI You bathe as if enraged at the people, Charidemus: so you wash your groin all over in the tub. Nor would I have you wash even your head here, Charidemus. And look, you do wash your head: I'd rather you washed your groin.
LXXXI 'Thirty epigrams in the whole book are bad.' If as many are good, Lausus, the book is good.

LXXXI Not by the mystic rites of Dindymene, nor by the bull of the Nile's heifer, nor, in short, by any gods or goddesses does Gellia swear, but by her pearls. These she embraces, these she covers with kisses, these she calls brothers, these she calls sisters, these she loves more fiercely than her two children. If by some chance the poor wretch should lose them, she says she would not live a single hour. Alas, how well now, Papirianus, the hand of Annaeus Serenus would do its work!
LXXXI Reader and listener approve my little books, Aulus, but a certain poet says they are not polished. I don't much care: for I'd rather the courses of my dinner pleased the guests than the cooks.
LXXXI When two had come one morning to fuck Phyllis and each desired to take her naked first, Phyllis promised to give herself to both at once, and did: one lifted her foot, the other her tunic.

LXXXI The eunuch Dindymus and an old man trouble Aegle they share, and the girl lies dry in the middle of the couch. The one isn't up to the work in strength, the other in years: so for both the labour itches without effect. She, a suppliant, prays for herself and the two wretches, that you make this one a youth, Cytherea, that one a man.
LXXXI On winter days and the holidays of Saturn, poor Umber used to send me a little cloak; now he sends me spelt-gruel: for he's become rich.
LXXXI. Turbots Though the broad dish carries a turbot, Still the turbot is broader than the dish.
LXXXI. A Beggar's Wallet Lest it bring a beggar's lunch to the bearded naked man, And sleep with a surly dog, the wallet asks for alms.

LXXXII This portico, scattered in much dust, That unfolds its long ruins, See by what a chance it lies, finished off. For only just now Regulus had been Carried beneath those roofs, and had withdrawn, When suddenly it was overcome by its own weight, And, after it had nothing to fear for its master, It fell, bloodless, in a harmless loss. After such fear, such a complaint, Regulus— Who would deny that you are the care of the gods, For whose sake the very ruin was innocent?
LXXXII Why, Ponticus, do you crucify your slave with his tongue cut out? Do you not know that the people speak the very thing he keeps silent?

LXXXII Whoever can be a guest of Zoilus, Let him dine among the whores of Summemmius And drink sober from the chipped jar of Leda: This, I maintain, is lighter and cleaner. He lies, dressed in pale green, on a couch he fills, And shoves his guests aside with his elbows on either hand, Propped on purple and silken cushions. A worn-out catamite stands by and supplies him, as he belches, Red feathers and toothpicks of mastic, And, as he sweats, a reclining concubine fans A faint coolness with a green fan, And a boy drives off the flies with a myrtle branch. A masseuse runs over his body with nimble art And spreads her skilled hand on all his limbs; A eunuch knows the signal of his snapping finger And, the inquirer into his dainty bladder, Guides the drunken member of his drinking master. But he himself, turned back to the crowd at his feet, Among the lapdogs licking the entrails of geese, Divides the boar's sweetbreads among the wrestlers And gives the turtle-doves' rumps to his catbamite; And while Ligurian rock-wine is served to us Or must boiled in Massilian smoke, He toasts his fools with Opimian nectar In crystal and in murrine cups. And himself, dark with Cosmus's flasks, He does not blush to share out among us, in golden-purple flagons, A poor adulteress's pomade. Then, undone by many a half-pint, he snores: We recline, and, bidden to keep silence for his snorts, We pledge each other with nods. Such insolence of shameless Malchio we endure, Nor can we be avenged, Rufus: he sucks cocks.

LXXXII Commend these little books too to Venuleius, Rufus, and ask him to charge a little leisure to me, and, forgetting a while his cares and his own works, not to weigh my trifles with a sour ear. But let him read them neither after the first cup nor the last, but when Bacchus in the middle loves his battles. If it's too much to have read both books, let one roll be folded back: so the work, divided, will be brief.

LXXXII Why did you promise me two hundred thousand, Gaurus, if you couldn't give me ten thousand, Gaurus? Or can you and won't? I ask, isn't that more shameful? Go, may you perish, Gaurus: you're a paltry man.

LXXXII A certain man, Rufus, having lately inspected me carefully, like a buyer or a trainer, when he'd marked me with face and finger, "Are you," he said, "are you that famous Martial, whose naughtiness and jokes are known to everyone who hasn't a Batavian ear?" I smiled modestly, and with a slight nod didn't deny I was who he'd said. "Why then," he said, "do you have a bad cloak?" I replied, "Because I'm a bad poet." That this may not happen too often to the poet, send me, Rufus, good cloaks.

LXXXII So large a sheath clothes Menophilus' penis that it alone would be enough for all the comic actors. I had believed — for we often bathe together — that he was anxious, Flaccus, to spare his voice: but while he played in the middle of the wrestling-ground, with the crowd looking on, the sheath slipped off the poor man: he was circumcised.

LXXXII Since the crowd gives you their querulous little books, Augustus, and we too give our small songs to our lord, we know that a god can find leisure alike for affairs and the Muses, and that these garlands too please you. Bear with your bards, Augustus: we are your sweet glory, we are your earlier care and your delight. Not the oak alone becomes you, nor Phoebus' laurel: let our civic crown of ivy be made for you too.

pr. Greetings, my Toranius, dearest brother. The epigram that stands outside the order of the pages I wrote to Stertinius, a most distinguished man, who wished to set up my likeness in his library. About this I thought I should write to you, lest you not know who this Avitus is who is addressed. Farewell, and prepare a lodging.

Bard renowned, whether you wish it or not, with a lofty heart, to whom your late ashes shall bring worthy rewards, let this brief poem live for you beneath my likeness, which, Avitus, you join with men of no obscure name: 'I am that man, second to none in the praise of trifles, whom you, reader, do not admire, but, I think, love. Let greater men sound greater things: for me, who speak of small matters, it suffices to come often back into your hands.'

LXXXII The astrologer had said you would soon perish, Munna, nor, I think, had he lied to you when he said it. For while you feared to leave anything behind after death, you devoured your father's wealth in luxury, and your two million melted in less than a year: tell me, Munna, is this not to perish soon?

LXXXII If my distress adds anything to your affairs, in the morning or at midnight I'll wear the toga and bear the shrieking blasts of the unkind north wind and endure the storms and take the snow. But if you grow no richer by a single quadrans through my groans and freeborn torments, spare me, I pray, worn out, and let go these vain labours that profit you nothing and harm me, Gallus.

LXXXII The guest Philostratus, returning from the waters of Sinuessa to his hired lodging at the bidding of night, nearly died, like Elpenor, by cruel fate, as he tumbled headlong down the long stairs. He'd not have suffered such great perils, Nymphs, if he'd drunk your waters instead.

LXXXII There's no escaping Menogenes in the baths and around the bathhouse, however you may wish to, by every art. He'll catch the warm ball with right hand and left, so as to charge you often with the catches he made. He'll gather and bring back the slack bladder from the dust, and, even if he's already bathed, even if already in slippers. If you take up your towels, he'll say they're whiter than snow, though they be filthier than a baby's bib. As you comb your scanty hairs with the cut comb, he'll say you've arranged the locks of Achilles. He'll himself bring you a swig from the dregs of a smoky flagon, and keep gathering the sweat of your brow. He'll praise everything, marvel at everything, until, having endured a thousand vexations, you say, "Come!"
LXXXII. Oysters I have just come, a shell drunk with Baian Lucrine: Now in my luxury I thirst for noble garum.
LXXXII. Brooms The palm-broom bears witness it once was prized. But now the cleaner-up has left the broom at leisure.
LXXXIII Your little dog licks your mouth and lips, Manneia: No wonder, if a dog enjoys eating filth.

LXXXIII You disfigured the wretched adulterer, husband, And the maimed features, robbed of nose and ears, Seek for what they were before. Do you believe you are sufficiently avenged? You are wrong: that man can still force the mouth.
LXXXIII You advise me, Cordus, to make my epigrams shorter. "Do for me what Chione does": I could not be briefer.

LXXXIII Nothing is worse than you, Naevolus, when carefree; the same man when anxious, nothing is better than you, Naevolus. Carefree, you return no greeting, you despise everyone, no man is free in your eyes, no man born: anxious, you give gifts, you greet your lord and king, you invite to dinner. Be anxious, Naevolus.
LXXXIII You pursue, I flee; you flee, I pursue; this is my disposition: I don't want what you want, Dindymus, and I want what you don't.

LXXXIII As much as anxious Etruscus's father's fortune, so much, highest of leaders, do they both owe you. For with your right hand you recalled the thunderbolts you'd hurled: I'd wish such conduct were in the fires of Jove; if your nature, Caesar, belonged to the supreme Thunderer, a hand would rarely use the whole thunderbolt. Etruscus attests to both gifts of yours, that it fell to him both as companion and as returnee.
LXXXIII While the barber Eutrapelus goes round Lupercus' face and paints his cheeks, a second beard comes up.

LXXXIII Among the great wonders of your arena, Caesar, which surpass the famous shows of leaders of old, the eyes confess they owe much, but the ears more, to you, because those who used to recite now watch.

LXXXIII You gather your sparse hairs from here and there and cover the broad field of your gleaming bald head, Marinus, with the hair from your temples; but at the wind's bidding the disturbed locks return and restore themselves, and ring your bare head with great curls on this side and that: between Spendophorus and Telesphorus you'd think Cyda's Hermeros was standing. Won't you confess yourself an old man more simply, so you may at last seem to be a single person! Nothing is uglier than a bald man with hair.
LXXXIII No one lives free of charge at your house unless rich and childless. No one, Sosibianus, lets a house for more.

LXXXIII Fabianus, the mocker of ruptures, whom all balls lately feared as he spoke against swollen hydroceles, more than two Catos could say, suddenly in the Neronian baths saw himself, poor wretch, and began to keep silent.
LXXXIII. Prawns The blue Liris loves us, whom Marica's wood Shelters: from there we prawns come, a vast throng.
LXXXIII. An Ivory Back-Scratcher This hand will guard your shoulders from the biting nuisance Of the flea, or anything fouler than a flea.

LXXXIV Quirinalis does not think he should take a wife, Though he wants to have sons, and has found A way to manage it: he beds his maidservants, And fills his house and lands with home-bred knights. Quirinalis is a true father of a family.

LXXXIV Soft and yielding to men was the Poeantian hero: So Venus is said to have avenged the wounds of Paris. Why Sicilian Sertorius licks the cunt, this is the reason: . . . By him, Rufus, Eryx seems to have been slain.
LXXXIV What does your adulteress say? I did not say a girl, Gongylion. What then? Your tongue.
LXXXIV There is no one in the people or the whole city who can prove by his own account that Thais has gone to bed with him, though many desire and many ask. Is Thais so chaste, I ask? No—she sucks.

LXXXIV Now the gloomy boy, his nuts abandoned, is called back by his bawling schoolmaster, and, badly betrayed by the coaxing dice-box, just dragged from his secret cookshop, the soaked gambler begs the aedile off. The Saturnalia have all gone by, and you've sent me no little gifts, not even smaller ones, Galla, than you used to. Well, let my December pass like that: you know surely, I think, that your own Saturnalia are coming now, the Kalends of March; then I'll give you back, Galla, what you gave.
LXXXIV Philippus is carried, in good health, by eight bearers, Avitus. If you think him in health, Avitus, you're mad.

LXXXIV While my likeness is being shaped for Caecilius Secundus and the painted panel breathes from a skilful hand, go, book, to Getic Peuce and the recumbent Hister: he holds those places, the peoples thoroughly tamed. You will give small, but sweet, gifts to a dear comrade: my face will be surer in my song; proof against any chances, blottable by no years, it will live, when the work of Apelles dies.

LXXXIV When your sacred loyalty stood, Norbanus, for our lord Caesar against sacrilegious frenzies, I was playing these things, safe in the Pierian shade, a known cultivator of your friendship. The Raetian told of me to you on the Vindelician shores, nor was the North unaware of my name: oh, how often, not denying an old friend, you said, 'That poet is mine, mine!' All my work, which for twice three years now joined my reader gave you before, the author will now give.
LXXXIV You wonder why Afer doesn't go off to bed? You see, Caedicianus, the one he reclines with.

LXXXIV Whoever does not yet seek to descend to the Stygian shades, let him flee, if he's wise, the barber Antiochus. White arms are torn by less savage knives when the god-frenzied crowd raves to Phrygian measures; gentler Alcon cuts through tangled ruptures and dresses broken bones with a workman's hand. Let this man shear the destitute Cynics and Stoic chins and strip the horse's neck of its dusty mane. Let him scrape wretched Prometheus beneath the Scythian crag, he'll call for the executioner bird with its hard breast; Pentheus will flee to his mother, Orpheus to the Maenads, only let the barbarous weapons of Antiochus sound. These scars, however many you count on my chin, such as sit on an old boxer's brow, no heavy wife made with angry nails: it's the steel of Antiochus and his criminal hand. Of all animals the goat alone has sense: he lives bearded, so as not to endure Antiochus.

LXXXIV I'd not wanted, Polytimus, to violate your hair, but I'm glad to have granted this to your prayers. Such were you, lately shorn Pelops, and you gleamed with your locks laid aside, that the bride could see all the ivory.
LXXXIV. Parrot-Wrasse This parrot-wrasse, which comes half-eaten from the sea's waves, Is good in its innards; the rest tastes cheap.
LXXXIV. A Book-Rest Lest your toga or cloak make your books bristle, This fir will give your scrolls a long span of life.

LXXXV When the witty auctioneer was selling well-tended hills And the lovely acres of suburban soil, "He is wrong," he said, "who thinks Marius is forced To sell: he owes nothing—rather, he is a lender." "What is the reason, then?" "He lost all his slaves there, And his cattle and crops; he does not like the place." Who would set a price, except a man who wanted to lose Everything? So the unlucky land clings to Marius.

LXXXV A guard of snow-white cooled drink, enclosed in light wicker, This shall be your gift at the season of Saturn. Because I sent you the gifts of summer in the month of December, If you complain, send me back a threadbare toga.

LXXXV Who persuaded you to cut off the adulterer's nose? It was not with this part, husband, that you were wronged. Fool, what have you done? Your wife has lost nothing here, Since the prick of your Deiphobus is safe.
LXXXV We drink from glass, you from myrrhine ware, Ponticus. Why? So that a clear cup won't betray your two kinds of wine.

LXXXV See, the sixth book is published for me without you, Rufus Camonius, nor does the book hope for you as reader, friend: the impious land of the Cappadocians, seen by you under an ill star, returns ashes and bones to your father. Pour out tears, Bononia, bereft of your Rufus, and let the lament resound through all Aemilia: alas, what piety, alas how brief an age has perished! He had just seen the fifth rewards of the Alphean games. You, who used to unroll our sport in a mindful breast, you, Rufus, used to hold all my jokes by heart, receive, with weeping, the brief poem of your grieving friend, and consider these to have been the incense for one absent.
LXXXV That you write certain quatrains not without wit, and a few couplets prettily, Sabellus, I praise, but do not marvel. It is easy to write epigrams prettily; but to write a book is hard.

LXXXV Whenever our Paulus is rather indisposed, Atilius, he keeps not himself but his guests from food. You, indeed, suffer a sudden and feigned indisposition, but my dole, Paulus, has stretched out its feet.

LXXXV Old Ladon now, a boatman of a Tiber barge, bought a farm near the waters he loved. And since wandering Tiber often pressed it with rushing waves and broke up the fields with its wintry flood, he filled with stones his discharged boat, which stood on the high bank, and set it against the shallows. So he turned aside the excessive waters. Who could believe it? The sunken boat brought aid to its master.
LXXXV Your tongue was suddenly struck by lightning, Zoilus, while you were licking. Surely, Zoilus, now you'll fuck.
LXXXV You say buggerers' mouths smell. If this is true, Fabullus, as you say: what do you think cunt-lickers' mouths smell of?
LXXXV. Coracinus You are first snatched up, coracinus, in the Nile's market: No fish has higher glory for the Pellaean gullet.
LXXXV. A Peacock-Couch The bird of Juno gives the bed-frame its most lovely name With its painted feathers — but it was Argus before.

LXXXVI Novius is my neighbour, and from our windows He can be touched by the hand. Who would not envy me, and think me Blessed at every hour, For having a yoked companion to enjoy? He is as far from me as Terentianus, Who now governs Nilotic Syene. I cannot dine with him, nor even see him, Nor hear him, nor in the whole city Is anyone so near to us and so far. One of us must move further off. Let a man be Novius's neighbour or lodger If he does not wish to see Novius.

LXXXVI That I do not glory in verse read backwards, Nor read in reverse the catamite Sotades, That no Greekish echo anywhere chimes back, Nor does the brilliant Attis dictate to me A galliambic soft with its enfeebling: I am not, Classicus, so bad a poet for that. What if you bade Ladas, against his will, Take to the slender paths of the spring-board? It is base to have trifles that are hard to make, And foolish is the labour of silly things. Let Palaemon write poems for the schoolboy rings; It pleases me to please a few choice ears.

LXXXVI That you should not, chaste lady, read the wanton part of the book, I foretold and warned you: yet, look, you are reading it. But if you watch Panniculus and Latinus, chaste lady,— These things are no more shameless than the mimes—read on.

LXXXVI If you wish to win approval from Attic ears, I urge and advise you, little book, to please learned Apollinaris. Nothing is more exacting and erudite, but nothing more candid and kind: if he holds you in his heart, on his lips, you need fear no sneers from the spiteful, nor will you give the mackerel troublesome coats. If he condemns you, you may at once run to the fishmongers' shelves, fit paper for boys to scribble on the back.

LXXXVI Setine wine and the master's snows and thick goblets. When shall I drink you with the doctor not forbidding? Foolish and ungrateful and unworthy of so great a gift is he who would rather be the heir of rich Midas. Let him possess Libyan harvests and the Hermus and the Tagus, and let him drink warm water, who envies me.

LXXXVI I used to be invited to your birthday feasts, back when I was not your friend, Sextus: what has happened, I ask, what has suddenly happened, after so many pledges between us, after so many years, that I, an old comrade, am passed over? But I know the reason: no pound of refined Spanish silver came to you from me, no light toga, no fresh cloaks. A dole that drives a bargain is no dole; you feed gifts, Sextus, not friends. Now you'll say to me, 'Let the summoner be flogged.'

LXXXVI That Silius, more than once mighty in Ausonian speech, groaned at the hastened fate of his Severus, I sadly complained with the Pierian band and Phoebus. 'I myself wept my own Linus,' said Apollo: and he looked back at his Calliope, who stood nearest his brother, and said: 'You too have a wound. Look at the Tarpeian and the Palatine Thunderer: Lachesis, daring the unspeakable, wounded both Joves. When you see godheads subject to harsh fates, you may free the gods of the charge of envy.'

LXXXVI No one ever burned so inflamed with a new mistress as Laurus blazed with love of the ball. But he who was the prime player while his prime years flowered, now that he's ceased to play, is the prime ball.

LXXXVI That a doctor may soothe your throat, which a harsh cough constantly vexes, Parthenopaeus, he orders you given honey and nuts and sweet cakes and whatever doesn't let boys be fierce. But you don't stop coughing all day long. This is no cough, Parthenopaeus, it's greed.
LXXXVI You have thirty boys and as many girls: you have one prick, and it won't stand. What will you do?
LXXXVI. Sea-Urchins Though it pricks your fingers with its sharp shell, Once the rind is off, the sea-urchin will be soft.
LXXXVI. A Saddle-Cloth Hunter, take the housing for your girt-up cob: For a sore tends to rise from a bare horse.

LXXXVII That you may not reek heavily, Fescennia, of yesterday's wine, In your excess you devour the lozenges of Cosmus. That breakfast coats your teeth, but stops nothing When the belch comes back from the depths below. What of it, that the poison, mixed with perfume, smells the worse, And the doubled odour of your breath travels further? So drop these tricks now too well known, these thefts found out, And be simply, honestly drunk.
LXXXVII You say, Sextus, that pretty girls burn with love of you, You who have the face of a man swimming under water.

LXXXVII Rumour reports, Chione, that you have never been had And that nothing is purer than your cunt. Yet you bathe covered, not in the part you should: If you have any shame, move your loincloth to your face.

LXXXVII Your Bassa, Fabullus, always keeps an infant by her, calls it her sport and her darling, and—what you'd wonder at more—she's no fond of children. What's the reason, then? Bassa is in the habit of farting.
LXXXVII May the gods give you, and you, Caesar, whatever you deserve: may the gods give me, and you, what I want, if I've deserved it.

LXXXVII After seven cups of Opimian wine, when I lie thick-tongued with deep draughts, you bring me some tablets or other and say, 'I have just ordered Nasta to be freed — he's a slave inherited from my father —: sign.' Tomorrow it will go better, Lupercus: just now my ring seals the wine-flask.

LXXXVII Come, let pious Rome feel the October Kalends of eloquent Restitutus: with all your tongues favour him, and with your prayers; we keep his birthday—be silent, lawsuits. Away with the wax candle of the dried-up client, and let the empty triple tablets and brief napkins wait for the jests of icy December. Let the richer compete in gifts: Agrippa's swollen trader should bring cloaks made by Cadmus' townsmen; the man charged with brawls and a drunken night should send dinner-clothes to his advocate; the girl who has bested her slandered man should present true sardonyx, but herself hand it over; the old man who admires our forefathers should give an embossed work of Phidian chasing; the hunter a hare, the farmer a kid, the fisherman should bring the sea's spoils. If each sends what is his own, what do you think the poet will send you, Restitutus?

LXXXVII You were rich once: but then you were a buggerer, and for a long time no woman was known to you. Now you chase old women. O what poverty drives one to! That woman, Charidemus, makes a fucker of you.

LXXXVII Cotta, having complained twice that he'd lost his slippers, while he brings a careless home-born slave to his feet, the only one to attend the poor man and make a crowd, devised—a shrewd and cunning man— a way not to suffer such a loss more often: he began to go to dinner unshod.
LXXXVII. Murex-Shells Dyed with our blood, ungrateful man, you put on Your cloaks — and that's not enough: we are food as well.
LXXXVII. A Dining-Couch Take the crescent-couch inlaid with horn: It seats eight; let whoever is your friend come.

LXXXVIII Alcimus, snatched from your master in your growing years, Whom the Labican earth covers with light turf, Receive no nodding weight of Parian marble, Which empty toil gives the ashes, doomed to fall, But pliant box and the dark shade of the vine And meadows green and dewy with my tears Receive, dear boy, as memorials of my grief: Here for all time shall your honour live. When Lachesis brings me to my final years, No otherwise do I bid my own ashes lie.
LXXXVIII You recite nothing, and yet you wish, Mamercus, to seem a poet. Be whatever you wish—provided you recite nothing.
LXXXVIII They are twin brothers, but lick different parts. Tell me, are they more unlike, or more alike?

LXXXVIII You sent back no gift for my small present, and now five days of Saturn have already passed. So not even six scruples of Septician silver were sent, nor a napkin from a grumbling client, nor a jar reddened with the blood of an Antipolitan tunny, nor one bearing small Syrian figs, nor a little basket of wrinkled Picene olives— so that you could say you remembered me? You'll deceive others with kind words and looks, for to me you'll now be a known dissembler.
LXXXVIII This morning I greeted you by your real name, by chance, and didn't call you my lord, Caecilianus. You ask how much such great freedom costs me? It cost me a hundred farthings.

LXXXVIII It is said, if the report is true, that lovely Vienna holds my little books among her delights: there every old man and youth and boy reads me, and the chaste girl before her grim husband. This I would rather than that my songs were sung by those who drink the Nile straight from its very mouth; than that my Tagus should fill me with Spanish gold, and Hybla and Hymettus feed my bees. So I am something, then, nor am I deceived by the gift of a flattering tongue: now, Lausus, I think I'll believe you.

LXXXVIII While you were angling for me, you sent me gifts: now that you've caught me, Rufus, you give me nothing. To keep what you've caught, send the caught one gifts too, lest the ill-fed boar flee from the cage.
LXXXVIII For many days now, Lupus, Charisianus says he can't bugger. When his comrades just now asked the reason, he said he had a loose belly.
LXXXVIII Tongilianus has a nose: I know it, I don't deny it. But now Tongilianus has nothing but a nose.
