LXXXVIII. Gudgeons Though banquets be lavish in the Venetian lands, The gudgeon is wont to be the start of the dinner.
LXXXVIII. A Relish-Tray If you believe a female tortoise is set in me, You're deceived: I'm the male prey of the sea.

LXXXIX You always whisper in everyone's ear, Cinna, Whispering even what may be said before a crowd of witnesses. You laugh in the ear, complain, accuse, lament, You sing in the ear, you judge, you are silent, you shout, And so deep has this disease settled in you, That often, Cinna, you praise Caesar in the ear.

LXXXIX That you delight in drawing out the night with too much wine, I pardon you: you have the vice, Gaurus, of Cato. That you write poems with no Muse and no Apollo, You ought to be praised: you have this from Cicero. That you vomit, is Antony's vice; that you live in luxury, Apicius's. But that you suck cocks—tell me, whose vice is that?
LXXXIX Eat lettuce and eat soft mallows: For you have the face, Phoebus, of a man straining at stool.

LXXXIX Stop now, enough now, little book, we've already reached the very end-knobs. Yet you want to go further on and on, nor can you be held back at the last sheet, as if your work were not yet done, which was done at the first page too. Now the reader grumbles and grows faint, now the copyist himself says it too: "Stop now, enough now, little book."

LXXXIX When, now at midnight, Panaretus, drunk, sought the late chamber-pot with snapping thumb, a Spoletine flask was given him, but one he'd emptied himself, nor had the whole jar been enough for him alone. He, with utmost faith of the vessel, measured back his wine and gave back the full weight of his wine-jar. You wonder the flask held as much as he'd drunk? Stop wondering, Rufus: he'd drunk it neat.
LXXXIX Go, happy rose, and with your soft garlands crown the hair of my Apollinaris. And remember to bind them, white — but only in time to come, so may Venus love you always — when his hair is grey.
LXXXIX By too hard a law you force a guest to write verses, Stella. 'One may, of course, write bad ones.'

LXXXIX This Juno, Polyclitus, your labour and happy glory, which Phidian hands would long to have earned, shines with so great a face that on Ida she'd have surpassed the goddesses convicted with the judge in no doubt. Did not her brother love his own Juno, Polyclitus, the brother could love your Juno.
LXXXIX Why do you send me untouched garlands, Polla? I'd rather hold roses rumpled by you.
LXXXIX That you bind your head with wool, Charinus, it's not your ears that ache, but your hair.
LXXXIX. Bass The woolly bass takes in the mouth of Euganean Timavus, Fed on fresh waters mingled with the sea's salt.
LXXXIX. A Citron-Wood Table Take these blessed woods, gifts of Atlas: Whoever gives gifts of gold will give less.

XC Because I never saw you, Bassa, joined to men, And no story gave you a lover, But a crowd of your own sex was always Performing every service round you, with no man coming near, You seemed to us, I admit, a Lucretia: But you, Bassa—the shame of it—were a fornicator. You dare to bring two female parts together, And your monstrous lust counterfeits a man. You have devised a marvel worthy of the Theban riddle: Here, where there is no man, there is adultery.

XC Quintilian, supreme guide of wandering youth, Glory, Quintilian, of the Roman toga, That I hasten to live, poor and not useless in my years, Forgive me: no one hastens enough to live. Let him put it off who longs to outdo his father's fortune And crowds his halls with too many ancestral busts. A hearth, and a roof that does not resent the black smoke, Delight me, and a living spring and untouched grass. Let me have a well-fed home-born slave, a wife not too learned, A night with sleep, a day without litigation.
XC Galla wants, does not want, to give to me, and I cannot say, Since she wants and does not want, what Galla wants for herself.
XC Gellia has only one lover. This is fouler still: she's the wife of two.
XC Matho boasts that I have made an uneven little book: if it is true, Matho praises my poems. Calvinus and Umber write even books: an even book, Creticus, is the one that is bad throughout.

XC So, reclining on the flowery grass, where here and there the curving wave with gem-like streams stirs the pebble, all troubles shut far off, may you pierce the ice with a dark draught, your brow red with stitched garlands; so may you have for yourself alone a catamite boy and a most chaste girl lust for you: the ill-famed Cyprus, in too great a heat, beware of, I warn and beg you, Flaccus, when the threshing-floor wears the crackling harvest and the burning mane of the lion rages. But you, goddess of Paphos, send back, send back to my prayers the young man unharmed: so may the Kalends of March serve you, and with incense and wine and victim may there be poured for you at your white altars many a cut square of cake.

XC Why do you pluck your old cunt, Ligeia? Why stir up the ashes of your own tomb? Such elegance befits girls —for you can no longer even seem an old woman—; that, believe me, Ligeia, is a charming thing not for Hector's mother, but his wife. You're wrong, if you think this a cunt to which a cock has ceased to belong. So if you've any shame, Ligeia, don't pluck the beard of a dead lion.

XC You approve no poems that run on a smooth path, but those that fall through ruts and over deep rocks, and you reckon a thing greater than Maeonian verse: "Here lies Metrophanes, little pillar of Lucilius;" and astounded you read "of the fruit-bearing earth," and whatever Accius and Pacuvius vomit up. You want me to imitate the old poets and your own, Chrestillus? May I die, if you don't know what a cock tastes like.

XC Maro made a vow for a sick friend—but loudly— who had a heavy and burning semi-tertian fever, that, if the sick man were not sent to the Stygian shades, a welcome victim should fall to great Jove. The doctors began to promise certain recovery. Now Maro makes vows, so as not to pay his vow.
XC. Gilt-Head Bream Not every gilt-head earns the praise and the price, But only the one whose sole food is the Lucrine shell.
XC. A Maple Table I'm not curl-grained, nor a daughter of the Moorish wood, But my wood too has known elegant feasts.
XCI Though you publish nothing of your own, you carp at my poems, Laelius. Either stop carping at ours, or publish your own.

XCI Sure salvation of all things, glory of the earth, Caesar, By whose safety we believe the great gods exist, If the poems of mine, so often read in hasty little books, Have held your eyes a while, Permit it to seem—what fortune forbids to be— That I be thought the father of three children. These shall be my consolation, if I have displeased you; These shall be my reward, if I have pleased.

XCI When a discharged soldier was seeking the fields of his native Ravenna, He joined his journey with the half-man troop of Cybele. A boy clung to him as companion, Achillas, runaway from his master, Remarkable for his beauty and his wantonness. The barren men perceived this: they ask in what part He would sleep. But he too perceived their silent treachery: He lies; they believe. After the wine, sleep is sought: At once the wicked crew seize the iron And geld the old man, who lay on the edge of the couch; For the boy was safe, guarded by the bedstead. There is a story that once a hind was substituted for a virgin, But now a prick was substituted for a hind.
XCI The holy censure of the supreme leader forbids and bans adultery. Rejoice, Zoilus: you don't go with women.
XCI From my little farm, eloquent Juvenal, I send you, look, some Saturnalia nuts. The rest of the fruit the lustful cock of the guardian god gave away to wanton girls.

XCI If to dinner amid opposite stars there summoned me, on this side Caesar's inviter, on that Jove's, though the stars were nearer, the Palatine farther off, these answers to the gods above I would give to bring back: 'Seek one who would rather become the Thunderer's guest: my Jupiter, look, keeps me on earth.'
XCI Almo has all eunuchs and can't get it up himself: and he complains that his Polla bears him nothing.

XCI Canace, daughter of Aeolis, lies entombed in this sepulchre, to whom, small as she was, a seventh and last winter came. Ah, the crime, ah, the outrage! you who hasten to weep, traveller, here it's not allowed to complain of life's brevity: sadder than her death is the manner of death: a hideous plague took her face and settled on her tender mouth, and the cruel disease itself devoured her kisses, nor were her whole lips given to the black pyres. If the fates were coming with so headlong a flight, they ought to have come by another road. But death hastened to close the path of her sweet voice, lest her tongue could bend the hard goddesses.
XCI Since you share a bed with your husband, Magulla, and share a catamite too, why, tell me, do you not share a servant as well? You sigh; the reason is, you fear the wine-jar.
XCI. Sturgeon Send the sturgeon to the Palatine tables: Let rare gifts grace the ambrosial feasts.
XCI. Ivory Tusks You who carry the bulls' great bodies, you ask Whether they could have borne up Libya's beams?

XCII Cestos often complains to me, with eyes not dry, That he is touched by your finger, Mamurianus. There is no need of a finger: have Cestos whole for yourself, If that, Mamurianus, is the only thing you lack. But if there is neither a hearth nor the frame of a bare cot, Nor the chipped cup of Chione or Antiope, If a threadbare and patched cloak hangs from your loins And a Gallic kilt covers half your buttocks, And you feed on the mere smell of a black kitchen And drink filthy water, bent down beside the dog: Then not your arse—for it is no arse that never shits— But the one eye you have left, that I will gouge with my finger: And do not call me jealous, or call me malicious. In short, Mamurianus, bugger on a full belly.
XCII The right of three children, which I asked for, He alone who could granted me, As the reward of my Muses. Farewell, wife. The gift of the master must not be wasted.
XCII My wife asks me to allow her an adulterer, Gallus—but one. Shall I not gouge out, Gallus, this fellow's two eyes?
XCII Though there's chased for you, Annianus, a serpent on your bowl by Myron's art, you drink Vatican wine: you drink poison.

XCII 'If you need anything, you know you've only to ask me' — this you say twice and three times a day, Baccara, in one breath. Grim Secundus duns me in a harsh voice: you hear, and don't know, Baccara, what I need. The rent is demanded of me in your presence, loud and open: you hear, and don't know, Baccara, what I need. I complain my cloaks are cold and threadbare: you hear, and don't know, Baccara, what I need. What I need is this: that you suddenly be struck dumb by some star, so you can't say, Baccara, 'If you need anything.'

XCII What are a master's ills, what a slave's advantages, you do not know, Condylus, who groan that you have long been a slave. A cheap little mat gives you untroubled sleep, while Gaius, look, lies sleepless on feathers. Gaius from first light, trembling, greets so many masters, but you, Condylus, not even a master. 'Pay what you owe, Gaius,' says Phoebus, and from over there Cinnamus: this, Condylus, no one says to you. Do you fear the torturer? Gout in foot and hand racks Gaius, and he would rather suffer a thousand lashes. Because you neither vomit in the morning nor lick cunt, Condylus, would you not rather be yourself three times over than Gaius?

XCII Marrius, cultivator and companion of a quiet life, by whom old Atina boasts as her citizen, to you I commend these twin pines, the glory of the wild grove, and the holm-oaks of the Fauns, and the altars of the Thunderer and rough Silvanus raised by the half-skilled hand of the bailiff, which the blood of lamb or kid has often stained, and the maiden goddess, mistress of the holy shrine, and him you see as guest of his chaste sister, Mars, the patron of my Kalends, and the laurel grove of dainty Flora, into which she fled when Priapus pursued her. All this gentle divinity of my little farm, whether you appease it with blood or incense: "Wherever your Martial is," you'll say, "behold, with this right hand he sacrifices to you with me, an absent priest; count him present, and grant to both whatever either shall ask."
XCII He lies who calls you vicious, Zoilus. You're not a vicious man, Zoilus, but vice itself.

XCII You often ask, Priscus, what sort I'll be, if I become wealthy and suddenly grow powerful. Do you think anyone can describe his future character? Tell me, if you became a lion, what sort would you be?
XCII. Hares Among birds the thrush, if my judgment counts for anything, Among four-footed beasts the hare is the first tidbit.
XCII. A Five-Foot Rule The holm-oak rule, marked with points and closed with a sharp tip, Often serves to expose the contractor's frauds.

XCIII Aquinus rests, joined to faithful Fabricius, Who rejoices to have reached the Elysian homes first. A double altar attests the gifts of the first rank: But there is more in what you read in the shorter line: "Each joined in the sacred bond of a praised life, And—what fame rarely knows—he was a friend."

XCIII "Where is the first," you say, "since this book is the second?" What am I to do, if that one has more modesty? Yet if you would rather, Regulus, that this become the first, You can take one iota from the title.

XCIII Since you have outlived three hundred consuls, Vetustilla, And have three hairs and four teeth, The breast of a grasshopper, the leg and colour of an ant; Since you wear a brow more wrinkled than your gown And breasts like the webs of spiders; Since, compared with your jaws, The Nile crocodile has a narrow gape, And the frogs of Ravenna croak more sweetly, And the gnat of Adria sings more tunefully, And you see about as much as owls see at morning, And you smell like a billy-goat, And you have the rump of a scrawny duck, And your bony cunt outdoes a Cynic graybeard; Since the bath-keeper admits you, with the lamp put out, Only among the whores of the graveyard; Since for you winter falls in the month of August, And not even the plague can thaw you out: You dare, after two hundred deaths, to want to marry And, mad, you seek a man to itch for your ashes. What if Sattia's tombstone wanted to wed? Who will call you spouse, who wife, You whom Philomelus lately called grandmother? But if you demand that your corpse be tickled, Let a couch be spread from Acorus's funeral parlour— The only one that suits your wedding, And let the corpse-burner carry torches before the new bride: Only a funeral brand can enter that cunt.

XCIII Thais smells as foul as not the old jar of a greedy fuller, just now broken in the middle of the road, not a he-goat fresh from love, not a lion's mouth, not the Transtiberine hide stripped from a dog, not a chick rotting in an aborted egg, not an amphora spoiled with tainted fish-sauce. That she may shrewdly swap this stench for another scent, whenever she lays her clothes aside and seeks the baths, she's green with depilatory or hides smeared with sour chalk or is covered three and four times with rich bean-paste. When she's thought herself well safe by a thousand tricks, when she's done it all, Thais smells of Thais.

XCIII Narnia, whom the river, white with its sulphurous current, girdles, scarcely to be reached by a double ridge, why does it please you so often to steal my Quintus from us and detain him with sluggish delay? Why do you ruin for me the worth of my Nomentan farm, which was precious because of its neighbour? But now spare me, Narnia, do not abuse my Quintus: so may you enjoy your bridge forever.

XCIII Why do you delay, boy, to add the immortal Falernian? Double my quarter-measure from the older jar. Now tell me, Catacissus, to which of the gods do I bid you pour six cups? 'It will be Caesar.' Let a stitched rose be fitted ten times to our hair, that there be one who set up the noble work of the sacred line. Now give me twice five kisses, that that name be made which the god bore from the Odrysian world.

XCIII If you should first see, Clemens, the Euganean shores of Helicaon and the fields painted with vine-clad ridges, carry to Sabina of Ateste my poems, not yet made public, but lately dressed in the purple toga. As a rose delights, plucked by the first thumb, so a fresh page, not soiled by the chin, pleases.

XCIII Flame took the Pierian household gods of the bard Theodorus. Does this please the Muses and you, Phoebus? O crime, O great outrage and reproach of the gods, that the house and its master did not burn together!

XCIII By what method she could kiss her lover in her husband's presence, Fabulla found out. She keeps kissing a little fool: him, drenched with many kisses, the lover snatches at once, and, filled up with his own, sends back straightway to the laughing lady. How much greater a fool is the husband!
XCIII. Boar The bristled beast, dreaded in the Diomedean fields, That fell to the Aetolian spear — such was its kind.
XCIII. Antique Cups This is no recent glory, nor work of our chisel: Mentor was the first to drink from these, while he made them.
XCIV You sang badly, Aegle, while you were being had. Now you sing well; but you are not to be kissed.
XCIV You say the hare is not cooked and call for the whip. You would rather, Rufus, carve up the cook than the hare.

XCIV Gold-inlaid dishes are always set before Calpetanus, whether he dines out or at home in the city. So he dines always, even in an inn, so in the country. Has he nothing else, then? No—and not even his own.
XCIV What the small onyx jar lately held was perfume: after Papylus smelled it — behold, it is fish-sauce.

XCIV With a Santonican herb-drugged drink Hippocrates gave me a cup: the cheek of the man! Now he asks me for honey-wine. Never were you so stupid even, I think, Glaucus, who gave golden gifts to one who gave you bronze. Does anyone ask for a sweet gift in return for a bitter one? Let him have it — but only if he drinks it in hellebore.

XCIV No Massylian serpent guards my orchards, nor does the royal land of Alcinous serve me, but my Nomentan garden buds in safety with its tree, nor do the leaden apples fear a thief. So these apples, just now born in the middle Subura, I send—the waxen fruits of my autumn.

XCIV That you're too envious and everywhere disparage my little books, I forgive: circumcised poet, you're wise. This too I don't mind, that while you carp at my poems, you plunder them: even so, circumcised poet, you're wise. This is what tortures me, that, born in Jerusalem itself, you bugger my boy, circumcised poet. Look, you deny it and swear to me by the temples of the Thunderer. I don't believe it: swear, circumcised one, by Anchialus.

XCIV I was writing epic; you began to write: I gave way, lest my poems should stand as rivals to yours. My Thalia transferred herself to the tragic buskins: you too fitted the long train to yourself. I moved the strings of the lyre, refined by Calabrian Muses: ambitious one, you snatch the new quills from me. I venture satires: you labour to be a Lucilius. I play at light elegies: you play at the same too. What could be less? I began to fashion epigrams: hence too my palm is now sought by you. Choose what you don't want—for what shame is it to want everything?— and if there's anything you don't want, Tucca, leave it to me.
XCIV. Does The boar is feared for its tusk, horns defend the stag: We unwarlike does — what are we but prey?
XCIV. Bold Cups We are the plebeian embossed-ware of bold glass, And our jewel is not cracked by boiling water.
XCV That you always shout, Aelius, that you bawl over the pleaders, You do not do this for nothing: you are paid to keep quiet.

XCV You never say "good day," but always return it, Naevolus, A thing the raven too often is wont to say first. Why, I ask you, Naevolus, do you expect me to say it: For I think, Naevolus, you are neither my better nor my elder. Each Caesar bestowed rewards on me, the praised, And gave the paternal rights of three children. I am read by many a mouth, and fame, without waiting for the pyre, Gives my name, known throughout the towns. There is something in this too: Rome has seen me a tribune, And I sit where Oceanus rouses you. As many as have been made citizens by Caesar's gift to me, I do not think you have so many slaves. But you are buggered, and prettily, Naevolus, you wag your rump. Now, now you are the better, Naevolus, you win: good day.

XCV It is winter, and rough December is stiff with cold, yet you dare, with a snowy kiss, to stop everyone you meet on this side and that, and to kiss all Rome, Linus. What heavier, what crueller thing could you do if you were struck and flogged? In this cold let no wife kiss me, nor my young daughter with her coaxing lips. But you are sweeter and more refined, you from whose dog's nostrils hangs a livid icicle, and whose beard is stiff, such as the Cilician barber reaps with upturned shears from a Cinyphian goatherd. I'd rather meet a hundred cunt-lickers, and I fear a fresh-castrated priest of Cybele less. So if you have any sense and shame, your winter kissings, Linus, I beg you put off till the month of April.
XCV He was Alfius before; now he has begun to be Olfius, since Athenagoras took a wife.

95b. XCVb You believe, Callistratus, that 'Athenagoras' is a real name. May I die if I know who Athenagoras is. But suppose I do speak a real name, Callistratus: it is not I, but your Athenagoras, who errs.
XCV Your husband sent back an infant to you, Galla, your lover too. These two, I think, plainly deny they've fucked you.
XCV Whenever you fall in with the kisses of cocksuckers, think you're plunging your head, Flaccus, into a bath-tub.

XCV The most pathic little books of Mussetius, which rival the Sybaritic little books, and the pages dipped in itching salt, read, Instantius Rufus; but let your girl be with you, lest you sing the wedding-song with lustful hands and become a husband without a woman.
XCV. Oryx Not the least prey of the morning's wild beasts, The fierce oryx — how many dogs' deaths it costs me!
XCV. A Chased Golden Bowl Though I redden, high-born, with Galician metal, I glory more in the art: for this is Mys' labor.

XCVI If it is no trouble, and you do not mind, limping verse, We ask you to say a few words to our Maternus, Whispered in his ear, that he alone may hear. That lover of gloomy cloaks, Dressed in Baetic grey and dull dun, Who thinks men in scarlet are no men And calls amethyst-purple the garb of women, May praise the natural and have, if he likes, forever His dusky colours—his morals are pale green. He will ask why I suspect a man is soft. We bathe together: he looks at nothing above, But watches the athletes with devouring eyes And cannot keep his lips off the sight of their cocks. You ask who this is? The name has slipped my mind.
XCVI You lick my girl, you do not have her, And you boast like an adulterer and a fornicator. If I catch you, Gargilius, you will hold your tongue.

XCVI Here I am buried, Bassus' grief, the infant Urbicus, to whom greatest Rome gave birth and name. Six months were lacking to me of my first three years, when the grim goddesses cut short my thread of life. What good to me was beauty, speech, or age? Give tears to my tomb, you who read this: so may the one you wish to outlive you not go down to Lethe's waters, unless later than Nestor.
XCVI The physician Herodes had filched a ladle from a sick man: caught, he said, 'Fool, why then do you drink?'

XCVI That I often speak too much of remote nations, Avitus, you wonder, made old in the Latian city, and that I thirst for gold-bearing Tagus and my native Salo and seek again the humble fields of a well-stocked cottage. That land pleases me, in which a small estate makes me blessed and slender means run to luxury: here the field is fed, there it feeds; here the hearth warms with a grudging fire, there it gleams with a mighty blaze; here hunger is costly and the market a bankrupter, there the table is laid with the riches of its own country; here four togas or more are worn through in a summer, there one covers me for four autumns. Go now, court patrons, when a place can provide you whatever a friend does not, Avitus.

XCVI Marcia, not the Rhine, leaps here, German: why do you stand in the way and forbid the boy the bounty of the rich pool? Barbarian, the conquering water ought not, with a citizen pushed aside, relieve a captive servant's thirst.

XCVI Since your husband's life and fidelity are known to you, and no woman oppresses or troubles your bed, why, foolish one, are you tormented, as if by rivals, over the servants, in whom love is both brief and fleeting? I'll prove the boys serve you more than their master: they make it so that you're your husband's only woman; they give what you, his wife, don't want to give. "Yet I do give it," you say, "lest my husband's wandering love should stray from our bed." It's not the same thing: I want a Chian fig, I don't want a marisca: in case you doubt which is the Chian, yours is the marisca. A matron and a wife ought to know her own limits: yield their own part to the boys, use your own part.
XCVI. Stag This was that stag tamed by your halter, Cyparissus. Or was this rather your stag, Silvia?
XCVI. Vatinian Cups Take the cheap memorial of the cobbler Vatinius — A cup; but his nose was longer.

XCVII When everyone is shouting, then alone do you speak, Naevolus, And you think yourself an advocate and a pleader. By that method no one could fail to be eloquent. Look, all are silent now: Naevolus, say something.
XCVII Lest Chione read this book, I commission you, Rufus. She was hurt by my poem, and she can hurt back.

XCVII If you know Caesius Sabinus well, my little book, glory of mountainous Umbria, the townsman of my Aulus Pudens, you will give him these, even when he is busy: though a thousand cares press and weigh on him, he will still have time for my songs: for he loves me, and reads me next to the noble little books of Turnus. Oh, what a name is being won for you! Oh, what glory! how frequent a lover! You will sound at banquets, at the forum, at mansions, crossroads, porticoes, taverns. You are sent to one, you are read by all.

XCVII A certain man bursts with envy, dearest Julius, because Rome reads me, he bursts with envy. He bursts with envy, because in every crowd I am always pointed at with a finger, he bursts with envy. He bursts with envy, because both Caesars granted me the right of children, he bursts with envy. He bursts with envy, because I have a sweet country place near the city and a small house in the city, he bursts with envy. He bursts with envy, because I am dear to my friends, because I am a frequent guest, he bursts with envy. He bursts with envy, because I am loved and approved: let him burst, whoever bursts with envy.
XCVII While the light pyre is built of papyrus soon to burn, while my weeping wife buys myrrh and cassia, the grave now ready, now the bier, now the embalmer, Numa wrote me his heir: he got well.
XCVII In one night I can do it four times: but if I can do you once, Telesilla, in four years, may I die.

XCVII Though you have a wife such as a shameless husband could scarcely ask for in his prayers, rich, noble, learned, chaste, you burst your flank, Bassus, but on long-haired boys, whom you got with your wife's dowry. And so the prick, bought back for many thousands, returns to its mistress and goes limp; nor, roused by coaxing words, nor begged with a soft thumb, does it rise. Have some shame at last, or let's go to court. This isn't yours, Bassus: you sold it.
XCVII. The Wild-Ass Foal While the wild ass is young and the foal still grazes On its mother alone, it has this name — babyish, but brief.
XCVII. Gold-Inlaid Platters Don't disgrace the big gold platters with a little mullet: At the very least it should weigh two pounds.
XCVIII Diodorus goes to law, Flaccus, and suffers from gout. But he hands his counsel nothing: that is gout of the hand.
XCVIII You ask how scrawny your arse is? You can sodomize, Sabellus, with your arse.
XCVIII You buy everything, Castor: so it will come about that you sell everything.
XCVIII The yield of the vintage did not everywhere fail, Ovidius; the great rain helped. Coranus made a hundred amphoras — of water.

XCVIII Though a servant adds my Caecuban, looser than an Idaean catamite, than whom no daughter reclines more elegant, no wife, no mother of yours, no sister, do you want me rather to gaze at your lamps or your old citron-wood and Indian tusks? But so you won't suspect me as I recline, provide from the herd and the squalid farmstead shaven, shaggy, raw, puny sons of a stinking swineherd for me. This jealousy will destroy you: you can't, Publius, have these manners and these servants both.

XCVIII There's no escaping the kissers, Flaccus. They press in, delay you, pursue, run to meet you, from this side and that, everywhere, on every road. No sharp ulcer or gleaming pustules, no grim chin or filthy scabs, no lips smeared with greasy salve, no drop from a frozen nose will help you. They kiss you sweating and they kiss you freezing, and they kiss you saving up your bridal kiss. It won't save you to have your head covered with cowls, nor your litter shut safe with leather and curtain, nor will a chair, however often closed, protect you: the kisser will get in through every crack. Not the consulship itself, not the tribunate nor the six rods, nor the proud staff of a bawling lictor will drive off the kisser: though you sit on a high tribunal and from the curule chair dispense justice to the nations, the kisser will climb up here and there. He'll kiss you fevered and weeping, he'll give a kiss to you yawning and swimming, he'll give one to you shitting. The sole remedy for the evil is to make a friend of someone you'd not want to kiss you.

XCVIII Baetis, your hair wreathed with an olive-bearing garland, you who dye golden fleeces in your gleaming waters; whom Bromius loves, whom Pallas loves; for whom Albula, ruler of the waters, spreads a ship-bearing path through the straits: with glad omens may Instantius enter your shores, and may this year, as the last, go well for the peoples here. He's not unaware what a burden it is to follow Macer: he who measures his own weight can bear it.
XCVIII. Wild She-Goat You'll see the wild goat hanging from the cliff's height, And hope it will fall: it looks down in scorn on the dogs.
XCVIII. Arretine Ware We warn you, don't too much scorn Arretine ware: Porsena was elegant with Tuscan earthenware.

XCIX Lately you had not a full two million, But you were so lavish and so liberal And so splendid, Calenus, that all Your friends wished you ten million. The god heard our vows and prayers, And within, I think, seven months, Four deaths gave you this. But you, as if it had not been left But snatched from you, your ten million, went off Into such wretched starvation That the more sumptuous dinners, Which once a year you get up for the whole year, You unfold with the dirt of black coin, And we seven, your old companions, Cost you half a pound of lead. What worthy of such merits shall we pray for you? We wish you a hundred million, Calenus. If this should fall to you, you will die of hunger.

XCIX You ought not to be angry, Cerdo, at my little book. It is your trade, not your life, that my poem has wounded. Allow my harmless wit. Why should I not be allowed To jest, if you were allowed to cut throats?

XCIX So may you ever see the Thunderer calm, Crispinus, nor may Rome love you less than your own Memphis: if my songs are read in the Parrhasian court — for they are wont to enjoy Caesar's sacred ear — dare to say of me, like a candid reader: 'This man brings no little credit to your times, and is not too far beneath Marsus and learned Catullus.' This is enough: the rest I entrust to the god himself.
pr. To the Emperor Domitian Caesar Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, Valerius Martialis sends greeting.

All my little books, my lord, to which you have given fame — that is, life — make their supplication to you; and on that account, I think, they will be read. This one, however, which is inscribed as the eighth of my work, enjoys the occasion of devotion more often. So there was less need to labour with my wit, since subject-matter had taken its place: this I have tried now and then to vary with some mixture of jests, lest every verse should heap up on your heavenly modesty its own praises, which might more easily weary you than satisfy me. Yet, although epigrams have been written even by the gravest men of the highest rank in such a way that they seem to have aimed at the verbal license of the mime, I have not allowed mine to speak as wantonly as they are wont. Since the part of the book that is both the larger and the better is bound to the majesty of your sacred name, let it remember that none should approach the temples unless cleansed by religious purification. That my readers may know I shall observe this, I have decided to declare it on the very threshold of this little book in a very brief epigram.

XCIX Marcus Antonius loves my Muses, Atticus, if the saluting paper now reports truly: Marcus, the not-to-be-denied glory of Palladian Toulouse, whom Quiet, the nursling of Peace, begot. You who can bear the long expense of the roads, go, book, a pledge of absent friendship. You were cheap, I confess, if a buyer now sent you; the author will be the great price of your gift: it matters much, believe me, whether water be drunk that flows from the source, or that stagnates in a sluggish pool.
XCIX If these were the Roman features of Socrates, they'd have been such as Julius Rufus has in his Satires.

XCIX Whenever you rise from your chair—I've often noticed it— your wretched tunics bugger you, Lesbia. When you've tried with your right hand, tried with your left, to pluck them out, you extract them with tears and groaning: so they're gripped by the twin Symplegades of your arse and enter your over-large, dark-blue buttocks. You want to mend the unsightly fault? I'll teach you: Lesbia, I advise you neither to rise nor to sit.
XCIX. Gazelle You'll give a pet gazelle to your little son: The crowd, tossing their togas, is wont to ask for it.
C Afra has her "mammas" and "papas," but she herself Can be called the greatest mamma of papas and mammas.

C I sent the courier back to you, Rufus, at the sixth hour, And I think he carried my poems soaked through: For by chance the sky was crashing down with measureless rains. No otherwise ought that book to have been sent.

C For three denarii you invite me, and bid me in the morning, gowned, attend your halls, Bassus, then cling to your side, walk before your chair, go with you to ten widows, more or less. My little toga, indeed, is worn and cheap and old: yet for three denarii, Bassus, I do not buy it.

C Why, fool, do you mix your verses with mine? What have you to do, wretch, with a book that's at war with you? Why do you seek to herd foxes with lions and make owls like to eagles? Though you had one of Ladas' feet, you'd run in vain, idiot, with a wooden leg.

C I don't want a girlfriend, Flaccus, so thin that my rings would circle her arms, who'd scrape me with a bare hip and prick me with her knee, whose loins jut out like a saw, whose arse like a spear-point. But I also don't want a girlfriend of a thousand pounds. I'm a lover of flesh, not a lover of fat.
C. Wild Ass Here's a handsome wild ass: the hunt of Erythraean Tusk must be staged: now away with the curtains.
C. A Drinking-Bowl If the land of learned Catullus is not unknown to you, You've drunk Raetian wines from my crock.

CI That hand, once faithful to my studies, And blessed in its master, and known to the Caesars— Demetrius, in his green years, has forsaken the prime of life: A fourth harvest was added to his three lustres. Yet, that he might not go down a slave to the Stygian shades, When the wicked plague was burning him in its grip, I took thought, and remitted to the sick man all a master's rights: He deserved by my gift to have recovered. Failing, he felt his reward, and called me his patron, Free, as he went to the infernal waters.

CI Appian Way, whom venerable Caesar, in the likeness of Hercules, hallows, greatest fame of the Ausonian road, if you wish to know the deeds of the earlier Alcides, learn: he tamed the Libyan, carried off the golden apples, unbelted the shield-bearing Amazon of her Scythian knot, added to the Arcadian boar the lion's hide, took the bronze-footed stag from the woods, the Stymphalian birds from the stars, came back from the Stygian water with the dog, forbade the fruitful hydra to be renewed by deaths, washed the Hesperian cattle in the Tuscan stream. These the lesser Alcides did: hear what the greater has done, whom the sixth milestone from the Alban citadel worships. He claimed the Palatine, possessed by evil rule, and as a boy waged his first wars for his own Jove; when he alone now held the Julian reins, he handed them over and was third in his own world; thrice he crushed the treacherous horns of the Sarmatian Hister, thrice he washed his sweating horse in Getic snow; sparing, often refusing to lead triumphs, he, victor, won a name from the Hyperborean world; he gave temples to the gods, manners to peoples, rest from the sword, stars to his own, constellations to heaven, garlands to Jove. The godhead of Hercules is not enough for such deeds: let this god lend his face to the Tarpeian father.

CI If perchance old Gabba, released and sent back from the Elysian field, happy in his own Caesar, who'd have heard Capitolinus and Gabba jesting together, will return and say: "Hold your tongue, country Gabba."
CI Could you, Flaccus, even see Thais, she's so thin? You, I think, can see, Flaccus, what isn't there.
CI. Venafran Oil This the Campanian Venafrum's berry sweated for you: Whenever you take perfume, this scents it too.
CI. A Mushroom-Dish Though mushrooms have given me so noble a name, I serve — for shame, alas! — the first-cut cabbage-shoots.
CII The painter who painted your Venus, Lycoris, Was flattering Minerva, I think.

CII You hand me back, Phoebus, the tablets for four hundred thousand: rather lend me, Phoebus, a hundred thousand. Seek another to whom you may boast of so empty a gift: what I cannot pay you, Phoebus, is mine.
CII By what method, you ask, was Philinus made a father, who never fucked? Let Gaditanus tell you that, Avitus, who writes nothing and yet is a poet.

CII He didn't lie who told me you have a beautiful body, Lydia, not a beautiful face. It's so, if you keep silent and recline as mute as a face is silent in wax or on a painted board. But whenever you speak, Lydia, you ruin your body too, and no one's tongue harms anyone more than yours does you. Take care the aedile neither hears nor sees you: it's a portent, whenever a statue begins to speak.
CII. Allies' Garum From the first blood of the still-gasping mackerel Take the proud garum — a costly gift.
CII. Surrentine Cups Take cups born from no cheap dust, But the smooth chiseled work of the Surrentine wheel.

CIII "If the gods above should give me ten times a hundred thousand"— So you used to say, Scaevola, when not yet a proper knight— "How I would live, how lavishly and how blessedly!" The easy-going gods laughed and granted it. After this your toga is much dingier, your cloak worse, Your shoe patched in its leather three and four times: And of ten olives, more are always kept back, One table unfolds two dinners, And the thick dregs of red Veientan are drunk, A penny buys warm chickpeas, and a penny a girl. Let us go to law, you cheat and welsher: Either live, Scaevola, or give the gods back their million.

CIII What new Leda bore servants so like you? What Spartan woman was taken naked by another swan? Pollux gives his face to Hierus, Castor to Asylus, and in each face the Tyndarian sister shines. Had that beauty been at Therapnaean Amyclae, when lesser gifts overcame the two goddesses, you would have stayed, Helen, and Dardanian Paris would have returned to Phrygian Ida with a twin Ganymede.

CIII Townsmen, whom Augustan Bilbilis on its steep mountain bore me, girt by Salo's rushing waters, does the glad glory of your bard please you at all? For I am your honour and name and fame, nor does Verona owe more to its slender Catullus, and she'd be willing for me to be called no less her own. A thirtieth summer has been added to four harvests, since without me you give country cakes to Ceres, while I dwell in the loveliest walls of mistress Rome: the Italian realms have changed my hair. If you welcome my return with a calm mind, I come; if you bear harsh hearts, I'm free to go back.
CIII So great, Safronius, is the goodness of your spirit and face, that I wonder you could have become a father.
CIII. A Jar of Fish-Brine I am, I confess, the daughter of the Antibes tunny: Were I the mackerel's, I'd not have been sent to you.
CIII. A Snow-Strainer Break my Setine wine, I advise, with our snow: With cheaper wine you can wet the linen.

CIV That the leopard bears the dainty yoke On its painted neck, and the savage tigers Submit patiently to the whip, That the stags bite the golden bit, That Libyan bears are tamed by reins, And a boar as huge as Calydon is said to have borne Obeys the purple halter, That ugly bisons drag the chariots And the beast, bidden to give soft dances, Does not refuse its black master: Who would not think these the shows of gods? Yet a man passes all this by as lesser, Whoever sees the humble huntings of lions, Whom the swift fear of hares tires out. They let go, they fetch back, they love their captives, And the prey is safer in the mouth, To which they delight to give loose, open jaws And to hold their timid teeth, Ashamed to crush so soft a spoil, Just when they have come from slaughtered bullocks. This clemency is not got by art, But the lions know whom they serve.

CIV Go, my little book, go as companion to our Flavus on the long sea—but of a favouring wave—, and with easy course and your own winds make for the citadels of Spanish Tarraco: from there a wheel will lift you, and swiftly carried you'll see, perhaps in the fifth carriage, high Bilbilis and your own Salo. What do I charge you with, you ask? That you greet my few comrades, but old ones, and seen by me before thirty and four winters, at once, straight from the road, and remind our Flavus now and then to procure me a pleasant, not laborious retreat at a wholesome price, to make your parent lazy. That's all. Now the swollen master calls and chides the delays, and a better breeze has opened the harbour: farewell, little book: a ship, you know, I think, waits for no single passenger.

CIV Wife, out the door, or fall in with my ways: I'm no Curius nor Numa nor Tatius. Pleasant nights drawn out over cups delight me: you, having drunk water, hurry sourly to rise. You take joy in darkness: but I take joy in playing with the lamp as witness and in bursting my flank with the light let in. A band and tunics and dark cloaks hide you: but no girl lies naked enough for me. Kisses that mimic the coaxing doves win me: you give me such as you give your grandmother in the morning. You deign to help the work with neither motion nor voice nor fingers, as though you were preparing incense and wine: the Phrygian slaves used to masturbate behind the door whenever Hector's wife sat on the steed, and though the Ithacan snored, chaste Penelope was always used to keep her hand busy there. You refuse to be buggered: Cornelia gave this to Gracchus, Julia to Pompey, Porcia, Brutus, to you; before the Dardanian servant mixed his sweet cups, Juno was Ganymede to Jove. If gravity delights you, you may be a Lucretia all day long: at night I want a Lais.
CIV. Attic Honey This noble nectar was sent you by the bee That plunders the woods of Theseus' Pallas-loved Hymettus.
CIV. A Snow-Bag Our linens too know how to thin the snow: No water leaps from your strainer colder.

CV The wine that is born, Ovidius, in Nomentan fields, As often as it has gained long years, Strips off, in its aged old age, its character and its name: And whatever it pleases, the old jar is called.
CV You used to send a pound, Garricus; you send a quarter now. At least pay me half, Garricus.
CV. Sicilian Honeycombs When you give Sicilian combs from the hills of central Hybla, You may call them Cecropian if you like.
CV. Serving-Jugs Cold won't be wanting, nor hot, to him who asks. But you — spare us your game of fastidious thirst.

CVI You keep adding water now and then, Rufus, And if forced by a comrade, you drink a scant Ounce of diluted Falernian. Has Naevia promised you a blessed Night, and do you prefer the sober Naughtiness of a sure embrace? You sigh, you keep silent, you groan: she has said no. So you may drink your goblets thick and fast And throttle the harsh grief in wine. Why spare yourself, Rufus? You must sleep alone.
CVI Vibius Maximus, if you've leisure to be greeted, read only this: for you're both busy and not too fond of labour. You skip these four lines too? You've shown sense.
CVI. Raisin-Wine The Cnossian vintage of Minoan Crete Bore you this, the mead that tends to be the poor man's drink.
CVI. An Earthen Pitcher Here a red pitcher with a splayed handle is given you. The Stoic Fronto used to ask for cold water in this.

CVII You often tell me, Lucius Julius, dearest of friends, "Write something great: you are an idle fellow." Give me leisure—such as Maecenas once made For his Flaccus and his Virgil: I would try to fashion works to live through the ages And to snatch my name from the flames. The oxen will not bear the yoke onto barren fields: A rich soil tires, but the labour itself delights.

CVII You hand me back a book unrolled clear to its very horns and as if read through, Septicianus. You've read it all. I believe it, I know it, I'm glad, it's true. I read through your five books the same way.
CVII. Pitched Wine That this pitched wine has come from vine-bearing Vienna, Do not doubt: Romulus himself sent it to me.
CVII. Wine-Baskets The Satyrs love us, Bacchus loves us, the drunken tigress, Trained to lick its master's drenched feet.

CVIII You have a house—and long may it stand and grow through the years, I pray— Lovely, indeed, but across the Tiber: But my garret looks out on the Vipsanian laurels, And in this quarter I have grown old already. I must move, to greet you at home in the morning, Gallus: It is worth it, even if it were further off. But it is no great thing to you if I furnish one client in a toga: It is much, Gallus, if I deny you that one—my own self. I myself will greet you, often, at the tenth hour: In the morning my book shall say "good day" to you for me.

CVIII Though you might be sated with so long a little book, reader, you still ask a few more couplets from me. But Lupus demands his interest and the boys their rations. Reader, pay up. You're silent and pretend not to hear? Farewell.
pr. Valerius Martialis to his friend Priscus, greetings.

I know I owe a defence for three years of most obstinate idleness; for which idleness there would be no excuse even amid those urban occupations by which we more easily achieve the look of being a nuisance rather than dutiful—much less in this provincial solitude, where, unless we even study to excess, I have withdrawn both without solace and without excuse. So receive my account. In which this is the chief and first point, that I miss the ears of the city, to which I had grown accustomed, and seem to myself to be pleading in a foreign court; for if there is anything that pleases in my little books, it was the audience that dictated it: that subtlety of judgment, that genius for subject-matter, the libraries, the theatres, the gatherings, in which pleasure does not feel itself to be study—in short, all those things which, grown soft, I left behind, I now miss as though abandoned. To this is added the rust of small-town teeth, and ill-will in the seat of judgment, and one or two malicious men—in a tiny place, a great many; against which it is hard to keep a good temper day by day: so do not wonder that what used to be done by an eager spirit is now cast off by an indignant one. Yet, lest I deny anything to you, both arriving from the city and demanding it—to whom I am ungrateful if I render only what I can—I have commanded myself to do what I used to indulge in, and have studied for very few days, so that I might receive your most intimate ears with their welcoming-gift. I should like you not to grudge the trouble of carefully weighing and sifting these things, which are at risk only with you; and—what is most difficult for you—of judging my trifles with elegance set aside, lest, if you so decide, we send to Rome not a Spanish-style book, but a Spaniard.
CVIII. Mead You stir Attic honey into nectarous Falernian. This drink deserves to be mixed by Ganymede.
CVIII. Saguntine Cups What no anxious servant need hold and keep, Take — cups made of Saguntine clay.

CIX Issa is more naughty than Catullus's sparrow, Issa is purer than a dove's kiss, Issa is more winning than all girls, Issa is dearer than Indian pearls, Issa is the pet, the lapdog of Publius. If she whimpers, you will think she is speaking; She feels both sorrow and joy. She lies leaning on his neck and takes her sleep, So that no breathing can be heard; And when forced by the need of her belly, She has never stained the coverlet with a drop, But with a coaxing paw rouses him and warns him She must be set down from the couch, and asks to be lifted. So great a modesty is in the chaste lapdog: She knows nothing of love; nor have we found A mate worthy of so tender a girl. That the last day may not snatch her away entire, Publius renders her in a painted tablet, In which you will see an Issa so like That she herself is not so like to herself. In short, set Issa beside the picture: Either you will think both are real, Or you will think both are painted.
CIX. Alban This the mild vintage from Caesar's cellars sent, The vintage that pleases itself on the Julian hill.
CIX. Jeweled Cups See how the gold gleams jeweled with Scythian fires. How many fingers this cup has stripped!
CX You complain, Velox, that I write long epigrams. You yourself write nothing: you make shorter ones.
CX. Surrentine You drink Surrentine? Take neither painted murra-ware Nor gold: these wines will give you cups of their own.
CX. A Drinking-Flask From this jewel, which keeps the name of Cosmus, You may drink, voluptuary, if your thirst is for spikenard.

CXI Since your fame for wisdom equals your devotion to the gods, And your piety is no less than your genius, He knows nothing of giving gifts to merit, who wonders That a book is given you, Regulus—or incense.
CXI. Falernian The Massic came from the presses of Sinuessa: You ask under what consul it was laid down? There was none.
CXI. Crystal Ware While you fear to break it, you'll break the crystal: hands Too careless and too anxious both go wrong.
CXII When I did not know you, I called you lord and king: Now I know you well: now you shall be plain Priscus to me.
CXII. Setine Setia, hanging high, that looks on the Pomptine plains, Sent these old casks from her tiny town.
CXII. A Glass Storm-Cloud The cloud that comes from Jove will pour rich waters For mixing in the cups: this will give you wine.

CXIII Whatever I trifled at, a young man and a boy once, And our trifles, which now I myself no longer know, If you wish to misspend good hours And grudge your leisure, reader, You may seek them from Quintus Pollius Valerianus, Through whom my nothings are not allowed to perish.
CXIII. Fundan This Fundan the happy autumn of Opimius bore. The consul pressed the must and drank it himself.
CXIII. Murra-Ware If you drink hot, the murra suits burning Falernian And the flavor turns out better than the neat wine.

CXIV These gardens near you, Faustinus, Telesphorus Faenius holds, and a small estate and watery meadows. Here he buried the ashes of his daughter and consecrated the name You read, Antulla's—though he himself were worthier to be read. It had been just that the father should have gone to the Stygian shades: But since that was not allowed, let him live, to tend her bones.
CXIV. Trifoline I am not of the first rank, I admit — Trifoline Lyaeus — Yet among wines I'll be the seventh vine.
CXIV. A Cuman Bowl This bowl, ruddy with Cuman clay, The chaste Sibyl sent you, her fellow townswoman.

CXV A certain girl desires me—envy me, Procillus!— A girl whiter than the washed swan, Than silver, snow, the lily, the privet. But I want a certain girl blacker than night, Than the ant, than pitch, the jackdaw, the cicada. Already you were plotting a cruel hanging: If I know you well, Procillus, you will live.
CXV. Caecuban The noble Caecuban is mellowed at Fundan Amyclae, And the vine, born in the middle of the marsh, grows green.
CXV. Glass Cups You see the wit of the Nile: how often, while its maker Longs to add more, ah, he has ruined the work!

CXVI This grove Faenius consecrated to the eternal honour of the ashes, And the lovely acres of well-tilled soil. In this tomb Antulla, snatched too soon from her own, is covered; In this both parents shall be mingled with Antulla. If anyone desires this little field, I warn him: let him not hope for it: That land shall serve its own masters forever.
CXVI. Signine You'll drink Signine to bind a loose bowel? Lest it bind too much, let your thirst be sparing.
CXVI. A Snow-Flask You drink Spoletine, or wine laid down in Marsian cellars: What do you want with the noble chill of boiled water?

CXVII Whenever you meet us, Lupercus, "Shall I send my boy," you keep saying, "To whom you may hand the little book of epigrams, Which, once read, I will return to you at once?" There is no need, Lupercus, to trouble your boy. It is a long way, if he should want to come to the Pear-tree, And I live up three flights of stairs—and high ones. What you seek you may look for nearer. You often go down, I suppose, to the Argiletum: Opposite Caesar's forum there is a shop, With its doorposts written over on this side and that, So that you may quickly read through all the poets. Seek me from there. You need not ask Atrectus— That is the name the master of the shop bears: From the first or second pigeon-hole he will give you Martial, smoothed with pumice and adorned with purple, For five denarii. "You are not worth so much," you say? You are wise, Lupercus.
CXVII. Mamertine If Mamertine of Nestor's age be given you, It can bear whatever name you like.
CXVII. The Same Not to drink snow, but to drink fresh water Brewed from snow — that is ingenious thirst's invention.
CXVIII The man for whom it is not enough to have read a hundred epigrams, For him no amount of trouble is enough, Caedicianus.
pr. Valerius Martial to his friend Decianus, greetings.

"What have we to do," you say, "with a preface? Are we not doing enough for you if we read your epigrams? Besides, what are you going to say here that you could not say in verse? I can see why tragedy or comedy should be given a preface, since they may not speak for themselves: epigrams have no need of a herald, and are content with their own tongue—that is, a wicked one: on whatever page it pleases them, they make a preface. Do not, then, if you please, do a ridiculous thing and bring on a character dancing in a toga. In short, consider whether it pleases you to face the net-fighter with a ferule. I sit among those who shout you down at once."

By Hercules, Decianus, I think you speak the truth. What if you knew with how long a letter, and what sort, you would have had to deal? So let it be done as you require. Whoever falls upon this book will owe it to you that they reach the first page not yet wearied.
CXVIII. Tarraconese Tarraco, yielding only to Campanian Lyaeus, Bore these wines that rival the Tuscan casks.
CXVIII. The Same Mixing the smoke of Massilia with snow-cooled waves — Go easy, boy, lest your water cost you more.
CXIX. Nomentan The Nomentan vintage gives you my Bacchus: If Quintus loves you, you'll drink something finer.
CXIX. An Earthen Chamber-Pot While I'm called for with a snap of fingers and the slave delays, Oh, how often the bolster has become my rival!
CXX. Spoletine You'd rather have the matured wine of Spoletine flasks Than drink the new Falernian must.
CXX. A Silver Spoon Though knights and senators call me a ligula, The unschooled grammarians call me a lingula.
CXXI. Pelignian The Pelignian tenants send their muddied Marsic: Don't you drink it — let your freedman do that.
CXXI. Snail-Spoons I'm handy for snails, but no less useful for eggs. Do you know, then, why I'm rather called a snail-spoon?
CXXII. Vinegar Don't think the jar of Nile vinegar beneath you: When it was wine, it was cheaper still.
CXXII. Rings Once a frequent, now a rare, friend gives us. Happy the man whose comrade is a knight not stranger-born.
CXXIII. Massilian When your dole strikes a hundred citizens off the list, You may set out the smoky wines of Massilia.
CXXIII. A Ring-Case Often the heavy ring slips from greasy fingers, But your gem will be safe in my keeping.
CXXIV. Caeretan Let Nepos serve Caeretan, you'll think it Setine. He doesn't serve the crowd: he drinks it with three friends.
CXXIV. A Toga The Romans, lords of the world, the nation of the gown, He made, who gave the stars to his great father.
CXXV. Tarentine Aulon, noble in its wools and happy in its vines, Gives precious fleeces to you, wines to me.
CXXV. The Same If you find it easy to lose your morning sleep, The dole will often come with a threadbare toga.
CXXVI. Perfume Never leave perfume or wine to your heir. Let him have the cash — give all of these to yourself.
CXXVI. A Greatcoat It's a poor man's gift, but no poor man's use: This greatcoat we send you in place of a mantle.
CXXVII. Rose-Garlands Midwinter, Caesar, gives you these hurried garlands: Once the rose was spring's; now it has become yours.
CXXVII. Dark Canusian Wool This Canusian, just like clouded mead, Will be your gift. Be glad: it won't soon turn old.
CXXVIII. A Hooded Cape Gaul clothes you in a Santonian hooded cape. It was lately the cloak of long-tailed monkeys.
CXXIX. Red Canusian Wool Rome dresses more in dark, Gaul in red, And this color pleases boys and soldiers.
CXXX. A Leather Cape Though you set out on the road under an ever-clear sky, Let the leather never fail you against sudden rains.
CXXXI. Scarlet Cloaks If you back the Blues or Greens, why take scarlet? Take care lest that lot make you a turncoat.
CXXXII. A Felt Cap If I could, I'd wish to have sent whole cloaks: As it is, I send a gift only for your head.
CXXXIII. Baetic Cloaks My wool tells no lies, I'm not changed in the cauldron. Let Tyrian dyes please thus: my own sheep dyed me.
CXXXIV. A Breast-Band Band, hold in check your mistress' growing breasts, So that there be something for our hand to grasp and cover.
CXXXV. White Cloaks We commend ourselves by their use at the amphitheater, When the white cloak covers the chilly togas.
CXXXVI. Dinner-Clothes We know no courts and no court-summonses: Our task is to recline on painted couches.
CXXXVII. A Neck-Wrap If perhaps I give you a little book to recite, Let this neck-wrap stand surety for your ears.
CXXXVIII. A Frieze-Mantle In wintertime smooth fabrics are not much use: My shaggy nap warms your cloaks.
CXXXIX. A Hand-Towel Let shaggy linens better guard your citron table: There can be a ring-mark on our table-tops.
CXL. Liburnian Hoods You never knew, you fool, how to attach cloaks to us: You'd put on white — strip off the green ones.
CXLI. Cilician Foot-Socks No wool gave these, but the beard of a smelly he-goat: The sole can hide in the Cinyphian fold.
CXLII. A Dinner-Suit While the toga is glad to rest through the five days, You may by your own right put on this attire.
CXLIII. Paduan Tunics Paduan triple-weaves use up much wool, And a saw could cut the thick tunics.
CXLIV. A Sponge This sponge falls to you by lot, useful for wiping tables, Light as it is when it swells with squeezed-out water.
CXLV. A Frieze Cloak Such whiteness is in me, such grace of nap, That you'd want to put me on even in mid-harvest.
CXLVI. A Bolster Dip your head in Cosmus' nard, and the bolster will smell of it: When the hair loses the perfume, the feather keeps it.
CXLVII. Frieze Bed-Coverlets The shaggy spreads gleam with purple tapestries. What use, if your old wife freezes you?
CXLVIII. Blankets Lest the bare couch lie open with no spread, We sisters have come, joined, to you.
CXLIX. A Shoulder-Wrap I fear the big-bosomed; hand me to a tender girl, That the linen may enjoy a snow-white breast.
CL. Damask Bedspreads This the Memphian land gives you as a gift: Babylon's needle Is already beaten by the loom of the Nile.
CLI. A Girdle I'm long enough now; but if the belly swells With a sweet weight, I'll become a short girdle for you.
CLII. A Square Coverlet The land of learned Catullus sends you blankets: We come from the region of Helicaon.
CLIII. A Half-Apron Let the rich man give a tunic: I can gird you up. Were I rich, I'd give both gifts.
CLIV. Amethystine Wools Drunk as I am with the blood of the Sidonian shell, I don't see why I should be called a sober wool.
CLVI. Tyrian Wools A shepherd gave us to his Spartan love: The purple of mother Leda was inferior.
CLVII. Pollentine Wools This land yields not only mourning wools of dark fleece, But it is wont to give its own cups as well.
CLVIII. The Same A drab wool, true, but made for the sheared attendants — The sort the table does not summon from the first rank.
CLIX. Leuconian Stuffing Is the cover too close upon the pressed-down feathers? Take fleece scraped from the Leuconian saddle-cloths.
CLX. Circus Stuffing Chopped marsh-reed is called Circus stuffing. The poor man buys this litter in place of Leuconian.
CLXI. Down Weary, you can rest on Amyclaean down, Given you by the inner wool of the swan.
CLXII. Hay Let the frail mattress swell for you, the mule cheated of its feed. Pale care does not come to a hard bed.
CLXIII. A Bell Give back the ball: the bath-bell sounds. You keep on playing? You want to go home washed by the Virgin spring alone.
CLXIV. A Discus When the gleaming weights of the Spartan discus fly, Keep away, boys: let it harm only once.
CLXV. A Lyre It gave Eurydice back to the bard: but he lost her, Trusting himself too little, loving without patience.
CLXVI. The Same Often it was thrown out of the Pompeian theater — The lyre that led the woods and held the beasts spellbound.
CLXVII. A Plectrum Lest a hot blister rise on your rubbed thumb, Let a white plectrum adorn the docile lyre.
CLXVIII. A Hoop The wheel must be set rolling: you give us a useful gift: This hoop is for boys, but for me it will be music.
CLXIX. The Same Why does the chattering ring wander round the loose circle? So the crowd it meets may yield to the tinkling hoops.
CLXX. A Golden Statue of Victory This is given him without a lot, on whom the Rhine Bestowed a true name. Pour ten cups of Falernian, boy.
CLXXI. An Earthenware "Boy of Brutus" The glory of so small a statuette is not obscure: Brutus was the lover of this boy.
CLXXII. A Corinthian "Lizard-Slayer" Spare the lizard creeping toward you, treacherous boy: It longs to perish by your fingers.
CLXXIII. A Painted Hyacinthus on a Panel The Oebalian boy turns his dying eyes from the hated discus — Phoebus' fault and grief.
CLXXIV. A Marble Hermaphroditus Male he entered the spring, and rose up both: One part has the father's, the rest the mother's.
CLXXV. A Painted Danaë Why did Danaë take a price from you, ruler of Olympus, If Leda gave herself to you for nothing?
CLXXVI. A German Mask I am a potter's joke, the mask of a redheaded Batavian. The face you laugh at, a child fears.
CLXXVII. A Corinthian Hercules The infant crushes the twin snakes and does not even look: Already the Hydra might have feared his tender hands.
CLXXVIII. An Earthenware Hercules I'm fragile: but you, I warn you, don't scorn the statuette: Alcides is not ashamed to bear my name.
CLXXIX. A Silver Minerva Tell me, fierce maiden, since you have helmet and spear, Why have you no aegis? "Caesar has it."
CLXXX. A Painted Europa You could have done better to change into a bull, best father of gods, Back then, when Io was a heifer to you.
CLXXXI. A Marble Leander Bold Leander cried out amid the swelling waves: "Drown me, you floods, when I am on my way back."
CLXXXII. An Earthenware Figure of a Hunchback Drunk, I think, Prometheus made these monsters on earth: He too played with the Saturnalia's clay.
CLXXXIII. Homer's Battle of the Frogs Read right through the frogs sung in Maeonian song, And learn to unknit your brow over my trifles.
CLXXXIV. Homer on Parchment Tablets The Iliad and Ulysses, foe to Priam's realm, Lie hidden, stored together in many a fold of skin.
CLXXXV. Virgil's Gnat Take, eager reader, the Gnat of eloquent Virgil, Lest, the nuts put aside, you read "Arms and the man."
CLXXXVI. Virgil on Parchment How small a parchment holds the boundless Virgil! The first leaf bears his very face.
CLXXXVIII. Cicero on Parchment If this parchment is your companion, imagine You're traveling long roads in Cicero's company.
CLXXXIX. Propertius' Monobiblos Cynthia — the youthful song of eloquent Propertius — Won fame, and gave no less than she received.
CXC. Livy on Parchment Vast Livy is compressed into scanty skins, Whom my library cannot hold whole.
CXCI. Sallust This man, as the hearts of learned men declare, Crispus, will be the first in Roman history.
CXCII. Ovid's Metamorphoses on Parchment This mass, built up of many-folded leaves, Carries Naso's fifteen books of song.
CXCIII. Tibullus Wanton Nemesis fired her lover Tibullus, Whom it pleased to be nothing in his whole house.
CXCIV. Lucan There are some who say I am no poet: But the bookseller who sells me thinks I am.
CXCV. Catullus Great Verona owes as much to her Catullus As little Mantua to her Virgil.
CXCVI. Calvus' "On the Use of Cold Water" This paper, which tells you of springs and the names of waters, Itself swam better in its own waters once.
CXCVII. Dwarf Mules You need fear no fall from these mules: You often sit nearly higher on the ground.
CXCVIII. A Gallic Lapdog If you want to hear the charms of the little lapdog, The whole page is too short for my telling.
CXCIX. An Asturian Pony This little Asturian, who gathers his swift hoof to the beat, Came from the gold-bearing tribes.
CC. A Greyhound The keen greyhound hunts not for himself but for his master, And will bring you the hare unharmed in his teeth.
CCI. A Wrestling-Master I don't love him for winning, but because he knows how to lose And has better learned the art of the bedroom-bout.
CCII. An Ape The clever ape, dodging the spears flung at me — If I had a tail, I'd be a long-tailed monkey.
CCIII. A Girl from Cadiz She wriggles so quivering, itches so caressing, that she'd make A masturbator of Hippolytus himself.
CCIV. Cymbals The bronze that mourns the Celaenaean loves of the Mother, The hungry Gallus is often wont to sell.
CCV. A Boy Let mine be a boy smooth by his years, not by pumice, For whose sake no girl can please me.
CCVI. A Love-Girdle Bind to your neck, boy, pure love itself, A girdle warm from Venus' bosom.
CCVII. The Same Take the girdle steeped in Cytherean nectar: This belt fired even Jove, the lover.
CCVIII. A Shorthand-Writer Though the words run fast, the hand is faster still: The tongue has not yet finished, the right hand has.
CCIX. A Cuttlefish-Shell Let the light Mareotic bark be made of a sea-shell: The reed-pen will run an unhindered course.
CCX. A Fool His stupor is not feigned, nor cunningly counterfeited. Whoever is no wiser than he ought, he is wise.
CCXI. A Ram's Head You cut the soft neck of Phrixus' woolly mate. Did he deserve this, the cruel man who gave you a tunic?
CCXII. A Dwarf If you look only at the man's head, you'd think him Hector: If you see him standing, you'd take him for Astyanax.
CCXIII. A Shield This shield, often vanquished, rarely victorious, Will be your buckler, a dwarf's.
CCXIV. Boy Comic Actors None in the troupe will play your "Hated Man": But anyone can be your "Double Deceiver."
CCXV. A Buckle Tell me plainly, buckle, what you do for comic actors And lyre-singers. "Make them screw at a higher price."
CCXVI. A Fowler The bird is fooled not only by limed reeds but by song, While the cunning reed grows up in a silent hand.
CCXVII. A Hawk He was the robber of birds: now, the fowler's slave, the same one Decoys them, and grieves at the birds he catches not for himself.
CCXVIII. A Caterer Say how many you want for dinner and at what price, and don't add A single word: the dinner is ready for you.
CCXIX. An Ox-Heart Poor pleader, since you write poems that bring back No money, take the heart you have.
CCXX. A Cook Art alone is not enough for a cook: I don't want A slavish palate: a cook should have his master's taste.
CCXXII. A Pastry-Cook This man's hand will raise for you a thousand sweet Shapes of his craft: for him alone the thrifty bee toils.
CCXXIII. Lard-Cakes Get up: the baker is already selling boys their breakfasts, And the crested birds of dawn are crowing on every side.
